title: Optimal strategies for reject option classifiers
evidence: Sec. 2.4: "the three rejection models are equivalent in the sense that they lead to the same prediction strategy".
method: Theory of reject-option classifiers: optimal strategies for cost-based, bounded-improvement and bounded-coverage models are the Bayes classifier plus a randomised Bayes selection function; proper uncertainty scores; Fisher-consistent SELE loss.
evaluation: Proved: Theorems 1-6 optimal strategies; Theorem 7 regression consistency; Theorem 8 AuRC <= 2x SELE; Theorems 9-11 SELE minimisers order-preserving. Experiments: 11 UCI sets, ordinal regression, 300-W; SELE mean rank 1.36 vs MCP 2.73.
contribution: Proves that cost-based, bounded-improvement and bounded-coverage rejection models share one optimal strategy, and gives a Fisher-consistent loss for learning the uncertainty score that realises it.
flag: (v): foundational reject-option theory with proved optimal rules and consistency results, plus experiments. runtime_interceptor no as instructed for pure theory, though the learned selection function is an inference-time reject rule. One-shot setting; no human or fallback, rejected inputs are simply abstentions; no latency (only BMRM training in minutes on a PC). The fetch covered characters 0-100000 of 125979: main body read in full, appendix proofs from A.4 onward and references NOT read, so proofs were not checked. arXiv header shows a template placeholder for venue; record is the JMLR version by the ACM id. 300-W AuRC values appear only in a figure. SELE loses to MCP on PENDIGIT (1.55 vs 0.69).

title: An analysis of robustness of non-Lipschitz networks
evidence: "We prove that classifiers with the ability to abstain are provably more powerful than those that cannot in this setting" (Abstract).
method: Nearest-neighbour classifier in feature space that outputs don't-know when the nearest training feature is farther than threshold tau; tau tuned data-driven with regret and generalisation bounds.
evaluation: Proved: impossibility without abstention (Thm 4.1), robust-error bound with abstention (Thm 5.1), abstention-rate bound (Thm 5.3), threshold-tuning regret (Thm 6.1-6.2). CIFAR-10 contrastive features vs linear protocol: adversarial error 100% vs 26-61%.
contribution: Proves that under random-subspace adversaries in feature space a classifier must abstain to be robust, and gives a thresholded nearest-neighbour rule with bounded robust error and abstention rate.
flag: (v) theory of abstention, here for adversarial robustness. arXiv abs page title matches the record, but the PDF text I read carried the earlier title 'On the Power of Abstention and Data-Driven Decision Making for Adversarial Robustness' (same arXiv id, same paper, possibly an older version than the JMLR text); only the first 100k of 110k characters read. Table 1 was garbled in extraction: per-row values (e.g. tau=2.0 self-supervised E_adv 26.2%, abstention 28.7%) need checking against the PDF. Robustness-specific threat model, one-shot classification, no deferral to anyone; maintainer may judge it too far from the reject-option core and prefer E4.

title: Toward Verifiable Real-Time Obstacle Motion Prediction for Dynamic Collision Avoidance
evidence: Sec. V: 'v_safe is guaranteed to avoid a collision for the next m timesteps with a given probability'; Algorithm 3 applies v_safe in place of the desired velocity.
method: Online-trained LSTM with dropout predicts obstacle motion as uncertainty ellipsoids; a nonlinear probabilistic velocity obstacle then picks the collision-free velocity closest to the hand-designed desired velocity.
evaluation: Stage-ROS simulation, single obstacle; GP and plain-RNN prediction baselines compared only qualitatively (Fig. 5, no error numbers); statistical model checking Table I SAT-UNSAT over theta=0.9-0.75 and sigma2=0-0.05 (N=20, alpha=beta=0.1); proved bounds 1-theta, (1-theta)^2, 1-theta^N; 2 Hz on an i7 laptop; no collision rate, no ablation.
contribution: Wraps an online-learned LSTM obstacle predictor in a probabilistic velocity-obstacle filter and uses statistical model checking to approximately verify that real motion stays inside the predicted bounds.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - the LSTM sits inside the filter as its predictor; what is guarded is a hand-designed desired-velocity controller, which is what the 2026-11-13 scope ruling calls E1. Check whether the maintainer counts the learned predictor as enough to keep (a). E2 is the alternative: no collision or violation rate, no numeric prediction error against GP or RNN, no ablation, so the only safety result is the theorems plus Table I SAT-UNSAT. Proofs of Theorems 1-2 are deferred to a longer arXiv version, the multi-agent reciprocal case is theory with no simulation, and the abstract's 'real-time' is 2 Hz on a 32 GB i7 laptop.

title: Towards Safety-Aware Computing System Design in Autonomous Vehicles
evidence: Sec. 3.1: 'once LiDAR perception latency exceeds 100ms, the system response time increases at a much higher rate'; Sec. 4.1 derives a situation-dependent response-time window theta from distance and vehicle dynamics.
method: An RSS-derived 'safety score' mapping computing response time to nominal safety, a fitted perception-latency model, and offline-planned plus online-monitored heterogeneous CPU-GPU resource management for an AV pipeline.
evaluation: In-house AV and architecture simulators replaying 200+ hours and 2000 miles of industrial L4 fleet traces; against CPU and CPU+GPU baselines the scheme gives 4.6x and 1.3x safety score, 2.4x and 35% lower response time, 2.6x and 45% lower LiDAR perception latency; latency-model MSE 1.7e-4; perception is 74% of response time; Xeon CPU plus Volta GPU; no ablation, no collision rate.
contribution: Defines a safety score that ties an autonomous vehicle's computing response time to RSS-based nominal safety and uses it to drive latency-aware CPU-GPU resource management on the vehicle.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: partly - the pipeline contains deep perception modules, but the contribution is classical scheduling and it budgets compute rather than intercepting a decision, so (a) is no and the record rests on (d) alone. Check that a safety score is accepted as a safety metric: no collision or violation rate is reported, the paper only says the score is 'in line with' collision probability in simulation, and there is no ablation. Simulators and traces are proprietary and in-house, the latency model is fitted for LiDAR perception only, and the score's shape depends on user-set sigma=0.05 and eta=0.1.

title: Reciprocal Collision Avoidance for General Nonlinear Agents using Reinforcement Learning
evidence: Abstract: 'safety is ensured by introducing linear constraints from the optimal reciprocal collision avoidance (ORCA)'; Sec. III-B: the agent selects the action closest to the RL-combined action subject to those constraints.
method: A two-agent RL policy trained by evolution strategy; at runtime the pairwise outputs are distance- and velocity-weighted and then projected by a convex program with ORCA linear constraints for nonlinear bicycle-model agents.
evaluation: Simulation only, 3 to 42 agents, 0.05 s steps, 450-parameter policy trained in about 20 minutes on an eight-core i7-7700K; no tables and no collision, success, distance or per-step computation numbers; no numeric baseline and no ablation, only trajectory figures called free of collision, congestion and deadlock.
contribution: Combines a tiny two-agent RL policy with an ORCA-derived convex projection applied at execution time to give decentralised reciprocal collision avoidance for agents with general nonlinear dynamics.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an ORCA convex projection filters the RL policy's action before it is executed, so (a) and (c) both hold on reading and this would otherwise be a strong include. It fails the evaluation floor: the paper has no results table and reports no collision rate, success rate, minimum distance or runtime, compares no baseline numerically (ORCA and prior RL work are discussed only in prose) and runs no ablation, so 'ORCA significantly improves system safety' is unmeasured. The authors also concede that linearising the nonlinear dynamics 'can introduce small errors' and suggest inflating the agent radius.

title: Learning to Optimize Autonomy in Competence-Aware Systems
evidence: Sec. 4.2: at level 1 (verified autonomy) the agent must request and receive human approval before acting, and at level 2 a human supervisor can override the action; feedback signals are approval, disapproval and override.
method: A competence-aware system composing a stochastic shortest path domain model with an autonomy model and a learned human-feedback model, so the planner picks an autonomy level per action and learns its own competence online.
evaluation: Simulated campus delivery robot (fixed and random tasks) and AV obstacle passing, means over 10 trials; level-optimality about 100% by episode 150 after about 275 feedback signals (about 375 for random tasks) and about 90% with under 60 signals on the AV; level-1 approval actions fall 45.8% to 0.0% while unsupervised actions rise 41.7% to 87.5%; convergence proved in Prop. 5.6 and Thm. 5.7; no baseline, no ablation.
contribution: Learns online, from human approval, disapproval and override signals, the level of autonomy at which an agent should execute each action, converging to the agent's true competence.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the system's own planned actions are gated, with level 1 requiring human approval before execution, so (a) and (e) hold and the Pillar 3 deferral test passes on hand-off plus sequential setting. Check the evaluation floor: there is no experimental baseline or ablation, so it rests on the convergence theorems, which assume an epsilon-consistent stationary human and no starved state-action pairs, plus the feedback-count curves; expected cost is shown as a curve with no numeric values, and no unsafe-action, violation or separate takeover count is reported. Single agent with one human authority, so no multi-agent aspect; transfer of control is explicitly not modelled; the intro mentions an AV prototype but every reported result is simulated.

title: Multimodal Trajectory Prediction via Topological Invariance for Navigation at Uncontrolled Intersections
evidence: Sec. 4: a GraphNet encoder over a directed graph of agents (node attributes position and velocity, edge attributes relative position with a one-hot winding-number sign) predicts the future states of all agents under each topological mode.
method: MTP predicts multimodal joint future trajectories by conditioning a graph-network and GRU encoder-decoder on winding-number topological modes; MTPnav then scores the predicted modes in a cost-based planner that hands a trajectory to a tracking controller.
evaluation: Simulated 2-4 agent datasets plus a CARLA Town04 four-way intersection, 50 trials per condition; minADE-minFDE 0.301-0.611 to 0.264-0.588 m against GRU 0.929-1.578, MFP 0.834-0.825 and the MTP-fc ablation 0.523-1.063, i.e. 78.24% better minADE than MFP and 33.82% better than MTP-fc, Wilcoxon p<0.001; navigation collisions near zero at 2-3 agents, still high at 4; no inference-time or hardware figures.
contribution: Uses winding numbers as topological invariants to enumerate interaction modes, letting a graph network predict multimodal joint futures at uncontrolled intersections and feed a cost-based navigation planner.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: not applicable - this is a criterion (b) prediction record with no interception; the planner selects its own minimum-cost trajectory and overrides no nominal action, so (a) is no, and (c) fails the primacy test because displacement accuracy is the primary outcome and collision frequency is reported next to time to destination. RQ5 is capped at 2 per the protocol for predictor papers. The non-generative inference cell is a judgement call, since the mode predictor is described as VAE-like. Table 2's navigation numbers are garbled in the PDF text layer so per-method collision rates could not be assigned reliably, the four-agent collision rate stays high (attributed to 162 possible modes and a small dataset), and the reported '1,180M' three-agent trajectory count looks like a typo that disagrees with Appendix B.1.

title: Learning how to approve updates to machine learning algorithms in non-stationary settings
evidence: "The key reason L2A is able to control the error-rate is that it can abstain for some fixed cost delta." (Sec. 6, Discussion)
method: L2A: online approval policy that at each time point approves or rejects candidate model updates and deploys a selective predictor that may abstain, combining strategies by exponential weighting.
evaluation: Simulations (T=50, 4 shift settings), MIMIC-IV mortality, Yelp ratings; baselines: blind approval, abstain-only, repeated T-tests, MarkovHedge; cumulative average risk; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Online learning-to-approve policy that gates updates to a deployed model under distribution shift and keeps average risk bounded by letting the deployed predictor abstain at fixed cost.
flag: (ii), arguably (iv): BORDERLINE. The main contribution is an online gate that approves or rejects MODEL UPDATES; abstention of the deployed predictor is the enabling component, not obviously the headline. If the maintainer reads the ruling as requiring abstain or defer on decisions (not on updates) this is exclude-E1. Empirically L2A does not beat simple baselines: MIMIC-IV blind approval 0.075 vs L2A about 0.08; Yelp repeated T-tests best. Simulation results in figures only. Theorem 1 bounds average risk, no regret bound. No human in loop; referral of abstentions to clinicians is mentioned only as a possibility.

title: Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning through Decentralized Multiple Control Barrier Functions
evidence: Sec. III: 'the composite CBF corrects the action of an agent only if it tends to violate safety constraints'; Algorithm 1 overwrites the MADDPG action with the QP solution before execution.
method: Decentralized multiple control barrier functions combined by Boolean intersection; a per-agent QP projects each MADDPG action to the nearest action satisfying cooperative and non-cooperative barrier constraints at every step.
evaluation: Multiagent Particle Environment, 2 patrolman agents, 3 obstacles and a wall; 5 runs x 5000 episodes; baseline MADDPG; collisions 0 vs 12,634 (50.5% of episodes); reward stable near 40,000; no hardware or latency reported.
contribution: Decentralized multi-CBF safety filter that corrects each learned MADDPG agent's action at execution time, eliminating collisions (0 vs 50.5% of episodes) while keeping reward high from the first episode.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - two MADDPG policies filtered by a per-agent CBF QP. Check: no ablation separating cooperative from non-cooperative CBFs, only 2 agents in one toy environment, the baseline's reward value is never stated so the reward comparison is not like-for-like, no latency or hardware figures, and the Sec. IV guarantee covers only the pairwise collision case.

title: Latent Variable Nested Set Transformers & AutoBots.
evidence: Sec. 3: a discrete latent variable with alternating temporal and social multi-head attention decodes scene-consistent joint future trajectories for all agents in a single forward pass (AutoBot-Joint).
method: Latent variable sequential set transformer: encoder alternates temporal and social attention, seed-matrix decoder emits one mode per latent value as bivariate Gaussians, trained by exact likelihood plus an entropy regulariser.
evaluation: nuScenes, Argoverse, TrajNet and TrajNet++, Omniglot; baselines Trajectron++, WIMP, GOHOME, CoverNet, Scene Transformer; nuScenes minADE(10) 1.05, off-road 0.03, Argoverse minADE 0.89 and minFDE 1.41, TrajNet++ scene collisions 139 vs 1144 ego-only; one GTX 1080 Ti, above 30 FPS.
contribution: Latent variable set transformer that predicts joint, socially consistent multi-agent futures in one forward pass, cutting scene collision counts roughly 8x versus ego-only prediction at a fraction of the compute.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: n/a - nothing is guarded, this is a pure predictor with no runtime interception, so only (b) holds and RQ5 is capped at 2 per protocol. Check: the record title 'Latent Variable Nested Set Transformers & AutoBots' is the v1 title of the same arXiv id, later renamed 'Latent Variable Sequential Set Transformers for Joint Multi-Agent Motion Prediction', so this is not a wrong paper. The collision counts are offline prediction metrics, not hazard rates of an acting system, and the maintainer may read this as a generative trajectory regressor (exclude-E1) rather than a Pillar 2 world model; the 30 FPS figure is a throughput claim with no per-step latency budget.

title: Least-Restrictive Multi-Agent Collision Avoidance via Deep Meta Reinforcement Learning and Optimal Control
evidence: Sec. IV-A: a single learned policy chooses per step between letting each agent's default controller run unchanged and overriding it with a maximum-actuation left or right turn, triggered by the pairwise Hamilton-Jacobi safety value.
method: Least-restrictive collision avoidance module trained with PPO and MAML over an LSTM-VAE encoding of a variable number of observed neighbours; it overrides the default controller only when the HJ reachability value signals conflict.
evaluation: Gazebo/ROS simulation plus TurtleBot3 Burger hardware, 3-6 agents and an unseen 8-agent task, 100 trials per scenario repeated 5 times; baseline HJ plus mixed-integer programming of Chen et al.; success above 90% and at least 30 points above baseline, 0.85-0.91 on 8 agents, interruption fraction 0.46 vs 0.54 for the distance-reward ablation; Jetson Nano, no latency given.
contribution: Learned least-restrictive supervisory layer that overrides any default controller with maximum-actuation evasion only when Hamilton-Jacobi reachability signals conflict, raising multi-agent success while intervening on under half of steps.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: which - the interceptor itself is a learned meta-RL policy, but the guarded default controller may be classical, learned or even human-driven, so the protected system is not necessarily learned. Check: no standalone collision, deadlock or travel-time metric (success is defined as reaching the goal without collision), baseline numbers are only legible in figures, the Jetson Nano is named but no inference latency or control frequency is reported so the edge deployment cell rests on hardware alone, and the 6-agent restrictiveness ties the ablation (0.48 vs 0.48) so the claimed 10% restrictiveness gain holds only for 4-5 agents.

title: Safe Deep Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Agent Systems with Continuous Action Spaces
evidence: Sec. 2.3: 'we augment the policy networks by introducing an additional centralized safety layer' - a QP projects the joint MADDPG action onto a linearised safety set before execution, and the filter is still required at test time.
method: Centralized safety layer solving a QP that projects joint MADDPG actions onto a linearised collision-constraint set learned by a neural sensitivity model, with a soft-constrained variant that penalises otherwise infeasible projections.
evaluation: Multi-agent particle environment, 3 agents and 6 pairwise constraints, 8000 episodes over 10 seeds, unsafe-initialisation and exogenous-disturbance cases; baselines unconstrained and hard-constrained MADDPG; test collisions 52.8 soft vs 137.4 hard vs 1386.5 MADDPG (unsafe init) and 40.8 vs 678.1 vs 1499.8 (disturbance); no hardware or solve-time figures.
contribution: Centralized QP safety layer over learned MADDPG actions that cuts training collisions by about 98% versus unconstrained MADDPG and stays feasible where a hard-constrained projection fails.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the MADDPG actor networks. Check: the projection is soft and the authors say it 'does not necessarily guarantee zero constraint violations', 20.9% (unsafe init) and 56.7% (disturbance) of hard-constrained episodes hit infeasible QP conditions, the filter is centralized and still needed at test time so there is no decentralised runtime story, the soft variant's reward is far worse under unsafe init (-136.4 vs -84.1) and goes undiscussed, there is no separate ablation beyond the hard/soft comparison, and no QP solve time is reported.

title: UMBRELLA: Uncertainty-Aware Model-Based Offline Reinforcement Learning Leveraging Planning
evidence: Sec. 3.2: the conditional VAE dynamics model 'models the stochasticity of other agents' behavior at time t with a continuous latent variable' and is rolled out inside a sampling-based MPC loop that executes only the first action; no layer sits between plan and execution.
method: Offline model-based RL: CVAE stochastic dynamics model, behaviour-cloned policy prior ensemble and truncated value function combined in return-weighted sampling-based MPC; the pessimistic variant keeps only the worst ensemble head's rollouts.
evaluation: NGSIM I-80 (5,596 trajectories) and CARLA Town04 unprotected left turn with 6 other agents, 30 in-distribution and 30 out-of-distribution scenarios; baselines MBOP, 1-step IL, MPUR, human, no-action; success 0.60 vs 0.50 (NGSIM), 0.63 vs 0.27 (CARLA ID), 0.43 vs 0.20 (OOD); Titan X and i5-3550, authors state the planner is not real-time capable; no prediction error reported.
contribution: Uncertainty-aware offline model-based RL that plans through a generative model of other agents' futures, roughly doubling collision-free success over MBOP in CARLA while remaining too slow for real time.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - nothing is intercepted, safety lives inside the MPC objective and model, so (a) fails per the runtime-override rule. Criterion (b) scope is arguably met (a generative latent model of other agents' future behaviour) but the protocol's predictive floor is not: prediction quality appears only as qualitative videos (Fig. 7) and no prediction error is reported, hence exclude-E2. This is the record most likely to be overturned: the closed-loop collision-free success rates do beat MBOP (2.33x CARLA ID, 2.15x OOD) with baselines and a pessimism ablation, so the maintainer may prefer include as method and architecture evidence with RQ5 capped at 2, or exclude-E1 since other agents are non-reactive logged trajectories and the multi-agent safety property is not the primary claim. Also a NeurIPS 2021 workshop paper, and Fig. 8 runtime has no numeric values.

title: Multi-UAV Conflict Resolution with Graph Convolutional Reinforcement Learning
evidence: "Sec. 5.1: the model manages to always avoid near misses in both cases, as the NMAC distance is never breached" - conflict resolution among 3-4 UAVs is the paper's sole objective and sole measured outcome
method: Cooperative MARL with graph convolutional communication (DGN) over a UAV relation graph; each agent picks turn-left, turn-right or do-nothing every 2 s; conflicts and severity penalised in the reward
evaluation: BlueSky ATC simulator, 3 then 4 UAVs, 10k episodes each; only comparator is the average unmitigated case; average LOSS per episode <1, zero NMAC breaches; trained on Tesla K80, no inference latency
contribution: Graph convolutional cooperative MARL resolves multi-UAV conflicts, holding losses of separation below one per episode with no near-midair-collision breaches in 3-agent and 4-agent airspace.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, the RL policy is the actor but nothing guards it - safety is reward shaping only, so (a) fails and runtime_interceptor is no. Check the evaluation floor: the only comparator is a dashed "average unmitigated case" line in Fig. 2, with no rule-based or learned baseline and no no-communication ablation, so exclude-E2 is defensible. Table 1 counts of solved compound conflicts (5650 for 3 agents, 4461 for 4 agents) are not normalised to an episode total, and the claimed "time in LOSS <5 s" appears only in prose.

title: MDPFuzz: Testing Models Solving Markov Decision Processes
evidence: "Abstract: We present MDPFuzz, the first blackbox fuzz testing framework for models solving MDPs" - the Sec. 7.4 abnormal-behaviour detector flags activation patterns offline and is never described as intervening in a live action
method: Blackbox fuzzing of sequential decision models: mutate initial states, keep seeds that crash, cut cumulative reward or add fresh state sequences (GMM density); offline anomaly detector and fine-tuning repair
evaluation: Five targets (CARLA RL and IL, ACAS Xu, MARL cooperative navigation, BipedalWalker), 12 h campaigns, 3 runs, 598 crashes; freshness ablation adds 37 crashes; detector AUC-ROC >0.78; repair cuts ACAS Xu crashes 139 to 29; RTX 3090
contribution: MDPFuzz fuzzes models solving MDPs by mutating initial states under a state-sequence freshness measure, exposing hundreds of collision-triggering states in RL, imitation, MARL and ACAS Xu policies.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (RL, IL, DNN and MARL policies are the systems analysed), so the Pillar 1 scope ruling is satisfied, but this is offline test-case generation with no execution-time override, so (a) fails, and multi-agent is 1 of 5 benchmarks rather than the primary claim, so (c) fails the primacy test. Most likely record in this batch to be overturned: the Sec. 7.4 detector (AUC-ROC >0.78 on 6000 samples) reads as a runtime monitor if the maintainer relaxes the intervention requirement, and the repair result (139 to 29 crashes at unchanged reward 30.73 to 30.74) is exactly RQ5 evidence. No external fuzzer baseline is compared quantitatively; the abstract's 598 crashes do not match the Table 3 per-model means, which sum to about 590.

title: Multi-Agent Vulnerability Discovery for Autonomous Driving with Hazard Arbitration Reward
evidence: "Abstract: Safety Test framework by finding Av-Responsible Scenarios (STARS) based on multiagent reinforcement learning" - attack success rate, i.e. the rate of AV-responsible collisions produced by 1-3 learned adversaries, is the primary measured outcome
method: Multi-agent RL (MAPPO, parameter sharing) trains 1-3 surrounding vehicles as adversaries; a Hazard Arbitration Reward penalises collisions the attackers themselves caused, isolating AV-responsible hazards
evaluation: highway-env Highway, Merge and Roundabout against four defender policies (Value Iteration, Robust VI, PPO, D3QN); ablation over 1, 2, 3 attackers; attack success rises e.g. 47.88 to 76.08 to 72.75 percent on Highway VI and 20.20 to 87.98 percent on Merge VI; no hardware or latency reported
contribution: STARS trains cooperating adversarial traffic agents with a hazard arbitration reward so that discovered collisions are attributable to the autonomous vehicle, exposing vulnerabilities even in safety-enhanced planners.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, two of four defenders (PPO, D3QN) and all attackers are learned, though Value Iteration and Robust VI are dynamic programming over a finite MDP abstraction and carry the highest reported attack rates, so the headline numbers lean on the non-learned defenders. Scenario generation only, no runtime override, so (a) fails. Check the evaluation floor: the only ablation is attacker count, there is no ablation removing the Hazard Arbitration Reward and no quantitative comparison with prior single-attacker or multi-attacker attack methods, which are discussed qualitatively only. The acceleration threshold lambda in HAR is never specified, and AV-responsibility is judged by the authors' reward design rather than independent rating.

title: Detecting danger in gridworlds using Gromov's Link Condition
evidence: "Abstract: Serendipitously, we discover these failures occur exactly where undesirable or dangerous states appear in the gridworld" - Theorem 5.2 (Sec. 5) characterises Link Condition failures as knight-move or 2-step-bishop-move agent pairs
method: Modified Abrams-Ghrist-Peterson state complexes with added dance generators for multi-agent gridworlds; failure of Gromov's Link Condition (positive curvature) is proved to coincide with collision-prone agent configurations
evaluation: Exhaustive enumeration of small rooms (3x3 with 0-9 agents, plus 2x2, 2x3, 4x1, 4x4) in a custom Python tool on a laptop; comparison is original versus modified complex; e.g. 3x3 with 3 agents gives 84 states and 184 link failures, mean 2.19, max 14; Remark 6.1 notes infeasibility at scale
contribution: Filling in agent dance squares makes gridworld state complexes fail Gromov's Link Condition exactly at collision-prone configurations, giving a proved, bounded-foresight geometric signal for multi-agent danger.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - the gridworld agents are abstract tokens with no policy, the authors state that mapping this geometry to neural network representations is ongoing work (Sec. 7), and no learned planner is guarded or analysed, so the Pillar 1 scope ruling of 2026-11-13 makes criteria (a) and (c) fail and this is exclude-E1 rather than exclude-E2. It does clear the evaluation floor on its own terms (Theorem 5.2 plus Table 1 enumeration against the unmodified complex), and the proposed "detour" response and bounded-foresight remark in Sec. 6 are future work only, so there is no runtime interception. Second most likely overturn in this batch if the maintainer counts gridworld RL environments as learned systems by setting; note the authors themselves "caution against hasty real-world implementation" (Sec. 7).

title: Designing Closed Human-in-the-loop Deferral Pipelines
evidence: "we propose to use prior information about human experts' similarity with input samples" (Sec. 1, Contributions)
method: Deferrer outputs a distribution over m experts (classifier is one); k are sampled and majority-voted. Strict- and Smooth-Matching initialise or mix the deferrer with a similarity prior (dSim).
evaluation: Synthetic cluster task and 25k-tweet offensive-language task with 40 synthetic experts; baselines: two prior deferral methods, random committee; accuracy overall and per dialect group; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Closed deferral pipeline that routes each input to a committee drawn from several fallible experts and a classifier, using a weak similarity prior to avoid amplifying biased expert labels.
flag: (i) and (iii): deferral to human experts among multiple experts. All experts are synthetic, no real human study (authors say future work). One-shot classification, not sequential. Results: content moderation overall 0.82-0.83 vs 0.79 random committee; cluster 0.92 (single run) vs about 0.60 baseline. Theorems 2.5 and 2.6 concern expected weight updates only. Expert-count sweep given in figure only. Focus is fairness across groups as much as deferral accuracy.

title: Confounding-Robust Policy Improvement with Human-AI Teams
evidence: "We present a deferral collaboration framework for incorporating the sensitivity model into offline policy learning" (Abstract)
method: ConfHAI: offline-learned router sending each instance to a human or an algorithmic policy, using a marginal sensitivity model for unobserved confounding; a variant routes among several experts.
evaluation: Synthetic, HELOC lending, International Stroke Trial with three simulated humans, FOCUS with five real annotators; baselines Human, AO, ConfAO, HAI; regret only in figures, no numeric tables. No hardware.
contribution: ConfHAI learns from confounded observational logs when to defer to human decision-makers and when to apply an algorithmic policy, with high-probability regret and improvement bounds under a marginal sensitivity model.
flag: (i) deferral to human experts, also (iii) multiple experts and (v) proved bounds. TITLE DIFFERS but same paper: the current arXiv version is titled "Confounding-Robust Deferral Policy Learning" (Gao, Yin); the record title appears to be the earlier version title - maintainer should confirm. Evaluation-floor doubt: I found NO numeric experimental result in the text, results are only in Figures 3 and 4 which I could not read, so the empirical floor rests on figures; the theory (Theorem 2 regret bound, Corollary 2.1 improvement over the human policy) is stated and proved in the appendix. Appendix theorem numbering does not match the main text. Humans simulated except FOCUS annotators. One-shot offline setting, not sequential. Added tag causal-inference.

title: Online Decision Mediation
evidence: "we first formalize this sequential problem of online decision mediation" (Sec. 1); UMPIRE is built to "explicitly trade off (immediate) system risk with expected improvements" (Sec. 3.2)
method: Online mediator between a fallible human and an expert oracle: each round accept the human action, override it, or request the expert; UMPIRE weighs immediate risk against model improvement.
evaluation: Six streaming tasks incl. LunarLander and two clinical, 11 baselines, 10 seeds; erroneous acceptances UMPIRE vs Matched Decaying Request: 4 vs 15, 112 vs 154, 64 vs 102. No hardware.
contribution: Formalises online decision mediation, where a learner sitting between a fallible human and an expert accepts, overrides or escalates each decision under abstentive feedback, and proposes UMPIRE, which lowers regret against bandit baselines.
flag: (ii) sequential/online setting, also (i) hand-off to an expert oracle and override of a human. The mediator can override the human at execution time, a genuine interception. Humans are simulated (ground truth perturbed with probability 1/2); the LunarLander expert is a PPO2 agent. Appendices with proofs (Theorem 1 bound on expected improvement, hardness versus contextual bandits) were NOT in the text I could read, so the proofs are unverified. Regret curves are in figures I could not read; Table 2 was partly garbled in extraction and the HighEnergy abstention value may be wrong, so re-check any number before citing. Rounds are i.i.d. contexts, not trajectories with irreversibility.

title: FiFAR: A Fraud Detection Dataset for Learning to Defer
evidence: "we introduce the Financial Fraud Alert Review Dataset (FiFAR), a synthetic bank account fraud detection dataset" (Abstract); "rejection learning performs best, despite our attempts to model human behavior" (Sec. 4.3)
method: Benchmark dataset for learning to defer: bank-account-fraud data plus predictions of 50 synthetic fraud analysts and per-batch work-capacity constraints; three capacity-aware assignment baselines (ReL, ReL-greedy, ReL-linear ILP).
evaluation: Bank Account Fraud data, LightGBM model, 300 capacity scenarios; cost-sensitive loss: Model Only 918 vs ReL 746-768, ReL-greedy 773-790, ReL-linear 765-789; predictive equality 0.29-0.37. No hardware or latency.
contribution: FiFAR is a public fraud-detection benchmark for learning to defer with 50 synthetic analysts and capacity limits; simple rejection-learning assignment cuts cost-sensitive loss from 918 to about 750 against the model alone.
flag: (i) deferral to human experts, also (iii) multiple experts. Dataset/benchmark paper, not a new method: maintainer should decide whether a dataset counts as a deferral contribution. All experts are synthetic, no real humans. Authors admit (Sec. 5) the baselines include no established L2D method. One-shot batch assignment, not sequential. A column sigma_d in the scenario table was not clearly explained in the text I read. Paper read through the fetch tool's extraction; figures not seen.

title: Multi-Agent Dynamic Relational Reasoning for Social Robot Navigation
evidence: "Sec. IV-A: the encoder infers relation graphs and hypergraphs in the latent space" from historical states without relation supervision, and the decoder predicts future displacements conditioned on those evolving latent structures
method: Latent-variable encoder infers dynamically evolving relation graphs and group-wise hypergraphs among agents, with smoothness, sharpness and sparsity regularisers; predicted trajectories feed a PPO social navigation policy
evaluation: ETH-UCY, SDD, NBA and a synthetic group dataset against MID, GroupNet, Graph-TERN and EigenTrajectory; ETH-UCY minADE20/minFDE20 0.18/0.30 versus 0.21/0.36, NBA 1.16/1.64 versus 1.46/2.19; crowd simulator 96.31 percent success and 3.59 percent collision versus CrowdNav++ 93.21 and 6.66; real RosMaster X3 robot; RTX A6000, no latency reported
contribution: Inferring dynamically evolving relation hypergraphs among agents improves multi-agent trajectory prediction and, fed to a reinforcement learning policy, lowers collision and group-intrusion rates in dense crowd navigation.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: which - nothing is guarded; safety comes from reward penalties and learned behaviour, and the authors concede it "still cannot achieve a zero collision rate in very dense scenarios" (Conclusion), so (a) fails and runtime_interceptor is no. (c) fails the primacy test because collision rate is one of seven navigation metrics alongside success, path length and group intrusion. Admitted under (b) as Pillar 2 method evidence, not safety evidence, so RQ5 is capped at 2 - check whether the maintainer counts a latent-hypergraph VAE decoder as a world model or dismisses it as a trajectory regressor, which is the pivot for this record. Text claims state of the art on SDD but the table shows minADE20 8.1 tied with EigenTrajectory, and claims shorter path length though 20.53 m exceeds CrowdNav++ 20.37 m. No inference latency or onboard compute figure, so edge deployment and latency cells are not claimed despite the real-robot trial.

title: TrustAgent: Towards Safe and Trustworthy LLM-based Agents
evidence: 'the inspection method interrupts the trajectory whenever the agent repeats a mistake after being notified and criticized' (Section 4.2); the post-planning inspector vets each action before execution.
method: Agent Constitution of safety regulations enforced in three stages: pre-planning hindsight finetuning, in-planning retrieval of relevant regulations, and a GPT-4 post-planning inspector that vets every action.
evaluation: 70 tool-use cases in 5 domains (ToolEmu sandbox); 5 LLM backbones vs no-strategy baseline; GPT-4-judged safety 0-3 rose GPT-3.5 1.22 to 2.02, Claude-2 1.83 to 2.57, GPT-4 2.15 to 2.56, Mixtral 1.33 to 2.44; helpfulness also up; prompting-only vs inspection-only ablation on medicine; no hardware or latency reported.
contribution: TrustAgent wraps an LLM tool-using agent in a rule-based Agent Constitution plus a runtime action inspector, raising judged safety across five backbones without reducing helpfulness.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an LLM tool-calling agent. Check (c): this is one planning agent plus an inspector, so the multi-agent primacy test fails; safety is GPT-4-judged inside a GPT-4-emulated sandbox over only 70 cases; no latency, cost or false-halt analysis, and no human handoff; body says GPT-4 average safety is about 2 while Table 2 gives 2.15; Mixtral has no with-strategy results for food or chemistry.

title: Safe Road-Crossing by Autonomous Wheelchairs: a Novel Dataset and its Experimental Evaluation
evidence: 'crossing is not recommended until the vehicle slows down or surpasses the crossing location' (Sec. 3); the danger function only issues a recommendation and is itself analytical, not learned (Sec. 4).
method: Analytical explainable danger function over car distance, velocity and acceleration, thresholded to tag unsafe road-crossing states, with fusion across wheelchair range sensors, wheelchair camera and a drone camera using YOLO detection.
evaluation: 15 lab runs of three RoboMaster robots (car, wheelchair, drone) with 18-camera OptiTrack ground truth; three single sensors vs distance, danger and voting fusion; best results distance fusion accuracy 0.92, recall 0.91, precision 0.95, danger fusion RMSE 0.361 vs 0.582 range-only; sensors at 10-30 Hz resampled to 100 Hz; no decision latency and no compute platform given.
contribution: A multi-sensor laboratory dataset and an analytical, explainable danger function for autonomous-wheelchair road crossing, with a preliminary comparison showing distance fusion most accurate.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - the crossing decision and the danger function are hand-designed; only the YOLO perception stage is learned. Most likely record in this batch for the maintainer to overturn: hazard detection over three agents is the primary measured outcome and he may count the autonomous wheelchair as an AI system; against that, there is no runtime override (recommendation only), no ablation, 15 short runs, and Table 1 vs Table 2 disagree on camera resolution.

title: Characterization and Mitigation of Insufficiencies in Automated Driving Systems
evidence: 'the ADS has to perform an emergency brake or disengage from the AD mode to hand over control to the human' (Section 4); the DMV and video studies count human takeovers caused by output insufficiencies.
method: Taxonomy of 16 output-insufficiency types for automated driving in four categories, plus Daruma, an unimplemented design pattern using cross-channel analysis, safety fusion and a high-level arbiter to switch between heterogeneous driving channels.
evaluation: DMV 2021 reports (over 2500 disengagements, insufficiency-caused five times more often than fault-caused), 32 road-test videos over 10h17m giving 71 insufficiency scenarios of which 62 (87%) safety-critical, and open-loop LGSVL runs of Apollo 5.0, Autoware.Auto and openpilot with 42 insufficiencies and 23 missed objects; no baseline or ablation for Daruma, which is never implemented.
contribution: Characterises the output insufficiencies behind automated-driving disengagements using DMV reports, road-test videos and simulation, and sketches Daruma, an arbiter that switches between heterogeneous driving channels.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: which - the analysed Apollo and openpilot channels contain deep networks, but Daruma itself is unimplemented and unevaluated, so no safety metric is reported against a baseline or ablation and (a) fails. Maintainer may instead prefer E3 since the paper is part survey and part position paper, or may argue the takeover analysis under (e) earns inclusion. Channels were run sequentially in open loop, so switching was never tested; body says Autoware and openpilot missed twice as many objects as Apollo while Table 5 gives 4 and 17 vs 2.

title: Delay-Aware Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Adaptive Cruise Control with Model-based Stability Enhancement
evidence: Algorithm 1 lists the step 'Output action with stability check': Eq. (15) replaces the RL acceleration with a model-based ideal acceleration whenever the latter scores at least as well (Sec. IV-C).
method: Multi-agent delay-aware MDP for cooperative adaptive cruise control; attention-based CTDE policies emit acceleration and filter gains, and a velocity-optimisation action filter can replace the learned action at execution time.
evaluation: Catchup and Slowdown platoons of 5, 8 and 10 vehicles, 0.5s total delay (k=5 steps), 50 test trials, 3 seeds, vs MADDPG, ConseNet and NeurComm; collisions at size 8 are 0 vs 27 and 50 (Catchup) and 3 vs 12, 50, 50 (Slowdown); average reward -36.6 vs -30.9 to -667.8; Xeon Silver 4214R and RTX 3090; no inference or control latency measured.
contribution: Delay-aware multi-agent RL for vehicle platooning adds a model-based action filter that overrides unstable learned accelerations, cutting collision counts to zero or near-zero against MARL baselines.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a MARL platoon policy whose action is filtered at execution. Check (d): the 0.5s delay is actuation and communication delay inside the environment, not inference latency, and no compute latency is reported, so (d) is weak. (c) is borderline: the primary claim is delay handling and stability, with collisions one of three metrics. There is no ablation isolating the action filter, so its contribution is unproven; the filter selects by reward, not by a formal guarantee; the paper claims it beats all baselines in every scenario but ConseNet has higher reward at Catchup size 5; only one delay setting is tested despite the abstract's 'various delay conditions'; collisions are counts, not rates.

title: Cooperate or Collapse: Emergence of Sustainable Cooperation in a Society of LLM Agents
evidence: 'all but the most powerful LLM agents fail to achieve a sustainable equilibrium in GOVSIM' (Abstract); five LLM agents share one common-pool resource and the measured outcome is collapse (Sections 2.3, 3.1).
method: GOVSIM, a common-pool-resource benchmark where five LLM generative agents harvest and negotiate over 12 simulated months in fishery, pasture and pollution scenarios; universalization prompting is proposed as a mitigation.
evaluation: 15 LLMs, 5 seeds, 3 scenarios; survival rate 53.3% GPT-4o, 46.7% Claude-3 Opus, 20% Qwen-110B, 6.7% GPT-4, 0% Llama-3-8B; ablations remove communication (over-usage +22%, p<0.001) and add universalization (about +4 months survival, +24% efficiency, p<0.001); greedy-newcomer test drops GPT-4o to 33.3%; sub-skill accuracy correlates with survival (R2=0.92); up to 4x RTX 3090 or 2x A100, about 4h per run.
contribution: GOVSIM shows that most societies of LLM agents collapse a shared resource within months, and that communication and universalization reasoning measurably extend sustainable cooperation.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - societies of LLM agents are the analysed system. No runtime interception of any kind, so (a) fails and this enters as emergent multi-agent failure evidence, not safety-mechanism evidence. All three scenarios are logical simulations, so there is no physical domain and no cross-domain cell; humans in the loop are future work only; the reported hours and GPUs are wall-clock simulation cost, not decision latency; metrics are judged on 5 seeds per model-scenario pair.

title: BELLS: A Framework Towards Future Proof Benchmarks for the Evaluation of LLM Safeguards
evidence: Section 5.1 Baseline detection: 'It achieves a 0.97 AUPRC score after 80 steps in the environment.' - the only implemented test supervises an LLM agent's trace.
method: Benchmark framework of three test categories for LLM input-output safeguards; implements one next-gen-architecture test on MACHIAVELLI plus a trajectory-harm detector that flags unethical steering.
evaluation: 200 MACHIAVELLI traces (134 games, 33.6k API calls); detector thresholded against 100 random agents; AUPRC 0.97 at step 80, above 0.9 after step 29; no safeguard compared, no ablation, no hardware or latency.
contribution: BELLS proposes a three-category benchmark structure for LLM input-output safeguards and contributes the first next-gen agent test, a MACHIAVELLI trace dataset and a trajectory-harm baseline detector.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - safeguards over an LLM application/agent. Check: safeguards only produce reports from traces, nothing overrides or halts an action, so (a) fails; the single quantitative result (AUPRC 0.97) has no comparator safeguard and no ablation, so the evaluation floor fails; existing tools (Lakera Guard, Llama Guard, GPT-4 moderation) are discussed but never run with numbers; only one agent, multi-agent is named as future work, so exclude-E4 is also arguable, as is E3 for a framework/position paper with one implemented test.

title: A Superalignment Framework in Autonomous Driving with Large Language Models
evidence: Section I Contributions: the framework is a guardrail 'effectively censoring the data interacting with cloud-based LLM'; Section V adds 'a safety assessment agent', but no module is specified.
method: Conceptual security layer between vehicle and cloud LLM: driving-safety, data-safety and alignment conditions over models P_phi, P_psi, P_omega, stated as subset and limit requirements with no rejection rule.
evaluation: AutoGen harness, 250 nuScenes-QA pairs, 11 published LLM-driving system prompts on gpt-3.5-turbo and llama2-70b-chat; accuracy 16.4-93.0 percent, GPT-4-assigned alignment 45-92; the proposed framework itself is never evaluated; no hardware.
contribution: Sketches a cloud-LLM autonomous-driving security framework with driving-safety, data-safety and alignment conditions, and benchmarks eleven published LLM driving prompts on nuScenes-QA for accuracy and alignment.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a cloud LLM in a driving stack, but the guardrail is only a sketch: no module list, no architecture detail, no threshold or veto rule, so (a) fails. Check: the abstract's claim that the framework's efficacy was 'successfully demonstrated' is unsupported - every experiment benchmarks other papers' prompts, and Table III safety rates are copied from those papers rather than measured. Multi-agent is nominal (Section III sets P_phi=P_psi=P_omega for a single-agent structure). Table IV and V 'Time' columns have no units and no hardware. exclude-E1 is arguable if the maintainer reads it as a prompt benchmark rather than a safety mechanism.

title: Harmonizing Safety and Speed: A Human-Algorithm Approach to Enhance the FDA's Medical Device Clearance Policy
evidence: Policy recommends "acceptance, rejection, or deferral to FDA's committees" (Abstract); a device is deferred when its predicted recall risk lies between two optimised thresholds (Sec 4.1).
method: Gradient-boosting recall-risk model plus a two-threshold accept-reject-defer policy for FDA 510(k) clearance, thresholds optimised under acceptance, rejection and committee-workload constraints.
evaluation: FDA 510(k) and recall data 2008-2020, 70-30 split, 9,582 test devices, vs current all-committee practice; AUC 0.77, 38.9% recall-rate improvement, 43.0% workload reduction. No hardware or latency.
contribution: Designs an accept-reject-defer policy for FDA device clearance that sends only mid-risk applications to human committees, cutting workload 43% while rejecting 38.9% of later-recalled devices.
flag: (i), BORDERLINE with E4: a one-shot classifier with a reject band applied to one regulatory domain, and deferral shares the contribution with the risk model and the threshold optimisation. Deferred devices are assumed to get today's committee recall rate, so the human side is not modelled or studied ('e' not claimed, no handoff gap cell). Only baseline is current practice (100% human review); no single-threshold or other deferral baseline. 13.7% of rejected devices were never recalled and some settings reject over 42% of safe devices. Text says 51.5% workload reduction for M-L-M while Table 5 implies 48.5% workload - check which. Retrospective, not deployed. Read first 100k of 137k characters; e-companion not read.

title: EARBench: Towards Evaluating Physical Risk Awareness for Task Planning of Foundation Model-based Embodied AI Agents
evidence: Section 2.1: EARBench is 'the first automated physical risk assessment framework specifically designed for EAI scenarios'; average Task Risk Rate over 12 foundation models is 95.75 percent.
method: Automated four-module pipeline (safety-guideline generation, risky-scene generation, embodied task planning, GPT-4o plan assessment) producing EARDataset, which scores physical risk in foundation-model embodied task plans.
evaluation: 2636 textual and visual scenarios, 28 scenes, 7 physical domains, 12 LLMs and VLMs; TRR 95.75 percent average and 94.03 for GPT-4o; mitigation ablations cut TRR to 67.85 (Llama-3.1-70B) and 45.64 (GPT-4o); human kappa 0.85; no latency.
contribution: EARBench automates physical-risk assessment of foundation-model embodied planners, finding a 95.75 percent average task risk rate and showing prompt-level mitigation still leaves risk above 40 percent.
flag: RULED OUT by the between-agents ruling of 2026-11-13: Benchmark of single-agent embodied planners; physical risk arises within one planner, no second agent in the system under test. | original draft was include. learned or AI system guarded: yes - foundation-model embodied planners are the system assessed. Check: there is no runtime interception at all (RM-Implicit and RM-Explicit are prompt text, plans are judged after generation and never executed), so (a) fails and inclusion rests on the 'safety evaluation of LLM agents' clause of (c); the multi-agent cooperative system is the evaluation harness, not the system under test, and planning is single-agent, so exclude-E4 is arguable. GPT-4o generates the scenarios, judges the plans and is itself evaluated. No robot or simulator execution; visual scenes are Midjourney-V6 images. GPT-4o TRR is reported as 94.03, 94.12 and 94.53 textual with 93.52 visual in different places.

title: MAPPO-PIS: A Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization Method with Prior Intent Sharing for CAVs' Cooperative Decision-Making
evidence: Section 3.3: 'if the intention trajectory of CAV overlaps with that of other vehicle, the intention is considered unsafe, and it will be replaced with a new safe intention'; Algorithm 1 replaces it before execution.
method: MAPPO for connected-vehicle merging plus an Intention Generator Module (8-step PID rollout of each agent's intent) and a Safety Enhanced Module that priority-checks shared intents and substitutes a max-min-margin action.
evaluation: highway-env merging, easy and hard, homogeneous and heterogeneous human drivers, 2M steps, 3 seeds; baselines MAPPO, MAACKTR, MAA2C and a module ablation; collision 0.01 vs 0.03 hard and 0.04 vs 0.09 heterogeneous-hard, reward 33.27 vs -36.58, speed 21.61 m/s, PET 1.6 s; no latency.
contribution: MAPPO-PIS shares predicted intent among connected vehicles and adds a runtime module that replaces conflicting intentions, lowering collision rate from 0.09 to 0.04 against MAPPO while delaying merge bottlenecks.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the Safety Enhanced Module vetoes and replaces the MARL policy's own chosen intention before it is executed, so (a) is clear. Check: (c) is arguable but I did not claim it - the headline gains are reward, average speed and bottleneck delay, and collision rates sit between 0.00 and 0.04 with little separation from MAA2C. No module-isolating ablation exists (only full MAPPO-PIS vs MAPPO, i.e. both modules together), no SEM intervention-frequency or false-halt figures, and no latency or onboard hardware despite the CAV framing. Text and tables disagree: Section 4.4 says hard-mode collision 'grow to 0.02' while Table 1 gives 0.01, and Section 4.3 cites speeds 24.5 vs 22.5 m/s against 25.69 vs 25.06 in Table 1. PET is used without definition. Gap cell non-generative inference is my judgement because intent prediction is PID plus IDM-MOBIL rollout, not a generative model - drop it if too generous.

title: Learning To Help: Training Models to Assist Legacy Devices
evidence: "we formalize the reverse problem of training the expert for a fixed (legacy) client" (Sec I).
method: Learning to Help: jointly trains a rejector and a server classifier for a fixed legacy client model with offload and error costs, using a convex exponential surrogate loss.
evaluation: Proved: Bayes-optimal rejector and server rules, O(sqrt(1/n)) generalisation bound, surrogate consistency. CIFAR-10 binary pairs vs confidence and random rejection; figures only, Table I accuracies. No hardware or latency.
contribution: Derives Bayes-optimal rules and a consistent surrogate for training a server model and rejector around a fixed legacy client that offloads hard inputs.
flag: (v), weakly: theory of a learning-to-defer variant (fixed client, trained expert). BORDERLINE with E1/E4: machine-to-machine offloading motivated by cost, one-shot binary classification, no human, no safety setting. Empirical floor is thin: the comparison with confidence-based rejection is shown only in Figures 2-3 with no numbers in the text; Table I gives per-pair accuracies (e.g. deferred airplane-vs-car 46.6 client vs 92.2 server) but is not a baseline comparison. Consistency holds only for an idealised alpha that needs the unknown P(x) and assumes conditional independence; appendix has typos and the Rademacher step is not fully justified. 'Edge' is a framing only, nothing is deployed.

title: Online Decision Deferral under Budget Constraints
evidence: Paraphrase (Sec 3-4): each round the learner observes a context and either defers to a human at a cost or uses the fixed ML model at zero cost, subject to a known budget B.
method: Online learning to defer as a budgeted two-armed contextual bandit: UCB-style estimates of reward and human cost with a dual variable pacing the deferral budget; linear and NeuralLinear variants.
evaluation: Regret bound O(sqrt(T)) via Agrawal-Devanur (proof sketched). Synthetic, Knapsack (396 humans) and ImageNet16H vs ModelOnly, HumanOnly, BestReject oracle; results mostly in figures. Colab T4; no latency.
contribution: Casts deferral to a human as a budget-constrained contextual bandit with a sublinear regret guarantee, evaluated on real human decision data with time-based deferral costs.
flag: (i) and (ii): deferral to a human as an online action over time under a budget. Checks: almost all quantitative results are in figures, the text gives no table of values (only qualitative statements and an observed regret growth near t^(2/3) on Knapsack, worse than the proved sqrt(T)); the method does not clearly beat the BestReject oracle and degrades at tight budgets on ImageNet16H. The regret proof is a sketch that 'follows identically' to prior work and needs a large budget. Human responses are replayed from recorded studies; the handoff itself is not studied, so 'e' not claimed and the human-handoff gap cell is generous. Evidence is a paraphrase, not a verbatim quote.

title: NetSafe: Exploring the Topological Safety of Multi-agent Networks
evidence: Abstract and Table 1: under misinformation injection the Star topology falls from 95.03 to 66.80 on Fact, a 29.7 percent decrease; Section 4.2 names 'Agent Hallucination' spreading through the network.
method: NetSafe models an LLM multi-agent system as a graph with a RelCom iterative communication protocol, injects misinformation, bias or harmful content at chosen nodes across five topologies and measures network safety.
evaluation: GPT-4o-mini agents, 6-node Chain, Cycle, Tree, Star and Complete graphs, 0-5 attackers, 3 runs, datasets Fact 153, CSQA 127, GSMath 113, Bias 103, AdvBench; Star 95.03 to 66.80, Complete GSMath 89.38 to 44.25, moderation 0.097 vs 0.920 attacker; static-metric Kendall tau APV 0.367, NE 0.067, EC -0.567; no defended baseline, no latency.
contribution: NetSafe shows that an LLM multi-agent network's safety depends on its topology, with misinformation in a star graph cutting accuracy 29.7 percent, and names Agent Hallucination and Aggregation Safety.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the agents are LLMs and multi-agent safety is both the primary claim and the primary measured outcome, so (c) holds. No defense, filter or monitor is proposed, so (a) fails and runtime_interceptor is no. Check: the comparison is across topologies and attacker counts rather than against a defended baseline, so the maintainer may hold that the evaluation floor's baseline requirement is unmet; outcomes are task accuracy and OpenAI Moderation scores, not a hazard or intervention rate; every network has 6 nodes averaged over 3 runs with no scaling study; the proposed static topology metrics correlate weakly (NE Kendall tau 0.067, EC -0.567 i.e. inverted); text-only agents, no physical or robotic setting, so no cross-domain cell.

title: Optimal Query Allocation in Extractive QA with LLMs: A Learning-to-Defer Framework with Theoretical Guarantees
evidence: "defer only when an expert exhibits strictly lower expected risk than the main model" (Sec 4.2, Lemma 1).
method: Learning-to-defer for extractive QA: a small TinyBERT rejector allocates each query among an on-device Llama-3.2-1B and two ALBERT experts under consultation costs, trained with a surrogate deferral loss.
evaluation: Proved: Bayes rejector, surrogate upper bound, (R,G)-consistency, Bayes-consistency. SQuADv1, SQuADv2, TriviaQA vs random, ensembles and three routers; EM 84.2 tie, EM-per-cost 12.16 vs 3.36. H100; no latency.
contribution: Proves a Bayes-consistent surrogate for multi-expert learning to defer in extractive QA and shows a tiny rejector matching router accuracy at lower compute cost.
flag: (iii) and (v): deferral among multiple experts with consistency proofs, but BORDERLINE with the E1 cost-router clause: all experts are models (no humans in experiments) and the deferral is motivated by compute cost (GFLOPs), not safety. One-shot per query, not sequential. Accuracy ties the routers at beta0=0 (EM 84.2 for all); the advantage is only in EM-per-cost, whose unit is unclear. The '4x efficiency vs Llama-3-8B' claim and Figures 2-3 values could not be found as numbers in the text. Corollary 2 proof looks thin (assumes uniform convergence). Efficiency is a GFLOPs proxy, no measured latency.

title: Joint Training for Selective Prediction
evidence: The ideal policy would "defer to a human if and only if an algorithmic decision is incorrect" (Introduction); a deferral policy network is trained jointly with the classifier.
method: Jointly trains a classifier and a separate deferral-policy network with cross-entropy plus a policy-gradient reward over correctness and defer action; deferred items go to a human.
evaluation: Four student-answer grading datasets (BEETLE, SciEnts, Mid-PHYS, ISTUDIO); vs softmax threshold, logistic-regression deferral, separate training, no-reward ablation; BEETLE accuracy 85.33% vs 79.35% at 8.2% deferral; no hardware.
contribution: Joint training of a text classifier with a learned deferral policy improves selective-prediction accuracy on automated short-answer grading over threshold and separately trained deferral baselines.
flag: none of (i)-(v) in substance: one-shot selective prediction applied to a domain (short-answer grading). It nominally defers to a human, so a lenient reading of (i) would include it - maintainer may flip - but the human is never modelled (deferred items are scored with gold labels, i.e. a perfect oracle), there is no expert model, no theory, no sequential aspect. I included arxiv:2507.14406 on a similar human-oracle basis, so the two should be decided consistently. No seeds, variance or significance tests; deferral rates differ across methods so accuracy comparisons are not at matched coverage; Thresh. on ISTUDIO/SFRN degenerates to 100% deferral; one cell (Mid-PHYS/BERT) is not won by JTSP. Policy gradient here is a training device, not a sequential setting.

title: SafeAgentBench: A Benchmark for Safe Task Planning of Embodied LLM Agents
evidence: Sec. 5.6: the GPT-4 chain-of-thought safety filter "inspected each planned step and terminated execution if unsafe"; Table 2 reports rejection rates on 450 hazardous tasks.
method: Benchmark of 750 tasks (450 hazardous, 300 safe) in AI2-THOR-based SafeAgentEnv with execution-based and GPT-4 semantic evaluators; a chain-of-thought safety filter is tested as an add-on runtime defense.
evaluation: 9 embodied LLM planners and 5 LLMs in SafeAgentEnv; rejection of hazardous tasks only 0-10 pct, risk rate up to 0.69, unsafe completion up to 0.28; RTX 4090, 21-97 s per task.
contribution: SafeAgentBench shows embodied LLM planners execute most hazardous instructions, rejecting at most 10 percent, and that a chain-of-thought safety filter over-rejects safe tasks without fixing long-horizon hazards.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - embodied LLM task planners. Check that criterion (a) is not over-credited: it rests only on the add-on chain-of-thought safety filter in Sec. 5.6, whose numbers live in Figure 6 and not in the text, so the over-rejection and no-improvement claims could not be verified from the body; the benchmark itself intercepts nothing. Multi-agent only incidentally (CoELA, MAP are two-agent). Text calls the semantic evaluator GPT-4 while App. C.4 names gpt-4o-2024-08-06, and Table 14 renames CoELA as Co-LLM-Agent.

title: MARL-OT: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Guided Online Fuzzing to Detect Safety Violation in Autonomous Driving Systems
evidence: Sec. 3.4: "Once the online fuzzer is triggered, it takes control of the surrounding vehicle."; violation rate against GA, single-agent RL and random baselines is the primary outcome (Table 3).
method: MADDPG trains surrounding vehicles to cooperatively encircle an ego ADS; its high-level guidance triggers a rule-based finite-state online fuzzer running four pre-crash action patterns to expose ego safety violations.
evaluation: MetaDrive, IDM and PPO ego policies, 7 scenario types, 200 runs x 5 repeats; violation rate 9.3-14.9 pct vs GA 0.2-6.7, single-agent RL 4.7-11.0, random 0.1-5.4; RTX 3090, about 15 min training.
contribution: MARL-OT couples MARL high-level guidance with a rule-based online fuzzer over surrounding vehicles, roughly doubling the detected safety-violation rate of autonomous driving systems versus offline genetic and single-agent RL fuzzers.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes for the PPO end-to-end ego policy, no for the hand-designed IDM policy. Check (a) is correctly denied: there is no runtime interception anywhere - the fuzzer controls only surrounding vehicles and never overrides the ADS, so this is adversarial testing, and a maintainer who reads the review as about safety reflexes rather than hazard discovery could call exclude-E1. Included on (c) because the multi-vehicle collision rate is both primary claim and primary measured outcome against three baselines. The abstract's up to 136.2 pct improvement does not reproduce from Table 3, where the best pairwise gain over single-agent RL is about 94 pct. No ablation other than the stripped single-agent RL variant; no human role beyond a 5-tester realism rating.

title: Identity-Free Deferral For Unseen Experts
evidence: "The deferral mechanism in EA-L2D is implemented via a feedforward neural network" taking classifier confidences and the expert's per-class accuracy representation (Sec. 4.2).
method: Represents each expert by Beta-Binomial per-class accuracy estimated from a few context predictions; a rejector compares classifier confidence to that profile, so unseen experts need no retraining.
evaluation: CIFAR-10, HAM10000, GTSRB, three medical MNIST sets; synthetic experts; vs L2D-Pop, Pop-Avg, multi-expert L2D; AURSAC/AURDAC e.g. 0.81/0.76 vs 0.62/0.35 on unseen experts; no hardware or latency.
contribution: A learning-to-defer rejector conditioned on a Bayesian per-class accuracy profile of the expert instead of expert identity, generalising deferral to experts never seen in training.
flag: (i) and (iii) learning to defer to experts drawn from a population, including unseen ones. TITLE DIFFERS: the fetched PDF is titled 'Expert-Agnostic Learning to Defer' (EA-L2D), not 'Identity-Free Deferral For Unseen Experts'; content matches the record topic exactly, so I treated it as an earlier-titled version of the same paper, but I could not confirm the retitling from the arXiv listing - please verify, and if it is a different paper this row should be exclude-E6 WRONG PAPER. All experts are synthetic oracles-on-one-class, no humans. Propositions 1-2 are proof sketches; Proposition 3 (expert-agnosticism) is an informal argument. Gap on Breast Ultrasound is small (0.77/0.73 vs 0.73/0.64). Abstract claims 1-16% (seen) and 4-28% (unseen) gains; I saw only selected Table 1 rows and did not verify the ranges. RQ4 scored 2 for generalisation to unseen experts, not unseen hazards.

title: Learning to Defer for Causal Discovery with Imperfect Experts
evidence: "L2D-CD learns which causal discovery predictor" - statistical method or metadata-based expert - returns the correct causal direction when the two differ (Sec. 2.4).
method: Post-hoc learning to defer for pairwise causal direction: a random forest on text embeddings decides per variable pair whether to trust a statistical method or an imperfect expert (LLM).
evaluation: Tuebingen cause-effect pairs, 50/50 split; LiNGAM, RECI, bQCD; GPT-4o and synthetic experts; vs random deferral and each alone; accuracy e.g. 0.883 vs 0.593; H-consistency lemma proved; no hardware.
contribution: Applies learning to defer to causal discovery, learning from variable descriptions when an imperfect expert such as an LLM should override a statistical causal-direction method.
flag: (i) learning to defer to an expert, but weakly: the expert is an LLM or a synthetic expert, never a human, and the task is offline pairwise causal discovery, not an acting system. A strict reading could call this a reject-option method applied to a domain (E4); maintainer should decide. Training sets on the disagreement set are tiny (11 to 36 pairs), domains were assigned by hand, baseline is only random deferral. One row (CEP under LiNGAM) has L2D-CD at 0.691 vs expert 0.692. Lemma 2.1 is a small extension of Mao et al. 2024, not foundational enough for (v) on its own. v1 read.

title: Why Ask One When You Can Ask $k$? Learning-to-Defer to the Top-$k$ Experts
evidence: "each query is allocated to a set of the k most suitable agents." (Sec. 4, Top-k Learning-to-Defer, Motivation).
method: Two-stage learning to defer where a rejector routes each query to the k highest-scoring pre-trained agents; a selector learns a per-query number k(x) under consultation cost.
evaluation: Proves (R,G)-consistency bound (Thm 4.6), Bayes-optimal rejector set and cardinality. CIFAR-100, SVHN, California Housing; vs top-1 L2D, random, oracle; RMSE 8.53 vs 10.08 at equal budget; A100; no latency.
contribution: Generalises two-stage learning to defer from one expert to the top-k experts, with a k-independent surrogate, consistency bounds and an adaptive per-query number of experts that subsumes model cascades.
flag: (iii) deferral among multiple experts and (v) foundational theory. Fetched version is titled 'Why Ask One When You Can Ask k? Two-Stage Learning-to-Defer to the Top-k Experts' - same paper, later version adds 'Two-Stage'. Companion to arxiv:2505.10160. Bayes-consistency is claimed in the abstract but appears only as a remark (Remark 4), not a numbered theorem. Agents are synthetic experts or trained models, never humans; SVHN gain is small (70.81% vs 70.05%); CIFAR-100 results given only in figures. Cascades are covered as a special case, which touches the cost-router exclusion, but deferral is the main contribution. Last ~18k characters (appendix tail) not read.

title: Characterizing the Robustness of Black-Box LLM Planners Under Perturbed Observations with Adaptive Stress Testing
evidence: App. D.2: timesteps whose entropy exceeds a first-quartile threshold are flagged to alert engineers; Sec. 4.2: "we use MCTS to intelligently search for perturbation action trajectories".
method: Adaptive stress testing with MCTS over prompt perturbations (sensor-field removal, noise, prompt style, few-shot removal), scoring LLM driving-action diversity as a black-box uncertainty proxy; offline trees reused for runtime alerting.
evaluation: highway-env with Llama 3.2, Dolphin 3.0 and DeepSeek-R1 planners; OPD tree-search comparator on unperturbed driving; alert rates 0.57-0.88 across MCTS depth and iteration settings; 24000 generations; no latency reported.
contribution: Adaptive stress testing with MCTS over prompt perturbations exposes unsafe black-box LLM planner behaviour and yields an entropy threshold that flags unpredictable timesteps at runtime without access to model internals.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - black-box LLM driving planners. Title check: the fetched PDF carries the earlier title Adaptive Stress Testing Black-Box LLM Planners, while the abs page shows the record title and four versions through 2026-05-11, so the figures above may come from an older version - worth re-reading v4. Criterion (a) fails: the runtime flag only alerts engineers and cannot veto, halt or defer. Primary metrics are action-diversity and entropy proxies plus alert rate with no baseline for the uncertainty method itself; collision, speed and inconsistency numbers appear only in figures, so the evaluation floor is met only if alert rate counts as a detection rate and the MCTS-setting variants count as ablations. A single planner in traffic, so (c) is multi-agent only nominally; exclude-E2 or exclude-E1 is defensible.

title: One-Stage Top-$k$ Learning-to-Defer: Score-Based Surrogates with Theoretical Guarantees
evidence: The model "learns a shared scoring function to simultaneously classify and select the most cost-effective entities" (Sec. 1, Introduction).
method: One-stage score-based learning to defer that ranks labels and experts jointly and consults the top-k entities; a k-independent convex surrogate plus a learned per-input cardinality k(x).
evaluation: Proves H-consistency bounds (Thm 4.8) and Bayes-optimal top-k set (Lemma 4.7). CIFAR-10, SVHN, synthetic experts; vs top-1 L2D and random; 95.53% vs 94.7% majority-vote accuracy; A100; no latency.
contribution: Extends one-stage learning to defer from a single decision-maker to the top-k labels and experts, with a k-independent surrogate, H-consistency bounds and an input-adaptive number of consultations.
flag: (iii) deferral among multiple experts and (v) foundational theory (surrogate consistency bounds). Companion to arxiv:2504.12988 by the same authors (that one is two-stage); maintainer may want to treat them as a pair. Abstract claims Bayes-consistency but no separately named Bayes-consistency theorem was found in the body; it follows from the H-consistency bound. The reader noted internal inconsistencies (two differing statements of Lemma 4.4, sign conventions in Thm 4.8 vs its proof) - proofs not checked by me. Experts are synthetic or trained models, no humans; gain over fixed k is under 1 point. Last ~6.7k characters of the PDF (end of appendix) not read.

title: DeCoDe: Defer-and-Complement Decision-Making via Decoupled Concept Bottleneck Models
evidence: Strategy pseudo-label rule: "Defer-to-Human if at least one expert is correct while the AI is not" (Sec. 3.3, Surrogate Loss Design and Optimization).
method: Decoupled concept bottleneck model with a gating network over explicit concepts choosing per instance among AI-only, AI+human combination, or full deferral to the human.
evaluation: CUB-200, Derm7pt, CelebA with simulated noisy human labels; baselines CE, OvA and realizable L2D surrogates; accuracy vs human-participation curves; RTX A6000; no latency.
contribution: A concept-bottleneck learning-to-defer model that selects per instance among autonomous prediction, human-AI complementary prediction and deferral, with the gate conditioned on interpretable concepts.
flag: (i) learning to defer to a human expert, one-shot image classification. Evaluation floor is met only thinly: comparisons against L2D baselines are shown as curves (Fig. 3, Fig. 5a) and the reader I used found no tabulated accuracy, coverage or deferral-rate numbers for DeCoDe or baselines in the main text; only base-model accuracies (CUB 80.9%, Derm7pt 78.9%, CelebA 35.3%) are numeric. Fig. 3(a) reportedly shows DeCoDe slightly behind L2D-REAL at low human participation. Humans are simulated by label noise, no user study, interpretability claims are qualitative. Appendix B derivations not read; no theorem in main text.

title: VLMLight: Safety-Critical Traffic Signal Control via Vision-Language Meta-Control and Dual-Branch Reasoning Architecture
evidence: Sec. 3.2: "Rather than issuing control actions directly, AgentModeSelector interprets the set of textual scene descriptions"; AgentCheck rejects an unvalidated LLM phase after N_check attempts and the system falls back to the RL action.
method: A VLM turns four camera views into text; an LLM meta-controller routes each decision interval to a PPO policy or to three reasoning LLM agents for safety-critical scenes, with RL fallback.
evaluation: SUMO-based image simulator on three real intersections; 9 baselines plus component and backbone ablations; emergency-vehicle wait 7.48, 2.17, 2.60 s vs best RL 22.04, 5.17, 7.81 s; 9.4-11.5 s decision latency on A100s against a 13 s phase buffer.
contribution: VLMLight routes traffic-signal decisions between a fast RL policy and a slow multi-agent LLM reasoning branch, cutting emergency-vehicle waiting time by more than half at small routine-traffic cost.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a PPO traffic-signal policy and the LLM reasoning branch. Criterion (a) rests on the AgentCheck validator plus RL fallback, which vetoes an LLM phase at execution time; the meta-controller otherwise only routes, so a maintainer could read the whole thing as architecture rather than interception. No collision, violation, intervention or throughput metric is reported - the only safety evidence is emergency-vehicle delay - so exclude-E2 is defensible under a strict reading of the floor. Abstract claims over 60 pct reduction in both AETT and AEWT and under 1 pct routine degradation; tables give about 29 pct AETT at Songdo and about 5 pct ATT degradation at Yau Ma Tei and Massy. Sec. 4.3 quotes a 48 s to 58 s ablation as AEWT where Table 2 places those values under AETT. Latency of 9-11 s on five A100s is real-time only against a traffic phase buffer, not edge.

title: From Virtual Agents to Robot Teams: A Multi-Robot Framework Evaluation in High-Stakes Healthcare Context
evidence: Sec. V-A: "Overall, these results suggest that a detailed KB helped increase performance across most dimensions"; Issue Handling scores 0 in both conditions.
method: Stress test of a four-robot CrewAI hierarchy (manager plus navigation, information-collection and display robots) driven by GPT-4o in a simulated emergency-department onboarding task, with and without a knowledge base.
evaluation: Simulation only, no real robots and no participants; 5 runs per condition; overall success 45.29 pct baseline vs 72.94 pct with knowledge base; delegation accuracy 0.333 vs 0.733; issue handling 0 in both; cost 0.077 vs 0.154 USD per run.
contribution: Stress-testing a CrewAI robot team in a simulated emergency department exposes five persistent failure modes of multi-agent LLM frameworks and yields three design guidelines for embodied deployment.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a GPT-4o multi-robot team - but nothing guards it. No runtime override, veto or halt, and the primary measured outcomes are task-success and delegation-accuracy scores rather than any hazard, collision or violation rate, so the (c) primacy test fails and I recommend exclude-E1. Escalation to a human supervisor exists only as prompt and knowledge-base text and is never implemented or evaluated, so (e) fails. If the maintainer instead reads a multi-robot LLM failure-mode study in a high-stakes healthcare setting as (c), the evaluation floor still fails for lack of any safety metric, which would make it exclude-E2. Only 5 runs per condition, no hardware or latency figures, and the healthcare stakes are asserted rather than measured.

title: DURA-CPS: A Multi-Role Orchestrator for Dependability Assurance in LLM-Enabled Cyber-Physical Systems
evidence: Step 7 of the orchestration loop: "Controller may halt, log details, or activate the RecoveryPlanner", and the RecoveryPlanner "overrides the Generator's decision" with emergency_brake (Sec. III.C, Fig. 3).
