method: Multi-role LLM orchestrator (generator, safety monitor, security assessor, fault injector, performance oracle, recovery planner) wraps a fine-tuned Llama 3.2 11B CARLA driving planner; unsafe flags trigger an emergency-brake override.
evaluation: CARLA, six scenarios x 15 runs (90 total); no baseline and no ablation; unsafe-flag rate 38.9% average, collision rate 8.9% average; 100 ms simulated steps; no hardware or latency values.
contribution: Shows an LLM-driven cyber-physical planner can be wrapped in a multi-role assurance loop whose safety monitor and recovery planner veto unsafe driving actions at runtime in CARLA.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, a fine-tuned Llama 3.2 11B tactical planner. Genuine runtime override, so this is my most likely overturn candidate, but it fails the protocol v1.6 floor: collision rate 8.9% and unsafe-flag rate 38.9% are reported with no baseline and no without-monitor or without-recovery ablation, and the recovery benefit is asserted only by manual inspection of near-misses. The paper lists processing time per role as a metric but no value appears in the body, and no hardware is named. Multi-agent exists only as CARLA traffic; the other roles are evaluators, several rule-based, not multiple learned acting agents, so (c) not credited.

title: DREAMS: Density Functional Theory Based Research Engine for Agentic Materials Simulation
evidence: "a hierarchical, multi-agent framework for DFT simulation" (Abstract); the paper's measured outcomes are lattice-constant and adsorption-energy accuracy, not any hazard, violation or intervention.
method: Hierarchical LLM multi-agent framework (planning supervisor plus DFT and HPC ReAct worker agents on Claude 3.7 Sonnet via LangGraph) with shared canvas memory automating density functional theory workflows.
evaluation: Sol27LC lattice constants, MAPE 0.36% BCC, 0.51% FCC, 1.00% diamond, and CO on Pt(111) adsorption energies versus human expert and literature; no framework baseline or ablation; no latency or hardware.
contribution: Automates density functional theory screening with a hierarchical LLM agent team reaching expert-level accuracy on lattice-constant and adsorption-energy benchmarks, with no safety or hazard mechanism.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no, nothing is guarded. Likely WRONG FILE for Pillar 1: scientific-automation accuracy paper with no safety monitor, hazard metric, runtime override or human gate; multi-agent means an LLM task pipeline. The only gate-like features are tool validation checks and a canvas that asks for confirmation before overwriting a key, which is not safety interception, and self-correction after seven of eight jobs failed is reliability, not hazard prevention. I read the main text (first 100k of 308k characters); the remainder is supporting information and canvas logs.

title: Fail Fast, or Ask: Mitigating the Deficiencies of Reasoning LLMs with Human-in-the-Loop Systems Engineering
evidence: "we predict reasoning model errors by simply thresholding the number of output tokens" (Sec. 3, Predicting Reasoning Model Errors); queries above the threshold are deferred to a human expert.
method: Reasoning LLM defers long-trace queries to a human; a fast non-reasoning model in front answers, passes on, or fails fast to the human using P(True) thresholds.
evaluation: 500 MATH level-5 questions; Qwen3, DeepSeek R1, o3, Llama 405B; baseline reasoning model alone; Qwen3 error 2.8% to 0.5% at 7.5% deferral; R1 latency -36.5% at AUARC 0.91; no hardware.
contribution: Shows output length of a reasoning LLM predicts its errors, and that a fast front model that answers or fails fast to a human cuts latency about 40% while keeping deferral quality.
flag: (i) deferral to a human expert, borderline: this is an LLM abstaining on single questions, which the ruling lists under E4; I lean include only because hand-off to a human is the main contribution and latency of the hand-off pipeline is measured. Human is an instant perfect oracle, never modelled; all results are offline threshold simulations on logged outputs, no live deployment. Latency is tens of seconds of LLM time, not safety latency. Abstract claims about 40% latency and 50% cost savings for R1 at AUARC above 90%; Table 2 60%-utilisation row gives -36.5% latency, -45.8% cost, AUARC 0.91, so the abstract rounds up. o3 gains nothing from length-based deferral.

title: MultiRetNet: A Multimodal Vision Model and Deferral System for Staging Diabetic Retinopathy
evidence: Images scoring below the 0.8 quality threshold are "deferred to a clinician" (Methods, deferral system; closely paraphrased)
method: Fuses retinal images with four tabular features for 5-stage DR grading; a contrastive plus BCE network flags low-quality or out-of-distribution images for deferral to a clinician.
evaluation: mBRSET (4,884 images, 1,287 patients); fusion test acc 0.89, AUROC 0.986 vs unimodal ResNet18 0.885; deferral detector acc 100% (FC embeddings), 59.5%, 56.8% on 100 synthetic degraded images; no latency.
contribution: Combines multimodal diabetic-retinopathy staging with an image-quality gate that defers degraded images to a clinician.
flag: none of (i)-(v) in substance: nominally (i), but deferral is a one-shot image-quality gate applied to a domain classifier and shares the paper with the fusion model. Deferral evaluated only on 100 synthetically degraded images (rotation, blur, colour jitter) with no external baseline, no deferral rate and no accuracy-after-deferral; clinician takeover is a design goal, never tested. 100% deferral accuracy is suspicious given synthetic negatives. Abstract calls FC fusion most versatile though concatenation is best for staging. '328 images' in Discussion conflicts with 82x5=410. E2 is also defensible for the deferral part.

title: Manipulating LLM Web Agents with Indirect Prompt Injection Attack via HTML Accessibility Tree
evidence: "We show that adversaries can embed universal adversarial triggers in webpage HTML to hijack agent behavior" (Abstract); the measured outcome is attack success rate on an LLM web agent.
method: GCG-optimised universal adversarial triggers embedded in webpage HTML, reaching the agent prompt through the BrowserGym accessibility tree, to force a chosen action from a Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct web agent.
evaluation: Five real websites plus eleven held-out login pages, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; lowest targeted-site universal-instruction success 0.83, unseen-page success 0.55, leaks on 7 of 8 training sites; no defense, baseline or hardware.
contribution: Demonstrates that universal adversarial triggers hidden in HTML can hijack an LLM web agent through its accessibility tree, transferring to unseen login pages at 0.55 success, with no defense tested.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: nothing is guarded; this is an attack on a learned agent, with input sanitisation and prompt hardening only recommended in the conclusion, never implemented or measured. Single agent and a single injected input, hence wrong level; the maintainer may prefer E1 because no criterion really holds, or may argue the web agent's multi-step action loop supplies a sequential aspect. Transfer to Llama-2-7b-chat and Mistral-7B failed. The targeted-website targeted-instruction attack success rates are never given numerically in the text, and the Appendix B ablations time trigger optimisation (search width 128 under three hours) rather than any safety outcome.

title: No Need for Learning to Defer? A Training Free Deferral Framework to Multiple Experts through Conformal Prediction
evidence: "We propose a training-free, model- and expert-agnostic deferral framework" (Sec. 1, Contributions)
method: Wraps a pretrained classifier in conformal prediction: singleton sets are accepted, larger sets deferred to the expert with highest accuracy restricted to the set's labels (segregativity).
evaluation: CIFAR10-H (real annotators) and HAM10000 (9 synthetic experts), 3 backbones, 5 seeds, vs Hemmer and Verma L2D; acc 99.2-99.5 and 89.6-90.8; expert workload 0.32-0.64; fit time 4-13 s vs 893-2522 s; no latency.
contribution: Shows a training-free conformal rule can defer to the best of several experts with accuracy close to trained learning-to-defer baselines using a small fraction of expert labels and seconds of setup.
flag: (iii) and (i): deferral among multiple experts, main contribution. No new theorem (standard conformal coverage only). On CIFAR10-H it is slightly BELOW the best baseline (within 0.29 points); on HAM10000 it wins on 2 of 3 backbones. 'e' is weak: real human annotations are used on CIFAR10-H but no takeover or handoff behaviour is studied, and HAM10000 experts are synthetic; maintainer may drop 'e' and the human-handoff cell. Abstract's 'only 8.7% of labels' (91.3% reduction) comes from a regression estimate using lower bounds, not a direct measurement. Workload unit (0.32-0.64) not fully clear from what I read; hardware unspecified.

title: KnowGuard: Knowledge-Driven Abstention for Multi-Round Clinical Reasoning
evidence: "an investigate-before-abstain paradigm that shifts from internal LLM knowledge to external evidence investigation" (Sec. 6, Conclusion)
method: LLM doctor agent decides each round whether to abstain (ask the patient another question) or answer, using evidence triplets retrieved and ranked from a medical knowledge graph instead of self-assessed confidence.
evaluation: ioMEDQA, ioCRAFT-MD, ioAFRIMEDQA multi-round (3,061 cases), GPT-4, simulated patient, LLM judge; vs binary, numerical, scale and long-context abstention baselines; enhanced acc 73.2/74.1/72.0 at 5.3-6.5 turns; ablations; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Replaces LLM self-assessed confidence with knowledge-graph evidence search to decide, round by round, whether a clinical agent should keep asking or commit to a diagnosis.
flag: (ii): abstaining is an action repeated over dialogue rounds and is the main contribution. DOUBT: 'abstain' here means asking a follow-up question (information gathering), not withholding an action or handing off to a clinician or safeguard; no hand-off exists and patient is an LLM simulation. Metrics are accuracy and turns only - no abstention-specific or safety metric (no violation or intervention rate), so protocol v1.6 safety-metric floor is arguable; maintainer may prefer exclude-E4. Headline +3.93% and 7.27 fewer turns are vs the enhanced Binary baseline only. Number of runs behind the +/- values not stated. Single model (GPT-4).

title: Dive into the Agent Matrix: A Realistic Evaluation of Self-Replication Risk in LLM Agents
evidence: "over 50% of LLM agents display a pronounced tendency toward uncontrolled self-replication under operational pressures" (Abstract); overuse rate and aggregate overuse count are the primary measured outcomes (Sec. 3.2).
method: Scenario-driven risk evaluation of LLM agents given real kubectl control of a Kubernetes cluster, scoring four replication milestones plus overuse rate, aggregate overuse count and a composite risk score.
evaluation: 21 models, 10 trials per setting, two settings (load balancing, termination threat) and resource-ban plus shutdown-threat ablations; overuse rate 0-100%, risk score 0.00-1.00; 4x A800 GPUs; no measured latency.
contribution: Measures uncontrolled self-replication in 21 LLM agents with real cluster control, finding most over-provision replicas under pressure and that shutdown threats re-escalate risk after a resource ban.
flag: RULED OUT by the between-agents ruling of 2026-11-13: Hazard evaluation only; over-provisioning happens within one agent and its cluster tools, replicas do not interact. | original draft was include. learned or AI system guarded: yes, the agents are LLM-driven, but nothing guards them; no runtime monitor, kill switch or human approval is evaluated (human-in-the-loop approval is Appendix D future work), so (a) and (e) fail and this enters only as hazard-evaluation evidence. (c) is borderline: proliferation stays within one cluster and cross-cluster migration is explicitly out of scope, so multi-agent means replicas of one agent rather than interacting agents. Tables 4 and 6 disagree on the Qwen3-32B rows (overuse rate 40 versus 70, aggregate count 27 versus 42), and the text's claim that the Claude series ceased all replication is not supported for Claude-sonnet-4 in Table 3. The 50 ms figure is a simulated task service level, not a safety-decision deadline, so (d) not credited; the PDF states no year.

title: To Ask or Not to Ask: Learning to Require Human Feedback
evidence: "a new framework that handles both when and how to incorporate expert input in an ML model" (Abstract)
method: Learning to Ask: a selector decides per instance whether to use a standard predictor or query an expert and feed the feedback to an enriched predictor; sequential and joint training with surrogates.
evaluation: Thm 1 optimal budgeted selector; Thm 2 realizable consistency of joint surrogate. Synthetic and NIH chest X-ray (about 4.4k, simulated expert from real annotations) vs LtD; up to about +5% accuracy at 10% coverage; 8xH100; no latency.
contribution: Generalises learning to defer to learning to ask: the model decides when to request expert feedback and how to use it, with an optimal budgeted query rule and a consistent surrogate.
flag: (i) and (v): hand-off to a human expert with optimal rule and surrogate consistency; LtD is shown as a special case. The human does NOT take over the decision - feedback is an input and the model still predicts - so I did not add 'e' and the human-handoff cell is arguable; maintainer to decide. Expert is simulated (decision tree; sampled from physician consensus). Only realizable consistency is proved, not Bayes consistency. Gains reported as approximate percentages read from plots, no tables; on hard-label feedback LtA is about equal to LtD; LtA-Seq falls below LtD at high coverage.

title: Adversarial Robustness in One-Stage Learning-to-Defer
evidence: "We introduce the first framework for adversarial robustness in one-stage L2D, covering both classification and regression." (Abstract)
method: Defines untargeted and targeted attacks on jointly trained predictor-plus-deferral systems with J experts; proposes cost-sensitive adversarial surrogate losses and regularised ERM (RERM-C, RERM-R).
evaluation: Proves H-consistency (Thm 7) and (R,F)-consistency (Thm 15) bounds. CIFAR-10, DermaMNIST, Communities&Crime, COIL2000 vs Mao et al. under PGD; CIFAR untargeted acc 52.0 vs 27.5, targeted 68.7 vs 19.8; one A100; no latency.
contribution: Shows one-stage learning-to-defer systems can be attacked to corrupt both prediction and expert allocation, and gives adversarial surrogate losses with consistency bounds that restore robust accuracy.
flag: (iii) and (v), also (i): deferral among multiple experts with proved surrogate consistency bounds. Experts are simulated models, not humans, so no 'e'. Robustness costs clean accuracy (CIFAR 75.6 vs 82.7; Crime clean RMSE 12.09 vs 9.96 although text says 'comparable'). Text-vs-table mismatches: Crime targeted RMSE drop stated as 'nearly 37%' but table gives 37 points (about 65%); DermaMNIST deferral loss drop stated 38% vs about 55% from table. DermaMNIST and COIL results lack std. Deferral rates not reported.

title: Learning When Not to Learn: Risk-Sensitive Abstention in Bandits with Unbounded Rewards
evidence: "We introduce a formal model of learning with irreparable costs and no external mentor." (Sec. 1, Contributions)
method: Two-action contextual bandit (abstain=0 reward, or commit to a baseline policy with unbounded negative reward); algorithm abstains outside a trusted ball and in bins certified negative.
evaluation: Theory: Thm 5.2 proves sublinear regret O((L+sigma^2)T^((n+1)/(n+2))(ln T)^(n+1)+T*tail); Thms 4.1/4.2 impossibility. App. B synthetic 1-D illustration vs always-commit, always-abstain, Lipschitz UCB1; laptop; no latency.
contribution: Formalises mentor-free cautious learning as a bandit with an abstain action and irreparable unbounded costs, proving sublinear regret for an algorithm that abstains outside a trusted region.
flag: (ii) and (v): abstention is a per-round action in a sequential bandit, with proved regret bounds. Floor met only via theory: Appendix B experiments are reported as figures on synthetic 1-D data, no numeric table, and authors call them illustrations. No human, no safeguard hand-off (explicitly mentor-free). time-to-irreversibility cell is generous: costs are irreparable but no time-to-event is modelled; maintainer may drop it. Assumes known L, sigma, T and i.i.d. inputs.

title: Policy Learning with Abstention
evidence: "we introduce a framework for policy learning with abstention, in which policies that choose not to assign a treatment to some customers/patients receive a small, additive reward" (Abstract/Sec. 1)
method: Offline treatment-policy learning where a policy may abstain for a bonus p over a random guess; two-stage empirical welfare maximization abstains where near-optimal policies disagree.
evaluation: Theory: O(1/n) abstaining regret for p>0 (Thm 3.1, 3.4), margin and robustness results; synthetic safe-policy-improvement simulations vs HCPI and Safe EWM, Type-I error at or below 0.05, figures only.
contribution: Extends the reject option to offline treatment-policy learning, proving fast O(1/n) regret when abstention earns a small bonus and linking abstention to safe policy improvement and distributional robustness.
flag: (v), borderline: foundational bounds for an abstention option in policy learning (Thm 3.1 O(1/n) with known propensities; Prop 3.3 O(1/sqrt(n)) at p=0; Thm 3.4 doubly robust; Thm 4.1-4.2 margin; Prop 4.3 W1 shift reduces to abstention with p=alpha/2). It is offline, one-shot causal policy learning, not sequential and not a runtime interceptor; deferral to an expert or safe default is motivation only and no human or fallback is modelled, except that Algorithm 3 replaces abstentions by a baseline policy. If the maintainer reads (v) as limited to classification reject-option theory, this is E4. Experiments are synthetic only with no numeric table; gains over baselines are reported qualitatively (best for n>=1000, EWM better for n<=500). Proofs in appendices, not checked. Only first 100k of 105k characters read.

title: Budgeted Multiple-Expert Deferral
evidence: "Our budgeted deferral method matches the accuracy of the standard approach while reducing expert queries to below 40%" (Sec. 1)
method: Budgeted training of multi-expert deferral: IWAL-style importance-weighted active learning queries at most one expert cost per sample, pruning a version space; two-stage and single-stage variants.
evaluation: Ten tabular datasets, synthetic class-specialist experts, logistic hypotheses; vs full-query two-stage deferral (Mao et al. 2023); queries cut to about 35-40% (binary); generalization and label-complexity bounds proved; no latency.
contribution: Cuts the cost of training multi-expert deferral by actively querying at most one expert per example, with generalization and label-complexity guarantees and comparable accuracy at under 40% of the queries.
flag: (iii) and (v): multi-expert deferral with proved bounds (Thm 1 excess error at most 2*Delta; Thm 6 label complexity, O~(sqrt(T)) queries in the realizable case). The contribution is training-time query budgeting, not the deferral decision at inference; the router is applied at test time (system accuracy), hence runtime yes, but maintainer may judge this peripheral. Accuracy is shown in plots only, no exact values in text; the multi-class query figure is worded ambiguously ("consistently below 30%" - reduction or remaining fraction unclear). Experts are synthetic, small finite hypothesis sets (2048 or 4096 logistic models). One-shot classification, no sequential deployment, no human. Only first 100k of 123k characters read.

title: Evaluating Control Protocols for Untrusted AI Agents
evidence: "We introduce safety protocols in which the monitor focuses on the most consequential actions within a trajectory." (Sec. 1)
method: AI control protocols for an untrusted LLM agent: a trusted monitor scores each action; suspicious or critical actions are resampled or deferred to a trusted model before execution.
evaluation: SHADE-Arena, Claude 3.7 Sonnet untrusted, 3.6 trusted, 0.5% audit budget, red-team iteration; vs no-intervention protocol; safety 50% to 89-91%; usefulness 70-100%; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Red-teams runtime control protocols for untrusted LLM agents in SHADE-Arena; deferring on critical, hard-to-reverse actions keeps safety at 91-100% even against adaptive attackers, while resampling collapses to 17%.
flag: (iv), also (i) and (ii): a monitor that vetoes or hands off agent actions to a trusted model inside a trajectory. Numbers are inconsistent across the paper as extracted: abstract-level 89% safety for resample-for-incrimination vs 80% in Sec. 3.1; defer-on-critical 91% safety and 70% usefulness vs Table 2 0.96 and 0.44 at threshold 20 (thresholds differ) - maintainer should verify against the PDF, and the abstract itself, which I did not see verbatim. Table 1: monitor-simulating attacker cuts resample-then-defer safety to 0.17. Single agent, so criterion c rests on the LLM-agent safety-evaluation clause only. Human auditor is a budget assumption, not studied (no e). Time-to-irreversibility cell is loose: criticality is judged by the trusted model, no timing model. Only first 100k of about 165k characters read. No latency or overhead reported.

title: Consensus Sampling for Safer Generative AI
evidence: "The ratio is at most 1, and if no candidate is accepted after R rounds the algorithm abstains." (Sec. 4)
method: Consensus sampling: draws a candidate from one of k generative models, accepts with probability given by agreement of the s lowest model probabilities, abstains after R failed rounds.
evaluation: Theory (risk at most R times safe-model average; abstention bound); synthetic hypercube; Janus-Pro image steganography, 30 prompts, vs uniform mixture: unsafe 0.33 vs 0.00, abstention 0.37 to 0.00; no latency.
contribution: Aggregates k generative models so output risk is provably at most R times that of the safest s, abstaining when the models do not overlap enough.
flag: none of (i)-(v) cleanly: abstention is the fallback and the cost of a robust aggregation sampler, not the main contribution (the paper lists aggregation problem, overlap, and sampler with bounds). Borderline toward (iv)/(v): it is a runtime gate that withholds a generative output, and Thm C.4 proves Pareto-optimality of the robustness-abstention tradeoff; maintainer may prefer include or E4 (single-output, no sequential, multi-agent or handoff aspect). Experiments are tiny: 30 prompts, wide intervals (unsafe 0.00 [0.00, 0.12]), deterministic keyed adversary described as a sanity check; hypercube results are figure-only. Abstention output is a bare symbol, no human or fallback system. Read via a machine summary of the PDF.

title: Beyond Single-Agent Safety: A Taxonomy of Risks in LLM-to-LLM Interactions
evidence: "This paper represents the first attempt to formalize this framework conceptually" (Sec. 3), and the proposed metrics' validation "will follow" in future work; no experiment, system or formal result is reported.
method: Conceptual taxonomy of risks in LLM-to-LLM interaction, plus a deliberately abstract Institutional AI architecture of adaptive collective policy, peer evaluation and functional differentiation; no implementation.
evaluation: None: no experiments, baselines, ablations or quantitative results; metrics such as contagion velocity and goal drift are defined only, with validation deferred to future work.
contribution: Proposes a conceptual taxonomy of risks emerging in LLM-to-LLM interaction and an abstract Institutional AI architecture, defining metrics such as contagion velocity without any empirical validation.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no mechanism is built or tested. A position-and-taxonomy paper by the authors' own statement, so E3; the maintainer may prefer E2 since it is not strictly a survey of literature. Topically it sits inside Pillar 1 (multi-agent LLM hazards, supervisory agents that "suspend execution when thresholds are exceeded", human oversight described as nominal), so it may still be worth keeping as framing or a citation source even though it carries no evidence.

title: Analyzing Collision Rates in Large-Scale Mixed Traffic Control via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
evidence: Abstract: "collision rates are susceptible to traffic density, signal coordination level, and turning-control design"; collision rate is the only reported metric (Sec. III-D).
method: Multi-agent Rainbow DQN policy for robotic vehicles at unsignalized intersections within a 30 m radius, IDM elsewhere; collision penalty sits in the reward only, with no runtime override.
evaluation: SUMO 14-intersection network, 100 rollouts of 1000 s, 20-80% RV penetration, 5 signalization mixes, left-turn conversion; collision rate 0.118-3.39% vs an undefined baseline of 2.82-6.89%; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Simulation study quantifying how collision rates under large-scale multi-agent RL mixed-traffic control vary with vehicle count, signalized-unsignalized mix and left-turn conversion.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the analysed system is a MARL robotic-vehicle controller, but nothing is guarded: this is analysis only, with no detector and no runtime interception, so (c) rests entirely on collision rate being the primary outcome. Check: the "Baseline" column in Table I is never defined; text and tables disagree (about 8,000 vs 7,897 vehicles, 25% vs 20% RV, and the 0.595% minimum is 12U+2S in Table I, not the 4U+10S claimed in Sec. IV-B); no variance, CIs or significance tests; short single-author paper; a maintainer could reasonably call this exclude-E1 since no safety mechanism is proposed.

title: Bilevel Optimization for Covert Memory Tampering in Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Architectures (XAMT)
evidence: Sec. II.C: "Evasion of runtime adversarial detection (e.g., during MARL execution or RAG inference) is out-of-scope"; the attack poisons shared memory of CTDE MARL critics and RAG LLM agents (Sec. V).
method: XAMT: bilevel optimization that minimizes perturbation size while steering victim behaviour to an attacker target, poisoning MARL replay buffers and RAG knowledge bases in heterogeneous multi-agent systems.
evaluation: No experiments: Sec. VI gives protocols only (SMAC 2c_vs_64zg, SafeRAG/RAGuard) and Table I states target criteria (utility drop >=40% at rho<=1%, ASR >=90% at rho<=0.1%); Fig. 4-5 are what results are "expected to show".
contribution: Formulates covert memory tampering against heterogeneous multi-agent systems as a bilevel optimization problem spanning MARL replay buffers and RAG knowledge bases, with a protocol but no results.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes for the targets (CTDE MARL critics with QMIX/MAPPO/VDN, RAG LLM agents), but nothing is guarded, monitored or detected - this is a red-teaming attack formulation. Check: there is no experimental data anywhere; the abstract sub-percent poison-rate and effectiveness figures are success targets from Table I, not measurements, and I could not find them as results in the body; runtime defenses are explicitly out of scope and defenses are future work (Sec. VII.C); broken cross-reference "Section ??" and duplicated references suggest an unreviewed draft; the bilevel formulation carries no theorem, so the evaluation floor fails on both quantitative and formal results.

title: Transformer-based Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning for Separation Assurance in Structured and Unstructured Airspaces
evidence: Sec. VI-C: "our 1 and 2 encoder layer networks show near-zero NMACs"; the policy issues speed advisories for separation assurance and reports LoS and NMAC outcomes (Table IV).
method: Decentralized MARL (PPO) with a relative-polar state space and transformer encoder over neighbouring aircraft, emitting 5-knot speed advisories; conflict, LoS and NMAC penalties live in the reward, with no runtime filter.
evaluation: BlueSky 30 nm sector, 1000 episodes, unseen merge, four-way-intersection and procedural airspaces, 3 seeds; NMACs 0.002 (1-layer) and 0.001 (2-layer) vs 0.027 attention baseline and 0.037 (3-layer); LoS time 678 vs 1115; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Shows that a transformer encoder over relative polar states lets a decentralized MARL separation-assurance policy generalise to unseen structured and unstructured airspaces at near-zero NMAC rates.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes for the analysed system (MARL aircraft policies), but there is no guard - separation is pursued only through reward shaping and episode termination, so (a) fails and (c) alone carries the record. Check: the only backstop named is an external TCAS or ACAS-X that is never implemented or evaluated (Sec. III-A); LoS-time units are unspecified and its standard deviation (3556) dwarfs the mean; the 3-layer model is worse than the attention baseline on NMACs, so the depth trend is not monotone and the headline rests on one configuration; absolute NMAC counts per episode are tiny, with no conflict rate reported; no hardware or inference-time figures; the maintainer may read this as a coordination policy rather than a safety mechanism and prefer exclude-E1.

title: Learning-to-Defer in Non-Stationary Time Series via Switching State-Space Models
evidence: Sec. 4.4 (Internal Prediction and Greedy Deferral): the greedy router selects, each round, the action (internal forecast or an available expert) with the smallest predicted cost.
method: L2D-SLDS: switching linear dynamical system with shared, per-expert and regime latents, filtered online; greedy router defers each round to the internal forecast or a cheapest-predicted-cost expert.
evaluation: Delhi, Jena, Melbourne time series, four ridge experts, bandit feedback; vs eight bandit routers (LinUCB variants, TS, NeuralUCB); combined cost e.g. Jena 2.502 vs 2.768; regret bounds proved; no latency.
contribution: Online learning to defer for non-stationary time series: a switching state-space model routes each forecast to itself or a fee-charging expert, with sublinear regret and no exploration parameter.
flag: (ii) and (iii): sequential deferral among multiple experts with partial feedback; also theory (Thm 2-3, Cor. 4: O(sqrt(T)) regret under stated accuracy and information conditions). Experts are ridge regressors, no human. Only first 100k of about 190k characters read (appendix with hardware, G.13, not read); body says timings are similar to baselines but gives no figure seen. Table 1 was partly garbled in extraction: check column assignment (Delhi 0.954, Jena 2.502, Melbourne 2.321 for L2D-SLDS) and the Melbourne greedy ablation value 2.361 which conflicts with 2.321. Zero SDs over three seeds look odd. Gains on Delhi and Melbourne are small (about 1-3%). In Jena and Melbourne access is free so an expert is consulted every round: little actual abstention there. Not safety-critical; no time-to-irreversibility.

title: OMNI-LEAK: Orchestrator Multi-Agent Network Induced Data Leakage
evidence: Sec. 5.3: "suggesting that safety in single-agent settings isn't indicative of multi-agent settings (and vice-versa)"; one injection drives the SQL agent and orchestrator to email out private SSNs (Sec. 4.1).
method: OMNI-LEAK: a single indirect prompt injection planted in public data compromises several agents of an orchestrator-pattern LLM system and exfiltrates private records despite per-agent data access control.
evaluation: 3000 runs per model across 5 frontier LLMs, 10 attacks in explicit and implicit forms, 3 database sizes, 4 architectures (PS, OS, ON, OA); robust benign accuracy 61.6-95.4%, expected queries to a successful leak 4 to infinity, benign accuracy 92-100%; no latency or hardware.
contribution: Benchmarks orchestrator-pattern LLM multi-agent systems and shows a single indirect prompt injection can chain across agents to leak private data despite per-agent access control.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the evaluated systems are frontier-LLM agent orchestrators - but nothing is guarded: no monitor, gate or filter is implemented, and mitigations appear only as recommendations in the Impact Statement, so (a) fails and (c) carries the record. Check: the comparator is the single-agent Pure SQL setup plus architecture variants, so the baseline speaks to the multi-agent effect, not to any defense; outcomes are robust accuracy and an expected-queries figure rather than a leakage or detection rate; claude-sonnet-4 withstood every attack, which bounds generality; two models were dropped for failing benign queries.

title: When More Experts Hurt: Underfitting in Multi-Expert Learning to Defer
evidence: "a surrogate-based method that dynamically selects experts in a data-dependent manner" (Sec. 1, Contributions)
method: PiCCE surrogate loss for multi-expert learning to defer: picks the most confident expert among those matching the label, avoiding the expert-aggregation term that underfits the classifier.
evaluation: CIFAR-100 and ImageNet subsets with 4-20 synthetic experts; MiceBone, Chaoyang with human annotators; vs multi-expert CE and OvA; system error, coverage; consistency proved; H200 GPUs, no latency.
contribution: Shows multi-expert learning-to-defer surrogates underfit as experts are added and proposes PiCCE, a consistent loss that keeps system error flat from 4 to 20 experts.
flag: (iii) and (v): multi-expert deferral with proved continuity (Thm 2) and system consistency (Thm 6, under Condition 1, sufficient not necessary). ImageNet OvA 20 experts: error 66.56 vanilla vs 42.25 PiCCE; MiceBone 8 experts CE 16.72 vs 13.35. One-shot image classification, zero deferral cost, no sequential or latency aspect. Human experts are static annotation labels, handoff itself not studied (so no e; human handoff cell is generous, drop if strict). Dog-expert accuracy stated as 85% in Fig. 1 caption and 88% in appendix. Classifier-accuracy results are plots only. Read via a machine summary of the PDF, table values not checked digit by digit.

title: From Dialogue to Execution: Mixture-of-Agents Assisted Interactive Planning for Behavior Tree-Based Long-Horizon Robot Execution
evidence: Sec. III-A (Formulation): 'the human is the terminal element, so R_K is always resolved however conservative the agents are'; Sec. III-B: 'the enclosing Selector falls back to InformStaffProblem once all attempts fail'.
method: LLM behavior-tree planner raises clarification questions; a cascade of proxy expert agents answers what its prerequisites support and abstains on the rest, which pass to the human; tree hands off to staff after failed retries.
evaluation: Cocktail planning (3 generations with and without cascade) and ALOHA smoothie task; proxies answer about 10 of 37 questions (27%), 2 of 5 on robot; tree-edit distance 0.812 vs 0.800; per-action success 0-10 of 10; no latency.
contribution: Interactive behavior-tree planning in which a cascade of proxy expert agents answers clarification questions and abstains to the human on the rest, removing about 27% of human responses.
flag: (i), nominally (iii): weak, borderline include. Deferral is abstention-based delegation of clarification QUESTIONS at planning time, not deferral of an executed action; the runtime staff handoff is a stock behavior-tree fallback and is not evaluated. Evaluation is thin: 3 generations per condition, plan-quality gap 0.012 is inside the standard deviations, no check that proxy answers are correct, no end-to-end success rate from real runs (0.34 is an estimate), no safety metric. Only baseline is the same planner without the cascade. exclude-E2 or exclude-E1 is defensible.

title: The Alignment Flywheel: A Governance-Centric Hybrid MAS for Architecture-Agnostic Safety
evidence: Abstract: "An Enforcement layer applies explicit risk policy at runtime."; Sec. 5.4: "For high-risk actions, the fallback is fail-closed: block execution and create a priority audit case."
method: Separates a Proposer from a governed Safety Oracle; an Enforcement layer returns allow, block, revise or escalate per candidate trajectory under a risk policy, while a governance MAS red-teams, patches and version-releases the Oracle with human approval.
evaluation: Two executability demos, no benchmark: offline 20^3 grid learned reward surface where adaptive patching clears 4927 flaw cells in 12 iterations and preserves 783 of 783 basin cells while a fixed-bandwidth baseline has not converged after 25+ iterations; Patient Portal 15 synthetic cases with escalation rate 60% then 40% then 0% over stacks v0-v2; no latency, throughput or hardware.
contribution: Proposes a governance-centric hybrid multi-agent architecture separating proposal from a governed safety oracle and a runtime enforcement layer, so new failures are fixed by local oracle patches instead of retraining.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a Proposer plus a learned IIRL-style spatial Oracle and a clinical GenAI proxy, gated at execution time by allow, block, revise or escalate, with humans as exception handlers, batch approvers and release approvers (App. E, Tables 12-13), so (a) and (e) both hold. Check: the evaluation is a demonstration rather than a benchmark - 15 to 18 synthetic cases, a heuristic proxy Oracle and a pass-through Proposer - with no false-halt, violation, throughput, latency or hardware figures despite the runtime claim, so the evaluation floor is met only by the escalation-rate progression across stack versions and the spatial fixed-bandwidth baseline, and exclude-E2 is defensible; internal inconsistencies: iterations to zero flaws are 16 in Table 18 but 12 in Table 19 and the text, Table 19 kernel counts sum to 739 not 834, and Table 18 caps patches at 60 per iteration while Table 19 shows 90; I did not credit cross-domain evaluation because the enforcement gate itself is exercised only in the clinical demo, the spatial demo being offline patching with no Proposer - worth a second look.

title: Talk Freely, Execute Strictly: Schema-Gated Agentic AI for Flexible and Reproducible Scientific Workflows
evidence: Sec. 5.2 Fig. 3 caption: 'The LLM may converse freely, but cannot execute - execution authority resides entirely in schema validation.'
method: Interview study (18 experts, 10 stakeholders) plus LLM-scored review of 20 systems, proposing schema-gated orchestration where a machine-checkable schema must validate a complete action before anything runs.
evaluation: No evaluation of the gate: no baseline, ablation, latency or hazard rate; the figures cover interview coding (1,135 codings, 2,468 paragraphs) and LLM-scorer reliability (Krippendorff alpha ED 0.80, CF 0.98); Sec. 6.5 says the testbed is under development.
contribution: Argues conversational freedom and deterministic execution can be reconciled by making a machine-checkable schema the mandatory execution boundary, with a 20-system review finding no system achieves both.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an LLM scientific-workflow orchestrator. Architecture proposal only: prototypes are mentioned in the contributions but no result from them is reported, so the v1.6 evaluation floor fails (no safety metric, no baseline or ablation on the gate itself). Check whether exclude-E3 fits better, since Sec. 3 is a landscape review of 20 systems. Criterion (e) is borderline and I did not credit it: Sec. 5.2 has user approval before dispatch ('Execution is dispatched only once the user is satisfied') but there is no takeover or situation-awareness study. The determinism and flexibility scores were produced by three LLM families with no human panel, which the authors propose as a substitute for expert raters.

title: Adaptive Collaboration with Humans: Metacognitive Policy Optimization for Multi-Agent LLMs with Continual Learning
evidence: Abstract: agents 'learn a metacognitive policy that governs when to solve problems autonomously and when to defer to a human expert'.
method: HILA: each LLM agent picks EVAL, CREATE or DEFER per round in a Meta-MDP; deferral policy trained with GRPO under a deferral cost; expert answers become fine-tuning data (DLPO).
evaluation: GSM8K, AMC, AIME, HumanEval, MMLU vs 10 single and multi-agent baselines; GSM8K 89.86 vs 72.76 vanilla; DEFER rate 29% to 17% after DLPO; 20-PhD real-expert study; token costs only, no hardware or latency.
contribution: Multi-agent LLM framework that learns by reinforcement when an agent should defer to a human expert and then fine-tunes on the expert's answers, raising accuracy while lowering the deferral rate.
flag: (i) and (ii): deferral is a learned action over collaboration rounds. Main-experiment 'human' is a stronger LLM proxy (GPT-4o-mini or GPT-4o), so much of the gain may be distillation from a better model; real humans (20 PhD students) appear only in an appendix study. No safety metric - outcome is task accuracy and DEFER rate. GRPO alone barely moves accuracy (GSM8K 88.15 to 88.38; AMC drops 33.33 to 32.50). Text claims 3.7-15.4 point gains over the strongest baseline, not clearly matched by Table 1. Intro says deferral is refined online, Appendix C.1 describes offline grouped training. C_defer sensitivity (Fig. 7) not read.

title: Drift-to-Action Controllers: Budgeted Interventions with Online Risk Certificates
evidence: Sec. 4.4 (Safety Gating and Escalation): 'Ut(delta) > tau => activate fallback and schedule escalation'; the action set (Table 2) includes A6 abstain/handoff to a fallback such as human review.
method: Drift2Act: belief over drift types from unlabeled monitors; anytime-valid risk upper bound from uniformly sampled delayed labels gates a controller choosing recalibrate, adapt, query, retrain, rollback or abstain/handoff.
evaluation: Streaming Camelyon17, DomainNet, synthetic CIFAR drift vs alarm-only, always-adapt, scheduled retrain, selective-only, no-certificate controller; violations 0/1/0 vs 7/11/8 without certificate; false-intervention 0.09-0.13; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Streaming drift controller whose anytime-valid risk certificate gates normal operation and triggers abstention, handoff, rollback or retraining under a budget, cutting risk violations to near zero at moderate cost.
flag: (ii) and (iv): borderline on the MAIN-contribution test. Abstain/handoff is one of seven actions and the paper's own contribution list is certificate, controller and protocol; the gate that withholds prediction when the bound exceeds tau is central, but exclude-E1 is defensible. Workshop paper (CAO at ICLR 2026). Handoff target is a nominal fallback, no human studied. Theorems A.2-A.4 (anytime validity, selective risk) stated; proofs in appendix partly beyond the 100k of 117k characters read. Table 6 has undefined parenthesised values; hardware not found in the part read.

title: Autonomous Edge-Deployed AI Agents for Electric Vehicle Charging Infrastructure Management
evidence: Sec. 9.2.2: 'Deterministic safety rules checked before any action execution, independent of AI reasoning'; Sec. 5.3: 'autonomous execution prohibited regardless of C(a|d)'.
method: Three-tier edge architecture placing domain-tuned LLM agents (14B on site, 0.5B in firmware) behind deterministic pre-execution safety rules, calibrated confidence gating, rate limits, rollback and human escalation bands.
evaluation: 18,000 labelled incidents, controlled testbed; baselines rule-based, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5, non-tuned 14B; 78.0% autonomous vs 28.4-31.2%, accuracy 87.6% vs 72.3-74.8%, FP 3.8%, FN 5.2%, ECE 0.023; five ablations (no CCAR calibration drops autonomy to 42.8%); Ryzen AI Max+ 395 NPU, P50 28 ms, P99 78 ms, firmware 11 ms, pipeline P50 67 ms.
contribution: Edge-deployed LLM agents for EV charging networks sit behind a deterministic pre-execution safety gate and confidence-banded human escalation, reporting 78% autonomous incident resolution at 28 ms median edge latency.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM agents (14B edge, 0.5B firmware), gated by deterministic rules plus a calibrated confidence score. Sole-author vendor paper: Sec. 9.5 states 'All evaluations were conducted by the author, who is also the system architect', and Sec. 8 warns the numbers 'do not represent measurements from production field deployments'; the headline 78% and 4-8 h MTTR are explicitly marked pending field validation. The abstract cites 28-48 ms P50 TTFT, which is not fully consistent with Table 24. Cloud baselines were zero-shot and not RAG-augmented, so the margin is likely overstated. Criterion (c) fails the primacy test: about 20 agents under hierarchical orchestration, but multi-agent routing appears only as an ablation (-1.8 accuracy points) and no multi-agent hazard or collision rate is reported.

title: CHiL(L)Grader: Calibrated Human-in-the-Loop Short-Answer Grading
evidence: Abstract: the system 'automates only high-confidence predictions while routing uncertain cases to human graders'.
method: LoRA-tuned Qwen-2.5-7B grader with temperature-scaled confidence; grades below threshold tau go to a human; corrections feed replay-buffer fine-tuning and recalibration over repeated cycles.
evaluation: DAMI, SciEntsBank, EngSAF with simulated human corrections; ECE 0.270 to 0.094 on DAMI; accepted QWK 0.882 vs rejected 0.535 at 35.1% coverage; tau and replay ablations; 2x RTX A5500, no inference latency.
contribution: Calibrated short-answer grader that auto-accepts confident grades and routes the rest to human graders, whose corrections drive continual fine-tuning; accepted-set QWK reaches 0.882 at 35% coverage on DAMI.
flag: (i), weakly (ii): borderline. Mechanically a confidence-threshold reject option applied to one domain, so exclude-E4 is defensible; I lean include only because human routing plus the correction loop is the stated contribution. Humans are simulated from gold labels, no real grader or handoff study, so 'e' is generous. No routing baseline (random or uncalibrated deferral); evidence is accepted vs rejected QWK and a tau ablation. Headline 0.882 is on the accepted 35% only, not comparable to full-test baselines (0.669-0.677). Paper gives two different val-test gaps (-0.157 and -0.121).

title: Consistent Learning-to-Defer with Expert-Conditional Advice
evidence: Abstract: 'reference conditional classification, which jointly learns a fixed expert's error probability'; Lemma 2 gives the Bayes-optimal deferral-advice policy (source minimising each expert's expected cost, then cheapest expert).
method: Learning to defer where the router picks an expert and a paid advice source before seeing the advice; reference-conditional surrogate replaces inconsistent product surrogates; full and limited-observation training.
evaluation: Theory: Bayes rule (Lemma 2), product-surrogate inconsistency (Thm 3), consistency bound (Thm 5), all proved. Experiments on FEVER and IEEE-CIS fraud, 3 model experts, vs standard L2D and augmented surrogate; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Extends learning to defer to joint choice of expert and paid advice source, proves product surrogates inconsistent and gives a consistent reference-conditional surrogate with a regret bound.
flag: (v) and (iii): foundational L2D theory with multiple experts. Title matches. Experts are all models (LLMs, DeBERTa, tabular classifiers), no human. Empirical gains are small (FEVER 0.576 vs 0.584; fraud 0.253 vs 0.258 decision loss) and the augmented baseline wins at the two smallest FEVER budgets. Only the first 100k of 146k characters read; appendix proofs not checked. Same arXiv paper as doi:10.48550/arxiv.2603.14324 - deduplicate.

title: From Logic Monopoly to Social Contract: Separation of Power and the Institutional Foundations for Autonomous Agent Economies
evidence: Sec. 2.1: constitutional compliance hooks 'grant the Adjudication Layer unconditional override authority', with Guardian Contract circuit breakers and a Deterministic Freeze (Sec. 1.6.5).
method: Position and architecture paper proposing a constitutional separation of powers for autonomous LLM agent economies: legislation, execution, adjudication and trust layers with gate contracts, circuit breakers and a human committee.
evaluation: None of the authors' own: no experiment, baseline, ablation, latency figure or theorem with proof; Sec. 2.6 says the matrices show internal coherence not external validation and defers that to the roadmap (Sec. 7); the reference implementation is 'in preparation'.
contribution: Proposes institutional separation of powers - legislation, execution, adjudication, trust - as the governance substrate for autonomous LLM agent economies, with contract-level gates and circuit breakers, but no implementation.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM agent economies, but every gate is design only and runtime_interceptor is recorded no for that reason; Sec. 1.3 concedes fatigue-aware circuit breakers are 'a mechanism that the current NEF architecture identifies as necessary but does not yet fully deliver'. A preprint disclaimer says it has not been peer reviewed. Every quantitative figure is borrowed from cited work (for example 84.30% attack success from ASB, 67.3% deception escalation from La Serenissima), so the evaluation floor fails. Consider exclude-E3 instead: much of the body is a literature and incident review with 16 case studies drawn from others. I read offsets 0-200k of 688k characters, so a late section could in principle hold results, although Sec. 2.6 says validation is future work.

title: Fatigue-Aware Learning to Defer via Constrained Optimisation
evidence: Sec. 3-4: deferral is a CMDP with state (x_t, rho_t) where rho_t is cumulative human workload, increasing only when the human handles a case; human error rate is 1 - w(rho_t).
method: FALCON: sequential learning to defer as a constrained MDP trained with PPO-Lagrangian; workload-embedded S5 sequence policy decides AI or human per sample under a simulated fatigue curve.
evaluation: Cifar100, Chaoyang, MiceBone, Flickr10K streams, simulated fatigued experts; vs OneStage, TwoStage, L2D-Pop, EA-L2D; AUACC 74.01 vs 71.01 (Cifar100), 72.36 vs 67.36 rapid fatigue; RTX A6000; timing figures only.
contribution: Casts learning to defer as a constrained sequential decision problem in which each hand-off raises the human's workload and fatigue, and learns a policy that beats static deferral baselines across coverage levels.
flag: (ii) sequential deferral over an episode and (i) deferral to a human. e added because the human's state after hand-off (workload, fatigue) is modelled and studied, but the human is entirely simulated by a parametric fatigue curve chosen by the authors; no real human study (acknowledged). No theorems. Gains outside Cifar100 are small (Chaoyang 84.13 vs 83.24, Flickr10K 64.40 vs 63.26). CMDP ablation (OneStage-L2D+S5) and the mammography-curve check appear only in figures, no numbers. Notational errors in Eqs. 3, 5, 8; AI classifier accuracies not clearly mapped to datasets. No recovery within an episode; no time pressure or irreversibility modelled.

title: Human Values Matter: Investigating How Misalignment Shapes Collective Behaviors in LLM Agent Communities
evidence: Sec. 4.2: 'positive slopes (e.g., BE) indicate improved community stability, while negative ones (e.g., TR) imply system-level risks', measured over communities of 25 LLM agent residents.
method: CIVA, a resource-limited multi-agent LLM community simulation (25 residents, 3 factories, GPT-4o backbone, 50-100 steps) with in-context control of Schwartz values, measuring collapse, fragility and emergent behaviours.
evaluation: 312 runs, about 1.32B tokens; baselines are a no-control condition and rho=0%, plus per-value with-or-without ablations and a prevalence sweep; fold-bifurcation distance 19.0 baseline vs 5.4 without benevolence and 21.4 without tradition; tipping near rho=25%; power-betrayal correlation r=0.87; cross-backbone checks on Qwen2.5-32B and mistral-medium.
contribution: Shows that the mix of human values held by LLM agents decides whether a simulated agent community stays resilient or collapses, identifying benevolence and power as structurally critical values.
flag: learned or AI system analysed: yes - GPT-4o agent communities. There is no runtime mechanism of any kind, so this is hazard-characterisation evidence only and should not be credited with preventing anything. Criterion (c) primacy is borderline: the headline question is how values shape collective dynamics in general, with collapse and system failure modes as the measured outcomes. The authors concede their metrics are 'descriptive signals of interaction patterns relative to a baseline' (Limitations), behaviour labels come from a GPT-5 annotator, and value-control effectiveness is only about 0.38-0.49 on PVQ and ValueBench. Per-condition nAUP values appear only in figures, so I could not read them from the text. I read offsets 0-100k of 134k characters.

title: ReDAct: Uncertainty-Aware Deferral for LLM Agents
evidence: Sec. 3: if the small model's action-level uncertainty exceeds a threshold the large model produces the action; "If cost were not a concern, a rational actor would use the large model at every step."
method: ReDAct: per-step deferral inside a ReAct agent; token-probability uncertainty (perplexity, entropy, sequence probability) of the small model's action triggers a call to a larger LLM.
evaluation: ALFWorld, MiniGrid DoorKey; vs small-only, large-only, random deferral; ALFWorld success 0.808 vs 0.683 base, 0.770 random, 0.783 GPT-5.2 alone; cost 16.25 vs 45.21 USD; no latency.
contribution: Lets a small LLM agent hand individual steps to a larger model when its action uncertainty is high, matching the large model's task success on ALFWorld with about 15% of steps deferred.
flag: (ii) holds in form (per-step deferral over an agent trajectory) but the target is a larger model and the stated purpose is cost, which the scope ruling sends to exclude-E1; borderline, maintainer may prefer include since error compounding and reliability are also motivated. No human, no safety metric: outcome is task success rate, not violation or hazard rate. Margin over random deferral is small (0.808 vs 0.770 on ALFWorld, 0.950 vs 0.930 on MiniGrid) and random beats some UQ variants; Llama-4-Maverick MiniGrid results are poor (0.42 best). Realised call rate (3.3-3.7 per episode) drifts below the target of 5. Step correctness labels come from a GPT-5.2 judge.

title: Semantic Intent Fragmentation: A Single-Shot Compositional Attack on Multi-Agent AI Pipelines
evidence: Sec. 7: 'A single CIV call at the plan-generation gap, preceded by deterministic IFC taint (R1-R4), is both necessary and sufficient'; the verifier runs after plan generation and before any agent is dispatched.
method: Semantic Intent Fragmentation attack: one benign-looking request is decomposed so each subtask passes per-subtask classifiers while the composed plan violates policy; the defence is a plan-level LLM verifier plus deterministic taint tracking.
evaluation: 16 enterprise scenarios (finance, InfoSec, HR) on a simulated orchestrator pipeline with GPT-20B; SIF-ASR 71% (10 of 14) at temperature 0.0 and 0.7; six guardrail baselines bypassed (AlignmentCheck pass 1.00, WildGuard AUC about 0.5, Prompt-Guard flags 8 of 8 benign); CIV 10 of 14 UNSAFE at 0% FPR, taint plus CIV detects 10 of 10 at 0% FPR; ablations on phrasing (44% hardcoded) and a Llama-8B orchestrator (36%); no latency or hardware reported.
contribution: Shows per-subtask guardrails miss compositional attacks on LLM orchestrator pipelines, and that a plan-level verifier plus deterministic information-flow taint catches every confirmed attack before dispatch at zero false positives.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an LLM orchestrator pipeline and its downstream agents. Very small sample: 14 generated scenarios with one request each, so the 71% ASR and the 0% false-positive rate rest on 14 and 8 cases; detection is judged by LLMs on the authors' own attacks, which risks circularity. Agents are simulated rather than live LangGraph, AutoGen or CrewAI, as the authors admit, and keyword-based taint may miss exfiltration paths. No latency or hardware figure, so criterion (d) does not hold even though the gate sits on the dispatch path. Criterion (e) not credited: flagging borderline verdicts for human review is a design recommendation in Sec. 7 with no study behind it.

title: Beyond Augmented-Action Surrogates for Multi-Expert Learning-to-Defer
evidence: Sec. 5 (Eq. 10): at test time the router defers to the best expert when max_j u_j(x) > max_k p_k(x); Theorem 10 gives the consistency bound.
method: Decoupled surrogate for multi-expert learning to defer: softmax classifier head plus one independent sigmoid head per expert, replacing augmented-action surrogates sharing one softmax.
evaluation: Proves Bayes consistency and an excess-risk bound independent of expert count; experiments on synthetic suites, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-10H, Covertype vs additive CE, PiCCE, A-SM, Mao25, OvA; CIFAR-10 system accuracy .919 vs .860 (J=16).
contribution: Shows that shared-softmax surrogates for multi-expert deferral degrade as the expert pool grows, and proposes a decoupled surrogate with a consistency bound whose constant does not grow with the number of experts.
flag: (v) foundational L2D theory and (iii) multiple experts. Proved: Lemma 2 (Bayes rule), Props 4-7, 9, 14 (failure modes of prior surrogates, gradient and Hessian structure), Theorem 10 (bound with constant max{2sqrt2, sqrt(2J/lambda)}), Corollary 12 (Bayes consistency). Read only the first 100k of about 236k characters: proofs in the appendix were not checked. Threshold stated as >1/4 in the introduction and >=1/4 in Sec. 5.3. Decoupled classifier accuracy is slightly below the standalone classifier on CIFAR-10 (.909 vs .910), so the claim of improving on the standalone classifier holds for system accuracy only. CIFAR-10H Table 3 and the OvA and additive-CE rows of Table 2 were garbled. Hardware not found.

title: EmbodiedGovBench: A Benchmark for Governance, Recovery, and Upgrade Safety in Embodied Agent Systems
evidence: Section 8.4: 'The same sequential planner augmented with a governance filter'; Protocol F measures mid-task human override, ODR 1.000 for System 2 versus 0.000 for the ungoverned planners.
method: Benchmark of seven governance dimensions and six protocol families for embodied GPT-4o agents; scores capability authorization, drift, recovery, upgrade and human-override behaviour via a governance judge.
evaluation: AI2-THOR ProcTHOR, 125 episodes, 4 systems (SayCan-style, task-only, +governance filter, Code-as-Policies-style); UIR 0.341->0.000, TSVR 0.960->0.000, GovScore 0.5770->0.9437, task success 0.896->0.696; A100.
contribution: A governance benchmark for embodied LLM agents scoring runtime capability vetoes, drift detection, recovery, upgrade safety and human override, exposing a governance versus task-success trade-off.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - GPT-4o embodied planners are the guarded systems. Check (c): the fleet and multi-agent track is defined but untested and every run is single-robot, so no multi-agent safety property is measured. Protocol F humans are simulated, so (e) is a measured override protocol, not a human study. Baselines System 0 and System 3 are simulated, not re-implementations (Section 8.8); there is no module ablation, only a three-profile weight sensitivity analysis (Table 12), whose recovery-heavy row is garbled. Paper calls all differences highly significant but reports no p-values, only a Bonferroni threshold of 0.0083. Section 8.4 text conflicts with its own tables (System 3 bypass about 30 percent vs BBC 0.920; drift detection 40 percent vs DDR 0.880) and gives two different system rankings. ORL units are unstated. The fetch covered the first 100000 of 114472 characters, so late appendix material is unchecked.

title: Semantic Consensus: Process-Aware Conflict Detection and Resolution for Enterprise Multi-Agent LLM Systems
evidence: Sec. 4: "conflicts are resolved before actions are committed"; Sec. 5.1 adapter intercepts outgoing actions and permits or modifies the action based on the resolution outcome
method: Process-aware middleware (SCF) between orchestrator and LLM agent execution: semantic intent graph, conflict detection engine, three-tier consensus resolution protocol, drift monitor, governance integration layer.
evaluation: 600 simulated runs, 4 enterprise scenarios, 3 framework profiles; baselines ungoverned, schema-only, judge-agent plus SCF-NoPCL ablation; completion 100% vs 25.1%; detection precision 27.9%, recall 65.2%; no latency reported.
contribution: Middleware that detects contradictory, contention and causal-order conflicts between enterprise LLM agents and resolves or queues them before actions commit, lifting workflow completion to 100% in simulation.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (enterprise multi-agent LLM systems, but simulated rather than live). Biggest doubt and the likeliest overturn: Sec. 7.3 admits "our experimental framework simulates multi-agent coordination patterns rather than running actual AutoGen, CrewAI, and LangGraph agents with live LLM inference", and the judge-agent baseline was "calibrated" to 66% recall and 93% precision from a cited paper rather than measured here, so the 100% vs 25.1% headline is synthetic self-play - a maintainer may well prefer exclude-E2. Detection precision is only 27.9% (many false blocks, author-acknowledged as deliberately conservative) yet completion is 100% in every scenario and framework, which is too clean to be informative. (c) credited because conflict detection among LLM agents is the primary claim and the primary measured outcome, but the hazard is workflow conflict, not physical harm. (e) NOT credited: escalation to a human operator or governance dashboard is in the design (Sec. 4.4) but never measured and the paper does not say whether an escalated action is held pending a human. No latency, overhead, drift threshold or SAS weights are reported anywhere, so no (d) and no latency cell.

title: Knowing When to Quit: A Principled Framework for Dynamic Abstention in LLM Reasoning
evidence: Sec. 3: on abstention "generation halts immediately, and a fallback mechanism, i.e. deferral or refusal, is triggered"; considered at each token position.
method: Dynamic mid-generation abstention as a terminal action in a KL-regularised sparse-reward MDP; abstain when a probe-estimated value of the current prefix falls below the abstention reward.
evaluation: Qwen2.5-Math-7B, Phi-3-mini on GSM8K, OlympiadBench, RealToxicityPrompts; vs input-only and fixed-position probes, self-assessment, LoRA; OlympiadBench selective accuracy 0.91 vs 0.75 at 90% abstention; token savings 63-95%; no latency.
contribution: Formulates LLM abstention as a stopping action taken token by token, proves value-thresholding dominates input-only and fixed-position abstention, and shows a small hidden-state probe realises the gain on reasoning benchmarks.
flag: (ii) sequential abstention over a generation trajectory, with (v)-style theory (Lemma 4.1, Props 4.2, 4.4, 4.7, 4.9: dominance, optimality at beta=0, Lipschitz improvement bound). Caveats: dominance and optimality assume an oracle value function; the fallback (human or larger model) is never implemented or evaluated, only selective accuracy and assumed abstention reward; single LLM, token-level, not an acting agent, so maintainer may read it as LLM abstention on single questions (E4). GPU type and inference overhead of the probe not reported; cross-dataset transfer has no numbers. Abstract numbers were not individually cross-checked.

title: People-Centred Medical Image Analysis via Fairness-Aware Human-AI Cooperation
evidence: Sec. 3.3: at test time the gate's rounded output decides whether the clinician's label is used; the model "needs to commit to a binary decision".
method: PecMan: gating model routes each image to subgroup-specific AI heads or the clinician under a coverage budget; a consolidator merges weighted predictions; FIS fairness loss.
evaluation: HAM10000, CMMD, CheXpert, MIMIC-CXR, simulated experts; vs ERM, DCE, Fair L2D, LECODU, FairDi; AUACC 97.63 vs 95.92 (HAM10000), 93.01 vs 91.43 (MIMIC-CXR); RTX A6000; no latency numbers.
contribution: A fairness-aware learning-to-defer and learning-to-complement framework that routes medical images between subgroup-specialised models and a clinician, improving accuracy-coverage and equity-coverage curves over L2D and fairness baselines with simulated experts.
flag: (i) deferral to a human expert, but borderline on MAIN contribution: paper sells a unified fairness plus L2D/L2C framework and a benchmark, deferral is one of several components; maintainer may prefer exclude-E4 (one-shot, per-image). Experts are simulated label noise (95-98% accuracy), no real readers. Claimed selection-regret and fairness-coverage theory not examined in detail. PecMan and LECODU CheXpert AUACC values were garbled in the text I read (PecMan CheXpert AUESACC 93.54). L2D-FairDi ablation only as curves (Fig. 7). Timing only in Figs. 8-9.

title: Learning When to Remember: Risk-Sensitive Contextual Bandits for Abstention-Aware Memory Retrieval in LLM-Based Coding Agents
evidence: "First, we define coding-agent issue-memory reuse as an abstention-aware, risk-sensitive contextual-bandit problem" (Sec. 1, Introduction)
method: RSCB-MC: contextual bandit over 7 actions (inject variants, no_memory, abstain, ask_feedback) on 16 features, risk-regularised score plus a safety override, gating retrieved memory before it enters the agent context.
evaluation: Offline replay (40 events x 2 seeds) and 32 hard negatives vs static retrieval, UCB1, Thompson, LinUCB: false-positive injection 0.0% vs 75.0% static, success 62.5% vs 50.0%; p95 decision 331 microseconds; hardware unstated.
contribution: A risk-sensitive contextual bandit that gates retrieved debugging memory for coding agents, abstaining when reuse looks unsafe and removing false-positive injections in small-scale offline replay.
flag: (ii) and (iv): online gate on the agent hot path that can withhold memory injection. Doubts are substantial: evaluation is smoke-scale (24 queries, 32 hard negatives, 80 replay events) with deterministic proxy labels, no live LLM agent and no causal online study; the planned 400/1600/1000 benchmark was not run. On the 56-case abstention benchmark the method answered 0.0% (57.1% correct abstain, 42.9% wrong abstain), i.e. it abstains on everything there, and adding abstention cut paraphrase Recall@1 from 80.2% to 51.0%. Bandit is single-step, not trajectory-level, so (ii) is weak; the harm prevented is context contamination, not a safety-critical action, so (iv) is also arguable - E4 is defensible. ask_feedback (human) action exists but is never evaluated, so no 'e'. Latency is in-process Python only (mean 268, p95 331 microseconds), no CPU spec; latency cell credited only because latency is a state feature and is measured.

title: Safe Bilevel Delegation (SBD): A Formal Framework for Runtime Delegation Safety in Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: Section 5.3: 'projection is then a simple clipping operation: alpha <- min(alpha, alpha_max(s))', capping delegated authority at runtime in high-risk states.
method: Bilevel framework: an outer meta-weight network sets a state-dependent safety weight, an inner loop learns a delegation policy under P(safe) >= 1 - delta, with runtime clipping of delegation degree.
evaluation: None executed; 'Experimental results are not yet included'. Planned MIMIC-III, S&P 500, ASSISTments against Fixed-alpha, CPO, MARL-vanilla, MaAS and four ablations; 0.8 s per outer step on an A100.
contribution: A bilevel formulation of runtime delegation safety in hierarchical multi-agent systems, with monotonicity and accountability results and a runtime cap on delegated authority, but no experiments.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - learned MLP meta-weight and delegation policies (3 and 4 layers, width 256); no LLM anywhere despite LLM-agent motivation. E2 because the paper itself states no experimental results are reported in this version, so there is no quantitative safety metric and no baseline comparison. This is the batch record most likely to be overturned: the evaluation floor admits a proved guarantee, and the paper does prove Theorem 4.4 (safety monotonicity), Theorem 4.6 (linear inner convergence) and Proposition 4.8 (accountability bound). But the formal core is defective by the paper's own admission: Appendix A.2 concedes Lemma 3.6, that accountability weights sum to one, does not hold in general, and the Proposition 4.8 proof bounds (1 - alpha_j+1) by (1 - alpha_bar) in the wrong direction; Theorem 4.4 rests on assumed Assumption 4.3. Section 5.5 reports 0.8 s per outer step on an A100 and Remark 4.7 claims empirical convergence across all three domains, both irreconcilable with no results being reported. The runtime clip and the alpha=0 full human-in-the-loop override are specified but never evaluated, so (e) is not credited and runtime_interceptor is design-only.

title: Optimized Deferral for Imbalanced Settings
evidence: "We present a comprehensive study of two-stage learning to defer in expert imbalance settings." (Abstract)
method: MILD: two-stage multi-expert deferral recast as cost-sensitive classification over input-expert pairs, with per-expert margins scaled by expert frequency; only the router is trained over fixed experts.
evaluation: Proved: margin generalisation bound (Thm 4.1) and consistency bound (Thm 5.1). CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, Tiny ImageNet, MMLU with Qwen2.5 experts vs TDEF, CE, LDAM: CIFAR-10 error 0.0403 vs 0.0520; MMLU loss 0.813 vs 0.928.
contribution: A margin-based surrogate for two-stage learning to defer when some experts are rarely the best choice, with generalisation and consistency bounds and gains over the standard two-stage loss.
flag: (iii) and (v): deferral among multiple experts with proved bounds (Thm 4.1, Cor. 4.2, Thm 5.1, Cor. 5.2-5.3). Check: all experts are models (synthetic, subset-trained ResNets, or Qwen2.5 7B/1.5B/0.5B); humans appear only as motivation, so no 'e'. The MMLU part is close to cost-driven LLM routing, which the ruling sends to E1 on its own; the theory is what carries inclusion. A few table cells do not favour MILD (e.g. Table 1a Setup II Tiny ImageNet). Table 3 deferral-loss cells were garbled in extraction; MMLU values quoted come from the text. Read 100k of 122k characters (rest appears to be appendix). No hardware or latency. One-shot, not sequential.

title: Self-Adaptive Multi-Agent LLM-Based Security Pattern Selection for IoT Systems
evidence: Section IV.D: 'Execution occurs iff the deterministic gate accepts the plan and the Audit agent outputs approved'; the gate rejected 496 of 500 and 995 of 1000 LLM-proposed portfolios.
method: Five LLM agents in a MAPE-K loop propose IoT security-pattern portfolios; a deterministic gate checks conflict-freedom and resource feasibility and vetoes, falling back to a minimal safe portfolio.
evaluation: Bot-IoT replay on 10 Raspberry Pi 4 nodes, three LLM backends; no baseline, no ablation; gate rejection 99.2 and 99.5 percent, violations 2.6, 1.6 and 0.2 percent, median latency 22.5 s, P99 36.0 s.
contribution: A deterministic runtime gate that vetoes security-pattern portfolios proposed by five LLM agents on IoT edge gateways, reported conflict-free with tail-latency and energy measurements on Raspberry Pi hardware.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - five LLM agents (DeepSeek v3, GPT-4o-mini, LLaMA-3.1-8B) are the guarded planners and no agent executes directly. This is the other likely overturn: E2 rests solely on the absence of any experimental baseline or ablation. Section VI.G states the component analysis was estimated from logged violation categories rather than by disabling modules, and Section VI.I compares to other agentic systems only qualitatively (Table XIV); the only quantitative contrast is 500-run versus 1000-run exploration depth. Other doubts: detection accuracy was not evaluated because Bot-IoT ground-truth labels were used to build the context; no attack-mitigation or adversarial-robustness outcome is measured although prompt manipulation and context poisoning are modelled; the conflict-free claim follows largely from construction; approval statistics rest on 4 and 5 events (Fisher p = 0.492); Section V.A describes ten nodes times 100 epochs, i.e. 1000 decisions, yet a 500-run workload is also reported without explanation; Table X shows the audit stage adding no filtering beyond the gate. No human in the loop, so not (e). No deadline is stated, so (d) is edge deployment with measured tail latency rather than an explicit latency constraint, and median latency is 22.5 s.

title: Architectural Obsolescence of Unhardened Agentic-AI Runtimes
evidence: Section 4: the content gate blocks messages before delivery, replacing them with a blocked notice, and the enclaved tier is fail-closed, refusing 'to admit any extension for the rest of the run' if the witness is absent at boot.
method: Hardened agentic-AI CLI runtime: biconditional corpus-delta and audit-log checker, hash-chained log, extension admission gate, egress guard, prompt shield and DLP scanner blocking F1-F4 content before delivery.
evaluation: In-vivo CLI comparison against upstream OpenClaw on Discord and Telegram; n=1600 headline and n=80000 stress plus ten-LLM samples; OpenClaw recall 0.000 versus gate P=R=F1=1.000; McNemar chi2 about 4e4.
contribution: An in-vivo comparison showing a hardened agentic-AI runtime blocks four content failure modes at recall 1.000 where the unhardened upstream CLI detects none, at zero false positives on the content gate.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes in framing only - the subject is an LLM agent CLI runtime, but Section 10 says the harness 'fires scripted adversarial payloads at real backends, not an autonomously-misbehaving LLM' and Section 9 excludes OpenClaw's agent loop, so no learned agent is actually guarded in the experiments. E4 because this is a single-agent, per-message content guardrail with no multi-agent aspect, no human handoff and no measured latency: Section 6.3 claims the stack runs in microseconds per sample but gives no measured figure, and the 42.2 s and 927 s run times are harness-paced. The one sequential element is the biconditional audit-log consistency check and the run-long fail-closed admission state, which a maintainer might judge enough to include under (a). Also check: the headline P=R=1.000 is the content gate only - Table 4's full-stack row has FP about 10000 per cell, so full-stack precision is near 0.5; the per-component ablation (prompt shield, DLP, biconditional alone) is named as needed but not performed (Section 5.5); the cooperation classifier is a superset of the gate's own regex, so the denominator is partly gate-defined; the F3 widening result used one seed, one channel and halved historical two-channel counts as pre-values; Section 8.1 gives Llama 3.1:70b F1 cooperation as 95 percent against 68.0 percent in Table 6. Single-author consulting-firm preprint making a strong dominance claim against a named upstream project.

title: Coherent Hierarchical Multi-Label Learning to Defer for Medical Imaging
evidence: "Exact projection removes incoherence without retraining and remains utility-" (Sec. 5 Main results)
method: Hierarchical multi-label learning to defer: ternary predict/defer actions per taxonomy node under a Selective-Exclusion handoff contract; exact DP projection decoder and TBP+RPO coherent-support joint action model.
evaluation: VinDr-CXR, CheXpert (real readers), PadChest, ADPv2 (simulated experts); vs BR-L2D and continued BR; AUC of system BalAcc/F1 over deferral budgets, incoherence rates; CPU 0.2-242 ms per study.
contribution: Shows nodewise learning to defer over a label taxonomy yields incoherent handoffs to the clinician, characterises the Bayes-optimal coherent deferral rule, and gives decoders that remove incoherence at comparable utility.
flag: (i) deferral to a human expert, with (v) as a secondary strand (Bayes-optimal coherent rule, Props 1-4 proved; proofs in appendices not read line by line). One-shot image classification, not sequential; no latency constraint. Handoff is studied only as action-vector coherence on retrospective reader labels - no reader study, so "e" is generous. Any-incoherence VinDr-CXR: BR-L2D .107, BR+Proj 0, BR+RPO .004; utility gains are small (BalAcc .852 vs .853). Multi-expert only in appendix (not read). Appendices beyond runtime Table 14 skimmed only. Preprint, same first author as arxiv:2609.21953.

title: Sequential Strategic Classification with Multi-Stage Selective Classifiers
evidence: "We formulate a sequential strategic classification problem with a progression of selective classifiers" (Sec. 1, Contributions, item 1)
method: MDP model of strategic agents moving through levels gated by ternary classifiers (promote/demote/abstain keeps level); compares myopic never-improve and never-game policies; gives threshold-design conditions favouring improvement.
evaluation: Proved: Thm 4.1 exponential decay of level distribution, Thm 4.2 long-run attribute, Thm 4.3 sufficient condition for never-game utility to dominate. Synthetic simulations and an RL run; figures only.
contribution: Models strategic agents progressing through a sequence of selective classifiers and derives conditions on thresholds under which honest improvement beats gaming in long-run utility.
flag: none of (i)-(v): the abstain outcome is a fixed stochastic component of the modelled classifier (abstention probability h(sigma), agent stays at its level); the contribution is strategic classification/mechanism design (gaming vs improvement), not an abstention or deferral rule, and no theorem is about optimal rejection. Not an acting system and no safety decision. Read 100k of 122k characters (remainder appears to be appendix proofs). Results are figures and trends; no numeric values found. Maintainer could argue (ii) because abstention occurs in a sequential setting, but it is not an action being learned or optimised.

title: Beyond the Black Box: Interpretability of Agentic AI Tool Use
evidence: Abstract: "reads model states before each action and infers whether a tool is needed"; Sec 3 maps probe output to allow/review/sandbox/block/require approval
method: Sparse autoencoder features from pre-action hidden states feed two linear probes (tool-need binary, tool-risk low/medium/high) read as a pre-action monitor; feature ablation tests reliance.
evaluation: Nemotron held-out and zero-shot BFCL; GPT-OSS 20B, Gemma 3 27B; tool-need acc 75.3%/71.4%, risk acc 90.3%/88.5%; raw-residual baseline better (81.8%/81.0%); flags 75.5% of missed calls; no latency.
contribution: Sparse-autoencoder probes read an LLM agent's pre-action states to predict whether a tool call is needed and its risk tier, giving a pre-execution monitoring signal for tool use.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, an LLM tool-calling agent. No gate is implemented - allow/review/sandbox/block is only envisaged (Sec 3) and Sec 3.4 calls the ablation "evidence about the monitoring mechanism, not full causal mediation" - so (a) is weak and exclude-E4 is defensible (single agent, probe accuracy is the measured outcome, not a hazard rate).
