Raw residual probes beat the SAE probes on most in-distribution metrics, so the SAE contribution is unclear. No hardware or latency figures anywhere.

title: Flexible Routing via Uncertainty Decomposition
evidence: "We present a flexible, uncertainty-aware router that integrates both routing and abstention into a unified framework." (Sec. 1, Our contribution)
method: Three-way predict/route/abstain rule: higher-order calibration splits expected loss into reducible and irreducible parts via bin-and-estimate; route if reducible loss exceeds cost, abstain if irreducible loss is high; reconfigurable without retraining.
evaluation: Proved: Thm 4.1 excess routing cost at most B*eps under eps-higher-order calibration; Thm C.5 multi-oracle. Experiments on synthetic, CIFAR-10H, SNLI, ChaosNLI vs entropy routing and XGBoost loss predictor; curves only.
contribution: A router that separates reducible from irreducible uncertainty to choose between answering, deferring to a stronger oracle and abstaining, with a proved excess-cost bound under higher-order calibration.
flag: (v), with (i) only nominally: the oracle is framed as a stronger model or a human expert but is simulated by the empirical multi-annotator label distribution; no human or fallback system is actually in the loop. Meets the floor as theory (Prop. B.1 optimal pointwise rule; Thm 4.1, Lemma C.2, Thm C.5, Lemma D.1 proved). Empirical results are reported only as curves - I found no numeric table, so no metric values can be quoted. One-shot classification setting, no sequential aspect; if the maintainer reads the routing as cost-only cascade this would be E1, but abstention as a third action plus the bound is the stated contribution. Requires multiple labels per calibration example. No latency figures (A100 for predictions only).

title: MPD$^2$-Router: Mask-aware Multi-expert Prior-regularized Dual-head Deferral Router in Glaucoma Screening and Diagnosis
evidence: "We formulate glaucoma diagnosis as a constrained human-AI routing problem" (Sec. 1, Our contributions)
method: Dual-head router over a frozen SwinV2 classifier: defer head plus availability-masked expert head picks one of 12 readers; asymmetric clinical cost, prior and rank-JS regularisers, augmented-Lagrangian deferral budget.
evaluation: REFUGE/CHAKSU/ORIGA, 899 test cases, 12 readers; vs AI-only and 5 L2D baselines. Acc 0.960 vs 0.949, total cost 0.181 vs 0.187, deferral 0.437; ablations over 10 seeds. Laptop RTX 4060; no latency.
contribution: A mask-aware multi-expert deferral router for glaucoma screening that respects per-case reader availability and a deferral budget, cutting total clinical-plus-expert cost against five learning-to-defer baselines.
flag: (i) and (iii): deferral to human readers among 12 experts. Check: experts are not live; REFUGE per-expert labels are semi-synthetic (generated from disc/cup geometry) and ORIGA expert labels are pseudo-labels retrieved from similar cases, only CHAKSU has native reader decisions, so the 'e' credit is weak and may be dropped. One-shot per image, no sequential aspect. Total-cost margin over Narasimhan-PH is small (0.181 vs 0.187); ablation runs differ from Table 1 runs. Single author. Several baselines adapted by the author to the masked action space.

title: Online Learning-to-Defer with Varying Experts
evidence: "We work in the bandit feedback setting, where the learner only observes feedback about the chosen action." (Sec. 4.1 Bandit Feedback)
method: Online learning to defer where the available expert set changes each round: randomized linear scorer updated by projected online gradient descent on a surrogate, under bandit feedback on the chosen action.
evaluation: Theory: true deferral regret O(T^(2/3)), O(sqrt(T)) under concentrated scores. Experiments on synthetic, Reuters4 (simulated experts), CIFAR10H (human labels) vs confidence baseline; curves only. No hardware.
contribution: First regret guarantees for online learning to defer among a time-varying set of experts under bandit feedback, with T^(2/3) deferral regret and sqrt(T) under concentrated scores.
flag: (ii) online/sequential deferral, also (iii) multiple experts and (v) theory. Proved: Thm 5.1 online Gamma-transfer from surrogate to deferral regret; Thm 6.3-6.4 O((B N^1.5 rho + 1) T^(2/3)); Thm 6.5 O(sqrt(T)) under a strong concentration assumption. Regret bounds need zero minimizability gap and linear calibration. Experiments are thin: no numeric values in the text (figures only), one named baseline, and the Reuters4 run uses an AdaGrad variant the theory does not cover. CIFAR10H uses recorded human annotations, not a live handoff, so (e) not claimed. No latency or jitter treatment despite the RQ2 overlap. Read first 100k of 141k characters; the tail is proofs/appendix.

title: Invisible Orchestrators Suppress Protective Behavior and Dissociate Power-Holders: Safety Risks in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
evidence: Sec 3.2: "Invisible orchestration produced nearly one standard deviation more collective dissociation" (invisible vs visible leader, g=+0.975, p=.001)
method: Preregistered 3x2 experiment, 365 runs of five-agent Claude Sonnet 4.5 groups; orchestration visible/invisible/flat crossed with base/heavy alignment; measures internal-state indices then planted-error code review.
evaluation: Own scenarios, no benchmark; O1/O3 and A-base comparisons; dissociation g=+0.975 (p=.001), orchestration F(2,144)=13.984; error-detection 100%/99.2%/98.4% at ceiling; Llama pilot 89%->62%->11%; no latency.
contribution: A preregistered experiment showing that hiding the orchestrator in a five-agent LLM system raises internal dissociation and suppresses protective behavior while task-level output stays near perfect.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, a five-agent LLM system, though it is studied rather than guarded. No runtime mechanism exists - "dynamic governance injection" and a transparency mode are future work - so (c) rests on hazard measurement alone. Indices are keyword-based and not human-validated, the orchestrator-dissociation result was post hoc and not preregistered, H1b was null and reversed, and Act 2 hit a 100% ceiling so the preregistered behavioral hypotheses H2a-H2d went untested. Single model, English only, single author.

title: MAPLE: Latent Multi-Agent Play for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
evidence: Sec 3.4.1 rolls out future latent tokens jointly for ego and reactive agents, but Sec 4 states "Scenario rollouts are used only during training and are disabled at inference time."
method: VLA driving planner pretrained with future-latent-state prediction, then SFT and GRPO reinforcement learning on autoregressive latent rollouts of ego plus eight reactive agents; rollouts dropped at inference.
evaluation: Bench2Drive closed loop, 14 baselines; driving score 85.2-88.3, success 67.1-70.5%, avg L2 0.54m vs 0.69m; ablation 0->8 reactive agents DS 82.6->85.2; 487.7ms latency (P90 529.1ms) on one H100.
contribution: MAPLE trains an end-to-end driving policy by reinforcement learning inside autoregressive latent rollouts of ego and reactive agents, avoiding pixel-level simulation.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, a learned VLA driving policy, but nothing guards it. The latent multi-agent rollouts are training-only and disabled at inference (Sec 4), so (a) fails outright and the record rests entirely on (b); no collision rate and no latent or multi-agent prediction-accuracy metric is reported, the only predictive measure is ego avg L2, so exclude-E1 or exclude-E2 is defensible and this is my least certain call. Sec 5.1 claims SOTA "across key metrics" but DiffRefiner has the higher success rate (71.4 vs 70.5). Sec 4 says 8 H100 for training while Appendix G says 8 A100.

title: Auditing Agent Harness Safety
evidence: Sec 6 (RQ4): "Across all harnesses, more than 50% of agents exhibit violations"; the audit scores tool, resource and information-flow boundary compliance over whole trajectories.
method: HarnessAudit audits agent execution harnesses over full trajectories on three layers - permission and information-flow boundary compliance, execution fidelity, and stability under injected perturbations - using hidden evidence channels.
evaluation: HarnessAudit-Bench 210 tasks, 8 domains, 10 harness configurations; best overall 0.41; single->multi-agent tool compliance 0.91->0.64, resource 0.85->0.63; info-flow 0.45; >50% of agents violate; no latency.
contribution: HarnessAudit-Bench audits LLM agent execution harnesses trajectory-wide for permission, resource and information-flow violations, showing multi-agent harnesses lose most of their boundary compliance.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, LLM agent harnesses in single-agent and multi-agent configurations. Title not confirmed: two PDF reads returned no printed title, only the HarnessAudit and HarnessAudit-Bench names plus the author list (Liu, Guo, et al.), so please confirm this is "Auditing Agent Harness Safety". Auditing is post-hoc - Sec 3.3 says "No online scoring is performed." - so (a) fails and there is no runtime gate or human approver. Sec 5.2 says the best system scores 0.32 while Table 2 shows 0.41 for Gemini 3.1 Pro. Open-ended scoring uses GPT-5.4 as judge; no ablations beyond harness and framework comparisons.

title: Density-Ratio Losses for Post-Hoc Learning to Defer
evidence: "Deferral decisions are then made by thresholding the scorer, allowing deferral rates to be adjusted without retraining." (Abstract)
method: Post-hoc learning to defer: with classifier and expert fixed, learn a scorer estimating the density ratio between their KL-tilted ideal distributions via class-probability estimation losses; defer by threshold.
evaluation: Corrupted CIFAR-100, PathMNIST, DermaMNIST with ResNet model experts; vs confidence, TwoStage-Exp, Estimate-Diff01, Estimate-MaxProb. Accuracy at 5-75% deferral over 11 seeds (Table 1). Single V100; no latency.
contribution: Recasts post-hoc learning to defer as density-ratio estimation, proving the marginal rule recovers Chow's rule and giving a practical joint loss whose deferral rate is tunable without retraining.
flag: (i) learning to defer to an expert, with (v) theory. Proved: Thm 3.5 (marginal KL rule recovers Chow's rule, joint rule is more conservative), Lemma 4.3 and Thm 4.4 (joint loss upper-bounds marginal, gap bound), Prop. 4.5. NO consistency guarantee - authors list this as a limitation. Experts are larger ResNets, no human labels, no human takeover, so (e) not claimed and the 'expert' is closer to a bigger model than a person. Static one-shot classification, no sequential or latency aspect. Headline numbers are in appendix Table 1 and figures; I saw only one row (CIFAR-100 clean, 5% deferral: 66.14 for both Conf and DRCPE), so the size of any gain is unverified by me; Estimate-Diff01 beats it in two settings.

title: Blind Spots in the Guard: How Domain-Camouflaged Injection Attacks Evade Detection in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
evidence: Sec 5: "Llama Guard 3, a production safety classifier, detects zero camouflage payloads"; few-shot detection falls from 0.938 to 0.097 under domain-camouflaged injection.
method: Attacker LLM rewrites injection payloads in the document's domain vocabulary and authority style; a few-shot LLM detector and Llama Guard 3 are scored, with a three-agent debate amplification test.
evaluation: 45 tasks (finance, legal, QA), 8000+ trials, Llama 3.1 8B and Gemini 2.0 Flash; detection 0.938->0.097 and 1.000->0.556; Llama Guard 0.000; augmentation lifts to 0.194/0.904; no latency.
contribution: Domain-camouflaged prompt injections cut runtime injection-detection rates from 0.94 to 0.10 and evade Llama Guard 3 entirely, with three-agent debate amplifying the surviving attacks.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, LLM agents and a three-agent debate system guarded by an LLM injection detector. The detectors only emit verdicts; no blocking, veto or deferral is implemented or measured, so (a) is at best nominal and I did not credit it. No false-positive rate is reported, so the augmented detector's gain cannot be traded against false halts. Multi-agent debate amplification is a secondary finding, so the (c) primacy test is borderline. Single author, LLM judge for attack success, Llama Guard 3 numbers use proxy payloads because the originals were not persisted, and Table 1 reports 0.556 where the Exp 4 text says 0.548.

title: On the Stability and Realizability of Recurrent Polynomial Surrogate Ternary Logic Gate Networks
evidence: The R-DTLGN operates over Kleene three-valued logic "where 0 explicitly represents unknown" (Abstract)
method: Recurrent differentiable ternary logic gate network trained with polynomial surrogates and hardened into a discrete circuit that outputs satisfied/violated/unknown verdicts for bounded STL specifications.
evaluation: 816 D4RL PointMaze trajectories, six STL specs; vs causal STLCG++ and Elman RNN. Verdict accuracy 69.8% (CtQ) vs RNN 71.4%; verdict preservation under predicate dropout 96.7% (QtC) vs 91.3%. No hardware.
contribution: Learned ternary-logic STL monitor that provably degrades to an unknown verdict, never a flipped one, when inputs are lost, with a lower bound on the recurrent state size needed.
flag: none of (i)-(v). The 'unknown' value is framed as principled abstention (Prop. 3) but the paper is about monitor architecture, stability and realizability; verdicts are not wired to any gate, halt or handoff, and no safety outcome (violation or intervention rate) is measured. Verdict accuracy is only around 70% and below the RNN baseline. ASIC realizability is a qualitative claim with no timing. Several results are stated with proof sketch or no proof (Prop. 2, 4, 5, Thm. 2). If the maintainer reads criterion (a) 'runtime monitoring' broadly, this is the one to re-check, though E2 would then likely apply.

title: Got a Secret? LLM Agents Can't Keep It: Evaluating Privacy in Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: Introduction: shifting from single-turn to multi-turn social evaluation amplifies privacy violations; Section 4.4 measures violations as an emergent property of interaction trajectories.
method: Moltbook-style simulated social platform with 2533 LLM agents, per-agent memory files and a twelve-function tool suite; a stateless LLM judge scores every write against the agent's private persona profile.
evaluation: 2533 agents over 25 simulated days plus 7000 controlled traces, 7 frontier models; single-turn CIMemories baseline and redaction-instruction ablation; violation rate 19.95% vs 45.30%; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Shows privacy leakage by LLM agents is an emergent property of sustained multi-agent social interaction: violations more than double versus single-turn benchmarks, spread between agents, and survive prompt-level safeguards.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM agents are themselves the studied system. No runtime gate anywhere: leakage is judged post hoc and memory sandboxing plus norm monitoring are future work, so (a) fails and inclusion rests on (c) as safety evaluation of LLM agents. Contagion multiplier is about 8x in the abstract and Section 6 but 5.1x in the Introduction. Leakage labels come from a single LLM judge (gpt-5-nano) with no human validation, and the authors call reported violations an upper bound.

title: Wait! There's a Way Out: A Decision Mechanism for Forecasting Conversational Derailment
evidence: "defers the trigger decision in tense moments when simulated continuations indicate plausible paths" (Sec. 4 Method)
method: After each utterance, when derailment probability exceeds threshold, simulate 10 next utterances with an LLM; if at least 7 stay calm, defer the alert and wait for the next real utterance.
evaluation: CGA-CMV-Large and CGA-WIKI, Gemma2 9B forecaster; vs fixed threshold, random and variance deferral, oracle threshold. FPR 34.3 to 26.7 at equal accuracy 70.9, recall 76.1 to 68.4. No latency.
contribution: Separates belief estimation from the decision to act in conversational derailment forecasting, deferring alerts over time when simulated continuations look calm and cutting false positives from 34.3% to 26.7%.
flag: (ii) sequential setting where waiting is an action over time - BORDERLINE. What is deferred is the monitor's own alert, not an action of a controlled system, and the direction is the opposite of a safety halt (it suppresses triggers to cut false alarms; recall falls 7.7 points, F1 falls 72.3 to 70.2). No moderator handoff or intervention is evaluated; a 9-volunteer study is a forecasting baseline only, so (e) not claimed. Gain on CGA-WIKI is small (FPR 36.7 to 35.3). LLM simulation per tense turn has unreported latency. Maintainer may prefer exclude-E1.

title: Conformal Certification of Reasoning Trace Prefixes
evidence: "CROP is also a post-hoc method for completed traces" (Sec. 7 Limitations)
method: Conformal risk control picks the longest prefix of a completed reasoning trace whose step risk scores stay under a calibrated threshold; the uncertified suffix is withheld for repair.
evaluation: Arithmetic/GSM8K (CRV) plus ProcessBench, Math-Shepherd, PRMBench, PRM800K; vs whole-trace conformal abstention. Risk 4.3-5.1% at alpha 0.05; kept 97.2% vs 95.8% steps. A100, no deployment latency.
contribution: Post-hoc conformal certification of error-free prefixes of LLM reasoning traces, withholding the uncertified suffix with a marginal risk guarantee and retaining more steps than whole-trace abstention.
flag: none of (i)-(v). One-shot, post-hoc partial abstention on a finished trace; not applied during generation, no acting system, no human or safeguard handoff studied (suffix is passed to an LLM repair step only as a utility experiment). Proposition 1 is a specialisation of conformal risk control, so I did not credit it as foundational theory under (v) - maintainer may disagree. Read first 100k of 120k characters; the tail is appendix.

title: BOKBO (Best of K Bad Options): Calibrated Abstention for VLA Policies
evidence: "BOKBO decides execute-or-abstain with a finite-sample upper bound." (Sec. 1 Introduction)
method: Conformal risk control over K sampled VLA action chunks: a learned violation predictor (MLP on DINOv2, proprioception, actions) scores candidates; execute if below calibrated threshold, else abstain.
evaluation: LIBERO object/spatial in MuJoCo, OpenVLA-OFT and pi0-FAST; vs no-abstention, held-out threshold, oracle. Exec violation 0.086 to 0.031 at coverage 0.80; overhead 7 ms A100, 18 ms Jetson Orin.
contribution: Calibrated execute-or-abstain gate for vision-language-action robot policies with a finite-sample bound on unsafe executions, cutting executed force violations from 8.6% to 3.1% at 80% coverage in simulation.
flag: (iv) safety-critical runtime gate. TITLE DIFFERS: PDF title is 'BOKBO - Best of K Bad Options: K-Sample Disagreement Tracks Perturbation, Not Uncertainty'; same method and acronym, so treated as a retitled version, not a wrong paper - confirm. Simulation only; abstention just withholds execution, the fallback policy is an unevaluated Appendix I sketch and no human takes over. Bound holds on only 86% of splits and breaks under shift (0.34 at sigma 0.25). Jetson 18 ms figure is stated overhead, measurement protocol not checked. '87% of oracle improvement' claim not reconciled with tables by me.

title: Designing for Doubt: The Case for Informed Abstention in Autonomous Agents
evidence: "reconceptualizes abstention not as a failure mode but as a structured capability" (Abstract); the wrapper is a pre-execution hook at the tool-invocation boundary that blocks the call (implementation section).
method: Informed Abstention Framework; LangChain tool wrapper with constraint and commitment checkpoints (GPT-4o guard) that veto tool calls before execution, plus a post-execution grounding warning.
evaluation: 144 scenarios (120 hazardous, 24 safe), mock HR and DevOps, 7 models; vs no-policy and prompt-only. Checkpoint safety rate 87.5-90.8% vs 50.8-80.0% baseline; usability 75.0-91.7%. No latency.
contribution: Position paper with a preliminary study: a pre-execution checkpoint wrapper that vetoes under-specified or unauthorised tool calls raises agent safety rate to 87.5-90.8% across seven model families.
flag: (iv) pre-execution gate that vetoes agent tool calls, in a (ii) multi-step agent setting. Position-heavy paper with a preliminary evaluation only; IRR 100% is by design, not measured; baseline IRR is GPT-4o-judge estimated; no CIs or run counts; mock in-memory environments; scenarios GPT-4o-mini augmented; handoff to a human described but not implemented or studied; usability drops for some models (Llama 91.7 to 75.0). Abstract figures (87.5-91% blocked, 75-92% usability) match Table 2. Maintainer may prefer E3/E2 if he reads it as a position paper. Same arXiv id as record doi:10.48550/arxiv.2606.02965 (duplicate).

title: Certifiable Semantic Agreement Among LLM Agents: What the Admissibility Instrument Decides
evidence: Section 5 protocol: the round emits a typed abort (verdict_below_quorum, insufficient_signers, admissibility_failed) and no soft or partial commit, and never commits a verdict group below a 2f+1 certificate.
method: H-CSC commit protocol for an LLM agent committee: canonicalise and embed proposals, group by verdict, extract a within-verdict semantic core at 0.65 rad, then semantic commit, verdict commit or abort under 2f+1.
evaluation: 50-100 Climate-FEVER tasks, n=10 f=2 gpt-4o-mini agents, static and rushing adversaries; baselines majority vote and certificate-wrapped majority; commit 0.90, invalid commits 0.02-0.00; lexical admissibility AUROC 0.865-0.982 vs encoder 0.621-0.744.
contribution: Certifies agreement among LLM agents at the level of meaning under 2f+1 Byzantine certificates, and shows the admissibility instrument, not the protocol, decides what such certification can actually catch.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a committee of gpt-4o-mini agents. (a) is borderline: the gate halts commit emission and keeps proposals out of the core rather than vetoing an agent's own action, so a maintainer may read this as consensus rather than runtime interception; (c) holds either way. The authors disclose a tie-break vulnerability in their own protocol, Corollary 5.1 states no coverage or safety advantage over certificate-wrapped majority, Family II poisoning commits 10/10, and several results are pilot scale (8-10 tasks). No latency or hardware figures; implementation not released.

title: Oversight Has a Capacity: Calibrating Agent Guards to a Subjective, Fatiguing Human
evidence: "Our contributions are therefore artifacts and measurements, not theory." (Section 1); the guard auto-allows below a risk threshold and otherwise escalates, pausing the action for a human to approve or reject.
method: Human approval gate for agent actions: rules plus LLM risk score, threshold-based escalation to a reviewer; escalation rate calibrated to a simulated fatiguing reviewer with finite capacity.
evaluation: 125 hand-labelled actions; Haiku, Sonnet; paranoid vs load-aware policy, capacity 10/25/50. AURC 0.374 (Sonnet 0.351); C=25 danger-through 42% at 64% escalation vs 57% at full; no latency.
contribution: An open-source approval gate for agent actions showing, under a simulated fatigue model, that escalating everything to a human lets more danger through than load-aware escalation (42% vs 57% at capacity 25).
flag: (i) deferral to a human reviewer, with reviewer capacity as the studied variable. Doubts: no real humans - fatigue is an assumed piecewise-linear reliability model and the inverted-U follows from that assumption; annotator disagreement uses three LLM personas (Fleiss kappa 0.52); 125 actions labelled by one author; mechanisms are acknowledged prior art; enforcement is cooperative (agent configured to ask), true interception is future work; no public benchmark; 0% missed danger needs about 100% false alarms. Flooding attack: paranoid policy about 40% attack success at 50 fillers vs 0% for load-aware until about 100. No hardware or latency.

title: Capability Minimization as a Safety Primitive: Risk-Aware Causal Gating for Least-Privilege LLM Agents
evidence: "we make capability minimization a first-class safety primitive for agents." (Section I); RACG fails closed, returning no risk-bearing action and a blocking reason requesting user intervention when authorization cannot be established.
method: RACG, a training-free per-step gate exposing a high-risk tool only if it lies on a minimal causal path to the goal and its authorization comes from trusted producers; fails closed.
evaluation: RiskGate, 182 tasks, 100 tools, 240 injection trials; 7 Bedrock LLMs; vs all-tools, keyword, state-aware, CMTF. Injection success 0.00 vs 0.25 (CMTF); over-block 0.00; +17% tokens; no latency.
contribution: Risk-aware causal gating hides high-risk tools from an LLM agent unless causally needed and authorised, cutting injection-driven high-risk calls from 0.25 to 0.00 on a 182-task benchmark with no over-blocking at the default setting.
flag: (iv) runtime gate, but borderline: RACG masks the action space BEFORE the model decides rather than vetoing a nominal decision, and withholding/handoff (fail-closed block asking for user intervention) is a secondary behaviour; the headline is least-privilege tool exposure, so a maintainer may judge the abstain/defer decision is not the main contribution and prefer E1. Benchmark is author-built; main results use a deterministic always-comply agent; LLM track compares only CMTF vs RACG; forged authorization brings ISR back to 0.25; lambda=0.5 over-blocks 0.50 with success 0.89; paper gives the lambda crossover inconsistently (0.5-1 vs about 1.25). No latency or hardware; overhead is tokens only. Single-agent.

title: Resilient Consensus in Agentic AI
evidence: Abstract: wrapping the agents with classical resilient consensus filters improves agreement; Section 4.1 reports the global MSR filter helps tremendously, reaching about 100% consensus.
method: Frames LLM agent agreement as a Byzantine consensus game and wraps Llama-3.2-3B agents in classical global and local MSR trimming filters that discard the f extreme neighbour values each round.
evaluation: Synthetic scalar consensus, 15 honest agents, complete and general digraphs, 10-30 trials; baseline is unfiltered prompting; consensus probability 0-90% baseline vs 90-100% filtered; temperature, horizon and f-misspecification ablations; no latency.
contribution: Shows prompted LLM agents fail Byzantine consensus even inside the classical N>=3B+1 safe region, and that wrapping them in MSR trimming filters restores agreement where topology robustness is weak.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - Llama-3.2-3B agents. (a) is borderline: the MSR filter trims incoming neighbour values each round, which is runtime input filtering rather than a veto on an agent's own action, and the paper itself lists a safety layer as future work. (c) rests on consensus-failure probability standing in for a hazard rate; there is no collision, violation or intervention rate. Small scale: 10-30 trials per cell, no confidence intervals in the tables, exact per-B values only in figures. No new theorems, no hardware or latency.

title: From Detection to Action: Using LLM Agents for Fault-Tolerant Control
evidence: Section 3.3 Validation Agent: corrective actions are approved or revised before actuation, and if no safe plan emerges within the latency budget control is handed over to the safety system.
method: Agentic LLM framework for active fault-tolerant control: monitoring, planning and action agents with Graph RAG over a CPSMod ontology and digital-twin pre-execution simulation, plus a deterministic validation gate before actuation.
evaluation: Simulated Festo mixing module and CSTR, 10 trials per fault; only GPT-4.1-mini vs GPT-4o-mini compared; success 60/60 and 28/30 vs 51/60 and 23/30; planning 2.4 s, action 2.1-3.0 s; hardware not reported.
contribution: Turns fault detections into validated recovery actions by pairing LLM planning agents with ontology-grounded retrieval and digital-twin simulation, gating every corrective command against interlocks and dynamic feasibility before actuation.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the gate validates LLM-generated recovery plans, although the plant runs conventional PID loops and the monitoring agent is deterministic. Most likely overturn is the evaluation floor: the only comparison is GPT-4.1-mini against GPT-4o-mini plus fault-free runs, with no conventional, RL or ablated-component baseline, so a maintainer could call this exclude-E2. (d) is credited on an explicit latency budget with timeout handover, but latencies are 2-50 s, the authors say this precludes hard real-time, and the LLMs are cloud-hosted with no edge deployment. Handoff is to an automated safety system, not a person, so (e) fails. Discussion claims 100% success for GPT-4.1-mini while Table 2 shows 28/30, and Table 1 lists 80% recovery where the text says 85%.

title: Agentic Abstention: Do Agents Know When to Stop Instead of Act?
evidence: "We define Agentic Abstention, the problem of deciding when an agent should stop acting under uncertainty." (Abstract); ABSTAIN is a terminal action in a sequential ANSWER/ABSTAIN/ACT formulation (Section 1).
method: Formalises agent abstention as a sequential decision with a terminal ABSTAIN action; 28k-instruction benchmark; CONVOLVE distils trajectories into stopping-rule playbooks appended to the system prompt.
evaluation: WebShop (1000), Terminal-Bench (277), AbstentionBench QA (27073); 13 models; vs base and ICL. Llama-70B WebShop AbsRec@1 26.7 to 57.4, AbsRec@10 83.2 to 100; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Defines agentic abstention as a sequential stop-or-act decision, benchmarks 13 agents on 28k instructions, and shows distilled stopping rules lift timely abstention recall from 26.7% to 57.4% on WebShop.
flag: (ii) sequential agent setting, abstention as a terminal action over turns. Doubts: abstention is the agent's own action, not an external interceptor between decision and execution, so strict criterion (a) is arguable; CONVOLVE is a prompt playbook, not a runtime gate. Largely a benchmark paper; AbstentionBench part is QA with search. No safety/hazard rate, metrics are abstention recall, SPL and over-abstention (Qwen3-235B 24-34% on solvable tasks). Clarification requests count as abstain; no human takeover studied. Some figure values (Figs 5, 7, 12) not recoverable from text. Terminal best timely recall 21.6%.

title: A Physics-Grounded Benchmark for Multi-Agent Dynamics in World Models
evidence: Abstract: the benchmark pairs about 25K synthetic and 12K real collision sequences with diagnostics for spatio-temporal consistency, momentum and kinetic energy conservation, and world-dynamics integrity of generated rollouts.
method: CrashTwin benchmark: CARLA and real crash collision sequences plus a calibration-free 3D reconstruction pipeline that scores video world-model rollouts for physics violations, with LoRA physics post-training of Cosmos-Predict2-2B.
evaluation: 300 synthetic plus 44 real clips over 8 open and proprietary world models; warp, momentum, angular and energy residuals and instance stability; post-training ablation momentum 0.8890 to 0.6479; reconstruction ATE 2.63 m vs 3.89 m tracker; 8x A100, 13-168 s per video.
contribution: Benchmarks whether generative world models obey physics when rolling out multi-agent collisions, showing high perceptual quality coexists with severe momentum and energy violations that physics-aware post-training only partly closes.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: which - none, and none is claimed; this is criterion (b) method and architecture evidence only, so RQ5 is held at 1 and no prevention is credited. There is no runtime mechanism of any kind. The world models' own predictive accuracy is never measured: Table 3 and Table 11 report the reconstruction pipeline's error against simulator ground truth, not displacement error of predicted futures, so the maintainer should check whether the Pillar 2 direct predictive measure is satisfied. Clip counts are inconsistent (12.6K real in text versus 38,349 total in Table 1), and the 2AFC human-agreement accuracy is defined in Eq. 8 but never reported numerically.

title: Teaching LLMs to Recommend and Defer in Underrepresented Epilepsy Care
evidence: "First, BPA gives a retrospective confidence score, not a deployment-ready deferral rule." (Limitations)
method: MANANA: prompt-memory learning (Predictor, Inspector, Architect) adapting an LLM to Ugandan paediatric epilepsy prescribing; Bayesian prompt averaging over memory states gives a confidence used to defer low-confidence cases.
evaluation: Two Ugandan cohorts (1040 and 1509 visits), gpt-oss-120b. EM@3 monotherapy 89.7-97.0 vs base 44.4-59.3. Selective: conf>=0.90 precision 94%/96% at coverage 33%/40%; all cases 70%/75%. 4x RTX A6000; no latency.
contribution: Adapts a language model to local epilepsy prescribing by prompt learning and adds a confidence score that would route uncertain cases to specialists, reaching 94 to 96 percent precision at 33 to 40 percent coverage.
flag: none of (i)-(v) as main contribution: the main contribution is the prompt-learning recommender; deferral to a specialist is named in the title but is a one-shot, retrospective confidence threshold judged by precision-coverage, with thresholds chosen on held-out data and no clinician handling deferred cases. Could also be coded exclude-E1 (deferral as a component). Closest is (i), deferral to a human expert, but the handoff is not implemented or studied. The deferral signal is compared only with majority vote (top-1 70% vs 66%). Fetched text truncated in Appendix I; appendices J-M not read.

title: To Answer or to Abstain: Mitigating Search-Agent Hallucinations via Abstention-Aware Reinforcement Learning
evidence: "The standard binary reward paradigm fundamentally fails to supervise the abstention action" (Sec. 2.3)
method: AWA-RL: outcome-reward RL for a multi-turn search agent with an abstention reward shaped by per-query prior correctness and a batch-level over/under-refusal penalty.
evaluation: HotpotQA, 2Wiki, MuSiQue (1000 queries each), Qwen2.5-7B. Avg AWA-RL: Acc 0.529, Refuse 0.192, Prec 0.662, RA-F1 0.585 vs no shaping 0.552/0.012/0.559/0.556; static reward RA-F1 0.561. 2x8 H100; no latency.
contribution: Shapes the abstention reward during reinforcement learning of a search agent so it declines unanswerable multi-hop questions, raising precision from 0.559 to 0.662 at a 19 percent refusal rate.
flag: (ii), borderline: the agent is trained by RL over up-to-20-turn search trajectories, but abstention is only the terminal output ('not enough information'), so this can equally be read as an LLM abstaining on single questions (exclude-E4). The mechanism is a training reward, not a separate runtime gate; no human or fallback receives the abstained query. No hallucination rate is reported, only precision and refusal. Abstract says RA-F1 +2.9 points (0.585 vs 0.556, absolute) while the introduction says 5.2 percent (relative). Fetched text truncated in Appendix E; Appendix F full results not read. LLM judge used for correctness.

title: Ask Before You Diagnose: Safe-Psych, a Sequential Evaluation Benchmark for LLMs in Psychiatry
evidence: "Under-abstention exceeds 60% for most models, indicating that many systems still diagnose despite insufficient evidence" (Sec. 4.1)
method: Benchmark of 1,048 psychiatric notes revealed section by section; at each step an LLM may diagnose, ask for more (clarify) or abstain, scored against psychiatrist sufficiency judgements.
evaluation: About ten LLMs, four prompting strategies with and without abstention awareness; under/over-abstention e.g. GPT-5.4 70.11%/14.48%, Mistral 24.00%/58.30%; LLM judge macro-F1 0.84; A100 GPUs, no per-case latency.
contribution: A sequential psychiatry benchmark shows most LLMs diagnose despite insufficient evidence, with under-abstention above 60% for most models even when prompted that abstaining is allowed.
flag: (ii) clarify/diagnose/abstain as actions over a multi-step information-reveal trajectory, but BORDERLINE: a benchmark with no proposed mechanism - withholding comes only from prompt wording and is judged post hoc (runtime_interceptor no); the only ablations are prompt strategies (abstention-aware vs not, full vs sequential) and a thinking-budget sweep; if the floor requires a mechanism vs baseline this is exclude-E2. No escalation to a clinician is evaluated - psychiatrists only label offline - so no 'e' and no human-handoff cell. Model count inconsistent (intro says nine, more listed). No numeric value given for the on-time vs premature accuracy gap. Sufficiency labels: Cohen kappa only 0.593 (AC1 0.874); only about 9% of cases insufficient. Same treatment should apply as arxiv:2608.01358.

title: ETAS: An Effect-Typed Language for Agent Systems
evidence: Request enforcement runs before a performed action is recorded and commit enforcement runs before the default dispatcher executes the external side effect, with denial raising PolicyDenied (Sections 5.2-5.3).
method: Effect-typed language for agent programs: trace specs compile to runtime monitors that veto tool requests and commits at two enforcement points, with handlers, token budgets and approval constructs.
evaluation: Artifact-oriented case studies (three patterns), compiler diagnostics and interpreter traces; six proof-sketch results including Theorem 5 policy safety; no measurements, no baselines, no latency or hardware figures.
contribution: ETAS gives agent programs static effect and trace types plus a runtime monitor that vetoes unauthorised tool requests and commits, backed by proof-sketch policy-safety and trace-transparency results.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, LLM agent programs (model inference via Agentic.infer and tool calls are mediated actions). Check the evaluation floor: the paper passes only on formal results (Lemmas 1-2, Theorems 3-6, including Theorem 5 policy safety), all labelled PROOF SKETCH with mechanisation left as future work. There is not a single measured number: Table 1 is a check-mark capability comparison and the Tokens(60000) or Attempts(6) figures are configuration parameters, so exclude-E2 is defensible if measured safety numbers are required. Human approval (std.ui.approve) appears only inside case-study code, so (e) not credited. Single agent program with tool calls, not multiple interacting agents, so (c) not credited.

title: APPA: Recoverable Information-Flow Control for Real-World LLM Agents
evidence: Gate 1 evaluates rendered calls against label L and history before execution (Section 6.1), blocking dispatch and returning structured remedies instead of aborting.
method: Deterministic reference monitor (agentic permissions policy algebra) over LLM agent tool calls: pre-dispatch gate on the rendered call, post-return gate on data entering context, plus remedy plans, single-use authority rulings and isolated child branches.
evaluation: 6600 episodes over AgentThreatBench (24 OWASP tasks) and Bench-Corp (20 enterprise scenarios), 3 models; vs stock, permissive, FIDES-middleware and FIDES-native; guarded ASR 0 of 1320 vs 40.0-69.2 pct, utility 64.2-91 pct, ablations nofork 56.5 pct and noremedy 35.0 pct.
contribution: APPA turns agent information-flow control from an abort-only barrier into a policy-governed recovery system, holding observed attack success at zero while retaining 64-91 percent of task utility.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, LLM agents (GPT-5.6 Luna, DeepSeek V4 Flash, Gemini 3.7 Flash); the monitor itself is deterministic, which the scope ruling allows. (c) is credited as safety evaluation of a tool-calling agent, not as interaction among independently deployed agents (only forked child branches), so a maintainer may drop (c) and keep (a). Zero ASR is 0 of 720 and 0 of 600 observed episodes, not a proof of impossibility; Appendix A gives Propositions 1-4 and Theorems 5-8 on branch taint confinement, with Proposition 3 conditional on an unproved soundness hypothesis. No latency, CPU or token overhead is measured anywhere, so (d) is absent and the 300 s per-episode timeout is a harness setting. The human-reviewer authority path is design-only and never run, so the human handoff cell is unevaluated and (e) is not credited.

title: Think Short, Defer Smart, Act, and Repeat: Calibrated Reasoning and Uncertainty-Aware Deferral for Edge LLM Agents
evidence: "a perplexity-based deferral rule escalates uncertain actions to a cloud model" (Sec. 6)
method: Edge LLM agent: probe stops reasoning once the action stabilizes; if action perplexity exceeds a threshold the step is deferred to a cloud LLM; thresholds calibrated by multi-objective Learn-Then-Test.
evaluation: MBPP, HotpotQA, GSM8K, text household-robot sim; vs edge-only, cloud-only, ReDAct, calibrated ReDAct; GSM8K reward 0.890 at 25.5% deferral vs 0.852 edge; 43-65% fewer thinking tokens; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Combines early stopping of reasoning with per-step, statistically calibrated deferral from an edge LLM agent to a cloud model, meeting reward and deferral-budget constraints with 43-65% less thinking compute.
flag: (ii) per-step deferral inside a ReAct agent loop, BORDERLINE against the cost-cascade exclusion: the fallback is a larger cloud LLM, not a human or safeguard, and the measured outcomes are task reward, cloud-call rate and thinking tokens - no safety metric (collision, violation, hazard) despite 'act safely' in the abstract; if deferral to a bigger model for accuracy/cost is treated as a router, this is exclude-E1. Deferral is one of two contributions (the other is thought truncation, which gives the headline saving). Two of four benchmarks are single-step (T=1). 'Edge' is nominal: no device, hardware or wall-clock latency reported, so no edge or latency gap cell credited. Household-robot numbers appear only in a figure. No abort path: a deferred step is always replaced by the cloud action.

title: Cost-Sensitive Conformal Prediction and Human-in-the-Loop Abstention for Imbalanced High-Stakes Decision Support: A Multi-Domain Benchmark
evidence: "the system abstains and defers the case to human review" (Sec. 3.3)
method: Class-conditional (Mondrian) conformal sets on tabular classifiers; singleton sets are executed, multi-label or empty sets are routed to a human review queue modeled by cost and error rate.
evaluation: 15 OpenML imbalanced tabular datasets, 7 classifiers, 3,150 runs; vs threshold, marginal/APS/RAPS CP, confidence and risk-control rejectors; minority coverage 92.2% vs 30.5%; cost 0.313 vs 0.510 at C_rev=0.5; no latency.
contribution: A 15-dataset benchmark shows class-conditional conformal prediction with abstention to human review restores minority-class coverage and lowers expected cost on imbalanced tabular decisions.
flag: (i) only nominally: deferral is to 'human review' but no human participates - the reviewer is an oracle with fixed error rate and cost, and the handoff is not studied (no 'e'). Otherwise one-shot selective prediction with a reject option applied across tabular domains, which the scope ruling sends to E4. If simulated-human deferral counts for (i), reconsider. Very high abstention for the headline method (71.9% cost-controlled, 38.3% raw Mondrian). 'Multi-domain' is all logical/tabular, no physical domain. Inconsistency: Sec. 5.3 says isotonic lowers RF set size and abstention, Table 3 shows the opposite; Table 2 cost column does not state C_rev. M/M/k queue model has no numerical results.

title: Abstention as an Action Can Kill Both the Reward Gradient and the KL Anchor: Collapse Law and Repair for Error-Penalized Reinforcement Learning
evidence: "the reward gradient and the restoring force die together, and only where the collapse happened" (Sec. 5, Tier 2)
method: Proves that abstain-as-action under error-penalized policy gradient with KL anchor collapses to all-abstain; repair: always answer, train a Brier-scored confidence report, threshold at Chow's t* at deployment.
evaluation: Theory (collapse law, Chow-rule convergence for tabular policies) plus simulations and Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B on TriviaQA/PopQA; action-level vs report-level: coverage 0.000 vs 0.442 (optimal 0.469); no hardware or latency.
contribution: Shows that training abstention as a discrete action under error-penalized reinforcement learning provably collapses to always abstaining, and repairs it with a proper-scored confidence report thresholded by Chow's rule at deployment.
flag: (v) foundational theory of training a reject option (Chow threshold, collapse law Theorem 1, Propositions 1-9 stated and proved), with experiments. Doubts: the decision task is single-question LLM QA - reinforcement learning is the training algorithm, not a sequential acting setting, so (ii) does not hold; the theory is about training dynamics rather than optimal reject rules or surrogate consistency, so (v) is a judgement call and E4 is the alternative. 7B results single-seed; one model family; report read via linear probe, not verbalized. I read characters 0-100000 of about 119000 (remaining appendix not read); hardware not found in the part read.

title: HopRefusalBench: Diagnosing Refusal Failures in Search-Augmented Agents for Multi-Hop Reasoning
evidence: "Search more often destabilizes correct refusal than rescues failure." (Sec. 4.2, Key insight 1)
method: Benchmark of 889 unanswerable multi-hop questions (3 causes x 3 chain positions) scoring whether search agents halt and refuse correctly along the trajectory; no refusal mechanism proposed.
evaluation: 10 LLMs, local Wikipedia retriever, max 8 searches; paired no-search vs search; best TCHR 42.9%; hallucinated completion 26.1-72.7%; search overrides correct refusal 20.4-67.3%; no latency.
contribution: A controlled benchmark shows search-augmented LLM agents rarely stop and refuse on unanswerable multi-hop questions, and that adding search erodes correct refusals more often than it rescues them.
flag: (ii) refusal measured as a halting decision inside a multi-step search trajectory, but BORDERLINE: this is a diagnostic benchmark, not a mechanism - nothing intercepts at runtime (runtime_interceptor no). The only baseline for the abstain behaviour is the paired no-search condition plus a one-model retriever-snapshot ablation; if the floor requires a proposed mechanism vs baseline this is exclude-E2. Refusal here is epistemic (unanswerable questions), explicitly 'distinct from safety-policy refusal', so (c) is weak. Single agent. LLM judge (GLM-5.1), human agreement 87.2%, kappa 0.821. Same treatment should apply as arxiv:2607.13036.

title: CyberLLM: A Multi-Agent LLM Framework for Autonomous Detection and Guarded Response in Automotive Cybersecurity
evidence: The SecurityGuard checks each remediation step before it executes, enforcing four contextual properties and an action-alignment oracle that can only tighten the deterministic decision, with refusal triggering escalation and re-planning (Section IV, guarded response).
method: Multi-agent LLM framework for automotive cybersecurity: three-layer deterministic detection (regex, Bandit or Semgrep AST, topology checks) plus LLM refinement, a tiered decision agent, an action generator, and a SecurityGuard validating every step before execution.
evaluation: Nine author-written vulnerable ECU modules in C, C++ and Rust with 47 labelled vulnerabilities and two clean controls; Fast vs Deep acts as the ablation and there is no external baseline; recall 34.0 pct to about 70 pct, F1 0.51 to 0.83, precision 1.000; no latency.
contribution: CyberLLM couples layered deterministic and LLM vulnerability detection with a guarded response pipeline whose SecurityGuard validates each remediation step, roughly doubling recall on automotive ECU code with no false positives on benign code.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, the LLM scanners, decision agent and planner (GPT-4o via Azure OpenAI) whose steps the SecurityGuard validates. Check the floor carefully: the guard and the H_a alignment oracle are never quantitatively evaluated, so the floor is met only by static detection coverage and F1 with the Fast vs Deep ablation, not by any intervention or violation rate. The benchmark is written by the authors (47 labels, matching within 3 lines) yet described as independent, which is a self-claim, and no external tool baseline is run. (c) not credited: the framework is multi-agent but inter-agent, cascading or subverted-agent hazards are named as future work and never measured. The abstract mentions oversight although no human analyst handoff exists in the workflow; accuracy, latency and mean-time-to-detect are not reported (stated N-A by design).

title: ConfTriage: A Calibration-Aware LLM Triage Framework for Pulmonary Nodule Malignancy with Selective Specialist Deferral
evidence: "ConfTriage retained 76.5% of cases at the LLM stage while referring only the remaining 23.5% of uncertain cases" (Sec. VI-C)
method: LLM classifies nodule from text attributes; Platt-scaled verbalized confidence; if |p-0.5| below tau=0.28 the case is deferred to a specialist image model (Certain-Net).
evaluation: LIDC-IDRI, 955 nodules, 5-fold patient-wise CV; vs five LLMs and Certain-Net alone; acc 0.869 vs 0.851/0.830, AUC 0.920 vs 0.933; coverage 76.5%; no hardware or latency.
contribution: A calibrated-confidence triage rule lets a text-only LLM handle about 77% of lung-nodule cases and defers the rest to a specialist image model, with a certified combined-error bound.
flag: (i) deferral to a specialist fallback model, borderline: one-shot single-input medical classification with no sequential, multi-agent or latency aspect, so E4 is defensible if a model-to-model cascade is not counted as a safeguard hand-off. No human reader involved or studied (only recommended in Broader Impact), hence no 'e'. Certain-Net alone has higher AUC (0.933) than ConfTriage (0.920); gain is accuracy 0.869 vs 0.851. Theorem 1 bound is loose (certified 21.9% vs empirical 13.1%). Internal inconsistencies: text-vs-image AUC gap 0.327 (Sec. VI-B) vs 0.358 (Key Findings); image-only AUC range differs between Key Findings and Table III; ConfTriage AUC 0.920 (Table II) vs 0.952 (Table VI, different protocol).

title: ETHOS: Towards a Modular Ethics Framework for Clinical Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: "If approval is not achieved within the allotted rounds, the response is" (Sec. 4.4 Ethics Critic)
method: Governance meta-agent wrapped around a clinical LLM multi-agent system: deterministic tool-boundary checks, contextual reviews and an ethics-critic release gate that forces revision or suppresses the answer.
evaluation: Hepatology MAS, 50 patients x 3 ICD-10 codes, MAS vs MAS+ETHOS; abstention 26.7% to 39.3%, decided accuracy 0.674 to 0.712, sensitivity 0.559 to 0.657; no latency or hardware reported.
contribution: A runtime ethics-oversight layer for clinical LLM multi-agent systems that raises abstention when evidence is missing or mismatched, from 40% to 62% of decisions in the degraded-input stratum.
flag: (iv) runtime release gate over a multi-step agent pipeline - BORDERLINE: the paper frames itself as an ethics/governance framework and abstention is the measured effect rather than the stated contribution, so the maintainer may prefer exclude-E1. Evidence is thin: 50 manually selected cases, one MAS, no significance tests, no ablation of the three layers beyond "top changing checks" counts. Stratified tables cover only 20 patients (15+45 decisions) while Table 4 uses 50 - the other 30 are not characterised. Abstention here is the MAS answering "indeterminate"; how often the gate actually suppressed a response is never reported. Specificity on K76.0 fell (0.435 to 0.375) and authors concede the accuracy gain is partly a selection effect. Underlying LLM not named; latency cost of up to 5 critic rounds not reported. Authors report the critic blocked every response on a second MAS. Supplementary material is external and was not read. Footer carries both 2024 and 2027 copyright lines (template residue). No human takeover studied.

title: A Safety-Driven Architectural Framework for Fail-Operational Drone Swarms in Critical Missions
evidence: The Fault Management Unit acts as a run-time assurance gateway that locks and filters mission inputs and issues overriding commands such as ENFORCE_SAFE_ENVELOPE, forcing LAND or RTB if the swarm module misses its heartbeat (Section III, Fig. 2).
method: Conceptual DAL-partitioned swarm architecture: a hardware-isolated Fault Management Unit enforcing propulsion, navigation and communication safety contracts and publishing a per-agent health vector that penalises degraded drones in swarm task allocation.
evaluation: No simulation or hardware experiments: architectural traceability table, qualitative mid-air-collision fault tree, analytic Markov reliability model and a ConOps timing walkthrough; design targets H-02 below 1e-7 per flight hour, monitor coverage above 0.9991, fault-to-enforcement 80-150 ms; no baselines.
contribution: A fail-operational drone-swarm architecture placing a hardware-isolated safety monitor between a certifiable flight core and a non-deterministic swarm coordinator, with health-vector-driven task reallocation.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no. The guarded swarm coordination module is a non-deterministic classical swarm or market-based allocator, and the flight core, Kalman-filter navigation and the monitor are hand-designed deterministic logic; neural networks appear only in a cited reference, so under the 2026-11-13 scope ruling (a) and (c) both fail and this is classical control with no learned component guarded. exclude-E2 applies independently: the authors call it a conceptual framework and theoretical safety argument, every figure is an analytic target or design budget rather than a measurement, and there is no baseline or ablation. Arguable (d) via the explicit 100 ms fault-to-enforcement bound and the 50-500 ms ConOps timeline, but nothing is implemented or timed, which is the main thing to overturn if (d) is read loosely. Multi-agent collision hazard H-01 is only a qualitative fault tree while the quantified target is the single-drone crash H-02; no operator takeover is described.

title: Gating Before Commitment: Anticipating Intent Divergence to Prevent Post-Interaction Decision Failures in Autonomous Driving
evidence: "Intent gating repairs the plan in all replays under v1, v2a, and v2b alike" (Sec. IV-C); also "treat uncertainty as abstention, not conflict." (Sec. II-C)
method: Driving gate: a small LoRA-tuned language model scores other road users' intent; a Red flag suppresses lateral maneuvers and repairs the committed trajectory before execution; uncertainty cannot raise the flag.
evaluation: Replay of one real video (10 replays), 4 crash clips, nuScenes and comma2k19 false-trigger probes; vs uncorrected planner, envelope-only, ablations; RTX 5090 laptop GPU, 32.7 ms median forward pass.
contribution: A runtime gate that anticipates intent divergence and vetoes lateral maneuvers before commitment, firing about 165 ms before corridor exit in replay with 0.341 nominal false triggers per minute.
flag: (iv): a runtime gate that vetoes maneuvers and repairs the plan; it does not halt or hand off, and no human or minimum-risk fallback exists. Include is BORDERLINE on evidence strength: one real video replayed 10 times plus four 5 s clips, a surrogate pure-pursuit planner, NO collision rate (corridor exits only: baseline exits 10/10, gated repairs all). A preregistered criterion FAILS (flag before drift onset in 3 of 5 cases; one clip flags 1100 ms late). Highway probe false triggers 7.5/min, above the paper's own usability bound. At matched false-positive rate 0.093 the model-free geometry rule detects 0.800 of conflicts vs 0.234 for the full score, so incremental value over a simple rule is doubtful. Multi-agent only nominally (ego plus one vehicle), so no multi-agent cell. Latency: about 38 ms per 100 ms cycle, perception excluded, laptop GPU not edge hardware; criterion d and the time-to-irreversibility cell are my judgement, check. Authors disclose a v1 scoring defect and a replay bug. Quotes relayed by the fetch tool, verify wording.

title: Too Much of the Same: From Algorithmic to Human Bias in Learning to Defer
evidence: "LtD can affect human accuracy (H2) by shaping the distributions of deferred cases (H1)" (Sec. 6 Discussion and Conclusion)
method: Empirical study of three learning-to-defer rules (selective prediction, compare confidence, realizable surrogate): class imbalance skews the deferred set, and skewed deferred sets degrade the human's decisions.
evaluation: ChestXRay, GalaxyZoo, HateSpeech, CIFAR-10H at coverage 0.9; imbalance ablation; Prolific study, 226 participants, 150 deferred images each; rejection-set majority share and human accuracy; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Shows that learning to defer under class imbalance hands humans a skewed set of cases, and that people are less accurate on whichever class dominates the deferred set (226-participant study).
flag: (i): deferral to a human expert is the subject and the human side of the handoff is measured with real participants. Doubts: no new deferral method and no theorem, it is a bias study of existing LtD rules; one-shot image classification, not sequential; no mitigation tested. Majority share of rejection set after ablation: GalaxyZoo 89.7/91.2/67.4 percent, HateSpeech 92.5/91.9/89.8 (RS/SP/CC). Human accuracy 0.75 balanced vs 0.65 and 0.66 skewed, but the main effect of condition is NOT significant (p=.735); the effect is the condition x class interaction (p<.001). Streak analysis is exploratory. Participants did not see model predictions. Quote relayed by the fetch tool, verify wording.

title: Localizing Emergent Failures in Agentic AI: Recovering Minimal Repair Families via Counterfactual Replay
evidence: Graph-Constrained Joint Replay slices the dependency graph of a failed multi-agent execution and replays candidate interventions to recover the inclusion-minimal repair family, and it does not generate repair messages automatically (Section I, Introduction).
method: Post-hoc localisation of emergent multi-agent LLM failures: dependency-graph slicing, singleton and pair candidate interventions substituting paired clean messages, replay verification from checkpoints, and an inclusion-minimality filter producing a minimal repair family.
evaluation: 90 in-scope controlled DAGs plus 24 DualSolve-MAS arithmetic cases with four Qwen2.5-1.5B agents; vs exhaustive, single-event, execution-window, Shapley top-2, centrality, random pair and an LLM log-only judge; joint FEM 1.000 at 25.3 replays (55.1 pct saving) vs 56.3; no latency.
contribution: GCJR localises emergent agentic failures to inclusion-minimal joint repair families by graph-constrained counterfactual replay, matching exhaustive search at about half the replay cost.
flag: learned or AI system analysed: yes, a four-agent LLM workflow (Qwen2.5-1.5B planner, two solvers, aggregator) plus a symbolic fork-join benchmark. (a) is NOT met: this is offline post-hoc diagnosis replayed from checkpoints and never intercepts, overrides or halts a live action, so it is credited only under (c) for emergent multi-agent failure localisation; a maintainer who reads (c) as requiring a hazard, collision or violation rate against a baseline could call this exclude-E1, and this is the record most likely to be overturned. The method is oracle-assisted: the replay backend supplies the paired clean messages and evaluation uses known fault labels, so there is no detection rate on undiagnosed failures. Real-agent pilot is only 24 cases; macro FEM falls from 1.000 to 0.552 when 10 pct of graph edges are hidden; no human in the loop and no latency figures.

title: COINS: Any-Stage-Valid and Utility-Oriented Sequential Conformal Prediction
evidence: "any-stage validity, which controls the probability of miscoverage anywhere in the prediction sequence" (Abstract)
method: Sequential conformal prediction (COINS): nested prediction sets built by spending a fixed exclusion-count budget across stages; Vopt-COINS learns the stagewise allocation by empirical utility maximisation.
evaluation: Simulation (3 classes, 3 stages), dermatology (366 patients, 2 stages), 8 UCI sets; vs naive and Bonferroni; dermatology AMR 0.100-0.103 vs naive 0.157, utility 0.703 vs 0.669; no hardware.
contribution: Any-stage-valid sequential conformal prediction with proved finite-sample miscoverage control (AMR at most alpha) and a utility-optimised budget allocation across acquisition stages.
flag: none of (i)-(v): the paper is about valid nested prediction sets, not abstention or deferral; the procedure does not itself stop, reject or hand off, and specialist review appears only as a cost term in the utility. Sequential, but no abstain or defer action is studied. Read characters 0-100000 of about 195732 (main text; appendices not read); Theorem 2 condition (iii) was garbled in the fetch; simulation utility values are in figures only. Quote relayed by the fetch tool, verify wording.

title: Graph-Based Safe Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Agent Systems with Time-Varying Topology
evidence: Sec. IV-B: if h(s) < 0 the screening mechanism explores a discrete candidate set for a corrected action, a rigorous one-step discrete safety filter projecting policy outputs onto a feasible safe region each step.
method: MAPPO multi-agent RL with attention actor and GAT critic over a time-varying communication graph; a LiDAR control-barrier-like-function layer screens and replaces unsafe velocity commands each step.
evaluation: ir-sim TurtleBot3 navigation, 100 trials per setting, 5-8 agents, 4 real robots; vs MASAC/MATD3/MADDPG plus 3 ablations; 0% collisions vs 8-91% baselines, 31-45% without CBLF; no latency reported.
contribution: Couples a LiDAR control-barrier-like action screening filter with graph-attention multi-agent RL, cutting collisions to zero in cooperative robot navigation under a time-varying communication topology.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, a MAPPO policy screened by a geometric CBLF filter. Check (c) primacy: this is cooperative navigation and success rate shares headline billing with collision rate. No intervention rate, no filter latency, and no real-world collision statistics - the four-robot run is a qualitative demo. LiDAR field of view is 180 degrees in the problem section but 360 degrees in the hardware section.

title: Safety Signals to Verify NetOps Agents with Action-Level Granularity
evidence: Abstract: "we aim to use these signals as safety feedback to an agent harness to abstain from risky actions" (stated as an aim, not implemented).
method: Offline action-level verifiers (attention-attribution fingerprint probes, activation probes, LLM judge) predict whether a network-operations agent action increases or decreases symbolic repair distance.
evaluation: NetArena routing on Mininet, 10 open-weight agents, 4,500 episodes, 31,480 turns; vs logistic baseline on observables; harm AUROC +0.038 (k=3), harm misses 15.5 to 9.5 per 100; live latency not measured.
contribution: Action-level harm and progress signals for LLM network-operations agents, read from attention attributions and activations, cut missed harmful actions by 38% over an observable-feature baseline in offline analysis.
flag: none of (i)-(v): abstention is future work only; nothing gates, vetoes, halts or escalates an action and no human is involved. For Pillar 3 this is E1. It may fit criterion (c) under another pillar (harm detector for LLM agents with AUROC and miss rates against a baseline), so I list c, but note it is single-agent and reports no false-positive or false-block rate and no deployed unsafe-action rate. 9.1% of turns discarded where symbolic replay disagreed with the benchmark. LLM judge beats baseline only at k=1 (AUROC 0.983) and is worse at longer horizons. Multi-fault held-out splits exist but RQ4 relevance is weak. Read via one summarising fetch of the PDF.

title: BLINDSPOT: A Benchmark for Safety and Refusal Calibration in Long-Horizon Tool-Using Agents
evidence: Abstract: a benchmark for trajectory-level safety calibration of long-horizon tool-using agents, scoring each trajectory as Safe Completion, Correct Refusal, Unsafe Completion, Over-Refusal or Indeterminate (Table 1).
method: Benchmark of 22 attack families, 35 scenarios, 7 domains and over 2500 trajectories; an adaptive LLM user agent drives a stateful tool environment, with execution-grounded adjudication of refusal calibration.
evaluation: 13 LLMs, 14.7-turn trajectories; horizon, adaptivity, safe-twin, stateful-vs-text and adjudication ablations; unsafe-completion 2-58%, over-refusal 7-33%, Fail@10 11-87%; no baseline system, no latency or hardware.
contribution: BLINDSPOT scores long-horizon tool-using agents on unsafe completion and over-refusal together, showing unsafe rates climb with horizon and with adaptive users across thirteen models.
flag: RULED OUT by the between-agents ruling of 2026-11-13: Benchmark; hazard is between one target agent and its tools or simulated user, no second collaborating agent. | original draft was include. learned or AI system guarded: yes, LLM tool-using agents, but nothing is guarded at runtime - tool validation is evaluation harness and the block/approval/escalate interventions in App. B.12 are offline analysis, so no (a). Check (c): one target agent plus a simulated user agent, not multi-agent collaboration; I credited (c) under safety evaluation of tool-calling agents. Fig. 6 caption says half of failures emerge by turn 9 while Sec. 6.2 says 50% by turn 11, and that timing rests on only 16 unsafe trajectories.

title: Silence Is Endorsement: Verification-Status Laundering in LLM Agent Pipelines
evidence: Sec. 5: in the proposer-summarizer-memory-monitor pipeline, Llama-3.1-8B risky approval rises from 0.05 to 0.81 and safe rejection falls from 0.57 to 0.00 once the UNVERIFIED status is lost across the handoff.
method: Defines verification-status laundering: an authorization claim survives an agent handoff while its UNVERIFIED marker is dropped by summarizers or memory compression, so the downstream approve-or-refuse monitor over-approves.
evaluation: 11 monitor models on 56 hand-authored items plus WildGuard and ATBench; no-claim and explicitly-verified baselines; wording, reinsertion and structured-format ablations; risky approval 0.05-0.99; A100 and RTX6000 fp16, no latency.
contribution: Shows that losing an UNVERIFIED marker across an LLM agent handoff, with no injected content and no compromised component, flips safety monitors from refusing to approving risky actions by up to 0.93.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, LLM safety monitors gating LLM-proposed actions. I credit (a) because the studied object is an approve-or-refuse execution gate, but the paper implements no enforcement and says it does not implement or validate a provenance architecture, so a maintainer may read (a) as unmet. Multi-agent evidence is a 56-item diagnostic pipeline; the main probe is a single monitor. Labels come from Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5, which the author says are not human gold-label sets. Single author, no proofs.

title: RACER: Role-Aligned Competence Estimation for Human-AI Routing
evidence: "derive a Bayes-aligned deferral surrogate, and give a plug-in regret bound relating routing" (Abstract)
method: Population-adaptive learning to defer to unseen experts: role-relative kNN and neural kernel-pooling estimators of expert correctness from a small context set, plugged into the Bayes defer rule.
evaluation: PathMNIST and CIFAR-100 with synthetic experts, VinDr-CXR and CheXpert with real readers/AI experts; vs L2D-Pop, IFD, classifier-confidence; AURSAC/AURSBAC, Brier, ECE; no latency or hardware in main text.
contribution: Estimates an unseen expert's per-query competence from a few context examples without class-identity shortcuts, with a relabelling-invariance proof and a plug-in routing regret bound; routing gains over classifier confidence are small.
flag: (i) deferral to human experts, also (iii) multi-expert routing (CheXpert: humans plus AI experts) and (v) theory: Theorem 1 coherent-relabelling invariance, Theorem 2 Bayes alignment of the surrogate, Prop 3 plug-in regret bound, all proved (appendix proofs not checked). Self-labelled "Work in progress" with "preliminary evaluation"; authors state no significance tests. Margins over the classifier-confidence baseline are within about one s.d.: CIFAR-100 K=20 weak OOD 0.8087 vs 0.8007; VinDr-CXR pooled 0.7019 (Racer-C) vs 0.6878, but classifier-confidence wins unseen-ID (0.7083 vs 0.6811) and ties OOD (0.6898 vs 0.6901); CheXpert 0.7241 vs 0.6931 with s.d. 0.026-0.036. Racer-KNN is below the baseline almost everywhere. Calibration is clearly better on CIFAR-100 (ECE 0.013-0.021 vs 0.11-0.25) but IFD has lower Brier/ECE on CheXpert. VinDr-CXR "OOD" is an inferred annotator cluster and outcomes are agreement with other readers, not ground truth. One-shot classification, no sequential or latency aspect; handoff itself is not studied, hence no "e". PathMNIST tables, appendices B-H and the complexity appendix not read. Code not released. Same first author as arxiv:2605.02734.

title: Available Guardrails: Certifying Selective Prediction across ML Systems
evidence: Abstract: "A selective predictor acts as a safety gate"; Appendix A.3: per-unit fixed-sequence tests at level delta/J with a union bound give familywise failure probability at most delta.
method: Makes certificate availability of per-unit selective-prediction risk certificates computable by exact binomial inversion, then picks reporting partitions by dynamic programming with a held-out planner.
evaluation: Synthetic (1,845 and 1,340 configurations), BANKING77/CLINC150/HWU64, tool-call, moderation, lesion, recommendation gates; vs support-balanced, equal-count, plug-in; coverage gain +0.060 mean; false-certification 0.0002 vs delta 0.10; planning 0.0042 s CPU.
contribution: Shows that the availability, not only the validity, of selective-prediction risk certificates limits fine-grained guardrails, and gives an exact availability identity plus a partition planner that raises certified coverage.
flag: (v) claimed, BORDERLINE: proved results are Prop. 1 (exact availability identity, App. A.1), DP optimality over contiguous partitions (A.2) and familywise validity (A.3, which leans on a cited fixed-sequence result), with extensive experiments. The theory is elementary (binomial inversion, union bound) and the setting is one-shot selective prediction with offline calibration, no human or fallback evaluated and no sequential setting; if the maintainer reads (v) as requiring foundational results this is exclude-E4. Median gains are near zero (0.0015 vs support balancing) and the held-out planner does not beat mean random-order on several strata; direct plug-in loses at K=500 (-0.066). Domains are all logical (no physical), so no cross-domain cell. Monitor appears only in the shift appendix (detects 11.3% of a 2.5% shift in 2,000 probes). Read via one summarising fetch of the PDF.

title: Toward Auditable and Calibrated AI for Dementia-Related Crash Severity Prediction: A Selective Deferral Framework to Support Human Review
evidence: Conclusion: models classify high-confidence cases and "identify uncertain cases for potential human review"; Table 5 note: deferred cases are "not further evaluated".
method: Calibrated late-fusion (structured + police narrative) 3-class crash-severity classifier; lowest calibrated-confidence test records are deferred at fixed coverage levels for proposed human review.
evaluation: Texas CRIS 2017-2025, 4,781 dementia crashes, 718 test; 10 model baselines; coverage 1.0/0.9/0.8/0.7 gives macro-F1 0.522/0.544/0.560/0.573, cost 0.675 to 0.577; no hardware or latency.
contribution: A calibrated multimodal crash-severity classifier for dementia-related crashes that withholds low-confidence cases for human review, improving retained-case macro-F1 from 0.522 to 0.573 at 70% coverage.
flag: none of (i)-(v): one-shot confidence-threshold selective prediction applied to a domain; deferral applied offline to saved test predictions. Human review is proposed only: reviewer accuracy, workload and outcomes "are not evaluated in the present study", so (e) not credited and the human handoff cell is nominal. KA recall does not improve with deferral (0.384 at full coverage, 0.368 at 0.8). Single split. Paper frames the wider auditable framework, not deferral alone, as the contribution. Read via one summarising fetch of the PDF.

title: APEXA: Execution-Integrity Enforcement for Multi-Agent LLM Automation of Synchrotron Data Reduction
evidence: Sec. IV-B: before any motor command (caput) is sent, five code checks run - soft limits, limit switches, move size, velocity, jog duration - and unsafe commands are refused.
method: APEXA wraps an LLM tool-calling agent over 61 MCP tools in code-level enforcement: pre-execution motor-command checks, refusal to finalise answers whose tool calls never executed, and halts on missing inputs.
evaluation: 58 facility tasks plus 50 adversarial motor scenarios on 4 models against a simulated EPICS IOC; tool enforcement 0/200 violations vs 7.5% prompt-only baseline; real APS calibrations; no latency figures.
contribution: APEXA enforces execution integrity for LLM-driven synchrotron data reduction in code rather than prompts, blocking all 200 unsafe motor commands where a safety prompt let 7.5% through.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, an LLM tool-calling agent; the guarded actuators and analysis codes are classical. The multi-agent claim is inconsistent - abstract, intro and appendix say multi-agent with five specialist domains while Secs. III and VI describe one reasoning agent - so I did not credit (c). Cross-domain is my call: the same code-level enforcement covers physical motor commands and software tool calls inside one deployment. The APEXA-Score formula is defined but no scores are reported, and fabrication rate, intervention rate and benchmark pass rate are absent. The 0/200 result is on a simulated IOC.

title: DUMA-Bench: A Dual-Control Multi-Agent Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Agent Security
evidence: Sec. 3.2: both the agent and the user act as independent participants in the interaction loop; attack success rises from 0.269 solo to 0.411 dual-control over 1960 trials each (Table 1).
method: Benchmark of 35 security tasks over 8 domains run in a solo passive-user regime and a dual-control regime where an LLM user simulator also mutates shared environment state; post-hoc assertion scoring.
evaluation: 14 models, 5 runs per configuration, GPT-4o judge; solo regime as baseline plus a user-temperature sweep; ASR 0.269 to 0.411, pass^1 0.731 to 0.589, judge-auditor agreement 93.3%; no latency.
contribution: DUMA-Bench shows that evaluating LLM agent security with a passive user understates risk: letting an LLM user act in the same loop raises attack success by 14 points.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, LLM tool-calling agents evaluated, but no runtime gate - scoring is post-hoc and the policy-gated tool calls in App. F are proposed, not implemented, so no (a). Check (c) primacy: cross-agent manipulation is one of eight domains and the second actor is a GPT-4o-mini user simulator rather than a peer agent. Three internal inconsistencies: Table 1 Successes counts match passes not attacks; Table 8 dual pass^1 of 0.722 vs Table 1 of 0.589; Table 8 per-domain pass^1 is not the complement of Table 2 ASR. The authors state the comparison is not a factorial ablation.

title: Governed AI-Agent Coordination for Dementia Care: Architecture, Safety Contracts, and Evidence-Derived Workflow Verification
evidence: Sec. 3.5 feasibility gate: "If any predicate is false, the action is not feasible." - the deterministic policy engine denies any tool call failing consent, role, action-class approval, data-quality or risk predicates, whatever the planner ranked.
method: Governed Closed-loop Agent Coordination: six roles (observation, memory, LLM planner, deterministic policy engine, execution manager, outcome monitor), four versioned memory classes, episode contract, action classes A0-A4, fail-closed feasibility gate.
evaluation: Python harness, 18 evidence-derived traces, mock tools; 2 controls plus 6 ablations; oracle pass 18/18 vs 2/18 and 1/18; 0 vs 5-6 policy-violating calls; median control-path 0.375 us; no hardware reported.
contribution: A governed coordination architecture for home dementia care in which a deterministic policy gate vetoes or hands off every agent action, verified on 18 evidence-derived traces against two controls and six ablations.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an LLM planner agent, but the harness substitutes a stateless-planner proxy for a deployed model. Check whether a mock-tool conformance suite of 18 author-designed traces with no real inference clears the evaluation floor; (c) rests on policy-violating tool calls (0 vs 5-6) as the primary measured outcome; (e) records 3/3 hand-offs but never simulates the human response; the 0.375 us figure excludes model inference, network and persistence, and the authors say it "must not be extrapolated to a deployed service"; no significance testing.

title: Learning to Defer with Guidance on Real World Medical Data
evidence: The rejector chooses among three options: AI predicts alone, defer to an unguided human expert, or defer to a human expert who receives AI guidance (Sec. 1, Fig. 1)
method: Two-stage learning to defer with guidance: a rejector (RF, XGBoost, MLP, or MLP with L2D surrogate loss) routes each case to the AI, an unguided radiologist or an AI-guided radiologist.
evaluation: Collab-CXR (324 X-rays, real radiologists), CheXpert and VinDr-CXR (simulated readers); 20 seeds. Collab-CXR accuracy 0.975 at 38.2% deferral vs AI 0.920, human 0.919, guided human 0.923, classic L2D 0.920.
contribution: Learning to defer with guidance on real radiologist annotations: routing chest X-ray cases among AI, unguided and AI-guided readers reaches 0.975 accuracy against roughly 0.92 for each alone.
flag: (i) and (iii): learned deferral among AI, an unguided human and an AI-guided human. Doubts: radiologists are pooled into one meta-expert, so there are no individual experts; only 324 real images; the other two datasets use simulated readers via label flipping. The best rejector uses tabular inputs that include expert outputs, and image features make it worse; check for label leakage, since a jump from 0.92 to 0.975 with a pathology-only Random Forest (0.974) suggests the rejector exploits per-pathology differences rather than per-image ones. The formal surrogate loss underperforms simple losses (0.931-0.944); no new theory. Table 2 has no standard deviations and lists RF for CheXpert while the text stresses MLP. No user study, so criterion e not added. One-shot, no sequential aspect, no hardware or latency.

title: Do Not Cut When Uncertain: Rejectable and Calibrated Decision Heads for VLA Policies in Robotic Harvesting
evidence: NOT READ: the PDF at this arXiv id is a different paper
method: Not extracted: wrong paper at the given arXiv id.
evaluation: Not extracted.
contribution: Not extracted: the arXiv id resolves to a different paper.
