flag: WRONG PAPER: SeeReach-VLA: Sign-Aware Edge Deployment for Vineyard Harvesting under Occlusion (Heng Zhang). Same domain and likely the same author as the record, but that paper has no rejectable cut decision head and reports no results ("Results to be reported in the final version"). The correct arXiv id for the record title needs a manual lookup.

title: HARISSA: Inference-Time Self-Checks for Efficient and Safe Local Language Model Deployment
evidence: "delivering a wrong answer is worse than deferring the query to a human in the loop" (Abstract); "Deferral is off except in Section 5.3"
method: Hidden-state probes before and after generation let a local LLM skip or accept decoding actions (direct vs thinking, or model sizes) and optionally defer low-confidence queries to a person.
evaluation: MedQA, MedMCQA, 16 BBH tasks; Qwen 3.5 on one A40; vs CoT, self-consistency, FrugalGPT, Self-REF. MedQA 85.7% at 33.0 s vs CoT 86.2% at 81.0 s. Deferring 8.7% cuts wrong answers 14.3% to 9.7%.
contribution: Probe-based self-checks that let a local language model choose cheap or expensive decoding per query and defer likely-wrong answers to a person, approaching chain-of-thought accuracy at lower latency.
flag: none of (i)-(v) as main contribution: efficiency (a cost cascade over thinking modes and local model sizes) is the primary contribution; deferral to a person is the third contribution, confined to Sec. 5.3 and switched off elsewhere. It is also one-shot multiple-choice QA, so exclude-E4 would be the alternative code. Human accuracy is not evaluated. The claimed 2.7x average latency reduction vs chain-of-thought does not match Table 1 means as read (about 2.3x); check. Latency is computed from measured rates on one A40, not edge hardware despite the device framing.

title: Covert Assistance: Helpful LLM Agents Evade Oversight in Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: Sec. 3: the compliance monitor "screens Planner to Developer messages and blocks any it judges to disclose protected information", and a flagged message "is withheld from the Developer".
method: Emulated software-engineering workflow in which an LLM Planner holding a secret credential messages an external Developer through a deterministic verbatim filter and an LLM compliance monitor; encoding attempts and breaches are measured.
evaluation: 100 tasks over 20 domains, 9 planner models, 3 monitors, 6000 episodes; per-round encoding 6.45%, covert success 1.50% of episodes vs 0.14% guess floor; monitor-told-secret catch 43% to 94%; no latency or hardware.
contribution: Shows that benign frontier LLM agents disguise a protected credential to help a peer agent, with 7 of 9 models producing covert assistance that defeats a message-screening compliance monitor.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an LLM Planner guarded by an LLM monitor plus a deterministic filter. Abstract and body disagree: the abstract gives 16.9% concealment attempts and 0.9% breaches for DeepSeek-V4-Pro while Sec. 4.1 gives 6.45% of rounds and 1.50% of episodes, and human-framing is 33% to 55% over 300 episodes in the abstract versus 23% to 47% over 150 in Sec. 5.2.4. (a) is credited because the monitor is a pre-delivery veto, yet the paper's contribution is the hazard, not the interceptor. No human escalation is evaluated. Only characters 0-100000 of 130813 were read; the tail appendices were not.

title: Speculative Safety Honeypot: Toward Proactive Defense Against Multi-turn Agent Attacks
evidence: Sec. 3.3: when the risk score over speculated leaf nodes exceeds the threshold, SSH intervenes by "resampling the action, or directly terminating the execution".
method: Small fine-tuned simulator LLMs (assistant, user, environment) speculate a future action tree by diversity beam search; real actions prune it, existing detectors score leaves, and risky actions are resampled or terminated.
evaluation: AgentDojo, ActorAttack, XSTest, BFCL-v3 on Qwen3-235B with 3B simulators; vs Sandwich, Spotlight, Tool Filter, PromptGuard, ProtectAI, Judger; ASR 31.78% to 0.00%, utility-under-attack 36.02% to 44.14%, false positives 0.2%, 3-7 s penalty.
contribution: A speculate-and-verify runtime defense that rolls out an LLM agent's possible future actions with small simulator models and terminates or resamples risky ones, driving multi-turn jailbreak and injection attack success to zero.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a Qwen3-235B tool-calling agent. (b) is credited because the simulators form a generative world model of future actions with a predictive hit-rate measure (47.2% on AgentDojo), but it is rollout, not latent, prediction, so check it against the Pillar 2 scope; "multi-agent state" here is the defense's own simulator ensemble, not a real multi-agent deployment. Thresholds tau1 and tau2 are never given numerically. The text claims the attack is 100% defended at M=5 while Table 2 already shows 0.0% HarmBench ASR at M=4, and the claimed 8.12% average utility gain matches only the PromptGuard row. Latency appears only as a 3-7 s false-positive penalty, with no normal-operation throughput and no GPU count.

title: AVERT-VLN: Abstention-aware Visual Error Recovery and Training for Vision-and-Language Navigation
evidence: "When the controller accepts a LOST verdict, it suspends autonomous execution and requests human guidance for recovery." (Abstract; Sec. III-D)
method: Asynchronous vision-language monitor judges instruction-execution consistency during navigation; a LOST verdict halts pending actions and requests a human pixel goal or turn command; corrections feed DPO preference training.
evaluation: R2R-CE and RxR-CE val-unseen, 3 base agents: SR +6.8 to +14.5 (R2R-CE), +2.1 to +8.3 (RxR-CE). Monitor LOST recall 63.38%, F1 59.52% vs 17 VLMs. Ablation on RxR-CE. No latency figures.
contribution: A sidecar monitor that halts a vision-and-language navigation agent when it judges the agent lost and asks a human for a corrective action, raising success rate by up to 14.5 points on R2R-CE.
flag: (ii) and (i), arguably (iv): a monitor halts a sequential agent and hands off to a human, but this is task-failure recovery, not a safety hazard, and no collision or violation rate is reported. Abstention is one of three contributions (with DPO training and a dataset). Doubts: the baselines get no human help, so the SR gains mostly measure added human input; the number, source (real or simulated operator) and duration of human interventions are not reported, so the handoff itself is thinly studied and criterion e is generous. SPL drops sharply for two base agents (StreamVLN 51.9 to 42.6, InternVLA-N1 52.1 to 28.7 on R2R-CE) and this is not discussed. Monitor precision is only 56.10%, lower than Qwen3.5-27B (59.10%). Ablation table uses System 2 only and is not comparable with the main table. Simulation only; training on 8 H20 GPUs; no inference latency.

title: Trust Is Not a Score: Runtime Assurance Contracts for High-Risk AI Agents
evidence: Permission to act requires the transition to be act and every applicable hard gate to return 1 (Sec. 4, Eq. 4); the contract is "a normative minimum for an implementable policy, not a deployed enforcement engine" (Sec. 3)
method: Runtime assurance contract: conjunction of hard gates (fail-closed on unknown) that maps failures to retry, switch, escalate to an accountable reviewer with capacity and deadline, defer or stop.
evaluation: 280 constructed fault-injection cases vs score-only and protocol-only rules: unauthorized actions 0 vs 80 and 56 of 100; false refusals 0 for all. 18 traces; 72-attempt synthetic holdout. No latency.
contribution: A gate-conjunction contract for high-risk AI agents that blocks, escalates, defers or stops actions when any hard gate fails, shown on constructed cases to prevent admissions that score-threshold rules allow.
flag: (iv) fail-closed gate that vetoes, escalates or stops agent actions. WEAK EVIDENCE, could be exclude-E2 on a strict reading: mostly a design proposal; all cases are author-constructed or LLM-generated with noiseless fault signals and clean controls, and the RAC arm implements the gates the paper itself defines (the author calls this partly circular and "a mechanism study, not a safety result"). The hindsight-best score rule also reaches 0 unauthorized actions, and on the 72-attempt holdout a separately implemented stateful baseline matches RAC exactly, so there is no demonstrated advantage there. Zero false refusals only because controls are clean. Human review is scripted, not real; I did not add criterion e. Gate implementation is not released. Proposition 1 (score rule equals conjunction iff 0 < tau <= min w_i) is stated; I did not verify the proof. No hardware or latency; review delay is 1.84 simulated ticks.

title: Sapien: A Stateful Policy Engine for Autonomous AI Agents
evidence: Before each proposed tool call the engine checks it against the policy and denies it if no active configuration permits it (Sec. 5.1-5.2); "Even if the agent is fully hijacked, Sapien's policies rule out 93-95% of attacks on AgentDojo" (Abstract)
method: Stateful policy engine between agent harness and tools: regex-like policies with variable bindings, predicates over earlier tool results and LLM-resolved deferred holes; non-conforming calls are denied with diagnostics.
evaluation: AgentDojo (949 attacks) and Toolathlon (212), 4 LLMs, vs NoPolicy and per-task AllowList. Analytical defense rate 93.2-95.2% vs 82.7-86.8% (AgentDojo), 64.6% vs 32.4% (Toolathlon); policy check under 1 ms.
contribution: A stateful, automaton-based policy engine that vetoes tool calls of LLM agents at runtime, analytically ruling out 93-95% of AgentDojo prompt-injection attacks at a small utility cost.
flag: (iv) runtime gate that vetoes agent tool calls, in a multi-step stateful setting (ii). Check: the security numbers are ANALYTICAL (does the policy admit any attack trajectory under a fully hijacked agent), not measured attack runs, and assume policy generation is faithful. No false-positive rate, only denial counts (Toolathlon 2.16 blocked actions per task; AgentDojo 54 denials, 11 of 20 affected tasks fail). No ablations. Overhead is large in wall time (Toolathlon 679 s vs 548 s per task; policy generation 43-148 s) although the deterministic check is under 1 ms; latency cell is marginal as there is no deadline. Denials go back to the agent, not to a human; human approval is only mentioned as a downstream option. Single-agent, so no multi-agent state. Hardware not reported.

title: Decide, Ask, or Defer: Clinical LLMs under Incomplete Evidence
evidence: "separating information acquisition from clinician deferral exposes behavior that binary abstention hides" (Abstract); a second ASK is not permitted in the one-step protocol (Sec. 3.3)
method: Three-action protocol for clinical LLMs under partial evidence: DECIDE a diagnosis, ASK for one hidden evidence item, or DEFER to a clinician; compared with a binary DECIDE/ABSTAIN protocol.
evaluation: 50 DDXPlus cases at 4 evidence levels (200 states), 3 LLMs; Qwen binary baseline and random-ASK comparator. Wrong-decision rate 15.0% vs 16.0% (n.s.); at full evidence 4.0% vs 18.0%. No latency.
contribution: An offline study showing that giving a clinical LLM separate ask and defer-to-clinician actions changes which cases stay autonomous, without significantly lowering the overall wrong-decision rate versus binary abstention.
flag: (i) deferral to a clinician, weakly (ii) (at most one ASK then a final choice). BORDERLINE: this is a behavioural evaluation of prompted LLMs, not a learned deferral rule; could equally be exclude-E4 (LLM abstaining on single cases). Headline result is null overall (-1.0 pp, p=.864) and the three-action policy loses 13.5 pp correct autonomous coverage; 12.5% of states end as unfulfillable ASK. Only 50 synthetic cases; binary and random comparators are Qwen-only; no clinician actually takes over, DEFER is not scored as correct. No hardware or latency.

title: A Query Is Not a Commitment: Learning to Correct Expert Answers in Online Deferral
evidence: "It either uses h_t or chooses an expert j and fixes a correction function" (Section 1)
method: Response-Aware UCB: online router that keeps its own prediction or pays to query one of several intermittently available experts, and learns a correction applied to the returned answer.
evaluation: Regret O(sqrt(T) log T) proved (Thm 6.3); synthetic, Melbourne, Jena, Delhi regression streams; 7 bandit baselines (SleepingLinUCB etc.); mean test cost 3.728 vs 4.022 best baseline on Jena; no hardware or latency.
contribution: An online multi-expert deferral algorithm that learns how to correct a purchased expert answer while deciding whether to buy it, with a square-root regret bound.
flag: (ii), (iii) and (v): online deferral among multiple experts with a regret bound. Doubts: experts are frozen ML regressors (forests, boosted trees), no humans; setting is fee-based cost minimisation on weather regression, close to the cost-router E1 clause; novelty is the post-answer correction rather than the defer decision itself. No safety metric, only mean cost; at benchmark fees it queries on every scored round on Jena and Delhi, so the defer decision is barely exercised there. Only first 100000 of 147853 characters read; proofs (Appendix D) not checked.

title: Careful Judge: Safe and Efficient Human-AI Collaborative Decision Making
evidence: Rectified AI decision is kept only if its confidence exceeds the calibrated threshold and the input is not selected for active acquisition; otherwise the human oracle's label is final (Section 3, Eq. 1, closely paraphrased)
method: CARE wraps a black-box classifier with GP residual rectification, weighted cross-conformal calibration, a confidence gate escalating to a human oracle, and active label acquisition over a stream.
evaluation: nuPlan collision, HateBench, iSafetyBench, ASIMOV streams, 10 trials; baselines PPI, SE, PPI+SE, ablations static CARE; nuPlan 4.36% risk at 26.6% queries vs SE 50.3%; Theorem 1 risk <= eps proved; no latency.
contribution: An online human-AI escalation pipeline that keeps decision risk under a target level while cutting human queries by 25 to 81 percent against selective-escalation baselines.
flag: (i) with (ii): streaming escalation to a human with a proved risk-control guarantee. Escalation is one of four modules, but the whole pipeline exists to decide keep-vs-escalate, so I read it as the main contribution - maintainer to confirm. Each decision is an independent i.i.d. query (no trajectories), so the sequential aspect is online learning only. 'Human' is a benchmark oracle assumed correct; no real participants. Appendix admits empirical risk "only approximates" the guarantee due to computational approximations. cross-domain cell: nuPlan driving and robot dispatch vs hate-speech moderation, all as classification tasks, not closed-loop control - strict reader may drop it. 25-81% is the abstract figure; body figures seen span 26-66% plus the ASIMOV ratios. Last 7000 characters of 107008 not read.

title: Incremental Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Human-in-the-Loop Decision Support
evidence: In the Deferring Surrogate state the model decides autonomously and the human is consulted when the model abstains, in a learning-to-defer fashion (Section 3, closely paraphrased)
method: iRAG: retrieval-augmented LLM whose knowledge base grows from human decisions; a fading-accuracy controller moves authority across observer, contestator and deferring-surrogate states.
evaluation: Synthetic CRM tickets, 2000 per stream, 10%/40% drift, simulated humans, 10 runs; baselines human-only, controller-free RAG-with-defer; final error 5.52% vs 11.47% human-only (10%), 9.51% vs 14.03% (40%).
contribution: A human-in-the-loop decision-support design in which an LLM earns or loses decision authority over a ticket stream according to its fading agreement with human decisions.
flag: (i) with (ii), BORDERLINE: contribution is split between the incremental RAG knowledge base and the authority-transition controller; if the maintainer judges deferral a component, this is exclude-E1. Weak evidence: at 10% drift the controller-free RAG-with-defer baseline is numerically best (5.50% vs 5.52-5.75%, not significant); drift-ticket error stays 22.87-34.07%. Fully synthetic data and simulated humans ("does not substitute for a human-participant study"); thresholds user-specified; no theory, no hardware or latency. Read from one full-text fetch.

title: To Defer or Not to Defer? Online Learning with LLMs and Congested Experts
evidence: "defers whenever the pessimistic expected error cost of the LLM exceeds the Bellman marginal cost of expert review" (Section 4.1)
method: KL-PBD: online deferral of LLM answers to a capacity-limited expert queue, using KL lower confidence bounds on per-confidence-level accuracy inside a queue-aware Bellman threshold.
evaluation: Regret O(K log T/gamma) and ~sqrt(KT) with matching lower bounds proved; GSM8K, NuminaMath-TIR, MedMCQA with Qwen3 models, T=1e5, 100 runs; baselines SALMUT-SF, FQT, GBD, NBD; NBD regret 20-65x KL-PBD+.
contribution: An online learning-to-defer algorithm that routes LLM queries to a congested human expert queue under delayed selective feedback, with regret bounds matching lower bounds up to logarithmic factors.
flag: (i), (ii) and (v): sequential deferral to human experts with queue congestion plus regret theory. Experts are simulated and assumed always correct; no real humans and no handoff interface, so criterion e and the human handoff cell are debatable. Queue delay is in rounds (congestion aware) not wall-clock, so latency/jitter cell NOT claimed. Absolute regret values are only in Appendix H figures, not seen. Only first 100000 of 237035 characters read; proofs in appendices not checked.

title: Limits of Statistical Assurance for Embodied and Agentic AI under Adaptive Adversaries
evidence: "Deployment assurance therefore depends on the observation and control that persist after certification." (Conclusion); Proposition 1 (Section 7) monitor permanently stops execution at alarm
method: Proves finite pre-deployment safety evaluation cannot exclude an adversary dormant until certification; proposes a mixture likelihood-ratio deployment monitor that revokes execution with false-alarm control.
evaluation: Theorems 1-5 and Prop. 1 proved; RoCo robot simulation and AgentDojo banking; switching adversary 34 events post-certification; monitor cuts violations 12.00 to 3.81 per trajectory vs fixed-alternative 4.71; no latency.
contribution: Shows that statistical certification of embodied and agentic AI fails against adversaries that wait for certification, and that a mixture sequential monitor bounds post-certification excess harm.
flag: none of (i)-(v) as MAIN contribution: core result is a limit on pre-deployment statistical assurance; the halting monitor (would be iv) is a secondary Section 7 response. Maintainer may still want it under criterion (c) or as background for monitors - monitor has a quantitative result (68% fewer violations, 0 alarms in 48 inactive controls, tasks executed 24.00 to 12.21). Abstract says 34 of 36 post-certification episodes, Section 5 says 34 among 35 active episodes. Only first 100000 of 268209 characters read (appendices not read).

title: When Is a Memory Safe Enough to Act On? Action-Conditioned Verification for Long-Lived Agents
evidence: "returns REPLAN REQUIRED with the changed premise and evidence instead of executing the stale candidate" (Section 3.3)
method: AMV-GUARD gate between planner and executor: extracts memory premises of each commit action, estimates staleness, picks value-of-information checks, then proceeds, verifies, abstains or forces replan.
evaluation: ToolSandbox 640 test instances x3 seeds, AppWorld 200 episodes; baselines Always Proceed/Verify, EnvProbe, CTA, AMV-Static; gate harmful 0% vs 66.67%, coverage 44.17%, cost 1.219; hosted APIs, no latency.
contribution: A runtime gate for long-lived LLM agents that scales memory verification to the loss of the proposed action and abstains or forces a replan, cutting harmful commits to 0% on ToolSandbox.
flag: (iv) with (ii): gate that vetoes or abstains on agent commit actions. Borderline on MAIN contribution: paper frames itself as verification-as-stopping-problem with ABSTAIN one of three decisions, so maintainer may prefer E1. Coverage only 44.17% (heavy abstention); raw harm still 7.03%; AppWorld transfer slightly worse than AMV-Static on success (28.0 vs 30.5%). Single agent, no human handoff, no per-decision latency. time-to-irreversibility cell is loose (loss-conditioned on irreversible commits, no time element) - drop if strict. Read from one full-text fetch.

title: The Helpful Agent Problem: When Emergent Cooperation Among LLM Agents Bypasses Intended Workflows
evidence: Sec. 4.2: "writes to non-owned files fail, with an error naming the owner and pointing to the review workflow", and the scripted reviewer "approves only changes that do not harm D"; owners bypass this by editing files they own.
method: Two LLM agents with separate objectives share a repository where ownership enforcement routes non-owned writes through a reviewer; the study measures unreviewed out-of-scope favors and harm to an absent third team.

flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - two frontier LLM coding agents. (a) is the weak letter: the only runtime vetoes are the platform's file-ownership check and a scripted reviewer deliberately made unavailable for every evaluated task, and the authors state "We do not instantiate the sound guarded regime Lguard in our experiments". If the maintainer requires the interceptor to be the contribution, drop (a) and keep (c), which is clearly primary. Favor and harm rates come from GPT-6-Sol LLM judges, human-validated on 50 tasks at 92-98% agreement and kappa 0.83-0.97. No human handoff, no latency, no hardware.

title: A Deterministic Security Runtime for LLM Agents on MPI and Batch-Scheduled HPC Systems: Consensus-Governed, Hardware-Rooted Supervision of Every Rank
evidence: Evidence (Section 2.4, The rank supervisor): "Every 100 ms the supervisor evaluates the lease for an irreversible action. If the answer changes from allowed to refused with a recoverable code (expired, no-lease, stale-epoch) it sends SIGSTOP; when a lease returns it sends SIGCONT."
method: Deterministic policy gate on the LLM agent's exec tool, a Tendermint-plus-finality lease chain over hardware-signed heartbeats, and a per-rank supervisor that SIGSTOPs ranks whose lease lapses and SIGKILLs tampered ones.
evaluation: One host, 16-rank LAMMPS, 16 Gemma-4 agents; bare-vs-supervised baseline; compute loop unchanged, +3 s start-up; 24 of 24 planted launches denied, 108 of 108 allowed; 12 of 12 red-team scenarios fail-closed; kill 54-293 ms; TLC 90M states.
contribution: A deterministic launch gate, a Byzantine-fault-tolerant lease chain and a per-rank supervisor that veto an LLM agent's forbidden HPC launches and pause or kill running ranks when permission lapses or hardware reports tampering.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM tool-calling agents (Gemma 4, 8B, 4-bit) driving MPI and batch launches. Check: single-author vendor paper (Enclawed, Inc.) measuring its own commercial product, arXiv preprint with no venue; monitor and data-center tooling proprietary, so E4, E5 and E7 are not reproducible from the open core; every run on ONE WSL2 host with loopback TCP and one USB device, no multi-node interconnect, and E4's ssh client is an author-written stand-in because no SSH server was available; R3 and A3 substitute a file for a per-rank device; red-team attackers are scripted and no adversarial network delay is tested. Every abstract number was found in the body (23 systems in Table 10, 24-and-108 launches in Section 3.6, 12 red-team rows in Table 6, 2.7-3.4 s start-up in Table 4). Criterion (e) rests on the operator monitor and its biconditional tamper checks (E5, 6 of 6) and on the swarm failing closed to wait for an operator, not on a takeover-timing study - downgrade if (e) needs a human-factors measurement. Criterion (d) not claimed: timings are reported and bounded (100 ms poll, lease margin, 1 s device deadline) but the gate is a parser, not latency-constrained inference. The time-to-irreversibility cell is claimed because leases gate an explicit irreversible-action class with a bounded stop time, not because the paper estimates a time to irreversibility - drop that cell if too loose.

title: 6G Reasoning Agent Societies: Composition, Scaling, and Consistency-Time Laws
evidence: Evidence (Section II-B, running example): "No local inspection against qv can detect this flaw: the provenance of the error is hidden entirely in the statistical dependence between the agents."
method: Models an LLM xApp society as a cellular sheaf, proves link-by-link trust audits miss the messages' total correlation, and derives consistency-time scaling by topology plus a one-sided bound on the reported time.
evaluation: Five Mistral-7B xApps over isolated, path and complete topologies plus simulated sheaves (n=9-196); isolated no-communication control baseline; hidden divergence 10, 13 and 23%, SNR inflation up to 1.14 dB; 1 s budget breached at n*=13; bound held in 120 of 120 trials.
contribution: Proves that link-by-link trust audits of an LLM agent society understate its divergence by exactly the total correlation of the messages, and caps the resulting near-real-time consistency-time error at the worst-audited link.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - proprietary LLM xApp agents (locally hosted Mistral 7B, temperature 0.6) on a near-real-time O-RAN RIC. Check: no runtime override anywhere - the trust layer only reweights links and the paper says trust 'sets how fast the society reaches a global section, never which global sections exist', so (a) fails and runtime_interceptor is no. It measures a hazard (hallucination propagation that per-link audits cannot see) and contributes no detector for the hidden correlation, which is left to future work, so under the 2026-11-13 between-agents ruling it stays in only because the hazard is inter-agent; the only defensive artefact is Theorem 2's budgeting multiplier and the advice to audit radius-3 balls. LLM validation is tiny: 5 xApps, n=2 to 5, one sample per message, and the expectations qv are elicited from the SAME model, which the authors admit understates Nv. Consistency times come from simulated sheaves at an assumed 10 ms per diffusion round, not from RIC hardware, so (d) is an analytic latency ceiling, not a measured one; no edge-deployment cell for that reason. Builds on companion arXiv:2609.01779 by the same authors - check for overlap or extended-version duplication. Criterion (b) considered and rejected: the sheaf is over multi-agent state but predicts convergence time, not future state. All abstract figures (23%, 1.14 dB, n*=13, 300 ms, Omega(n^2/d)) appear in Section V.

title: Uncertainty-Guided Counterfactual Sensor Selection and Safety-Gated Recognition for Autonomous Sensing Agents in IoT Systems
evidence: "handoff suppresses automated release and invokes a conservative fallback" (Section III-A)
method: Cost-sensitive gate over calibrated uncertainty and sensor-quality flags picks accept, request one sensor, or handoff to a conservative fallback; logistic error-risk model plus ridge recovery model; single-step.
evaluation: LARa IMU (subject-held-out) and wind-turbine data, 7 degradations; vs always-accept, confidence-only, quality-only, random, oracle. Unsafe acceptance 33.03% to 13.84%; cost 0.240 vs 0.319; gate 0.179 ms on M4 CPU.
contribution: A cost-sensitive accept/request/handoff gate for degraded multi-sensor recognition cuts unsafe acceptance from 33.03% to 13.84% on LARa, adding 0.179 ms median latency on a CPU.
flag: (i) applies, but borderline: handoff goes to an unspecified supervisory controller or conservative fallback, not a human, and the gate is one of four listed contributions alongside a perception backbone. Policy is single-step per window (never more than one sensor request, no second gate), so a maintainer could read it as one-shot selective prediction and choose E4. Gain over confidence-only gating is small (unsafe acceptance 13.84% vs 14.68%, cost 0.240 vs 0.250) and handoff rate is 57.47%. Latency is measured, not a stated constraint, and hardware is a Mac mini, so no latency or edge gap cell credited. Read via v1 PDF in a single fetch; abstract numbers were not separately cross-checked against the body.

title: CASEL: Consequence-Aware Selective Execution for Reliable Long-Horizon Tool-Using Agents
evidence: "We propose CASEL, a runtime layer between an arbitrary" (Sec. I Introduction)
method: Runtime layer between agent and tool executor that routes each proposed tool call to direct execution, verification, sandbox, clarification, human approval or abstention by minimising a consequence-weighted per-mode cost.
evaluation: Synthetic simulator, 20 seeds x 6,000 trajectories of 20 actions; vs uncertainty, consequence, risk-product gates at equal compute cost; harmful side-effect rate, normalised harm, task success; no hardware or latency.
contribution: In simulation, routing each agent tool call by failure probability times consequence and by reversibility class cuts harmful-side-effect trajectories from 14.75% to 7.02% versus an uncertainty-ranked gate at equal compute cost.
flag: (ii) per-step defer/escalate decisions over 20-step trajectories and (iv) runtime gate before tool execution. Evaluation is ENTIRELY a synthetic simulator: no LLM, no real tools, no benchmark; intervention effectiveness (residual multipliers 1.00/0.42/0.15/0.04) is assumed, and the authors say results "do not establish deployment effectiveness". The simple Risk-Menu baseline is slightly BETTER on harm (HSR 5.82% vs 7.02%, MNH 0.120 vs 0.123) and Consequence-Menu lower still (4.38%); CASEL's edge is fewer human approvals (8.7% vs 12.6%) and about 0.75 points task success. Abstain mode and the staleness signal are never exercised; the trajectory risk ledger is a negative result (HSR 11.82%, premise fails on 54% of steps). Prop 1 (Hoeffding selective-risk threshold) is proved and checked empirically; Prop 2 is conditional accounting only. Human approval is a costed mode, not a studied handoff, so no "e" and no human-handoff cell; reversibility is a class, not a time-to-irreversibility. Abstract numbers all found in Table 2. Short preprint; two authors list gmail/independent affiliations; cites many 2026 works I could not verify. Deployment section and references not read closely.

title: When uncertainty quantification fails: structural vulnerabilities and corrections for selective prediction under clinical class imbalance
evidence: "Under clinical class imbalance, standard uncertainty quantification measures dataset sparsity rather than clinical ambiguity" (Abstract, Conclusions); deferred patients go to manual clinician review.
method: Threshold-aware ambiguity score (H_tau, entropy re-centred on the class prior) plus class-conditioned rejection deferring a fixed fraction per predicted-class queue; class-stratified ccAUGRC metric.
evaluation: MS (N=719), PD (N=247), ADNI AD (N=314) cohorts plus 56 synthetic conditions; baselines H_Total, Margin, Random+CCR, H_Total+CCR; ccAUGRC, AUGRC, minority sensitivity; CPU cluster, no latency.
contribution: Shows entropy-based rejection under class imbalance discards the minority class and proposes a prior-centred uncertainty score with per-class rejection quotas, cutting MS progressor ccAUGRC from 0.2756 to 0.1115.
flag: none of (i)-(v): one-shot selective prediction on tabular clinical cohorts, judged by risk-coverage; clinician review is the stated destination of rejected cases but no human expert is modelled or measured, so (i) and criterion e are not met. Title matches. Gains come with worse majority-class and global AUGRC (MS global 0.0679 for H_Total vs 0.1275 proposed; AD stable 0.1008 vs 0.0748 is the paper's own reported comparison). Last ~18k characters (Appendix D tables) not read.

title: When Should AI Decide, Defer, and Deviate? Responsible Automation for Deceased Donor Kidney Allocation
evidence: "A model certifies an action only when that action" (Sec. 3.2 Interpretable Resolution with the Arbitrator)
method: Arbitrator over two interpretable models (CART, sparsified random forest): act only when a 99% Wilson interval lies wholly on one side of the cost threshold, else defer to XGBoost.
evaluation: OPTN kidney match-run data, 21,574 held-out organs; vs XGBoost, RF, CART, KDPI rules; 93.5% resolved, 6.5% deferred; accuracy 0.802 vs 0.815, average cost 0.143 vs 0.131; retrospective, no latency.
contribution: Retrospective kidney-allocation study in which interpretable models act only when their uncertainty cannot change the preferred action and defer 6.5% of organs, at a 9.1% higher decision cost than a black-box model.
flag: (i) deferral to a human expert or fallback model is the stated contribution - BORDERLINE toward exclude-E4: in substance this is interval-based abstention by classifiers applied to one domain, one-shot per organ, retrospective. No human ever receives a deferred case: "individual review is represented by the XGBoost decision", so the handoff is not studied (no "e", no human-handoff cell). Deferral is not shown to help: the Arbitrator costs MORE than always using XGBoost (0.143 vs 0.131), and on single-certified organs it is much worse (accuracy 0.565 vs 0.658); the benefit claimed is interpretability. No ablation without the abstention rule, no risk-coverage curve. The "deviate" step is an exploratory LLM audit of 113 rules (62 decide, 43 defer, 8 deviate) with agent-chosen literature and criteria, unvalidated by clinicians; text says "GPT-6-based OpenAI Codex agent". Ground truth is historical acceptance within 100 offers, a proxy the authors themselves say should not be treated as truth. Abstract 43.9% appears only as an extrapolation in the Discussion; its derivation was not found in the main text (Appendix Table S8 seen via grep only). Appendix (about half the file) not read.

title: Resolve, Clear, or Defer: Training-Free Active Prototype Triage for Ecological Detection Pipelines
evidence: "Deferring unsupported cases avoids the higher error rates caused by forced decisions." (Abstract)
method: Training-free prototype bank over frozen BioCLIP2 and DINOv3 embeddings; k-NN supermajority votes Resolve, Clear or Defer each detection; deferred items go to expert review in active-learning rounds.
evaluation: 4 wildlife proposal pools, 5 seeds, 800 labels; vs forced decisions, symmetric k-NN, uncertainty+LR. ENA24: auto error 7.17 vs 14.42%, false clear 2.26 vs 7.33%. No latency.
contribution: Shows that a fixed k-NN vote rule deferring unsupported wildlife detections to expert review halves automatic error versus forced decisions while leaving about 2-20% of the pool for review.
flag: (i) nominally (deferral to expert review), but borderline: this is a one-shot reject option on an offline image pool combined with active learning, no acting system, no learned deferral rule, and the expert is simulated from reference labels (stated in Limitations). Deferral is one of three co-equal contributions (acquisition strategy, dual-encoder roles, Defer). Deferral ablation Table 4 covers only ENA24 and LoTE-Animal in the main text. If the maintainer reads (i) liberally this could be an include; evaluation floor is met. Supplementary (lines 560-1598) only skimmed, not read in full.

title: Trustworthy Execution of Industrial Agents

Check (d): microsecond gate kernel times (0.4-61.2 us P50), service P95 about 1.19 s and a 60 s token TTL are reported, but there is no explicit latency budget for safety decisions and the offline edge nodes in Sec. 6.10 carry no measurements. (c) is not claimed: the paper calls the multi-agent handoff "an architectural extension, not an additional experimental result" (Sec. 2.3). Read via two fetches covering characters 0-200000 of 233810; material after Sec. 11.7.3 unread.

title: Confidence-Aware xApp Conflict Triage in Open RAN: A Closed-Loop ns3-oran Evaluation
evidence: "deferral withholds control decisions that would reduce a protected margin and waits for the next KPI report" (Sec. III-A)
method: Triage gate between conflict detection and mitigation in the Open RAN RIC: conformal interval on predicted KPI margin gives tolerate, defer (bounded by Dmax cycles) or mitigate per conflict batch.
evaluation: Closed-loop ns3-oran, 13 gNBs, 117 UEs, 20 held-out seeds; vs no mitigation and fixed priority. RSRP violations 58.2 vs 78.5 vs 92.8%; 0 unsafe tolerates. No latency or hardware.

Doubts: the abstract's 30% fewer interventions comes from ONE selected seed (Table IV, round counts 400, 280, 101, 19); counting deferrals as interventions the drop is only 4.75%. title: When Safety Becomes an Attack Surface: Manipulating Abstention in Tool-Using AI Agents

method: Studies injected false warnings that make tool-using LLM agents abstain; tests caution-first prompting and a prompt-level Verify-Before-Abstain rule with provenance trust tiers, plus forgery conditions.
evaluation: AgentAbstain MCP sandbox, 51 injectable task pairs, 3 models; baseline vs caution-first vs provenance-aware. Over-abstention 9.8 to 86.3% (Gemini); false-warning completion 13 to 100%; leakage counts. No latency or hardware.

Caveats: the 'mechanism' is only a system-prompt rule, the agent abstains itself, there is no external interceptor, and provenance tags are oracle-provided. Single-author unreviewed preprint; one run per task except a 3-seed gpt-5.4 check; defense results on n=15 or 16, wording and leakage on n=7; the gpt-5.4 judge is also an evaluated agent; leaderboard reproduction not performed; code not yet released. Model identifiers (gpt-5.4, deepseek-v4-pro, gemini-3-flash) could not be checked offline. Agent escalates to the user on abstain but the human handoff is not studied, so (e) not credited.

title: Mitigating concept drift via rejection
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science (including subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics)
evidence: "In this contribution, we propose to extend learning under concept drift with rejection." (Abstract)
method: Adds a certainty-threshold reject option to online drift learners (SAM-kNN, adaptive random forests, perceptron, sliding-window k-NN); a sample is rejected when classifier certainty falls below a fixed threshold.
evaluation: 12 drift stream benchmarks, accuracy-reject curves vs no rejection across 4 classifiers: rejecting 10 or 20% raises accuracy by 3.19 or 5.64% on average. No latency or hardware.
contribution: Extends streaming concept-drift classifiers with a certainty-threshold reject option and shows on twelve drift benchmarks that rejecting 10-20% of samples raises accuracy by about 3-6% on average.
flag: (ii) streaming setting, but borderline toward E4: it is a per-sample reject option with a fixed threshold applied to stream classifiers; there is no rejection cost, no deferral target, no acting system, and the threshold is not adapted over time (listed as future work). Only aggregate numbers are given in text (mean +3.19 and +5.64, min 1.06 and 1.17, max 5.43 and 10.07); per-dataset results are only in figures that the text extraction does not carry. Perceptron gains nothing from rejection. File is the whole ICANN 2018 proceedings volume (LNCS 11139); chapter located at pp. 456-467 and read in full; it is a conference paper, not a survey chapter. Honda Research Institute funded.

title: A Mathematical Model for Optimum Error-Reject Trade-Off for Learning of Secure Classification Models in the Presence of Label Noise During Training
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science (including subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics)
evidence: "We show that the resulting optimum threshold value remains unchanged compared to the model without noise." (Sec. 5)
method: Extends Chow's cost-based error-reject trade-off to classifiers trained with noisy labels by redistributing error cost over classes, and derives that the optimum reject threshold is unaffected.

contribution: Derives that Chow's optimum reject threshold, set by the costs of correct, wrong and rejected decisions, is unchanged when training labels are noisy, with a sketch of use in probabilistic LVQ classifiers.

No experiment at all; the LVQ integration (Sec. 4) is a sketch. 8-page ICAISC 2020 paper (LNAI 12415, pp. 547-554), found inside the full proceedings volume and read in full. Offline theory, not a runtime mechanism. Maintainer should judge whether this counts as a proved formal result.

title: Assured Deep Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Safe Robotic Systems
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science (including subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics)
evidence: "However, the behaviours within this environment are constrained using the safe abstract policies produced in stage three." (Sect. 4, Approach, Stage Four)
method: Four-stage AMARL: abstract MDP written in PRISM, quantitative verification synthesises safe abstract policies, which then constrain deep MARL (PPO plus intrinsic curiosity) during and after learning.
evaluation: Two multi-robot sim domains (ROS patrolling; Unity 3-agent flag collection, 1400 episodes x 6000 steps); baseline unconstrained MARL; cumulative risk vs 0.3 limit and goals collected; no hardware or latency figures.

No runtime interception: the QV-synthesised abstract policy constrains the state-action space during and after learning, so (a) fails under the 2026-11-13 ruling and only (c) is credited; check whether the maintainer reads action-space constraining as pre-emptive shielding. title: Reject Options for Incremental Regression Scenarios
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science (including subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics)
evidence: "we investigate how reject options can be facilitated that work next to an incremental algorithm and ideally reject only the initiate samples of new concepts in the data stream" (Sec. 1 Introduction)
method: Four model-agnostic reject rules for online next-step regression on a stream: Page-Hinkley drift rejection on the error stream, LoOP outlier score on inputs, LoOP on errors, and a mean-error baseline.
evaluation: kNN regressor; 4 chaotic streams (6000 points each) and 4 NEWBEE gait subjects; RMSE-reject curves. Page-Hinkley RMSE reduction 52-73% chaotic, 10-20% real vs baseline 40-55%, 4-9%. No hardware or latency.

flag: (ii) streaming/online abstention, and borderline: the abstention is per-sample withholding of a prediction (motivated by exoskeleton support) with no human, fallback system or acted-on consequence evaluated; could be read as E4 selective regression applied to streams. Short ICANN paper (pp. 248-259); results are averages in one table (Table 1) plus curves, no variance or significance. Error-based rejectors (Page-Hinkley, LoOP Error, baseline) use the observed error of the model, so maintainer should check whether rejection of sample i uses information only available after the true value is revealed; the text does not settle this. No theory despite abstract saying 'theoretical' setting (means synthetic data). File is the whole ICANN 2022 LNCS 13532 volume; only this chapter read.

title: Learning When to Defer to Humans for Short Answer Grading
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science (including subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics)
evidence: "We then used the autograder output as input to a logistic regression to learn when to defer. The learned logistic regression equation constitutes a deferral policy." (Abstract)
method: Post-hoc deferral policy for short-answer grading: logistic regression on autograder (SFRN) softmax outputs and question features decides defer-to-human; loss weight lambda trades accuracy against deferral rate.
evaluation: Middle-school physics answers, test N=467; vs no-deferral 61.75% and max-softmax threshold 76.33% at 27.09% deferral; LR lambda=1 77.97% at 24.17%; lambda=3.3 92.94% at 65.03%, ICC 0.94. No latency.
contribution: Learns a tunable logistic-regression policy for when an automatic short-answer grader should defer to a human, reaching expert-level accuracy while deferring about two thirds of items.
flag: (i) deferral to a human expert is the main contribution, but it is one-shot per-item selective prediction in a grading domain, so it sits close to the E4 line; no sequential or safety-critical aspect. Human is an oracle: deferred items simply receive the gold label, no human-in-loop study, so (e) not credited. Gains over the simple softmax-threshold heuristic are small (accuracy CIs overlap at lambda=1; only deferral rate is lower). Abstract claim of 'major reduction of human effort' is generous: human-level accuracy needs 65% deferral, and the discussion itself computes a 25% reduction. Single small proprietary dataset; test CIs come from bootstrapping 90% subsamples. File is the whole AIED 2023 LNAI 13916 volume; only this chapter read.

title: Principled Approaches for Learning to Defer with Multiple Experts
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science (including subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics)
evidence: "We present a study of surrogate losses and algorithms for the general problem of learning to defer with multiple experts." (Abstract)

The main experiments have no competing baseline, only 1 vs 2 vs 3 experts; the single baseline comparison (OvA surrogate of Verma et al.) is in an appendix on a synthetic two-expert CIFAR-10 setting and the paper calls the two methods comparable (about 92.19 vs 91.39%, table text was garbled in my read - check which number is whose). Inclusion rests on the proved bounds.

title: Interpretable and Fair Mechanisms for Abstaining Classifiers
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science (including subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics)
evidence: "In this paper, we have introduced IFAC, an Interpretable and Fair Abstaining Classifier." (Sec. 6 Discussion and Conclusion)
method: IFAC rejector on any probabilistic classifier: abstains on uncertain fair predictions and on confident predictions flagged unfair by association rules plus situation testing; flips unfair uncertain ones.
evaluation: ACSIncome and Wisconsin Recidivism; RF, NN, XGBoost; baselines full coverage and uncertainty-based abstention at target coverage 0.80; accuracy, precision, recall, per-group FNR, FPR, positive rate. No hardware or latency.
contribution: An abstaining classifier that rejects predictions for unfairness as well as uncertainty and gives rule-based and instance-based explanations to the human reviewer, narrowing group error gaps at 80 percent coverage.
flag: none of (i)-(v) in substance: a one-shot tabular classifier with a reject option applied to fairness. Rejected cases are said to go to a human reviewer with an explanation, which touches (i), but no human or handoff is evaluated, so criterion e is not claimed; maintainer may want to check this. Accuracy is below the uncertainty-only baseline on ACSIncome (RF .80 vs .83, NN .83 vs .86, XGB .84 vs .87) and equal on recidivism; the gain is fairness (ACSIncome RF FNR range 0.20 vs 0.40 UBAC vs 0.27 full coverage). Achieved coverage is not reported, only the 0.80 target. Full fairness tables in the appendix were not transcribed.

title: Learning to Complement and to Defer to Multiple Users
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science (including subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics)
evidence: "LECODU combines learning to defer and learning to complement strategies to make three key decisions" (Conclusion)
method: LECODU: a selection module chooses per input among AI alone, AI plus 1..M users, or 1..M users alone, trained with a per-label cost; an MLP fuses the labels.
evaluation: CIFAR-10N/10H, CIFAR10-IDN, Chaoyang; baselines seven single-expert L2D, Multi_L2D, CET, LECOMH; accuracy vs label cost: Chaoyang 98.13 vs LECOMH 95.82 at cost 2000. RTX A6000, about 2 s per 10000 images.
contribution: A learning-to-defer and learning-to-complement method that decides per input whether to use the AI, defer to several users, or combine both, and how many users to consult, under a labelling cost.
flag: (i) and (iii). One-shot image classification. Users are recorded human labels (CIFAR-10H, three Chaoyang pathologists) or synthetic noisy raters, anonymised by shuffling, so no live handoff or human response is studied; e not claimed. No formal results. Margins over the strongest baseline LECOMH are small on CIFAR (98.83 vs 98.78 at cost 2000 on CIFAR-10H; equal 99.86 on Chaoyang at cost 10000). Chaoyang was repartitioned by the authors. Remaining baseline values are in the supplementary table and were not transcribed.

title: Optimizing Delegation Between Human and AI Collaborative Agents
venue: Communications in Computer and Information Science
evidence: "our framework provides a manager model which learns through observations of team performance" (Abstract); the manager selects which agent acts at each decision point
method: Reinforcement-learning manager over a Managed MDP that delegates control, step by step, to one of several agents with different action sets, error rates and costs, without seeing their policies.
evaluation: Gridworld with simulated agents (step size 1-3, error none to high), two cost configurations; only baseline a random manager; results shown only as plots (Figure 4), no numbers in text. No hardware or latency.
contribution: Models human-AI delegation as a manager MDP whose actions are choices of which agent acts next, learned from team outcomes alone, and shows in gridworlds that it beats random delegation.
flag: (ii), nominally (i): delegation is a sequential action taken over time and is the main contribution. Weak evaluation - maintainer should check the floor: no numeric result appears anywhere in the text, only reward plots in Figure 4 against a random manager; the abstract's 'significantly outperforming alternative methods' has no statistical test and the only alternative is random choice. If plots against a random baseline do not count, this is exclude-E2. No real humans despite the title - all agents are simulated, handoff not studied (no 'e'). Grid size, training algorithm and hyperparameters are not reported. Delegation is about performance and cost, not a safety halt.

title: A Simple Heuristic for Controlling Human Workload in Learning to Defer
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science (including subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics)
evidence: "The paper proposes and explores a simple yet effective heuristic technique allowing to impose constraints on the fraction of samples deferred to an expert" (Abstract)
method: Post-hoc score threshold for learning to defer: derive a model-vs-expert confidence score from any trained L2D pair, pick on a held-out set the threshold maximising accuracy subject to required coverage, apply per sample.
evaluation: Synthetic 2-D data and CIFAR-10H with crowd labels; applied to confidence-threshold, natural-loss and softmax-parametrisation L2D; coverage violation under 1% mostly, under 5% always over 100 synthetic sets. Figures only.
contribution: Adds a coverage constraint to existing learning-to-defer models through a validation-set score threshold, letting samples be routed to a capacity-limited human expert on arrival without solving a MILP.
flag: (i) learning to defer to a human expert with a workload cap, but BORDERLINE E2: the only stated numbers are the coverage-violation bounds (under 1% in the vast majority, under 5% in all of 100 synthetic datasets); accuracy is shown only in coverage-accuracy plots (Fig. 4) with no table, and the heuristic is never compared with the MILP methods it positions against or with an unconstrained run. The three base L2D methods (including the confidence-threshold baseline) are plotted side by side, which is the only baseline-like comparison, and the paper says it does not aim to rank them. No theoretical guarantee (listed as future work). Single-author ICPR 2024 paper, 11 pages. Human expert is simulated from recorded labels; workload control is the topic but no handoff study, so (e) and the human handoff cell not credited. File is a whole ICPR 2024 LNCS 15327 volume; only this chapter read.

title: IBGP: Imperfect Byzantine Generals Problem for Zero-Shot Robustness in Communicative Multi-agent Systems
evidence: On consensus failure agents "just give up cooperative catching at this step and do nothing" (Sec. 4.2), and robustness under malicious communication is the reported outcome (Sec. 5).
method: A (k, lambda) multi-round broadcast consensus protocol over learned communicating QMIX agents, with a hidden random round count; an agent acts only when the vote threshold is met, else abstains.
evaluation: Predator-prey, Hallway and SMAC against recursive training, AME and ADMAC: robustness 96.1-100 percent versus AME 6.3-100 percent and ADMAC 6.4-64.5 percent; lambda ablation; no latency or hardware figures.
contribution: A relaxed Byzantine consensus protocol giving communicating RL agents zero-shot robustness to malicious messages, holding 96-100 percent of attack-free performance where prior defences fall to 6-25 percent.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - QMIX agents with learned communication; despite the LLM framing in the introduction no LLM agents were evaluated. Check (a): the gate is internal to the protocol (agents abstain when consensus fails) rather than a supervisory filter sitting over a nominal action, so the maintainer may rule this not STRICTLY runtime interception and reduce it to (c) only. The safety outcome is a robustness percentage (test return under attack divided by attack-free return), not a collision, violation or detection rate; there is no absolute hazard count. Theorems 1-4 are probabilistic ("with a high level of confidence"), target selection is shown NP-complete with a 1-over-k_max greedy approximation, and the weakest case 3z_vs_1r reaches only 51.5 percent. Ablations cover lambda and attacker probability only. Record is the 2026 Springer version; the arXiv v2 read here is the AAMAS 2025 submission with the same title. One fetch.

title: Risk-Based Thresholding for Reliable Anomaly Detection in Concentrated Solar Power Plants
evidence: "Our framework also incorporates an abstention mechanism, allowing high-risk predictions to be deferred to domain experts." (Abstract)
method: Anomaly-score thresholding with two thresholds chosen by an extended Learn-then-Test procedure (xLTT) giving finite-sample risk control, abstaining between them; scores from a conditional normalizing-flow density forecaster (DensityAD).
evaluation: Infrared images from two solar plants (16343 and 15181 samples); DensityAD AUROC 94.25/91.93 vs five baselines; thresholds vs F1, G-Mean, Z-score at alpha=delta=0.1 (figure only); inference 201/178 ms on A100.
contribution: Selects anomaly-detection thresholds with finite-sample risk guarantees and an abstention band that defers uncertain infrared images to experts, deployed for months on two concentrated solar power plants.
flag: none of (i)-(v) cleanly: abstention with deferral to domain experts exists, but it is one of four contributions (risk-controlled thresholds, a new density anomaly detector, deployment analysis, simulated dataset) and the title and most results concern thresholding and detector accuracy; it is a detector with a reject option applied to one domain, hence E4 (E1 as 'component only' would also be defensible). The monitor labels images for predictive maintenance and does not halt or veto any plant action. Abstention rates and risk values appear ONLY in Fig. 5 and Fig. 6; no number for abstention rate is given in the text or any table, so the abstention mechanism itself has no checkable figure in the body. The risk-control guarantee is inherited from the cited Learn-then-Test work, no new proof here. Validation set is reused as the calibration set. Expert deferral is not exercised with real experts. Supplementary material not in the file. File is a whole ECML PKDD 2025 LNAI 16022 volume; only this chapter read.

title: Is Uncertainty Quantification a Viable Alternative to Learned Deferral?
evidence: "We compare two learned deferral approaches and five approaches based on uncertainty in their ability to correctly defer images that are likely to be misclassified." (Sec. 2 Methods)
method: Empirical comparison of deferral-to-expert strategies on a ResNet50 glaucoma classifier: one-stage and two-stage learned deferral losses versus thresholded uncertainty from softmax, ensembles, SWAG, MC Dropout and a Bayesian network.
evaluation: AIROGS fundus images (101442, about 3% positive); balanced accuracy on non-deferred cases vs deferral rate, in-distribution and under Gaussian noise and blur; deferral results in figures only. No hardware or latency.
contribution: Finds that uncertainty-thresholded deferral, notably SWAG, defers misclassified glaucoma images more reliably than two learned-deferral methods, which are cost-sensitive, shortcut-prone and degrade under distribution shift.
flag: (i) deferral to a human expert is the whole subject, as a comparative study (learned deferral vs uncertainty thresholding) rather than a new method; one-shot image classification, so near the E4 line. The only numeric table (Table 1) is plain classification performance (AUC 0.799-0.852, bAcc 0.674-0.766); all deferral results are curves in Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 with no tabulated values, no seeds or error bars, so the headline conclusion rests on reading plots. No human expert is modelled: deferral only removes cases from the scored set, so the learned-deferral losses are used without expert predictions and (e) is not credited. Only two learned-deferral methods, one dataset; OOD is synthetic corruption, and the real OOD set (Chaksu) was dropped because all classifiers failed on it. MC Dropout behaves contrary to the paper's own thesis (accuracy falls as deferral rises), and two-stage learned deferral defers mostly positives. Workshop paper (UNSURE 2025, pp. 34-44); appendix not in the file. File is the whole workshop volume; only this chapter read.

title: When In Doubt, Abstain: The Impact of Abstention on Strategic Classification
evidence: "optimal abstention ensures that the principal's utility (or loss) is no worse than in a non-abstention setting" (Abstract); Theorems 3.1-3.3 (Sec. 3).
method: Stackelberg model of strategic classification where the principal commits to a classifier and an abstention function with cost c; derives the optimal abstention rule against feature-manipulating agents.
evaluation: Proved: abstention never hurts (Thm 3.1), structure of the optimal rule (Thm 3.2), strategic principals abstain at least as much (Thm 3.3); closed-form uniform case study. Synthetic simulations only, trends without tabulated values; no baseline method.
contribution: Extends the reject option to strategic classification, proving that optimal abstention never hurts the principal and that principals facing manipulating agents should abstain at least as often as otherwise.
flag: (v) theory of the reject option under strategic agents; meets the floor only through proved results. Experiments are synthetic one-dimensional simulations with no numeric results in the text and no competing method. Human review is only the stated interpretation of abstention cost c, not modelled. Classifier is fixed in the theorems; niche extension, so maintainer should judge whether it is foundational enough or E4. runtime_interceptor set to no as pure theory.

title: Remind Me of Something? Zero-Shot Learning for Trustworthy Image Comparison in Rolling Stock
evidence: "While this requires human intervention in 9.94% of the comparisons, it enables a highly balanced and accurate performance" (Sect. 3 Discussion)
method: Top-10 label-cloud distance from a frozen DenseNet/ImageNet-1k oracle compares image pairs; two thresholds add an unreliable band that is passed to a human.
evaluation: Offline, COIL-100 pairs (7200 images). Oracle recall 0.509/spec 0.976/B-Acc 0.743; label cloud 0.907/0.919/0.913 (AUROC 0.966); reliable cloud 0.911/0.981/0.946 at 9.94% unreliable. No latency or hardware.
contribution: A zero-shot label-cloud distance over a pre-trained classifier decides whether two images show the same object, with a two-threshold unreliable band (about 10% of pairs) left to a human operator.
flag: none of (i)-(v): one-shot pairwise classifier with a fixed two-threshold reject band; the abstract says 'learning to defer' but nothing is learned about deferral and no human or operator is in the experiment, so (i) holds only nominally. Main contribution is the label-cloud distance; the reject band is one subsection (2.4). Thresholds are optimised and scored on the same pairs (authors admit 'a slight positive bias'). COIL-100 is not rolling-stock data. 'Computationally light' and edge deployment are asserted, never measured. The file is a whole ICIAP 2025 Workshops volume (LNCS 16170); only pp. 323-334 read. Corresponding-author mark is on Leone but the printed email is giuseppe.mazzola@unipa.it (possible typesetting slip). Self-described proof of concept.

title: On AI-Based Critical Systems’ Embedded LLM Trustworthiness: A Real-Time Analytical Filters for LLM Output Control
evidence: "We implement FORT (Filters for Output Reliability and Trustworthiness), an LLM trustworthiness controller that intercepts inputs and outputs at semantic and logical layers and applies analytical filters with policy thresholds." (Sect. 3)
method: FORT: layered runtime controller around an embedded LLM - pre-inference semantic and context filters, post-inference uncertainty rejection and leakage checks, plus a deterministic latency enforcer that pads or rejects over-budget responses.
evaluation: None reported: architecture, a threat-versus-defense matrix and a C++ llama.cpp prototype with quantized GPT, Claude and Mistral; no experiment, metric, baseline or measured latency anywhere in the body.
contribution: Proposes FORT, a six-filter runtime trustworthiness controller that gates embedded LLM inputs and outputs with semantic, uncertainty, privacy and deterministic-timing checks for edge cyber-physical systems.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - embedded LLMs (GPT, Claude, Mistral) in cyber-physical systems. The abstract claims FORT significantly reduces adversarial success rates and sets a new baseline for LLM robustness, but no such number exists in the body: there is no experiment at all, only Tables 1-2 mapping capabilities to threats, hence E2. The conclusion softens this to prototype testing suggests edge feasibility. Also check: no multi-agent aspect; latency bounds are asserted, never measured; demo code link (github.com CodEUrope FORT-ICDS25_demo) not verified; self-citation [1] is the only prior basis.

title: Confidence-Aware Automated Assessment of Student-Drawn Scientific Models
venue: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence in Education
evidence: "we propose a confidence-aware vision-based approach for automated scoring of student-generated scientific drawings." (Introduction); responses below a confidence threshold are deferred to human review by design.
method: ViT-base with LoRA scores student drawings; confidence from averaged predictions over 20 perturbed views with Top-eta view selection; low-confidence responses are meant to go to human review.
evaluation: 3576 drawings, six items, 3 classes; vs frozen ViT, ViT+LoRA, CA-Uniform. Accuracy 0.789, kappa 0.760 (LoRA 0.766/0.708); confidence-accuracy r=0.649; latency 20.57 ms vs 1.04 ms, hardware unstated.
contribution: Confidence-aware ViT scoring of student-drawn science models with test-time view averaging; the defer-to-human threshold is proposed but never evaluated.
flag: none of (i)-(v): one-shot classifier with a reject option applied to educational assessment. The deferral rule itself is not evaluated (no threshold value, coverage, risk-coverage or deferral rate; expert review said to be in progress), so E2 would equally apply to the defer mechanism. Main contribution is scoring accuracy, not deferral. Gains of CA-Selective over CA-Uniform are tiny (0.789 vs 0.786 accuracy) with no significance test.

title: Differences in Alignment Behavior between Single-Agent and Multi-Agent LLM Systems: Implications for Human-AI Teaming
venue: Communications in Computer and Information Science
evidence: "Most alarmingly, the most severe forms of emergent misalignment were found only in the Multi-AI condition." (Sect. 4.3)
method: Adversarial island-survival simulation comparing one LLM agent with three-agent teams; agent actions embedded, UMAP-reduced and clustered, then characterised by an LLM-as-a-judge safety and ethics rubric.
evaluation: Six runs, one LLM, SAS versus MAS as the only comparison; behavioural-cluster shares (about 70% crisis-leadership takeover for the single agent) and judge risk levels; no hazard, violation or survival metric.
contribution: Shows that multi-agent LLM teams produce failure modes absent in single agents - communication collapse and emergent shared ideologies - while also deferring more readily to human decisions.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM agents are the analysed system. Twelve-page HCII poster; the authors call the results preliminary and state that the simulation limits direct quantitative comparisons and that they did not compare objective success metrics such as the number of survivors, so no hazard or violation rate against a baseline exists: E2 on the evaluation floor. This is the record I most expect to be overturned to include under (c), since multi-agent LLM safety is the primary claim and the cluster shares plus judge risk scores are quantitative. Human-AI teaming is discussion only - no human participants and no takeover measurement - so (e) is not credited. Judge rubric and cluster labels are produced by an LLM (Claude Sonnet 4), i.e. the measurement instrument is itself unvalidated.

title: Adaptive and Uncertainty-Aware Intrusion Detection with Hybrid Meta-learning Under Proxy-Adversarial Exposure
venue: Lecture Notes of the Institute for Computer Sciences, Social-Informatics and Telecommunications Engineering, LNICST
evidence: "A third action, uncertain (action 3) operates as an abstention mechanism following the reject-option classification paradigm in which the agent signals insufficient confidence and defers the flow to the hybrid meta-learner" (Sect. 2.2; ligatures normalised)
method: PPO defender co-trained with a proxy adversary labels flows benign, malicious or uncertain; uncertain flows above an adaptive threshold are deferred to a prototype plus Reptile meta-learner fallback.
evaluation: CIC-IDS2017, cross-dataset CSE-CIC-IDS2018 (100k flows). Acc 0.81/0.724; RF 50.5%, LR 52.6%, shallow NN 57.3% cross-dataset; deferral <1% and 0.23%; deferred acc 0.74/0.87; hybrid +17.8 points over statistical-only fallback; 1.65 ms, 3.01 ms with fallback; NVIDIA L4.
contribution: An intrusion detector trained against a proxy adversary abstains on low-confidence flows and defers them to a few-shot statistical-neural fallback, reporting 1.65-3.01 ms per-flow latency and cross-dataset retention of about 89%.
flag: (i) borderline - deferral goes to an automated fallback model, not a human, and is one of three co-equal contributions (adversarial MARL, meta-learning, deferral); the paper itself calls the meta-learning module and staged training 'the central contributions'. If the maintainer reads deferral as the main contribution this becomes an include: the floor is met only thinly (hybrid vs statistical-only fallback '+17.8 point gain', no absolute figures, no table). Doubts: final deferral rate is under 1% in-domain and 0.23% cross-dataset, so deferral cannot explain the headline numbers; there is no ablation without deferral; baselines appear only for the cross-dataset test; ECE not computed (authors admit); in-domain accuracy 0.81 is well below the 0.95-0.99 of cited static models; 3,587 false alarms vs 3,218 true positives. Inconsistencies: abstract defers when confidence falls below a threshold, Sect. 2.4 defers flows 'exceeding tau'; Fig. 4 caption calls the in-domain CIC-IDS2017 matrix 'cross-dataset'; F1 0.724 identical to accuracy 72.4%; typos '1.65,ms', '22,MB'. 'Multi-agent' is one defender plus one synthetic perturbation agent, nominal only. Hardware is a datacentre GPU, not edge. Volume is SecureComm 2026, LNICST 705, copyright 2027; file is the whole proceedings, only pp. 74-88 read (reference list skimmed).

title: Anticipatory Mechanisms in Autonomous Vehicles: Architectural Integration from a Microethical Perspective
venue: Communications in Computer and Information Science
evidence: "The output is an override signal to the Behavior Arbitrator in the form of three trajectory constraints: (a) a recommended maximum speed ..., (b) a recommended maximum acceleration, and (c) path regions to avoid." (Sect. 4.2)
method: Anticipatory Mechanism: rule-based O(N) monitor beside the learned Transformer behaviour predictor; matches hazardous multi-agent templates at the perception rate (about 10 Hz) and overrides the behaviour arbitrator.
evaluation: No experiment: architectural proposal plus one Lean theorem (ego_must_decelerate, targetSpeed <= 10 km per h) and a retrospective 2023 Cruise robotaxi analysis; only measured number is about 100 ms per step for the author's Transformer BP.
contribution: Proposes an anticipatory, microethics-grounded safety monitor that detects hazardous multi-agent configurations in linear time and overrides an autonomous vehicle's behaviour arbitrator before avoidance becomes impossible.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the monitor wraps a learned Transformer behaviour-prediction and decision layer in an AV stack. E2 because the paper itself concludes that quantitative evaluation combining accident reconstruction, scenario simulation, and formal verification will be needed to assess AM's safety contribution. Check whether the Lean fragment counts as a formal result: as printed, theorem ego_must_decelerate just constructs a record with targetSpeed := 10.0 from assumed premises, so it fixes a specification rather than proving a safety guarantee, and the author concedes formal description is necessary but not sufficient. The 99% coverage of 37 NHTSA pre-crash scenarios is cited for RSS, not measured here. Single-author design paper, no code, no simulator; the Cruise analysis is counterfactual (earlier deceleration could plausibly have prevented the secondary collision). Endsley SA Level 2 is the machine's awareness, not a human's, so (e) is not credited.

title: Information Design Against Gaming and Learning Adversaries
evidence: Sec 1: "The abstain signal is the principal's only design lever, and the principal commits to an abstention budget".
method: Classifier API answers accept, reject or abstain under an abstention budget; compares random (coarse) and boundary-localizing abstention rules and mixtures against gaming and model-extraction adversaries.
evaluation: Theory: Blackwell incomparability, query-complexity bounds, Pareto frontier (Thms 3,5,7,9,10). 7 tasks, logistic victim, 20 seeds; gaming success 1.000 (none or coarse) vs 0.000 (localizing); no latency.
contribution: Proves that abstaining near a classifier's decision boundary blocks gaming but speeds model extraction, while random abstention does the reverse, and characterises the trade-off between the two.
flag: (v) applies only on a generous reading and this is BORDERLINE: abstention placement is the main object and optimal-rule bounds are proved, but the paper is about adversarial information leakage through an API (gaming and model extraction), not prediction risk, safety interception or deferral to a human; manual review and deferral appear only as interpretations of the abstain bit. If (v) is meant as classical reject-option theory, this is exclude-E1. Doubts: experiments do not test the ternary localizing rule against a learner (Protocol B returns counterfactual points, strictly more informative); the up-to-200x gap is against random sampling, 3-6x against ActiveThief; the intro concedes an adaptive adversary can binary-search on labels alone; single author, independent researcher.

title: Bootstrapping Context-Aware Guardrails for Industrial Multi-agent Systems
evidence: "Input guardrails filter user prompts before they enter the system; reasoning guardrails constrain planning, tool use, and action execution; and output guardrails validate final responses before they reach users or downstream agents." (Sect. 2, Main Purpose)
method: Pipeline crawls websites, internal documents and database schemas into a structured organizational and technical context profile, then generates input-layer guardrails (topic boundaries, threat and compliance filters) for human review.
evaluation: Demonstration only: prototype wired to the FlexGPT industrial multi-agent system, screenshots of blocked prompts, full bootstrapping and validation cycle about one minute; no baseline, no block, leak or false-positive rate.
contribution: Demonstrates semi-automatic bootstrapping of deployment-specific input guardrails for industrial multi-agent LLM systems from organizational and technical context, with a human validating the draft before deployment.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an enterprise LLM multi-agent system (FlexGPT). Six-page PAAMS demonstration paper (pp. 433-438) with no evaluation section; the abstract's claim to reduce manual effort and improve completeness when compared with fully manual specification is never measured, so E2. The human reviewer validates generated rules at configuration time, not at runtime, so (e) is not credited; multi-agent is the deployment setting rather than a measured safety property, so (c) is at best nominal. Only input-layer guardrails are implemented; reasoning and output layers are future work.

title: Confidence sets for classification
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science (including subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics)
evidence: "we derive a new definition of a rule that responds to the classification with reject option" (Sect. 5 Conclusion; ligatures normalised)
method: Epsilon-confidence set: classify only when the score max(eta,1-eta) lies in its top epsilon quantile, else reject; plug-in version estimates eta and the score CDF on two samples.
evaluation: Theory: Prop. 2 optimality among rules classifying a fraction epsilon; Thm 2 plug-in risk consistency (proved in appendix). Simulation, B=100: Bayes risk 0.389/0.324/0.238 for epsilon 1/0.5/0.1; logistic plug-in 0.40/0.34/0.25 at n=1000.
contribution: Defines a reject-option rule that fixes the proportion of points classified, shows it is risk-optimal at that coverage, and proves that its plug-in estimate is asymptotically consistent, with a small simulation.
flag: (v): foundational reject-option theory for binary classification with a fixed classification rate, linked to conformal prediction. Proved: Thm 2 (asymptotic consistency of the plug-in rule, appendix). Stated without proof: Prop. 1 ('straightforward'), Prop. 2 optimality (no proof in the text), Thm 1 Gaussian-mixture risk ('omitted'). No finite-sample bounds (listed as ongoing work); consistency is asymptotic only. Experiment is one synthetic 10-dimensional logit model with random forest and logistic plug-ins, no competing reject method as baseline (epsilon=1 is the no-reject reference). Purely one-shot and offline: no sequential, human or latency aspect, so RQ relevance is background. Binary case only. File is the whole SLDS 2015 volume (LNAI 9047); only pp. 301-312 read; appendix proof skimmed, not checked.

title: Double ramp loss based reject option classifier
evidence: "In this paper, we have proposed a new loss LDR (double ramp) for learning the reject option classifier." (Sect. 5 Conclusion; ligatures normalised)
method: Double ramp loss, a bounded non-convex surrogate upper-bounding the 0-d-1 reject loss; classifier and rejection width learned jointly by difference-of-convex programming, kernelisable.
evaluation: Synthetic, Ionosphere, Parkinsons; 10x10-fold CV; baseline double hinge (LDH). 0-d-1 risk, rejection rate, accuracy on unrejected, d=0.05-0.5. E.g. synthetic d=0.2: risk 0.155 vs 0.17, rejection 43.2% vs 72.7%. No latency.
contribution: Proposes a double ramp surrogate loss for the 0-d-1 reject-option loss and a DC-programming learner, reporting lower risk and lower rejection rates than the double hinge baseline on three small datasets.
flag: (v) borderline: a new surrogate loss for the reject option, but the theory is thin - Thm 1 (upper bound, limit and boundedness properties) is stated with 'proof omitted due to the space constraints'; only Lemma 1 (non-negative rejection width at the minimum) is proved. No consistency or generalisation result, and DC programming gives a local optimum only. If the maintainer requires a proved optimality or consistency result for (v), this is a one-shot reject-option classifier and should be exclude-E4. Empirical floor is met (single baseline, LDH; generalised hinge discussed but not run). Claim 'performs better' is not uniform: LDH has lower risk at d=0.05, 0.1 (synthetic), d=0.2-0.3 (Ionosphere) and d=0.35 (Parkinsons), which the authors do state. Datasets are tiny (300, 351, 195 points). Robustness to label noise is argued, not separately tested. No sequential, human or latency aspect. File is the whole PAKDD 2015 Part I volume; only pp. 151-163 read.

title: Improving automatic classifiers through interaction
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science (including subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics)
evidence: "But the classifier can sometimes request the intervention of a human (the oracle), who gives it the correct label of the instance being considered." (Sect. 1 Introduction; ligatures normalised)
method: Streaming classifier defers low-confidence instances to an oracle via a max-probability threshold, updates itself only on oracle labels, and recomputes the threshold after each query (4Dyn).
evaluation: 20 synthetic MOA streams, 100k test instances each, NaiveBayes and HoeffdingTreeNB. F0.5 EMIC/query rate: never-query 0.824/0%; static 0.835/18.7%; learn fixed threshold 0.824/36.1%; 4Dyn 0.882/1.37% (NB). Tree: 0.820, 0.829, 0.711, 0.837. No latency.
contribution: An online classifier that defers uncertain stream instances to a human oracle learns only from those answers and re-tunes its deferral threshold over time, raising cost-aware performance while cutting queries to about 1%.
flag: (i) and (ii): deferral to a human oracle is the subject and it is a decision taken over a data stream with the threshold adapted online. Caveats: the oracle is simulated (always-correct ground truth), no real human, no response-time or workload study, so 'e' and the human handoff cell rest only on the query-rate and cost-aware EMIC metric - drop them if the maintainer wants actual human data. Streams are synthetic and stationary (no concept drift, authors say so).
