Learning with a fixed threshold makes things worse (tree EMIC 0.711 below the 0.820 no-query baseline; NB query rate doubles to 36%). The claim that the threshold can only stay or decrease is stated with the proof omitted. Results are averages over 20 streams, no significance test seen. The per-stream results and learning-curve passage between Table 5 and the conclusions was only skimmed. File is the whole ICAISC 2016 Part II volume; only pp. 3-13 read.

title: Detecting novel class for sensor-based activity recognition using reject rule
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science (including subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics)
evidence: Sec 1: "we have worked out a reject rule to reject uncertain data, and treat uncertain data as novel class sample"
method: Learn++.NSE incremental ensemble with ELM base classifiers plus a reject rule: batches whose L2 loss distance to class codewords exceeds a running-mean threshold are rejected as novel class.
evaluation: UCI Opportunity body-worn sensor data, 130 features, 1000-sample batches; baseline plain Learn++.NSE; test accuracy 0.826 vs 0.792 (T=20, 10 novel) and 0.813 vs 0.801 (100 novel); no hardware or latency.
contribution: Adds a loss-distance reject rule to the Learn++.NSE stream ensemble so that uncertain activity-recognition batches are flagged as a novel class, with a small accuracy gain over plain Learn++.NSE.
flag: none of (i)-(v) cleanly; nearest is (ii) since data arrive as a stream, but rejection is a novel-class detector applied per batch, not an abstain action studied over time, and the paper says testing 'is not time-ordered'. No human or fallback receives rejected data. Chapter located inside IDCS 2016 proceedings volume (LNCS 9864, pp. 34-44); only that chapter read. Weak evaluation: only accuracy is reported, no rejection rate or novel-class detection rate, one dataset, how rejected samples are scored in accuracy is not explained; algorithm figures (Fig. 2-3) not present in text. The second threshold needs true labels so only the first applies at test time.

title: Diagnosing Override Regimes in Multi-hop RAG Choosers: Decision-Relevant AUC and Rescue-Hurt Geometry
evidence: Sec 1: "we learn a binary gate that decides, per-question, whether to override the default with the challenger"
method: Diagnostic study of a learning-to-defer style override gate (LightGBM, 19 features) choosing between a default and a challenger RAG pipeline; introduces decision-relevant AUC on rescue-vs-hurt rows.
evaluation: 2WikiMultihopQA n=1000, Qwen3-8B; default-only baseline, drop-one ablation, LR/XGBoost, GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3 judges; OOF AUC 0.72 vs decision-AUC 0.575, delta EM 0.0 pp; Mistral slice +3.0 pp at 13% override; no latency.
contribution: Shows that override gates between RAG pipelines can look healthy on aggregate AUC while being near chance on the rescue-vs-hurt rows that change the answer, and proposes reporting decision-relevant AUC.
flag: none of (i)-(v) on my reading; nearest is (iii), but the 'experts' are two retrieval-pipeline configurations of the same LLM and the decision is one-shot per question, with no human, safeguard or sequential element. The paper is explicitly a diagnostic and evaluation-metric study, not a deferral method ('diagnostic probe rather than as a proposed new chooser'), and its headline result is a null. Maintainer may prefer E1 if he reads it as an evaluation-protocol paper. Chapter located inside APWeb-WAIM 2026 proceedings (LNCS 16995, pp. 355-368); only that chapter read, sections 7-9 skimmed. Record year 2027 is the volume copyright year. Model name 'Qwen3-8B' and judge 'DeepSeek-V3' are as printed. Mistral positive slice has default and challenger EM both 0.082, a very weak regime.

title: Knowing when to Defer: A Risk-Calibrated Deferral Policy for Agentic AI in Financial Decision-Making
evidence: Abstract: "an agent acts only when a conservative upper estimate of material-error risk falls below a threshold set by the consequence of an undetected error, the measured coverage of verification, the value of timely action and the cost of review"
method: Closed-form expected-cost act-or-defer threshold per decision, using a calibrated Clopper-Pearson upper risk bound, measured validator coverage q, materiality and review cost; outputs above threshold are deferred to human review.
evaluation: 44 facts from 6 issuers, 358+251 constructed outputs; baselines always-act, always-defer, global thresholds, Chow reject, L2D; coverage 34.9%, uncaught wrong 0.0 vs 8.0 always-act and 0.4 matched; held-out stress 7.2 uncaught; no latency.
contribution: Derives a per-decision act-or-defer threshold for financial AI agents that tightens with materiality and loosens with measured verification coverage, and shows its safety collapses when that coverage estimate is stale.
flag: (i) deferral to human review, also arguably (iv) an approval gate before write-back; (ii) is NOT met in practice. Doubts: single author listed as Independent Researcher; no agent or LLM is actually run - candidate outputs are hand-constructed perturbations of 44 public facts, each judged one-shot, so 'agentic' is framing only (paper admits it 'does not evaluate ... a fully autonomous agent'). Human reviewer is not real: residual human error e_H=0.005 and all costs are scenario assumptions; criterion (e) not credited because the handoff itself is not studied. Proposition 1 is a one-line algebraic result. Test splits are tiny (mean 65 items) and interior risk bins are nearly empty. Zero-uncaught result holds only on the in-grammar suite the validator was designed on; on held-out error families validator detection falls to 0.067 and the policy admits 7.2 uncaught per split or defers everything. Refers to an 'earlier version of this work', check for a duplicate record. Abstract numbers were all found in Tables 2-4. Chapter located inside MIWAI 2026 proceedings (LNAI 17148, pp. 135-149); sections 5.6 and 6 only skimmed. If the maintainer requires a real sequential or human element this drops to E4.

title: Provable Limits and Certified Deferral for Verbalized Uncertainty in Small Language Models
evidence: Sec 3.1: the policy answers when calibrated confidence is at least the threshold and "defers to a human otherwise".
method: Small LLM verbalises a confidence, Platt-calibrated; a Clopper-Pearson certified threshold answers or defers to a human; propositions on limits of temperature scaling for verbalised confidence.
evaluation: 11 open models (0.5B-14B) on ARC-Challenge and TruthfulQA MC; calibration baselines; at 20% risk only 3 of 22 pairs certified (coverage 99.8%, 93.3%, 43.6%); MacBook Air M4, 0.14-2.55 s per question.
contribution: Shows that verbalised confidence in small language models often cannot be fixed by temperature scaling and gives a certified answer-or-defer threshold, which certifies only the largest models at a 20% risk budget.
flag: (i) only nominally: the deferral target is called a human but no human or handoff is modelled or evaluated; in substance a one-shot selective-prediction threshold for a language model on single multiple-choice questions, built from standard tools, so E4 under the scope ruling. A maintainer could argue (i) or (v) (Props 1-3, Cor 1), but the results are elementary. Check: no certificate at 10% risk; i.i.d. assumption; 200-question calibration sets; runs on a laptop via Ollama, which is why edge deployment is listed (latency is reported, not constrained).

title: Decentralized Belief Propagation in LLM Agents: A Brain-Inspired Approach to AI Safety Analysis
evidence: "Misinformation resistance improves dramatically from 0.21 to 0.79, representing nearly a four-fold increase in the system's ability to prevent harmful information propagation." (Sect. 4.4)
method: Models belief diffusion among LLM agents as a Metropolis-Hastings naming game: a speaker proposes its belief, the listener accepts by an LLM-weighted utility, with adaptive learning rate and annealed temperature.
evaluation: Simulation of 100 agents on a scale-free graph against an SIS baseline; misinformation resistance 0.21 to 0.79, truth propagation 0.93 to 0.98, belief modularity 0.23 to 0.41, false-information peak 0.85 to 0.34, with standard deviations.
contribution: Replaces epidemic models of belief spread among LLM agents with a Metropolis-Hastings naming game, reporting higher misinformation resistance and monitorable belief clusters usable as early warning indicators.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: nominally yes - the analysed system is a network of LLM agents, but no model, prompt, implementation or code is ever named, so the agents may be numerical stand-ins. Serious doubts: the headline 0.21 to 0.79 gain compares two MODELS of the same network (MHNG versus SIS), not a safeguard against a baseline, so it is not evidence that any hazard was prevented; Fig. 1 reports modularity 0.000 while Table 1 reports 0.41 plus or minus 0.06; Sect. 4.5 presents 0.000 communication success rate, 0.000 average human comprehension and 0.000 total agents as findings and then interprets them, which reads as machine-generated prose over empty data; Theorems 1-3 are stated with only a proof sketch for the convergence proposition; DistilBERT [13] is in the reference list but never used. I recommend include only because quantitative safety metrics with a baseline are present and (c) is the primary claim; I expect the maintainer to overturn this to E1 (a model, not a safety mechanism) or E2.

title: Unchaotic agents
evidence: "Throughout the execution phase, the agent did not submit any material without first seeking my review and explicit permission." (Sect. 5.2 The execution phase)
method: Conceptual critique of Shapira et al. Agents of Chaos plus one unscripted single-case deployment of an LLM agent under relational-stability framing on a conference-submission task.
evaluation: n=1 unscripted deployment (Claude Cowork on Sonnet 4.6), 27 candidate talks, 15 conferences, about 4 h setup; no baseline, no ablation, no quantitative safety or hazard metric.
contribution: Argues that documented agentic failures follow from unstable relational deployment conditions rather than architecture, offering a single successful deployment as an existence proof.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (LLM agent) but no runtime interceptor at all. Open Forum commentary; the only evidence is one unscripted case with no baseline, ablation or quantitative metric, so the evaluation floor fails; maintainer may prefer E3 (essay). Leans on two self-cited Zenodo preprints (Hedberg 2025a,2025b) for its MEI framework; unaffiliated author, private e-mail address; the supporting corpus of 25 empirical studies is asserted, not tabulated.

title: WisdomNet: trustable machine learning toward error-free classification
evidence: Network outputs 'reject' via an added conjugate neuron instead of a class label so that it yields "only the true output" (Section 3.1, closely paraphrased)
method: Adds a conjugate 'reject' output neuron to a trained classifier and fine-trains on samples the base network misclassified, trading rejections for zero error.
evaluation: UCI BC/BN/IO, MNIST pairs, Dogs vs Cats; baseline is base MLP/ConvNet/ResNet50 only; test error 0% with reject 1.5-13.58% (BN 1.5, BC 10.05, IO 13.58, MNIST 4v9 4.2, cats-dogs 6.5); GTX 1080 Ti.
contribution: A classifier architecture with a learned reject neuron that reports zero test error on small binary benchmarks at reject rates of 1.5 to 13.6 percent.
flag: none of (i)-(v): one-shot classifier with a reject option; deferral to a human is mentioned but never studied; no theory. Title matches the record (minor wording 'Towards' vs 'toward'); arXiv id 2610.15299 is a 2026 id for a 2020 journal paper, so check the id mapping. No comparison with any other rejection method (threshold rejection discussed only qualitatively); cats-dogs 'testing results' appear to be on the validation set; 0% error claims rest on small test sets (57-137 samples for UCI).

title: SYNAPSE-X: a calibration-aware vision transformer framework for selective referral in multi-class brain tumor MRI classification
evidence: Sec 3.3: "if its calibrated confidence was greater than or equal to threshold tau, and referred if its confidence was below tau"
method: Vision Transformer four-class brain tumor MRI classifier with post hoc temperature scaling; cases with calibrated max confidence below 0.85 are referred for expert review.
evaluation: 7,023 public MRI images (1,311 test) plus 3,264 external; threshold sweep 0.70-0.95; at 0.85 referral 6.7%, retained accuracy 99.12% vs 98.41% overall; external 8.4% referral, 98.74%; ECE 0.041 to 0.018; no latency reported.
contribution: Applies temperature-scaled confidence thresholding to a Vision Transformer brain-tumor MRI classifier, referring 6.7% of low-confidence cases and raising retained-case accuracy from 98.41% to 99.12%.
flag: none of (i)-(v): nominally (i) since rejected cases go 'for expert review', but this is a fixed max-softmax threshold on a one-shot classifier applied to a domain, judged by risk-coverage; no expert is modelled or involved, and the paper itself calls for future radiologist-in-the-loop studies. No comparison of the referral rule against any other abstention method, only against no referral. Public image-level Kaggle-style datasets without patient identifiers, so leakage cannot be ruled out (acknowledged); 'corrected experimental cohort' wording suggests a revision after review. Hardware and inference time not found by keyword search; sections 2 and the literature table only skimmed.

title: Reliable prediction of anti-diabetic drug failure using a reject option
evidence: Sec 1: "the rejected instances can be conveyed to human experts for careful investigation"
method: Reject option for multi-class classification using a heterogeneous ensemble (SVM, RF, ANN) with two-phase fusion: fused posteriors give a confidence score for rejecting, a second fusion gives the prediction.
evaluation: 27,836 EMR prescription instances (Seoul National University Hospital), 3 HbA1c classes, tenfold CV; baselines single-classifier reject; integrated error 9.467 vs 9.837; at 80% rejection error 4.12% vs 5.33%; no latency.
contribution: Proposes a two-phase fusion reject option over heterogeneous classifiers for anti-diabetic drug failure prediction, giving a modestly better error-rejection trade-off than single-classifier reject options on hospital records.
flag: none of (i)-(v): a classifier with a reject option applied to a domain, one-shot per prescription, evaluated by error-rejection curves; human experts are mentioned as the destination of rejected cases but are not modelled or studied. No theory beyond restating Chow-style rule. Gains over baseline are small (integrated error 9.47 vs 9.84) though reported significant by paired t-test; useful accuracy needs 60-80% rejection. Published as an 'Industrial and commercial application' article; data are proprietary hospital records.

title: Effectiveness of symmetric rejection for a secure and user convenient multistage biometric system
evidence: "The core of a multistage biometric verification system is reject option which allows a stage not to give a genuine/impostor decision when it is not confident enough." (Abstract)
method: Symmetric rejection: each verifier stage sets a reject region [L,R] rejecting equal proportions x of genuine and impostor scores; rejected samples pass to the next biometric verifier, final stage forces a decision.
evaluation: Offline score sets: NIST 4-stage (2 fingerprint, 2 face) and 5-stage keystroke system; baselines SPRT and Marcialis et al.; AUC vs average number of stages (ANS). No hardware or latency.
contribution: Empirical study showing symmetric reject regions in a serial biometric cascade give an accuracy-cost trade-off close to the SPRT optimum (AUC 0.995 at 1.112 stages vs 1.139) and far better than rejecting the whole overlap region (1.725).
flag: none of (i)-(v): a reject option applied to one domain (biometric verification); the 'deferral' is a cascade to the next automatic verifier for accuracy and user convenience, not to a human or safeguard, and the stages are a fixed serial fusion, not a learned sequential policy. A maintainer could argue (i) fallback system, but the last stage is forced to decide and no human is involved. Reject option IS the main contribution and the floor is met (AUC/ANS vs two baselines). Keystroke results are given only as curves (Fig. 5), no numbers in text. Companion of doi:10.1007/s10044-022-01118-8 (same method, same lead author).

title: On error reduction by the symmetric rejection method in multi-stage biometric verification systems
evidence: "If the match-score falls inside the reject region, no binary (genuine/impostor) decision is made in the current stage and the verifier in the next stage is activated." (Abstract)
method: Theoretical analysis of the symmetric rejection method in an n-stage serial biometric verifier: two lemmas and a statement that system FRR and FAR fall below the best verifier's equal error rate.
evaluation: Proved: Lemma 1, Lemma 2 (Appendix A) and statement that FRR_n, FAR_n < EER_1. Validated on NIST 4-stage system: FRR cut up to 91.58%, FAR up to 56.16% vs EER_1=0.0463; no competing method.
contribution: Proves, and checks on NIST fingerprint and face scores, that symmetric reject regions in a serial multi-stage biometric verifier lower both false reject and false accept rates below the best single verifier's equal error rate.
flag: none of (i)-(v): theory is specific to one rejection heuristic in biometric cascades, not foundational reject-option theory (no optimal rule, surrogate consistency or generalization bound), so I do not credit (v); maintainer may want to confirm. Proofs assume a particular shape of the genuine/impostor score densities in the overlap region (Appendix A) - check the stated assumption. Only baseline is the single best verifier's EER; no comparison to SPRT or other rejection methods here. The 91.58% and 56.16% maxima occur at different settings of x (0.9K and 0.7K), not jointly. Same NIST setup and follow-up to doi:10.1007/s10044-020-00899-0.

title: LGA: lightweight design and privacy analysis of generative agents in social simulations
evidence: "a supervisory agent, Grace, who must approve any bank-related actions proposed by Alice before they can be executed" (Sect. 4.2 Defense Based on Multi-Agents Collaboration Verification)
method: Lightweight Generative Agent framework with page-table-style memory and shared database, plus three privacy defences: behavioural-guideline regulation, supervisory-agent approval, and step-back prompting.
evaluation: Sandbox social simulation, 5 agents, 4 identity scenarios, GPT-3.5-turbo to GPT-4o; privacy leakage rate falls from 53.33% to 12.50% (David) and 93.33% to 13.33% (Chris) vs no-defence baseline; separate 8-agent run shows 44.96% token-cost cut.
contribution: Rebuilds the Generative Agent architecture more cheaply and measures privacy leakage among interacting LLM agents, cutting leak rates by 50-80% with regulation, supervisory approval and step-back defences.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (LLM generative agents). Criterion (a) rests only on the Grace supervisory-agent approval gate, which is one of three defences and is agent-based, not human; the other two defences are prompt-level and would not meet (a) alone. Leak-rate cells come from 10-15 runs each, so percentages are coarse; the 60.67% cell (Disguised, Regulation) looks like a typo; cost and dissemination figures come from a different 8-agent party experiment, not the privacy runs; no latency figures.

title: Theory and algorithms for learning with rejection in binary classification
venue: Annals of Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence
evidence: "We introduce a novel framework for classification with a rejection option that consists of simultaneously learning two functions: a classifier along with a rejection function." (Abstract)
method: Jointly learns predictor h and separate rejection function r from different hypothesis sets under rejection cost c; convex max-hinge and plus-hinge surrogates; kernel-based CHR algorithms plus confidence-based variants.
evaluation: Proved: Rademacher generalization and margin bounds (Thm 1, 6, 8, Cor 7, 9), calibration and excess-risk bounds for surrogates (Thm 3-5). Experiments: synthetic and 9 UCI sets, CHR vs DHL, rejection loss; significant at 1% on 7 of 9.
contribution: Foundational theory of binary classification with a separately learned rejection function: data-dependent generalization and margin bounds, calibrated and consistent convex surrogates, and kernel algorithms that beat confidence-threshold rejection on UCI data.
flag: (v) foundational theory of the reject option. This is the journal version of Cortes, DeSalvo and Mohri 'Learning with Rejection' (ALT 2016); check the queue for the conference paper and dedupe. One-shot i.i.d. binary classification with fixed cost c: no human, no sequential setting, no latency; relevance to the review is as theory background for learning to defer, RQ scores are accordingly low. runtime_interceptor yes only in the sense that the learned r(x) withholds a prediction at inference. Tables 3-11 hold per-dataset numbers I did not transcribe; appendix proofs skimmed, not verified. Authors' own alternative confidence-based surrogates lose to DHL (Appendix E), reported candidly.

title: Evaluating Case Selection for Human Oversight in Clinical AI
evidence: "We propose neither a new allocation algorithm nor a new statistic." (Validate Case Selection)
method: Four-page Comment arguing confidence-based routing to clinicians should be audited against an independent reference standard, need for clinical deliberation ('selection validity'), with selection sensitivity and precision as reporting metrics.
evaluation: None. Hypothetical four-episode worked example (Table 1) and a 2x2 figure; no data, no implemented system, no baseline, no metrics computed. "No datasets were generated or analysed".
contribution: Viewpoint proposing 'selection validity': evaluating whether the rule that routes clinical AI cases to human review surfaces the decisions that need deliberation, independent of model confidence.
flag: (i) by topic (deferral to a clinician is the subject) but this is a journal COMMENT with no method and no evaluation: the text says the example is "illustrative rather than a report of an implemented system" and the specifications are "not a validated instrument". Fails the evaluation floor; E3 (commentary) would be an equally defensible code. Single author; AI Use Disclosure states ChatGPT and Claude assisted drafting and literature search. Useful only as a pointer for the human-handoff discussion (the high-confidence-but-needs-deliberation miss).

title: Soft Dice Confidence: A Near-Optimal Confidence Estimator for Selective Prediction in Semantic Segmentation
evidence: Proposes "a linear-time approximation, termed Soft Dice Confidence (SDC)" (Sec. 1) for image-level selective prediction, where rejected images are "fully delegated to a specialist".
method: Image-level confidence score for binary segmentation: soft Dice between predicted probabilities and thresholded mask, O(n), untuned; proved within a bounded ratio of the intractable ideal Dice confidence under pixel independence.
evaluation: Six medical segmentation tasks, three with OOD sets; AURC vs aMSP, PLA, AEF, oracle, e.g. breast 0.135 vs 0.341 aMSP, MS-OOD 0.338 vs 0.600; relative-error bound max 4.4e-3. No runtimes.
contribution: Soft Dice Confidence is a linear-time, tuning-free confidence score for rejecting whole segmentation outputs, provably close to the ideal Dice confidence and with lower AURC than other untuned estimators on six medical tasks.
flag: none of (i)-(v) clearly: an uncertainty estimator for one-shot selective prediction judged by risk-coverage, which the ruling sends to E4. Maintainer may consider (v) because Theorem 2 and Corollary 3 bound the estimator against the ideal one (relative error at most (3-2sqrt2)/s), but this is near-optimality of a confidence score for one metric under conditional independence, not general reject-option theory. Specialist deferral is motivation only; no human or workload measured. Skin cancer: AEF+SDC at 50% tuning slightly beats SDC (0.053 vs 0.055). Complexity claimed negligible, no timings. Read first 100k of 108k characters.

title: The black-box simplex architecture for runtime assurance of multi-agent CPS
venue: Innovations in Systems and Software Engineering
evidence: "control authority may switch from an unverified and potentially unsafe advanced controller to a backup baseline controller in order to maintain the safety of an autonomous cyber-physical system" (Abstract)
method: Black-Box Simplex: a decision module admits the advanced controller command only if a lookahead baseline controller can extend it to a provably permanently safe sequence; adds multi-agent command blending.
evaluation: Simulation: 11-16 robot MPC coordination (20 repeats) and 3, 7 and 15 F-16 aircraft with ACAS-Xu neural controllers; blending lifts goal success from 0-41.67% to 59.06-100%; zero collisions, min separation 1500.5 ft vs 175 ft for the unguarded system; two theorems proved; reachability check 1.5-2 ms on a 2.70 GHz Xeon E-2176M laptop, 55x faster than real time.
contribution: Shows runtime checks can replace static verification of the baseline controller, giving proved collision avoidance for multi-agent CPS driven by unverified MPC or neural-network controllers.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes in the F-16 study (ACAS-Xu neural-network controllers guarded); the multi-robot study guards MPC, which is not learned, so the learned-system condition is met by one of two case studies. Journal extension of two earlier conference papers (refs 7,8), so check for duplicate queued records. (d) is weak: millisecond check times and a proposed runtime cap, but no deadline or jitter study and a laptop CPU rather than edge hardware. All results in simulation; command-blending success rates degrade sharply with agent count (59% at 16 agents).

title: A co-training approach for sequential three-way decisions
venue: International Journal of Machine Learning and Cybernetics
evidence: "When available information is insufficient, a deferment decision instead of an immediate decision is made. With the increasing of available labels, the deferment decisions are classified definitely, which constructs a sequential three-way decisions model." (Sect. 7)
method: Cost-sensitive sequential three-way decisions (accept, reject, defer to boundary region) for face recognition; kNN-based co-training on two views labels new samples each step until the boundary region is resolved.
evaluation: Offline face databases incl. PIE; vs cost-sensitive and cost-blind sequential two-way models; decision cost, total cost (test cost 0.001*l^2), error rate, high-cost error rate, boundary size; 50 runs averaged. No latency.
contribution: Adds co-training to sequential three-way decisions so that uncertain face-recognition samples are deferred to a boundary region and resolved as more labels accrue, lowering decision cost and high-cost errors versus two-way decisions.
flag: none of (i)-(v), borderline (ii): deferment is the main idea and is revisited over decision steps, but the 'steps' are batch co-training rounds on a static face dataset, not online or trajectory decisions, and nothing is handed to a human or safeguard - effectively a reject-option classifier applied to one domain. If the maintainer reads sequential three-way decisions as (ii), the floor is met (costs vs two baselines, Tables 5-10). Doubts: costs are unitless and the cost matrix and test-cost function are author-chosen; overall error rate is WORSE for the three-way model (deferrals counted as errors); results values not transcribed (tables are garbled in the text extraction). Extension of the authors' own ICNSC 2019 paper [35]. 'Simulates a human decision process' is rhetoric only.

title: A cost-sensitive sequential multi-class three-way decision model
venue: International Journal of Machine Learning and Cybernetics
evidence: "S3WD inherits the idea of deferred decision-making from three-way decision and integrates the relationship between decision steps through a sequential process." (Section 1 Introduction)
method: Rough-set sequential multi-class three-way decision: class-specific attribute importance (grey relational analysis) orders granularity levels; penalty function adapts accept/defer thresholds from misclassification and delayed-decision rates.
evaluation: 8 UCI datasets, Matlab on a 3.0GHz CPU; vs SMTD and SMTD-CSL; decision result cost, process cost, normalised total cost, recall. Lowest total cost on 8/8; recall best on 4/8. No latency.
contribution: Cost-sensitive sequential three-way classifier that defers boundary objects to finer attribute granularity with adaptive thresholds, lowering combined result and process cost on eight UCI datasets versus two prior three-way models.
flag: none of (i)-(v) on a strict reading: 'sequential' means successive attribute granularity levels over a static table, not decisions over time, and deferral is to more attributes, not to a human or safeguard; if the maintainer reads (ii) liberally (defer = acquire more information at a cost) this is borderline. Weak evidence: cost matrices and attribute test costs are randomly set; no train/test split is described (regions computed on the whole dataset); single run, no variance or significance; total-cost gaps are tiny (e.g. 0.2081 vs 0.2086); abstract says 'high accuracy' but only recall is reported and it is lower than a baseline on 4 of 8 datasets. Deferred-decision rates are not tabulated.

title: Compliance without coherence: fluent failure and the ethics of alignment evaluation in multi-agent language models
evidence: "complementing behavioral monitors with structural audits of an agent's discourse" (Abstract)
method: Conceptual essay defining fluent failure in multi-agent LLM deployments and arguing, via Floridi levels of abstraction, for discourse-structural audits (graph modularity, betweenness) alongside surface monitors.
evaluation: None of its own. The pre-registered triadic multi-agent simulation is an unpublished companion preprint cited only as a plausibility anchor; no metrics, no baseline, no ablation, no formal result.
contribution: Argues deployed surface alignment monitors are in principle blind to fluent, compliant failure of LLM agents, and sketches discourse-structural auditing as a complementary evaluation layer.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (LLM agents) but nothing intercepts at runtime and nothing is measured. The author states plainly that the argument is conceptual and that the empirical companion is a preprint, not peer reviewed and not load-bearing, so the evaluation floor fails; Table 1 is an illustrative classification, not data. Maintainer may prefer E3, since AI and Ethics classes it as RESEARCH but it is self-described as an essay. Single author, dual affiliation.

title: Safe integration of Large Language Models into industrial process control: a multi-agent architecture with P&ID-grounded validation
evidence: "A deterministic Verification Agent validates every proposal against P&ID topology, SCADA constraints, and SOP compliance before any action is permitted" (Sect. 1 Introduction)
method: Four-layer AAE architecture: LLM Monitor agents propose, an Orchestrator ranks, a deterministic Verification Agent applies six P&ID graph-traversal checks plus a forbidden-action rubric, and an Execution Agent routes auto-execute, notify, approval or block.
evaluation: 5 synthetic scenarios (3 from Tennessee Eastman), Claude Sonnet 4 proposals and Qwen2.5-VL-3B for HMI parsing; 43 injected proposals give recall 1.000, FNR 0.000, FPR 0.750, precision 0.854, F1 0.921; LLMs propose unsafe actions in 10-70% of 50 runs and every one is flagged; B0-B3 graduated ablation; aggregation 24.2 ms (sigma 3.1 ms, 200 iterations, i7-1370P), LLM inference 2-8 s.
contribution: Confines LLM inference to an advisory monitor layer and gates every proposed control action through deterministic P&ID-grounded validation, catching all covered unsafe proposals across five process-control scenarios.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (LLM proposal generator and VLM). Strongest record of the batch but note: single-author industrial paper, all scenarios synthetic, ground-truth and forbidden-action rubrics written by the system designer (self-acknowledged evaluation bias), and prototype code and evaluation scripts generated with an AI coding agent. Recall 1.000 covers only the six structural checks plus scenario-specific rubric; FPR 0.750 rests on 8 negatives with Wilson interval about [0.41,0.93]. Escalation paths and operator console were not exercised in the evaluation, so (e) is architectural plus a qualitative alert-fatigue discussion, not measured. The 24.2 ms excludes file I/O, MQTT and LLM inference; P0 actions bypass the framework entirely. Multi-agent here means a software agent architecture, not reasoning over multi-agent state.

title: Balancing autonomy and oversight in reliable agentic artificial intelligence through adaptive human interaction architectures
evidence: "those falling below a lower safety threshold halt execution and escalate to a human operator through a purpose-built three-panel decision console" (Abstract)
method: Dynamic Intervention Framework: a Llama-3-8B Supervisor scores each GPT-4o Worker step by token log-probability plus goal-embedding cosine drift and routes to autonomous, async audit or human halt; DPO on operator corrections tunes thresholds.
evaluation: 5000 synthetic enterprise tasks in 3 logical domains against fully autonomous and static HITL baselines (human responses oracle-simulated); success 98.2% vs 84.3% and 99.1%; intervention 14.5%, false positive 3.2%, self-correction 76.4%; mean latency 4.8 s vs 45.6 s (89% cut); DPO drops intervention 21.0% to 11.5% over 5 epochs; 8x A100, 0.3 s per-step budget.
contribution: Treats human oversight as a dynamically allocated resource, scoring every agent step for confidence and goal drift to halt and escalate only the risky ones while matching static human-in-the-loop accuracy.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (GPT-4o Worker agent). Most relevant record in the batch for RQ3 and RQ5, but the maintainer should doubt the headline claim: the human baseline and every operator response are oracle-model simulations with ground-truth access, so statistical equivalence to full human oversight is not a human study (the authors concede this). The 14.5% intervention rate contradicts Tables 3 and 4, which both total 760 of 5000 decision steps (15.2%). ASYNC_REVIEW, one of three core routing states, fired 0% of the time, so a third of the mechanism is unevaluated. Data synthetic and only available from the corresponding author; a PRISMA-2020 literature search inside a systems paper, free-mail author addresses and no shared affiliation are worth a machine-generation check.

title: Act or ask: Interactive construction robots via vision–language models with confidence-guided decision deferral
evidence: "if the confidence falls below the threshold, the system can trigger a deferral mechanism that displays the marked image to human workers for decision-making" (Section 3.2-3.3)
method: VLM (GPT-4o family) picks SAM-derived keypoints for a Franka arm; sequence-likelihood confidence below threshold 0.9 withholds the action and asks a human supervisor to choose the keypoints.
evaluation: Real Franka Research 3, lab tabletop, 10 trials per case. Panel installation with vs without deferral: success 90% vs 60% (30 trials, 9 deferrals); threshold sweep 0.7-0.95. RTX 4090 PC; no latency numbers.
contribution: Language-instructed construction robot that asks a human instead of acting when VLM token-likelihood confidence is low; deferral ablation raises panel-installation success from 60% to 90% on a real arm.
flag: (i) and (iv): pre-execution confidence gate handing off to a human supervisor. BORDERLINE on 'main contribution': deferral is in the title but is one of three listed contributions and the paper is mostly a VLM keypoint control pipeline; the mechanism is a plain fixed threshold on summed token log-probabilities, not learned (the paper nevertheless calls it 'learning to defer'). Evaluation is thin: deferral tested on one of three tasks only, 30 trials each arm, no confidence intervals, human input implicitly assumed correct, no measure of human response time or workload (so criterion e not claimed). Two failures were wrong picks at above 95% confidence, which the gate cannot catch. Headline 60% and 78.5% success rates in the abstract are for tasks run WITHOUT deferral. Latency discussed only qualitatively; execution is open-loop. No safety-violation metric as such, only task success.

title: Hierarchical world models for joint trajectory and service caching optimization in low-altitude edge intelligence
evidence: "At the slow timescale, the macro-level dynamics model predicts the next-period latent state and period return under the current cache action" (Sec. 5.4; equation symbols omitted)
method: CoDeQ-HRL: hierarchical PPO with quantum-inspired encoder over the service-dependency graph, action-conditioned macro/micro latent dynamics models and multi-step latent imagination to rank candidate cache plans for multi-UAV edge computing.
evaluation: Trace-driven simulation (3 UAV clusters, 300 terminals, ISCX traffic) vs DDPG, MADDPG, MAAC, MAPPO, SAC, TRPO, GRL; task success, SLA, energy efficiency, backlog, cache hit; RTX 4090 training; no latency.
contribution: A hierarchical RL scheduler for UAV edge caching that uses action-conditioned latent dynamics over a service-dependency graph to imagine cache plans, evaluated only through downstream service-quality metrics.
flag: Topically (b): latent dynamics over a service-dependency graph and joint multi-UAV state, with imagination before execution. But ONLY DOWNSTREAM RESULTS are reported (reward, task success ~0.89 vs 0.55-0.65, SLA ~0.90, 20.3 vs 11-14 kb/J, 4.9-5.0 vs 2.6-3.5 GB, backlog 0.04 vs 0.08-0.10, cache alignment 0.79 vs 0.42-0.48, chain hit 0.91 vs 0.51-0.65); no direct measure of the world model's predictive accuracy (the prediction loss is defined but never reported) and no ablation of the dynamics model, QLSC or ECA, so gains cannot be attributed to the world model. Hence E2 per the maintainer's ruling. All figures are approximate values read off plots in the text, no tables of results, no seeds/variance stated. Abstract claims real-world mobility trajectories but the setup section names only the ISCX VPN-nonVPN traffic dataset; the mobility trace source is not identified. The constraint-aware residual execution layer is feasibility projection/masking of actions, not a safety interceptor. Quantum-inspired wording is classical linear algebra. Volume dated 2027.

title: Research on calibrated and cost-sensitive vulnerability alert governance for open-source software auditing
evidence: "The probability-band review rule routes uncertain calibrated probabilities to Review" (Section 4.3 Review-aware decision rules)
method: Governance layer over CodeBERT, CodeQL, Semgrep and SpotBugs alerts: post-hoc calibration, cost matrix and boundary flags choose Fix, Review (human) or Ignore per alert, with an audit record.
evaluation: OWASP Benchmark Java, 2740 rows (393 test). Unsafe ignores 69 (CodeBERT binary), 22 (Semgrep), 0 with rule-union Review but 392/393 reviewed; ECE 0.468 to 0.005; review-budget sweep; 3 Vul4J cases. No latency.
contribution: Calibrated, cost-sensitive Fix/Review/Ignore triage layer for vulnerability alerts; on OWASP Benchmark it removes unsafe auto-ignores only by sending nearly every alert to human review.
flag: none of (i)-(v) in substance: a one-shot three-way reject option applied to a domain; Review nominally means human review but no human is involved or studied and the review budget is simulated. Results are weak and close to degenerate: the neural detector is near chance (AUROC 0.5256, scores saturated at 0.997), calibration lowers AUROC for Platt/isotonic/histogram, and the 'zero unsafe ignore' policies route 392 of 393 test samples to Review (or to Fix with 184 false-positive fixes), i.e. no real selectivity. Table 8 hybrid rows are identical to the rule-union rows, so the uncertainty band adds nothing measurable. Vul4J study is 3 cases of artifact generation, not a quantitative evaluation. Heavy 'registered' protocol phrasing and received/accepted within 30 days (1 June to 30 June 2026); maintainer may want to check for templated or machine-assisted writing.

title: Knowing when to escalate: Prompt-based uncertainty quantification for selective automation of LLM-based intrusion detection
evidence: "Flows routed to accept are processed automatically without human intervention" (Section 3.3 Confidence-based routing framework)
method: Seven black-box prompt-based confidence estimators (self-report, multi-prompt voting, Monte Carlo, cross-variant sampling, penalty-adjusted variants) feed fixed thresholds (0.85/0.60) routing flows to accept, escalate-to-human or reject.
evaluation: 5 LLMs, CIC-IDS2017/2018, n=750 each. ECE: PA-MPV 0.217, MPV 0.243, Monte Carlo 0.597; AURC baseline 0.281; accepted accuracy 0.630 vs 0.95 target; median latency 3.0-52.1 s per sample.
contribution: Comparison of seven prompt-based uncertainty methods for accept/escalate/reject triage of LLM intrusion detection: none supports safe automation (accepted accuracy 0.63), sampling methods badly degrade calibration.
flag: none of (i)-(v): an uncertainty estimator judged by ECE and risk-coverage for an LLM abstaining on single independent flows; escalation to a human is only a routing label, no analyst is involved or studied. Largely a negative result: plain self-report baseline has the best AURC on CIC-IDS2017, PA-MPV/MPV gains are not significant after Bonferroni correction, and several model-method cells sit at the 0.500 chance floor. Authors admit feature selection is label-informed (leakage; accuracy drops 0.131 in the label-blind ablation), thresholds are set a priori, and latency is throttled free-tier wall-clock time (seconds, not real-time). Declares use of AI tools for code and drafting. Model names as given (e.g. 'Qwen3 80B', 'Llama 4 Scout') could not be verified from the text.

title: Classification with reject option for software defect prediction
evidence: "The rejected sample may be further analyzed by a specialist that will give the final decision." (Section 1 Introduction)
method: Two weighted extreme learning machines with opposite class bias; a module is rejected when they disagree. rejoELM tunes bias for accuracy-rejection risk; IrejoELM uses an F-measure-based risk for imbalanced data.
evaluation: 5 open-source Java projects (Bug Prediction Dataset, CK+OO metrics), 2/3 train; vs rejoNB, rejoRBF; accuracy-rejection and F-measure-rejection curves, hypothesis tests. Lucene: F 26.2% to 33.33% at 18.61% rejection. No latency.
contribution: ELM classifiers with a reject option for software defect prediction; the F-measure-optimised variant beats reject-option Naive Bayes and RBF baselines on five imbalanced open-source defect datasets.
flag: none of (i)-(v): a classifier with a reject option applied to a domain, one-shot per module. Handing rejected modules to an expert is motivation only; no human is in the evaluation (Table 4 is an illustrative look at process metrics of 43 rejected Lucene modules, by the authors). Check Table 3: IrejoELM F-measures of 84-99% look inconsistent with the worked Lucene example in the text (26.2% without rejection, 33.33% at 18.61% rejection) - the table values probably correspond to very high rejection rates, which the table does not report. Results otherwise shown mainly as curves; rejoELM itself has poor F-measure (0.85-4.35% on three datasets).

title: Safety-aware behavioral decision-making for construction robots: Semantic-driven hybrid framework for worker-robot collaboration
evidence: "During the execution phase, any worker intrusion that violates the guard condition triggers an immediate transition to the paused state, halting the robot's motion." (Sec. 4.3)
method: Extended Semantic Event Chain: symbolic multi-graph of worker/robot/object relations with transitions learned from VR demonstrations; graph matching selects behavior; FSM guard (separation distance > protective separation distance) pends, pauses or aborts motion.
evaluation: VR wall-panel installation, 30 participants, simulated camera/force sensor; 18/20 policies feasible (90%), 16/18 first-pass success (89%), 0.25 collisions per trial; no baseline, no ablation, no latency.
contribution: A symbolic semantic scene-graph model of worker-robot collaboration, learned from VR demonstrations, drives a construction robot whose motions are paused at runtime when a speed-and-separation guard is violated.
flag: Pillar 2 view: this is NOT a predictive world model. The 'semantic world model' is a hand-structured symbolic state-transition graph (ESEC) used for matching partial observations to known states; nothing is learned to predict future state and no predictive-accuracy metric is reported, so (b) is not met and E1 would be the Pillar 2 verdict. I list (a) because the FSM guard (SD > PSD, ISO 13855-style protective distance) does pause/abort robot motion at execution time; under (a) it still fails minimum evaluation: the only safety number is 0.25 active collisions per trial over 16 trials with NO baseline or ablation, so E2 (maintainer may prefer E1). Only downstream task results otherwise (90% policy extraction, 89% first-pass collaboration). Single worker + single virtual robot in VR only; authors state multi-agent scalability is unvalidated. 'Requesting intervention' in anomaly handling is mentioned but not implemented or evaluated, so human handoff is nominal. Waiting when state match is ambiguous is a deferral-like default, not evaluated separately. Small n; two failed policies blamed on demonstrations, two retries on participants.

title: A predictive safety filter for learning-based control of constrained nonlinear dynamical systems
evidence: The filter decides whether the learning-based input "can be safely applied to the real system, or if it has to be modified otherwise" (Abstract), modifying it "as little as necessary to maintain safe operation at all future times" (Sec. 1).
method: Predictive safety filter: an MPC solved each step certifies the learning controller's input against a probabilistic model or replaces it with a minimally modified safe input; terminal safe controller.
evaluation: Simulation only: pendulum (120 episodes) and Bullet quadrotor (240 episodes); baseline unguarded learned policy; constraints held in all 240 episodes; no violation counts or timings; Theorem 4.6 proves safety in probability.
contribution: A predictive safety filter that certifies or minimally modifies any learning controller's input at every step, proving constraint satisfaction in probability without constraining how the policy is learned.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes in intent - designed for black-box RL - but the policies actually guarded in the experiments are Bayesian-optimisation-tuned bang-bang and PD controllers rather than RL, and the terminal controllers are hand-designed, so a strict reading of the Pillar 1 scope ruling could push this to exclude-E1. Single-agent, single-input guardrail, so exclude-E4 on level is also defensible; the sequential aspect (MPC horizon, closed-loop episodes) is the only thing against that, and there is no multi-agent, latency or handoff aspect. Evaluation floor rests on Theorem 4.6 plus qualitative baseline trajectories: no violation counts, rates or cost values are reported (only that constraints held across all 240 quadrotor episodes) and there is no formal ablation, just 10 versus 18000 data points on the pendulum. The guarantee is probabilistic with existential constants, and Assumption 4.3's tracking policy and Lyapunov function are used in the proof only, never implemented. Real-time solution is claimed via Ipopt and CasADi but no solve times or hardware are given, so (d) does not hold. Human override appears only as a conceptual driver-assistance remark in the Discussion, which is not (e). Version read is v4, the 2021 Automatica preprint matching the record DOI. One fetch.

title: Semi-automatic wafer map pattern classification with convolutional neural networks
evidence: "Otherwise, the wafer map is subject to manual classification by a process engineer." (Abstract); "We assumed that manual classification by a process engineer was always correct with no errors." (Sec 4.2)
method: CNN wafer-map classifier with a reject option: thresholds one of eight predictive-uncertainty measures (softmax or MC-dropout based) and sends high-uncertainty maps to a process engineer.
evaluation: WM-811k, 9 classes, 10 seeds; eight uncertainty measures and random rejection compared; accuracy 96.73% at full coverage, 98.71% at 95%, 99.40% at 90%; AUC 0.9975 (Gini). No latency or hardware.
contribution: Thresholding CNN predictive uncertainty to route uncertain wafer maps to a process engineer lifts accuracy from 96.7% to over 99% while the CNN still covers about 93% of maps.
flag: none of (i)-(v) beyond a nominal (i): one-shot classifier with reject option applied to a domain. The human is simulated as an always-correct oracle, so the handoff itself is not studied (no engineer time, error or workload data). Single dataset, small custom CNN; differences among seven of the eight measures are statistically insignificant by the paper's own t-tests. Abstract figure (over 99% at 93% coverage) is consistent with Table 2 and Sec 4.3.

title: Toward feasible machine learning model updates in network-based intrusion detection
evidence: "If all evaluated classifiers reject the evaluated event, its alert is suppressed, and the event is stored for later model updates" (Sec 5.1)
method: Stream-learning NIDS ensemble (Hoeffding Tree, bagging, Oza) with per-class confidence thresholds; events rejected by all classifiers have alerts suppressed and are stored 30-90 days for incremental model updates.
evaluation: One year of MAWI traffic (2.6 TB); batch and stream ensembles with and without monthly updates as baselines; FP rate improved 12% at 8.5% rejection without updates, 2% rejection with updates; update CPU time 3.2%. Commodity hardware, no latency.
contribution: A stream-learning intrusion detector that rejects low-confidence events and later retrains only on those stored rejections keeps accuracy over a year of traffic with far less labelling and compute.
flag: none of (i)-(v) cleanly; BORDERLINE (ii): the setting is streaming and rejections feed later model updates, but the paper frames its main contribution as feasible model updates, with the reject option one of two parts, and each rejection is a per-event confidence threshold. Maintainer may prefer exclude-E4 or a lenient include under (ii). Rejection only suppresses the alert: no handoff to a human or fallback detector, and the security cost of silently dropped attack events is not measured. Labels come from MAWILab unsupervised detectors, not ground truth. Results are mostly figures with averages in prose; '12%' and '6%' appear to be absolute rate differences. Latency of the verifier is not reported.

title: U-PASS: An uncertainty-guided deep learning pipeline for automated sleep staging
evidence: Sec 2.4 (U-PASS pipeline): "Instead of making an incorrect prediction on these samples, it is better to defer them to a clinician."
method: Sleep-staging pipeline using uncertainty at three stages: channel and training-sample selection, active-learning finetuning on uncertain recordings, and deferral of uncertain test epochs to a clinician.
evaluation: 90 PSG recordings (45 train, 45 test), SeqSleepNet, 23 repeats; compares channel counts, discard fractions and several uncertainty metrics; accuracy 75% -> 85% with about 20% of epochs deferred; no hardware or latency.
contribution: An uncertainty-guided sleep-staging pipeline in which data selection, active learning and deferral of uncertain epochs to a clinician together raise accuracy from 75% to 85%.
flag: none of (i)-(v) as main contribution: deferral to a clinician is one of three pipeline components, evaluated only by ranking test epochs by uncertainty and reporting accuracy on the retained part; the clinician is simulated with ground-truth labels, no human study. If the maintainer treats the deferral stage as primary it would still be a one-shot reject option applied to a domain (E4). Single private dataset; several per-stage gains are given only in figures; the 85% figure combines all stages with about 20% deferral (89% excluding transition epochs; inter-rater agreement 82.6%).

title: A novel bone marrow cell recognition method based on multi-scale information and reject option
evidence: "we reject the identification of the sample and defer it to an expert" (Sec 2.2.2.3)
method: Crossformer backbone with two-stage Class Centroid Learning; a confidence derived from distance to class centroids is thresholded (calibrated cth) to reject low-confidence bone marrow cell images to experts.
evaluation: In-house Nanfang Hospital dataset plus public MLL; CNN/ViT/Swin backbones and an inductive conformal predictor as baselines, CCL ablation; accuracy 94.41%, rejection 21.07%, accepted accuracy over 98%; Titan XP, ICP 26.14 s per 2354 images, CCL over 3x faster.
contribution: A multi-scale transformer with class-centroid learning classifies bone marrow cells at 94.4% accuracy and rejects 21% of images to experts so that accepted predictions exceed 98% accuracy.
flag: none of (i)-(v) beyond a nominal (i): one-shot image classifier with a reject option applied to a medical domain. Reject option shares the contribution with the backbone and accuracy claims. Expert handoff is asserted, not studied: no expert reads rejected cells and no workload or reader study. Primary dataset is in-house and not public. Rejection comparison is against one baseline (ICP) reported for its best backbone only.

title: Verification-Gated Agentic Mission-State Governance for Intelligent Industrial Multi-Robot Systems
evidence: "can update the committed mission state only after deterministic verification and atomic commit." (Abstract)
method: Agentic/heuristic modules propose multi-robot assignments and repairs; a deterministic verifier gates commits to a task forest and governed blackboard; invalid proposals are rejected, else deferred or fallback-repaired.
evaluation: Mission-state simulator, 6-24 robots, 30 seeds. Medium: safe completion 0.921 vs 0.902 no-verifier (invalid events 0 vs 26.7), DART-DAG 0.579, Flat-BB 0.840. Decision time 17.67 s medium, 153.56 s large (Python).
contribution: A deterministic verification gate lets agentic planners propose multi-robot mission-state changes but commits only verified ones, giving zero invalid commitments and 0.92 safe completion against 0.58 for baselines.
flag: (iv): a gate that rejects proposed mission-state commits and defers when nothing verifies. Doubts: the gate acts on high-level state updates, not on physical actions; simulator only, explicitly no actuator faults, perception error or collision avoidance; no human escalation. No-verifier ablation still reaches 0.902 safe completion, so the gate's own increment is small on that metric (its effect shows in invalid events 26.7 to 0). Verification dominates runtime at seconds to minutes, far from real time. Table 1 and Table 6 node counts disagree slightly; hardware not reported; some table cells blank in extraction. Record DOI is the journal version; I read the arXiv copy.

title: A2C: A modular multi-stage collaborative decision framework for human–AI teams
evidence: "In this paper, we introduced A2C, a novel framework designed to accommodate flexible modes of decision-making." (Sec. 8 Conclusion)
method: Three-stage pipeline: a one-class rejector passes known-class inputs to the classifier, defers the rest to a human with context, who may open collaborative exploration with an AI collaborator.
evaluation: MNIST, FMNIST, CIFAR-10, KDDCup99 with simulated expert competence; baselines automation-only and deferral-only; F1: CIFAR-10 37.38, 64.75, 81.24; KDDCup99 33.43, 35.18, 96.24. GPT-4 persona study, success up to 85.7 percent.
contribution: A modular automated, augmented and collaborative decision framework in which a rejector defers unfamiliar inputs to a human who can escalate to joint human-AI exploration, raising F1 on unseen classes.
flag: (i). Main doubt: no real humans anywhere. Expert competence and collaboration success are set by parameters (class-recognition sets, resolution rates 50-100 percent), so the Table 6 gains follow largely from those assumptions; the persona study uses GPT-4 personas judged by one author's manual review, and real-human study is left to future work. Criterion e is therefore generous and the maintainer may drop it. All abstract numbers were found in Tables 4, 6 and 7. The rejector is an off-the-shelf one-class detector (rejector accuracy 92.97 to 96.41 percent). One-shot per input, logical domain (intrusion detection) plus image benchmarks. Persona run count (75 runs, seven categories) is unclear. Only latency: under 5 minutes per collaborative run. No hardware.

title: TriSV-CD: Selective verification with a do-no-harm arbitration gate for reliable remote sensing change detection
evidence: "The gate then applies a single do-no-harm rule" (Sec 4.1); "instead of abstaining on low-confidence inputs, V4-Safe rolls back edits in the high-confidence region" (Sec 2.2, ligatures and line-break hyphen normalised)
method: V4-Safe: training-free gate that restores the baseline change map when a test-time-augmentation correction edits pixels whose mean baseline probability exceeds 0.55; VLMs used only for offline diagnosis.
evaluation: 5 backbones x 3 change-detection datasets plus 2 external backbones; ungated TTA correction, VLM-informed thresholds and oracle as comparators; harmful edit rate 41.90% to 7.68% (PDEFM-SYSU), 10.87% to 4.88% (BIT-NJDS); RTX 3090, gate overhead 6.10 ms per sample, pipeline 14.57x baseline.
contribution: A fixed-threshold rollback gate that rejects test-time corrections where the baseline change detector was already confident cuts harmful edits several-fold with small, mostly positive F1 changes across fifteen backbone-dataset cells.
flag: none of (i)-(v) on a strict reading; WEAK (i): rollback to the baseline prediction is a fallback, but it is a one-shot per-sample post-processing rule on a segmentation map, with no acting system, no sequence and no human. F1 gains are tiny (order 0.003-0.005); the authors themselves call it an empirical layer, not a guarantee. Threshold 0.55 was selected on the SADE-SYSU test split (paper admits no test-independent selection; a validation audit selects 0.60), and the gate does not reduce harmful rate on the external SYSU cells. Harmful-rate reduction is concentrated on SYSU; LEVIR cells are near zero for both. Volume is dated 2027 for a 2026 article. Roughly the last third (supplementary tables after Sec 6) was only skimmed.

title: Calibrated selective prediction using deep ensembles for thyroid nodule ultrasound classification under dataset shift
evidence: Conclusion (Sec. 7): "a calibrated deterministic deep-ensemble framework for annotation-assisted thyroid nodule ROI classification"; high mutual-information images are sent to radiologist review.
method: Five-member ConvNeXt-Tiny ensemble with vector scaling; mutual information gates images; confident low/high probabilities give No-FNA/FNA suggestions, the rest go to radiologist review.
evaluation: TN5000 5-fold CV and external TN3K. AURC: MSP 0.0302, variance 0.0323, MI 0.0378, random 0.1098; triage review 52.9%, capture 99.83%; external AUC 0.787, review 83.7%. Tesla T4, no latency.
contribution: A calibrated deep ensemble for thyroid ultrasound defers uncertain images to radiologists; under dataset shift it sends 83.7% of external cases to review, and its mutual-information score ranks errors worse than plain softmax confidence.
flag: none of (i)-(v) as a main contribution: a classifier with a reject option applied to one domain, one-shot, retrospective. Radiologist review is the deferral target but no reader, workload or outcome is studied. The paper's own chosen gate (MI) has worse AURC than the MSP comparator (0.0378 vs 0.0302). External No-FNA NPV of 100% rests on 6 images. arXiv title is longer than the record title (adds ROI-Based and A Retrospective Evaluation) but it is the same paper.

title: Set-valued safety tubes for uncertainty propagation in multi-step AI pipelines
evidence: "If the intersection is empty, the system halts, abstains, or requests another observation; no artificial set-valued state is introduced after failure." (Sec 3.1, ligature normalised)
method: Random-set (zonotope) state for multi-step AI pipelines: affine prediction expands, observation filtering shrinks; three stopping times (feasibility failure, safety-tube exit, resolution) define halt, abstain and completion rules.
evaluation: Theory: proves measurability, contraction, maximal, Lyapunov, tube-exit and resolution bounds and a finite-horizon feasibility-failure probability bound. Synthetic only: 2-D contract toy vs scalar fuzzy score; 1e5-path Monte Carlo (rho 0.88, P(tau_feas<=50) 0.396 vs bound 0.50). No real pipeline, no latency.
contribution: A set-valued stochastic framework tracks accumulated uncertainty through multi-step AI pipelines as zonotopes and proves bounds on when a pipeline must halt, abstain or can declare its uncertainty resolved.
flag: BORDERLINE (ii)/(iv): a sequential pipeline with halt/abstain stopping rules and proved bounds on them, so a maintainer could include it as formal runtime-monitor theory. Recommended E1 because the paper states its contribution is the set-valued uncertainty-propagation and filtering mechanism (Sec 1: 'The contribution is the set-valued mechanism that produces this recursion'); the halt/abstain rule is a consequence, and the action at tau_feas is left unspecified ('halt, abstain, or obtain new evidence'). Not theory of the reject option in the (v) sense. No real LLM agent or dataset ('No empirical datasets were used'); the only baseline is a constructed scalar fuzzy score in a 2-D toy. Affine stage maps are an assumed interface, not verified for any model. runtime_interceptor marked yes for the defined rule, but it is never run on a live system; authors say real-time implementation is future work. Proofs were not checked line by line.

title: Adaptive alert prioritisation in security operations centres via learning to defer with human feedback
evidence: "the DRL agent reviews the alerts prioritised by the predictive AI and either (i) accepts the assigned priorities, or (ii) defers alerts that may be misprioritised to human analysts" (Sec 3.3)
method: L2DHF: a D3QN agent sits after an ensemble alert classifier and, per alert, accepts the AI priority or defers to an analyst; analyst feedback is the reward, under an analyst time budget.
evaluation: UNSW-NB15 and CICIDS2017, 2016 hourly steps, ~400 alerts/step; vs predictive AI, static L2D, DRLHF, AlertPro, A2C; per-class accuracy, misprioritisations, deferred alerts; ~15 s per step on Xeon CPU.
contribution: Learning to defer made adaptive: an RL deferral agent refines over time which security alerts go to a time-limited analyst, raising critical-alert accuracy while deferring fewer alerts than static deferral.
flag: (i) and (ii): deferral to a human analyst, learned online over 2016 time steps. Check: the analyst is SIMULATED with ground-truth labels (perfect, single analyst), so criterion e rests on a modelled time budget and workload counts, not a human study; noisy-analyst result (Sec 6.5) is preliminary and undetailed. Claim of beating SOTA is not uniform: on UNSW-NB15 L2DHF is slightly below A2C (small effect sizes), and on CICIDS2017 it leaves the most unprocessed alerts (avg ~363 per step) and less spare analyst time than L2D and A2C. Critical accuracy 0.977 (UNSW) and 1.0 (CICIDS) vs L2D 0.864 and 0.6; deferred alerts avg 13 vs 16 (L2D), 17 (DRLHF), 22 (A2C) on CICIDS. Baselines ran on different hardware, so execution times are not comparable; 15 s per hourly batch is not a latency result. Volume dated 2027, available online Sept 2026. Reward weights and analyst review times are assumed, not tuned or measured.

title: Physics-grounded multi-agent architecture for traceable, risk-aware human–AI decision support in manufacturing
evidence: The critic agent issues accept, revise or escalate decisions and "acceptance requires that the explicit checks above pass" (Sec. 3.4), escalating rather than forcing acceptance when its budget is exhausted.
method: MAKA: four LLM agents - central router, tool-only analysis, knowledge-graph retrieval, critic. The critic checks ids, schema and offset bounds before acceptance and escalates to human approval when verification fails.
evaluation: 75 tool-use questions, 6 models, 450 critic-ablation trials, Ti-6Al-4V blade digital twin; critic lifts tool F1 0.2919 to 0.6697, full recovery 61.19 percent; KG +0.1274; loop 4.3 s.
contribution: A physics-grounded multi-agent LLM architecture whose critic gates tool-based manufacturing recommendations, raising tool-selection F1 from 0.29 to 0.67 and escalating unverifiable cases to a human approver.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM agents (router, analysis, KG, critic); the critic's own checks look rule-based (id matching, bounds, schema) but the paper never states this. Most likely overturn: the evaluation floor is met only through tool-selection F1 and recovery rates (0.2919 to 0.6697 mean F1, 61.19 percent full recovery, 62.22 percent reduced-missing, no-critic ablation over 450 trials); no hazard, violation, collision or unsafe-recommendation rate appears anywhere, so exclude-E2 is defensible. (c) fails the primacy test - multi-agent safety is an architectural design goal, not a measured outcome. (e) is architectural only: humans approve recommendations and can override the critic ("the CRA decision can be overridden by an explicit human approval signal", Sec. 3.4), but no takeover timing, quality or situation awareness is studied and there is no user study, so the maintainer may strike (e). Nothing acts on the machine at execution time - outputs are recommendations gated before CAM implementation - which also weakens (a). Digital-twin deviation reduction (about 1e-2 in to 1e-3 in) is simulation only, with no point-to-point agreement to the 30 inspection points and a residual the authors say is not uniquely attributable to deflection. Latency 4.3 s and KG overhead 0.7305 to 2.6496 s are reported but edge deployment is motivation only, so not (d). The abstract's "up to 87.5 percentage points" tool-execution uplift is in the conclusion but stated as up to 87.5 percent on L2 and at least 32 percent on L3; Table 1's capability comparison is self-assessed. One fetch.

title: MSR77 A TALE OF TWO THRESHOLDS: ADAPTIVE THRESHOLDING WITH ABSTENTION FOR AI-ASSISTED SINGLE SCREENING (AISS)
evidence: "The two threshold strategy turns classifier output into one of three actions (include, exclude, postpone)." (MSR77 abstract, Methods)
method: Two adaptive thresholds on a title/abstract screening classifier give include, exclude or postpone; postponed records go back to manual human screening in AI-assisted single screening.
evaluation: Simulation on 160 Cochrane reviews (60 tuning, 100 test) with simulated human errors and two stress tests; recall, conflict rate, share deferred; no comparator method reported; no hardware or latency.
contribution: A conference abstract simulating two-threshold abstention for AI-assisted systematic-review screening: recall stays at or above 95% with 2-3% of records postponed to humans, but fails under automation bias.
flag: (i): abstention hands uncertain records back to human screeners and is the main contribution. The text file is a page of Value in Health conference abstracts (June 2026, S311); the record is the single ~300-word poster abstract MSR77, located and read in full, not a wrong file. Reason for E2: no baseline or ablation is reported (no single-threshold or no-abstention comparator), only the strategy's own behaviour across simulated scenarios, and humans are simulated. Numbers given: recall >=95% with 2-3% postponed under realistic error; model-collapse stress test 12.6% deferred, recall 97.5%; automation-bias test recall <90% with low abstention. No method detail on how thresholds adapt. One-shot per-record decision, so E4 is the alternative reading if the maintainer does not count the human handback. Authors are from a vendor (Evidence Prime); LLM evaluation described as ongoing.

title: Empirical fair auditing of high-confidence failures under distribution shift
evidence: "at deployment time, each incoming example is scored, restricted to the monitored high-confidence slice in Eq. (8), and ranked according to estimated failure risk. Finally, a budgeted alert set is selected" (Sec 3.6)
method: A detector head (TCP-M with tau-gating, multi-threshold supervision) scores failure risk among high-confidence predictions; a fixed review budget is allocated by global, parity or bounded group quotas.
evaluation: ACSIncome, Diabetic Readmission, CivilComments, CivilComments->Jigsaw; 20 seeds, shift severity sweep; vs TCP, SCOD, PSCOD plus ablations; HC-AUC, Precision/Recall/Lift@5%, alert-rate gap; Tesla P100, no latency.
contribution: A failure detector that ranks high-confidence predictions by risk of being wrong under distribution shift and allocates a fixed human-review budget with group-parity quotas.
flag: none of (i)-(v) cleanly: this is a one-shot failure/uncertainty estimator judged by precision and lift at a fixed budget, applied to batch pools of static classification data. Borderline (i): flagged cases are meant for downstream human review, but no reviewer is modelled or simulated and no post-review outcome is measured, so the handoff itself is not studied; selection is a top-K ranking over a batch, not a per-decision gate. Abstract numbers found in Table 4 (HC-AUC 0.944 and Lift@5 9.518 on Diabetic Readmission, Lift@5 4.561 on ACSIncome). I could not locate the abstract's 99.8% alert-rate-disparity reduction in the body text by search (may sit in a table I did not read). Abstract omits that SCOD beats the method on CivilComments (HC-AUC 0.833 vs 0.801; Precision@5 0.170 vs 0.114) and that its Equal Opportunity gap is higher than baselines on three datasets. Absolute Precision@5 is low (0.07-0.26). Some garbled prose in Sec 4.4 (Diabetic shift description). Ablation and sensitivity sections skimmed only.

title: Classification with reject option: Distribution-free error guarantees via conformal prediction
evidence: "By accepting only the singleton predictions, we turn CP into a binary classifier with reject option." (Sec 1)
method: Binary conformal predictor used as a rejector: singleton prediction sets accepted, empty and two-label sets rejected; derives the error rate on accepted predictions as a function of significance level.
evaluation: Proved: singleton error = (eps - P(empty))/P(singleton) online (Prop 2), PAC-type inductive bound. Illustrated on qsar-biodeg, spambase, California housing; no baseline; results in figures only.
contribution: Derives a distribution-free expression and estimator for the error rate of accepted predictions when a binary conformal predictor rejects every non-singleton set.
flag: (v), borderline: the contribution is a formal error guarantee for the reject option, but it is a short proposition (rearranged law of total probability) plus a PAC-type corollary resting on Vovk et al.; the batch-update result is a sketch. No baseline at all and the only number in the text is a maximum singleton rate of about 0.4 on qsar-biodeg (reject rate about 0.6); other results are figures only. Binary classification only, one-shot in practice (online protocol is the conformal validity setting, not abstention as an action over time). Rejected cases are not routed to anyone. Reader notes the 'unbiased estimator' claim is stronger than the asymptotic argument shown. If (v) is read as requiring substantial theory, this is exclude-E4.

title: Conformal validation: A deferral policy using uncertainty quantification with a human-in-the-loop for model validation
evidence: "the policy defers a subset of observations for which the predictive model is most uncertain and provides a human with informative prediction sets to make the ancillary decision" (Abstract)
method: Conformal Validation: RAPS conformal sets on a Swin classifier; any non-singleton set is deferred to a human, who optionally sees the prediction set.
evaluation: Food-101 subset with Gaussian blur; 30 human participants, 50 deferred images each; arms: model alone, human with sets, human alone; accuracy on deferred images, per-class accuracy, response time; no latency budget.
contribution: A conformal set-size rule defers 35% of blurred food images to people; in a 30-person study humans beat the model on deferred images by 15-19 points, with prediction sets adding an unproven further gain.
flag: (i): deferral to a human is the main contribution and the handoff is studied with real participants (IRB-approved, 30 people, in-house recruits). Doubts: one-shot image classification with a fixed, hand-inspected threshold (not learned); no comparison against another deferral rule (entropy, softmax) - the baseline is the model alone on the deferred subset, which is the weakest reading of the evaluation floor; maintainer may prefer E4. Numbers: deferral rate 35% (34.6% in Table 1) at alpha=10%; model accuracy 95% on non-deferred; humans +18.7% with sets and +15.2% without vs model on deferred images (p<0.01 each); sets vs no sets +3.5% (95% CI -1.2% to 8.2%, p=0.08, not significant). No end-to-end system accuracy for the combined human-AI pipeline is reported. Response times shown only in a figure; sets slow responses. Toy task (food images) standing in for high-risk use. Number of classes used is not clear from the text I read. Arithmetic: 2500 test samples, 1000 for calibration.

title: Conformalized classifiers with reject option
evidence: "Pick one instance from this sorted sequence to reject all instances with a lower confidence and predict all instances with a higher confidence." (Sec 3)
method: Binary conformal (and Mondrian) classifiers used as reject-option classifiers: instances are ranked by conformal confidence and expected accuracy or precision of the kept set is estimated from set-type proportions.
evaluation: 41 public binary tabular datasets, 100x hold-out; decision trees, random forest, XGBoost; vs uncalibrated, Platt, isotonic, Beta, Platt-binning; accuracy/precision estimation error at 10-90% rejection, Friedman/Nemenyi ranks.
contribution: Conformal prediction turned into a reject-option classifier whose accuracy or precision at any rejection level can be estimated in advance, more accurately than calibrated probabilistic predictors on 41 datasets.
flag: none of (i)-(v): a one-shot classifier with reject option evaluated on benchmark tabular data by how well it predicts its own accuracy/precision at each rejection rate. Not (v): the validity claim is inherited from conformal prediction under exchangeability and stated informally (Eq. 7-8); no theorem or proof appears in the text. Human referral is mentioned only as motivation; no human, no sequential setting. The authors state the procedure needs a batch of test instances and "cannot be used in a streaming scenario", and it is binary-only. Results are mostly rank-based significance figures (Conf significantly best for precision estimation at all rejection levels for XGB and RF); I did not find a single headline estimation-error number in the text. Conformal error rates match eps (means 0.010, 0.050, ~0.100). Extends the authors' own 2023 conference papers. Per-dataset tables skimmed, figures not readable in text.

title: “I do not know! but why?” — Local model-agnostic example-based explanations of reject
evidence: "we propose a model-agnostic framework that enriches classification with reject option by explanation mechanisms" (Abstract)
method: Fits a local surrogate (logistic regression or depth-3 tree) around a rejected input of a conformal-prediction reject option, then computes counterfactual, semi-factual and factual explanations of the reject.
evaluation: 6 tabular datasets, kNN/GNB/random forest, 5-fold CV; surrogate vs black-box Downhill-simplex solver; feasibility, fidelity (recall of perturbed features), sparsity; 0.16-0.43 s vs 0.70-6.18 s per explanation.
contribution: Explains why a conformal reject option abstained, using local surrogates to produce sparse counterfactual, semi-factual and factual examples about four to twenty times faster than direct black-box search.
flag: none of (i)-(v): the contribution is post-hoc explanation of an existing reject option, not the abstain/defer decision; the reject rule itself is a standard conformal threshold and is never evaluated (no error-reject or risk-coverage result). Handoff to a human expert is the motivation only; no user study, authors say so (Sec 7-8). Surrogate fidelity is clearly LOWER than the black-box baseline for counterfactuals (avg 0.25-0.47 vs 0.80-0.87, Table 4); the win is sparsity and time. Extended version of Artelt et al. 2022 conference paper. Hardware not stated. Appendix tables (decision-tree surrogate, sensitivity) skimmed only. Mild RQ3 relevance (slow explanation of a halt).

title: Performance visualization spaces for classification with rejection option
evidence: "We introduce a new visualization space called the cost reject space." (Abstract)
method: Analyses three spaces for displaying reject-classifier performance (ROC, error-reject, new cost-reject); derives an expected-value interpolation of the error-reject curve to replace linear interpolation.
evaluation: Illustrative only: synthetic 10-D two-class Gaussians, LDA vs SVM with posterior threshold; plots comparing linear vs proposed interpolation against large-sample true curve; no tables, no numeric metrics, no hardware.
contribution: Shows that linear interpolation of error-reject curves overestimates reject-classifier performance, gives an unbiased interpolation, and proposes a cost-reject space in which a classifier is a line.
flag: none of (i)-(v): an evaluation/visualisation methodology for one-shot classification with a reject option, offline analysis, no deferral mechanism proposed. Nearest is (v), but there is no stated theorem or proof: the interpolation is derived by a binomial-expectation argument and checked on one simulation by figure only (Fig. 2-3). No quantitative result against a baseline is reported in numbers, so exclude-E2 is an equally defensible code. Single-author paper; received 2017, published 2019. ROC section (Sec 5) read only in part. Possible use to the review is as a caution on how risk-coverage curves are drawn.

title: Learning to complement with multiple humans
