flag: (ii): defer and abstain are actions taken over time inside a trial; no human or fallback system receives the deferral (DEFER = wait for the next EEG window). Doubts: single independent author, self-described firsts. At matched encoder the agent ties or loses to hand-thresholded baselines on return (Table I; BCI-IV-2b LOSO row is identical to EEGNet-fixed: acc 0.65, ITR 1.9, latency 3.0 s, i.e. the policy collapses to waiting until trial end). The Lee2019 wrong-commit advantage is not significant (p=0.07) and LOSO vs random is significant on one of three datasets. Paper states RECAL and voluntary ABSTAIN are 'latent' (action share DEFER 92%, commit 6.3%, timeout-abstain 1.7%), so abstention is in practice a timeout. Headline 87.6% is on 3 easy subjects at 27% commit rate (task accuracy 0.234); 9-subject figure is 74.6% at 29%. CMDP budget 'satisfied in every configuration' sits beside per-seed wrong-commit rates up to 0.135. Panel described as six temperature-perturbed agents but five temperatures listed, three mixtures but four percentages; total is still stated as 12. All results are offline replay of logged trials, no closed-loop users; 0.25 s is the decision step, compute latency is not reported. I did not read Appendices A-H beyond the hardware line.

title: Detecting Attacks at Switching Speed: Ai/Ml and Active Learning for in-Network Monitoring in Data Planes
venue: IEEE International Conference on Network Protocols
evidence: "In HALIDS, an intelligent network device can either make a decision with a suitable level of confidence or defer the decision to an expert oracle." (Sec. I)
method: P4 data-plane intrusion detector: in-switch decision tree/random forest classifies each packet; below a confidence threshold the packet is exported to an off-band oracle model, whose labels also retrain the switch.
evaluation: BMv2 software switch on a laptop, UNSW-NB15 traces (~2M packets). Versus switch-only baseline: detection gain ~20% (M1), ~11% (M2), 0 (M3); oracle query rate <0.4%; packet loss unchanged. No latency.
contribution: HALIDS lets a programmable switch block or forward packets itself and defer low-confidence ones to an off-band oracle, improving malware-packet detection by up to about 20% while querying under 0.4% of packets.
flag: (i) with (ii) and (iv): per-packet streaming deferral from an in-line gate that drops or releases traffic to an off-band fallback model (the oracle is a larger random forest, not a human). Borderline against the E1 clause on cascades to a larger model: here the small model is forced by data-plane limits and the deferral gates a security action, but the paper frames itself as an implementation/automation prototype with active-learning retraining, not as a deferral study. Evidence is thin: all detection results are relative gains read from figures, no absolute recall/F1 values or tables, no seeds; M1 and M2 F1 are called 'rather poor'. No latency measured although the text admits oracle queries delay the packet; '@hardware' means a laptop running BMv2, no hardware P4 switch. Text says retraining gain is 'almost 50%' while the Fig. 9 axis runs 0-1.5. Oracle accuracy itself is never reported and the oracle serves as ground truth for retraining. Extension of a TMA 2024 poster by the same authors.

title: DAG-Net: Double Attentive Graph Neural Network for Trajectory Forecasting
venue: Proceedings - International Conference on Pattern Recognition/Proceedings/International Conference on Pattern Recognition
evidence: Method section: a variational recurrent neural network with 32-dim latent variables predicts future displacements while two attentive graph networks share predicted goals and recurrent hidden states across agents.
method: Per-agent VRNN with grid-cell goal prediction conditioning prior, encoder and decoder; two attentive GNNs (2 layers, 4 heads) share goals and hidden states across agents; decodes future displacements.
evaluation: NBA SportVU (10 observed, 40 predicted, feet) and Stanford Drone TrajNet (8-12, metres); vs STGAT, Social-Ways, Weak-Supervision, C-VAE; attack ADE-FDE 8.98-14.08 vs STGAT 9.94-15.80, defence 6.87-9.76 vs 7.26-11.28, SDD 0.53-1.04 vs 0.58-1.11; ablations vanilla VRNN 0.58-1.17 and A-VRNN 0.56-1.14; no hardware or timing reported.
contribution: Couples per-agent variational recurrent prediction with two attentive graph networks over shared goals and hidden states, improving multi-agent trajectory forecasting on basketball and urban drone data.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - predictor only, no runtime interception. Check: ADE and FDE are the only metrics, with no safety, collision or hazard outcome, and no latency or hardware figure anywhere, so it gives nothing for the edge or jitter questions; on the defence 20-30 long-term split its ADE 5.01 is slightly worse than C-VAE 4.98.

title: OptLayer - Practical Constrained Optimization for Deep Reinforcement Learning in the Real World
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Method section: OptLayer sits between the policy network and the robot and returns the action closest to the network prediction that satisfies joint, velocity, torque and collision constraints, and only corrected actions are executed on the real robot.
method: Differentiable quadratic-program layer appended to a deep RL policy projects the predicted action onto state-dependent joint, velocity, torque and collision-avoidance constraints; the CPC strategy trains on both raw and corrected actions.
evaluation: 2D reacher (TRPO) and UR5 6-DoF reaching in Gazebo and on hardware, 36 joint plus 20 collision constraints; vs unconstrained UP and CP, CC variants; all constrained strategies had zero collisions over 7000 episodes and 6h of from-scratch real-robot training while UP knocked over the obstacle; average reward 700 reached in 3250 (CPC) vs 5350 (UP) episodes; 64ms vs 60ms per step, about 4ms OptLayer overhead inside a 0.1s control step.
contribution: A differentiable constrained-optimisation layer projects a deep RL policy's action onto safety constraints before execution, giving collision-free real-robot training and faster learning than penalty-only reinforcement learning.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a deep RL (TRPO) policy; the filter itself is a QP, which the scope ruling allows. Check: the layer corrects or projects rather than vetoing or halting, so criterion (a) rests on reading projection as an override; collisions are reported as "never" rather than as counted rates, and the real-robot episode count is not stated; the 4ms overhead is measured but there is no deadline or jitter analysis, so I did not credit (d) or the latency gap cell; single arm, no multi-agent aspect.

title: Multimodal Probabilistic Model-Based Planning for Human-Robot Interaction
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. V-B: a CVAE with discrete latent z and LSTM encoder-decoder predicts GMM distributions over the human's future actions conditioned on interaction history and a candidate robot action sequence.
method: CVAE-LSTM human response model conditioned on candidate robot action sequences; a two-stage sampling planner scores 4096 sequences with about 100000 sampled human responses and executes the lowest expected-cost one, replanning every 0.3s.
evaluation: 1105 human-human traffic-weaving trials in the Vires VTD simulator (about 77000 exemplars) plus real-time human-in-the-loop runs; the only number for a model is the basic LSTM baseline eval NLL -9.70, its own CVAE NLL appears only in Fig. 4 and is described as "slightly" better; no collision, violation or success rate; policy step about 0.25s on a GTX 1080 Ti.
contribution: Conditions a multimodal CVAE human-response model on candidate robot action sequences and uses it inside a receding-horizon planner for interactive highway traffic weaving.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - the human is modelled and predicted, not guarded, and collision avoidance is only a cost term inside the planner, so criterion (a) fails by the ruling on planners with no runtime override. E2 because the paper reports no quantitative result for its own model: a second read of Sec. V and VI found only Table I (human pass fractions) and the LSTM baseline NLL -9.70, with its own NLL in Fig. 4 and the closed-loop and human-in-the-loop results purely qualitative. Most likely overturn if the maintainer counts the Fig. 4 NLL values as the (b) predictive measure.

title: Robust Model Predictive Shielding for Safe Reinforcement Learning with Stochastic Dynamics
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Algorithm 1: at each step the shield executes the learned policy only if the next state is robustly recoverable, and otherwise switches to a tube-based robust NMPC backup controller.
method: Model predictive shielding for stochastic dynamics: a sampling-based robust recoverability check per step switches between a DDPG policy and a tube-based robust tracking NMPC backup that drives the system into an invariant set, then an LQR-style stabiliser.
evaluation: Simulation only - cart-pole, holonomic and non-holonomic particle with obstacles, 50 scenarios and 3 seeds, N=1500 samples; vs the learned policy alone, non-robust MPS and linear-robust LRMPS; RMPS and LRMPS reach a stated "safety probability of 1.0" while the learned policy is frequently unsafe and MPS is only slightly safer; goal-reaching drops about 20% on the non-holonomic particle; LRMPS invokes the backup more often (Fig. 3); Lemma 1 and Theorem 1 give probabilistic one-step recoverability bounds; no wall-clock latency.
contribution: Shields a learned RL policy with a sampling-based robust recoverability test and a tube-based NMPC backup, achieving empirically perfect safety under stochastic dynamics at modest performance cost.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a DDPG policy, with a non-learned MPC shield, which the scope ruling allows. Check: single-agent throughout, so no (c); the per-environment safety, reward and backup-invocation numbers are in Fig. 3 rather than the text, so only "safety probability of 1.0" is quotable; the guarantee is one-step and high-probability, not infinite-horizon, and two heuristics (sampled invariant set, precomputed boxes) may weaken it; the authors call the method "still too slow for production systems" and report no measured latency, so I did not credit (d); the time-to-irreversibility gap cell is my reading of the recoverability check and can be dropped.

title: PredictionNet: Real-Time Joint Probabilistic Traffic Prediction for Planning, Control, and Simulation
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. III.A.2: a CNN encoder-decoder with two recurrent networks, one processing past-present observations and one rolling out the future, predicts future occupancy, velocity and backtrace vectors for all agents jointly in a single pass, about 5 ms on NVIDIA Drive AGX (Sec. IV).
method: Raster CNN encoder-decoder with recurrent rollout jointly predicts future occupancy, velocity and backtrace vectors for all traffic agents over 3 s; frozen trunk reused for an SAC ego-policy head.
evaluation: INTERACTION, internal 5,000 km LiDAR set, sim and 530 km real drives; vs analytic predictor, TNT, MultiPath, ITRA; ADE 0.458 m, FDE 1.030 m; sim collisions 4.1% vs 8.7%; 5 ms on Drive AGX.
contribution: Shows a single-pass raster world model can predict joint traffic futures accurately enough to drive planning, control and simulation within about 5 ms on embedded automotive hardware.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - prediction only, nothing can override or halt an action, so (a) fails and I rest on (b) plus (d). Check whether a raster occupancy-plus-velocity rollout counts as a world model under the Pillar 2 scope rather than a trajectory regressor, and whether (d) holds with no stated deadline; the non-generative-inference cell is my reading of a single-pass deterministic decoder despite the paper's 'probabilistic' title. PredictionNet-RL numbers (cut-in failures 2% vs ACC 88%, harsh brake 0% vs 100%) are simulation only; the abstract's 'hundreds of kilometers' real-world control is backed only by a 15% comfort improvement and 'no network-related safety disengagements', with no safety-metric baseline; authors note their ADE-FDE is single-trajectory against best-of-6 baselines.

title: Contingencies from Observations: Tractable Contingency Planning with Learned Behavior Models
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. III-B: a conditional autoregressive normalizing flow q(X|o) over joint multi-agent future trajectories is learned from observations, and Sec. III-C plans by stochastic gradient ascent on the robot's latent variables inside that model.
method: Learns a conditional normalizing flow over joint multi-agent futures from LIDAR-paired demonstrations; plans by gradient ascent in the robot's latent variables, giving a closed-loop contingent policy re-planned each step.
evaluation: CARLA left-turn, overtake and stop-sign right-turn at 3 held-out locations, 90 episodes per method; vs noncontingent ablations, MFP, PPO; goal-reached-without-near-collision 27-28/30 vs 9-16/30; no prediction error or latency.
contribution: Shows contingency planning becomes tractable by optimizing latent variables of a learned joint behavior model, producing closed-loop reactive driving from observational data without hand-specified multi-agent models.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - safety enters only as a prior and a constraint term inside the planner objective (App. F approximates a violated constraint with a large negative value), which the 2026-11-13 ruling explicitly excludes from (a). (b) holds on reading, but the Pillar 2 floor needs a direct predictive measure and the paper reports none (no ADE-FDE, no held-out likelihood), hence E2; a maintainer may prefer E1 on the view that this is a planner paper. Counter-evidence to weigh: the RG* metric does require no near-collisions and is reported against ablations and MFP, which can be read as a safety metric. No hardware, runtime or latency figures anywhere; CARLA only, experts are hand-crafted and suboptimal.

title: Pylot: A Modular Platform for Exploring Latency-Accuracy Tradeoffs in Autonomous Vehicles
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. VI-A: 'timely accuracy' scores each component against ground truth at the time its result is produced, and a 35 ms detector runtime halves mean timely AP50 in a pedestrian emergency scenario about 20 m ahead.
method: Modular dataflow AV platform on a Rust runtime with interchangeable detection, tracking, prediction and planning operators, pseudo-asynchronous simulation that defers control commands by measured pipeline runtime, and timely-accuracy metrics.
evaluation: CARLA city driving and pedestrian-emergency scenarios, 10-40 m/s sweeps; perfect components and 3 planners in fast-slow configs; timely mIoU 0.75 at 10 ms, AP50 halved at 35 ms, P99 15-760 ms.
contribution: Open platform and timely-accuracy methodology quantifying how component latency, not accuracy alone, decides whether an autonomous vehicle avoids a collision, with faster weaker configurations often safer.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a learned perception-and-planning pipeline, but there is no interceptor: the only deferral is a simulation synchronizer that buffers the control command until simulated time matches pipeline runtime, so (a) fails and I rest on (d) alone. Evaluation floor is thin: Table I's collision-avoidance results at 16-22 m/s are colour-coded and not recoverable as numbers from the text, ride comfort appears only in Fig. 4, no jitter figures, no deadline enforcement and no CARLA Challenge score beyond 'a high score'. Experiments ran on 2 Xeon Gold CPUs and 2 Titan RTX, not edge hardware, so I did not credit edge deployment; the real Lincoln MKZ port (434 lines) has no quantitative results. Judge also whether a platform-and-measurement paper is E3-adjacent; I read it as a system plus empirical study, not a survey.

title: Conformal Decision Theory: Safe Autonomous Decisions from Imperfect Predictions
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. V-A: 'Our approach (CC) adapts the reward weight lambda_t on the human collision cost' - the conformal control variable is a term inside the planner objective, and Sec. VI only proposes as an extension that 'we revert to a safe decision if lambda_t <= lambda_safe'.
method: Online gradient update of one conservativeness parameter lambda indexing a family of decision functions, with a proved bound on empirical risk under an eventual-safety assumption; batch variant via conformal risk control.
evaluation: Stanford Drone MPC navigation, simulated conveyor manufacturing, simulated trading; vs ACI, aggressive, conservative, UCB, LCB, oracles; safe at 1.142 m min distance and 29% faster to goal than ACI; no latency.
contribution: Conformal decision theory adapts a single conservativeness knob online so that actions taken from imperfect learned predictions meet a user-chosen risk level without distributional assumptions.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a learned autoregressive human-trajectory predictor in the robot study, simulated predictors elsewhere. MOST LIKELY OVERTURN. Under the 2026-11-13 ruling lambda is a cost weight inside the planner (and in the manufacturing study lambda IS the action, the belt speed), with no override, veto, halt or defer, so no letter holds and I record E1; a maintainer may instead rule that online conformal risk control over a learned predictor is a runtime safety mechanism, in which case Theorem 1's bound R_t <= eps + ((lambda_1-lambda_safe)/eta + K)/t plus the ACI and conservative baselines clear the floor, and the physical-plus-financial evaluation is a genuine cross-domain case. Robot safety is a boolean over one run per learning rate; manufacturing and trading numbers appear only in Figs. 5-6; no intervention rate, latency or hardware.

title: Conformal Policy Learning for Sensorimotor Control under Distribution Shifts
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. IV-D, Eq. 10: pi_switch uses pi_safe when the predicted distance plus its conformal quantile reaches the threshold and pi_speed otherwise, so the safe policy takes over the learned fast policy's actions at execution time.
method: An online P-controlled conformal quantile on a learned predictor's error serves either as a switching threshold between a fast and a safe DQN policy or as an extra observation for an end-to-end RL policy.
evaluation: highway-env 50-car driving, 500 rollouts, plus Unitree Go1 SLAM tracking in and out of distribution; vs dropout, ensemble, HAU, certificates, no-quantile; duration 37.8 s vs 19.4 s; coverage above 0.9; 10 Hz.
contribution: Treats a calibrated conformal quantile as a policy input so a robot switches to a conservative controller exactly when its predictions stop being reliable under distribution shift, at negligible extra compute.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a DQN driving policy and a SLAM-driven quadruped controller, overridden at runtime by pi_safe, so (a) holds and runtime_interceptor is yes. Check the evaluation floor: no collision, violation, intervention or switch rate is given numerically, collision frequency appears only in the Fig. 2 Pareto curves ('always achieves a higher speed than the baselines at the same collision frequency'), and the dropout, ensemble, HAU and certificate comparisons are qualitative plus those curves; I relied on Table I episode duration (rollouts terminate on collision) and speed against pi_speed and the no-quantile ablation. On the quadruped pi_switch only retunes the P gain, and pi_safe cannot stop because minimum speed is 20 m/s, so 'halt' is never available; deferral is always to another policy, never to a human, so not (e). Edge-deployment is credited on the 10 Hz onboard Go1 alone, with no latency measurement.

title: RiskBench: A Scenario-based Benchmark for Risk Identification
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Sec. V (closely paraphrased): each risk identifier outputs a per-road-user risk score and an object counts as a risk once the score passes a threshold; Table III then reports Influenced Ratio and Collision Rate for a privileged planner that sees only the identified risk.
method: CARLA scenario-based benchmark of 6916 scripted ego-plus-interacting-agent scenarios with risk ground truth, evaluating ten risk identifiers on localization, anticipation, temporal consistency and the driving outcome of a privileged planner.
evaluation: 1689 CARLA test scenarios (521 interactive, 375 collision, 322 obstacle, 471 non-interactive); ten baselines (Random, Range 5m and 10m, Kalman, Social-GAN, MANTRA, QCNet, DSA, RRL, BP, BCP); best overall F-1 53.6 for rule-based Range 10m vs 48.6 RRL and 15.1 Random; planning-aware collision rate 0.4% interactive and 5.3% obstacle with ground-truth risk vs 33.6% and 58.7% for CARLA autopilot, 10.0% and 57.2% for QCNet; temporal consistency 3 s before the critical point 18.5% QCNet to 1.9% BP; one ablation (full vs restricted observation); no hardware, no latency.
contribution: A CARLA benchmark that scores risk identification not only by localization and anticipation but by the driving outcome a privileged planner reaches when it is shown only the identified risk.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: which - seven of the ten identifiers are learned (Social-GAN, MANTRA, QCNet, DSA, RRL, BP, BCP) and the planning-aware test uses an imitation-trained privileged planner, but Random, Range and Kalman are rule-based. No runtime interception anywhere: risk-aware planning is named as future work, so this is a dataset-plus-protocol record and the maintainer may rule it E1 or E4 because risk is scored per object from the ego front view rather than as a property of agent interaction. Internal inconsistencies: the intro says 14 maps and 237 road structures while Sec. III says 8 towns and 231 Area IDs; the claim that RRL leads on F-1 holds only among learned models, since rule-based Range 10m scores 53.6. Vision methods are fed ground-truth tracklets and restricted to the front view; temporal-smoothing results sit in the video submission only; no mIoU, no hardware, no latency. The non-generative inference cell could also be credited, since generative trajectory predictors are benchmarked head-to-head against direct risk scorers and mostly lose.

title: Plug in the Safety Chip: Enforcing Constraints for LLM-driven Robot Agents
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: Method section: for black-box agents the chip 'stops execution when it detects an imminent unsafe state', and otherwise masks any action whose state change would leave the automaton's valid states, so it is pruned rather than executed.
method: English safety constraints translated to LTL by modular Lang2LTL-style prompting, expert-verified, conjoined into one automaton that masks or halts a GPT-4 robot agent's next action and re-prompts it with a generated violation explanation.
evaluation: VirtualHome 20 household tasks with five constraints each in two environments, plus a Boston Dynamics Spot with two mobile-manipulation tasks of ten constraints and three task-abortion tests; success-rate and safety-rate: Four Room 76% and 84%, Mobile Manipulation 88% and 94%, rising to 98% and 100% with expert-verified LTL, against NL-constraint prompting 100% and 56% and the unconstrained base model 90% and 38% in Four Room and 94% and 30% in Mobile Manipulation; on the robot 98% and 100% vs NL 98% and 34% and Code-as-Policies 53% and 55%, and above five constraints NL safety falls to 0% while Safety Chip aborts contradictory tasks without entering unsafe states; GPT-4-0613, no component ablation, no latency.
contribution: Compiles English safety constraints into one verified LTL automaton that masks or aborts an LLM robot agent's actions at execution time and explains each violation back to the planner.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a GPT-4 LLM robot agent, intercepted before execution, so (a) is clear. Single agent only: VirtualHome is described as a multi-agent platform but every experiment runs one agent, so (c) fails and the sequential multi-step LTL setting is what keeps the record off E4. Humans only author and verify constraints before deployment, so (e) does not hold - the fast-halt-then-explanation loop sends its explanation to the LLM, not to a person, and dialog-based confirmation is future work; RQ3 is scored on that mechanism, not on a human study. Monitoring assumes perfect proposition truth values, read from the simulator, so the 100% safety rate is conditional on perfect perception. The 76% vs 100% success-rate drop under unverified LTL is the paper's own false-halt cost. No component ablation, no token counts, no latency, VirtualHome trial counts unstated, robot tasks run twice at temperature 0. Not cross-domain: Spot and VirtualHome are both physical settings. Time-to-irreversibility is credited for the check that the automaton state can still reach an accepting state, which is a weaker reading than the review's usual one.

title: Reducing Oracle Feedback with Vision-Language Embeddings for Preference-Based RL
venue: IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation
evidence: Abstract: 'defers to an oracle only for samples with high uncertainty, identified through a filtering mechanism' - the deferral is a training-time preference-label query, not a withheld decision.
method: ROVED: preference-based RL where a vision-language embedding labels segment pairs and only uncertain pairs (KL-threshold band) are sent to a human or VLM oracle; adapters fine-tune the embedding.
evaluation: 8 Meta-World tasks, 5 seeds, vs PEBBLE, SURF, MRN, LIV, DecisionNCE, RL-VLM-F; oracle queries cut 50-80%, 75-90% with transfer; label latency under 0.009 s vs about 5 s per VLM query; no hardware stated.
contribution: Preference-based RL that labels most trajectory pairs with a vision-language embedding and queries a human or VLM oracle only for uncertain pairs, cutting oracle feedback by 50-80% on Meta-World.
flag: none of (i)-(v): the 'deferral' is active label querying during reward-model training, not abstention on an executed decision; nothing sits between a decision and its execution. Success rates appear only in figures; the 80% and 90% abstract figures are in the body. Title matches.

title: A Dynamic Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach for Eco-Safe Mixed Platooning
venue: 2026 11th International Conference on Intelligent Computing and Signal Processing, ICSP 2026
evidence: "the supervisor forcefully intervenes, overriding the DRL action ai,t with the maximum safe deceleration amin to physically prevent the crash" (Sec. III-D)
method: GAT over a dynamic graph fusing radar and V2V edges feeds MAPPO under CTDE with an eco-safe mixed reward; a one-step kinematic supervisor overrides unsafe accelerations at execution.
evaluation: SUMO co-simulation, 1 leader and 16 followers, NGSIM human-driver traces, 50% CAV penetration, penetration sweep 0-100%; baselines SFC-CTH, DDPG, DPPO; fuel 1.32 vs 1.45-1.60 ml/s, mean speed 14.3 m/s, dampening ratio 0.51 and 0.38; no collision, near-miss or intervention count and no supervisor ablation.
contribution: Cascades a one-step kinematic override on a graph-attention MAPPO platoon controller, reporting fuel, travel-efficiency and string-stability gains over classical and DRL baselines.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - MAPPO graph policy, so criterion (a) is met on reading, but the safety mechanism is never measured: no collision, near-miss, headway-violation or intervention rate anywhere, and no ablation with the supervisor removed, while the paper claims an "absolute mathematical guarantee against collisions" with no proof. exclude-E1 is also defensible because the primary claims and all measured outcomes are fuel economy, average speed and string stability. Draft residue in the body ("textcoloryelloweach", a section titled "PREPOSITION"); GAT is credited to Sperduti and Starita 1997 instead of Velickovic et al.; ref [13] is a 2026 TITS paper on the same eco-safe mixed platooning problem that this work tracks closely - check for overlap.

title: MedHAI: Improved Framework for medical diagnosis using human experts
venue: 2024 IEEE 5th India Council International Subsections Conference (INDISCON)
evidence: "we defer it to an expert for human annotations, which will subsequently be submitted to the defer model" (Sec. III-E)
method: Chest X-ray classifier with calibrated confidence and two validation-tuned probability thresholds; in-band cases with confidence below 90% are deferred to an expert whose annotation feeds a second defer model.
evaluation: ChestX-ray8 subset (1,964 images), four CNNs. Combined vs AI-only accuracy: InceptionV3 70.01 vs 65.64%, MobileNetV2 78.23 vs 74.34, InceptionResNetV2 72.11 vs 66.28, ResNet50 65.64 vs 63.92. No deferral rate or latency.
contribution: MedHAI defers low-confidence chest X-ray predictions to an expert-annotation-assisted model, raising accuracy by about 2-6 points over the classifier alone across four backbones.
flag: (i), weakly: deferral to a human expert is the stated contribution, but it is a hand-set confidence rule, not learned deferral, and close to a domain reject-option paper (maintainer may prefer exclude-E4). Serious evaluation doubts: the deferral rate (expert workload) is never reported, so the cost claim is unsupported; no comparison with random deferral, learning-to-defer or any cited baseline, only AI-alone. The 'expert' is the dataset's bounding boxes fed to a defer model with 95-99% accuracy, and boxes exist only for diseased images, so the label probably leaks. No sensitivity or specificity figures are given despite being the stated objective; no test-split description, seeds or CIs. Abstract says 'about 6%', best case is +5.83 points (InceptionResNetV2). Training accuracy below validation accuracy for three models; formulas for sensitivity/specificity/accuracy are printed inverted; 'Patt Scaling' described with the temperature-scaling formula. Methodology follows ref [2] (Gupta et al. 2023) closely.

title: Correct-by-synthesis reinforcement learning with temporal logic constraints
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Sec. IV: the permissive strategy is applied to the game to remove every transition it does not allow, yielding a game whose winning condition is True so that any strategy learned inside it is correct by construction; no module observes or overrides a nominal decision.
method: Extract a (maximally) permissive winning strategy for a temporal-logic two-player game offline with slugs, prune the game to its allowed transitions, run maximin-Q learning inside the pruned game, then map the learned strategy back.
evaluation: NxN grid-world motion planning against one adversarial robot; no external baseline, comparisons are against the theoretical optimum and across permissiveness levels; Table I extraction 0.10-300 s and learning 4.28-771.73 s over N=3-10 on a 2.4 GHz 8 GB laptop with up to 1.562e7 iterations; N=4 values converge to 10, 9, 8.1, 7.29, matching (1/(1-gamma))*gamma^k; Table II six counter-augmented permissiveness levels raise max discounted reward 5.7368 to 9.8616 while learning time grows 9.87 s to 275.88 s; formal results Prop. 1-2 and Theorem 1; no collision or violation rate.
contribution: Decouples correctness from optimality by pruning a temporal-logic game to a permissive winning strategy and learning the reward-optimal policy inside it, with linear-time maximal permissiveness for a Boolean fragment.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - maximin-Q learning is the learner, so the record fails on the runtime test, not on the scope ruling. This is the most likely overturn in the batch: pruning the game means that at every execution step the learner can only pick a permitted action, which is action masking in effect and the correct-by-synthesis ancestor of shielded RL, so the maintainer may read (a) as met even though the paper describes no interception of a nominal decision and all restriction happens before learning. Safety is by construction with no collision or violation rate anywhere; the formal content is Prop. 2 with its proof omitted and Theorem 1, which covers only phi0 AND phi1 with Boolean conjuncts, while learner optimality is borrowed from Littman's convergence results. The second agent is the environment player of a zero-sum game, not a learner, so (c) fails the primacy test, though the joint two-robot game state could arguably be credited the multi-agent state cell. General extraction is 2-EXPTIME, Example 2 admits no maximally permissive strategy and its reward loss (roughly 1.5-5.5 vs an optimum of 10) is never tabulated.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning on Autonomous Vehicles
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Sec. IV: 'The prediction module masks undesired actions at each time step' and 'Actions that are marked as safe are passed on to the network as permissible actions'; if no action is permissible the vehicle waits.
method: Constant-velocity Kalman predictions of surrounding traffic with quadratically growing uncertainty are overlapped with the ego's predicted maneuver footprint to mask unsafe accelerations before a DQN acts, with a Chebyshev plus union bound giving m/(2*kappa_n^2) < delta.
evaluation: SUMO unsigned-intersection left turn, IDM traffic with Krauss driver imperfection, 0.2 s steps, 100 m sensing, 0.1/s vehicle emission, 20000 training simulations per network, statistics over 1000 trials; 'There were no recorded collisions during the entire training process'; baselines a random policy inside the same mask and an enlarged fixed-margin rule-based policy that performs 'much worse', plus a timeout-penalty ablation z in {-1,-5,-10}; encounters under 10 m vanish by about 7000 iterations and density rises near 20 m; policy verified on a vehicle with six IBEO lidars and three radars; forward checking is O(mT) but no latency is measured.
contribution: Masks a DQN's intersection-crossing actions with an analytic multi-vehicle prediction check whose failure probability is bounded by a Chebyshev-union argument, letting the policy train with zero collisions.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a DQN driving policy, masked before execution. The weakness is evidence, not scope: every comparison lives in Fig. 4-6, the paper prints no table and no numeric collision rate, success rate or time-to-cross, so the whole quantitative safety claim is the sentence 'no recorded collisions' with no baseline collision rate beside it and the baselines beaten only 'much worse' in prose - E2 is defensible. Traffic vehicles are scripted IDM/Krauss and their number is given only as an emission rate, so (c) fails. The probabilistic bound assumes non-adversarial agents, neglects corrective ego control and a fixed 2 m detection uncertainty, and the authors themselves concede the guarantees are weaker than comparable approaches. The arXiv text prints no venue or year although the record says IROS 2018, so check this is the same paper as the DOI; the real-vehicle verification is asserted with no quantitative result and no measured runtime.

title: Conditional Generative Neural System for Probabilistic Trajectory Prediction
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Sec. V and Tables I-III: the system is evaluated only as a predictor, by ADE/FDE over 1-5 s horizons; the feasibility term of Eq. 13 that the authors call a differentiable barrier function is a training loss, not a runtime check, and no planner or controller consumes the predictions.
method: Conditional VAE with a two-dimensional latent space trained jointly with a least-squares GAN discriminator; soft block attention over neighbouring trajectories and a Gaussian image mask feed a frozen VGG-19, GRUs and fully connected layers.
evaluation: ETH and UCY pedestrians (8 observed, 12 predicted steps), Stanford Drone in pixel space and an INTERACTION roundabout set (4 observed, 10 predicted steps); nine baselines (CVM, LR, P-LSTM, S-LSTM, S-GAN, S-GAN-P, SoPhie, CAR-Net, DESIRE) and a four-way input ablation (T+CLSL, T+VDM, T+CLSL+VDM, T+I+CLSL+VDM); average ETH-UCY ADE/FDE 0.49/0.97 m vs 0.54/1.15 SoPhie and 0.58/1.18 S-GAN; SDD 15.6/28.2 px vs 17.8/32.1 SoPhie and 19.3/34.1 DESIRE; roundabout at 5 s 1.47/2.12 m vs 1.69/2.77 S-LSTM; no likelihood, collision or offroad metric, no hardware, no inference time.
contribution: Combines a conditional VAE with a GAN discriminator and attention over neighbouring trajectories and scene images to sample feasible multi-modal future trajectories for interacting road users and pedestrians.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - nothing is guarded or intercepted, so (a) and (c) fail outright. The judgement the maintainer is most likely to overturn: (b) holds on a literal reading, since this is a latent conditional generative model of FUTURE multi-agent state with a direct predictive measure, nine baselines and a four-way ablation, and the Pillar 2 ruling excludes only a 'plain trajectory regressor'. I read a CVAE-GAN trajectory-prediction paper with no dynamics model, no action conditioning and no closed-loop use as exactly that, but if the maintainer disagrees the record becomes (b) method-and-architecture evidence with RQ5 capped at 2. Interaction is attention only, no graph and no social pooling, which also weakens the 'over graphs' half of (b). The 'outperforms on all datasets' claim is overstated: LR wins HOTEL ADE at 0.39, S-GAN wins HOTEL FDE at 0.61, SoPhie wins ZARA1 ADE at 0.30 and CVM wins the 1 s roundabout ADE at 0.16. Units are unstated for ETH-UCY and the roundabout set, the sample count and whether ADE/FDE is best-of-N are never given, and diversity and realism are shown only as KDE plots.

title: Minimizing Safety Interference for Safe and Comfortable Automated Driving with Distributional Reinforcement Learning
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Abstract: 'the proposed framework can guarantee that actions generated from RL are fail-safe according to the worst-case assumptions'; Sec. V-B: an unsafe RL action is replaced by an emergency maneuver limited to 5 m/s3 jerk.
method: Deepset-IQN distributional RL driving policy wrapped in a proactive set-based safety verification layer that replaces unsafe actions with fail-safe emergency maneuvers; CVaR level tunes conservativeness at runtime.
evaluation: Simulated occluded merging and crossing, 30 randomized scenarios; baselines rule-based and DQN; crossing time and J_Interference (IQN 10.00 versus rule-based 83.59); zero collisions; no hardware or latency reported.
contribution: Shows a distributional RL driver can be trained to minimize how often its fail-safe verification layer must intervene, cutting safety interference up to 83% versus a rule-based policy.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a set-based verification layer shields a distributional RL policy and can veto its action at execution time. Check: the abstract's '8 seconds faster than DQN' reads as about 10 s in Table I, and the 83% interference reduction holds only for the comfort-tuned agent at zero perception noise (the speed-tuned variant is about 70%); other vehicles are simulated traffic rather than co-designed agents, so (c) fails the primacy test; no hardware, inference-time or real-vehicle evidence, so RQ1 credit is for the interception pattern only.

title: Learning Models of Adversarial Agent Behavior Under Partial Observability
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Sec. IV-B: an LSTM plus graph neural network encoder over tracker agents with a mutual-information-regularised latent mixture decoder predicts the adversary's current and future locations; Abstract: 'GrAMMI outperforms all baselines in both domains'.
method: GrAMMI: LSTM plus graph neural network encoder over multi-agent tracker state with a Gaussian-mixture latent decoder and mutual-information auxiliary loss, predicting a partially observed adversary's present and future position.
evaluation: Prison Escape and Narco Interdiction pursuit domains, 450 rollouts per dataset; baselines LSTM, VRNN, VAE-Opponent plus no-GNN and no-MI ablations; log-likelihood and ADE at 0, 30 and 60 min; no hardware.
contribution: Predicts a partially observed adversary's current and future location from multi-agent tracker histories using a graph encoder with a mutual-information objective, gaining about 31.68% average log-likelihood over baselines.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - nothing is guarded, so this enters only as Pillar 2 criterion (b) method evidence and RQ5 is capped at 2 per protocol v1.6. Check: there is no runtime override and the tracking team runs fixed heuristic policies; ablations beat the full model in several cells (Prisoner-Low 0 min log-likelihood 6.381 without GNN versus 5.230 full; Smuggler-Low 0 min ADE 0.122 without GNN and MI versus 0.127 full), so the 31.68% headline is an average over favourable cells; Sec. VII states the model cannot predict multiple horizons while Tables I-II report 0, 30 and 60 min.

title: CooperRisk: A Driving Risk Quantification Pipeline with Multi-Agent Cooperative Perception and Prediction
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Sec. III: the time-indexed risk maps built from cooperative multi-agent prediction 'function as the cost objectives for downstream motion planning', and the headline outcome is a 44.35% decrease in conflict rate (Abstract).
method: V2X pipeline: late-fusion cooperative LiDAR perception, transformer multi-agent multi-modal trajectory prediction, severity-and-exposure risk maps over time, consumed as a soft cost term by an MPC planner.
evaluation: V2XPnP dataset, 2 CAVs plus 2 infrastructure sensors; baselines CV, LSTM, QCNet, MTR and a no-fusion ablation; conflict rate 0.04 versus 0.08, minADE 0.74 versus 0.77; delays 100-500 ms tested; no hardware.
contribution: Quantifies driving risk from cooperative V2X perception and multi-agent trajectory prediction as time-indexed risk maps for an MPC planner, reporting a 44.35% lower conflict rate than single-agent baselines.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the stack analysed is a learned cooperative perception and prediction pipeline. Risk enters the MPC objective as a soft cost with no veto, halt or fail-safe, so (a) clearly fails and the include rests entirely on (c) with conflict rate as the headline measured outcome; a maintainer who reads the paper as prediction-first would call exclude-E1, and this is the record in the batch most likely to be overturned. Check: the 44.35% conflict-rate reduction does not follow from Table I (0.04 versus 0.08 is 50%) and the 37.31% average TOR reduction is not reproducible from the table; the ground-truth rows' EPA and TOR columns are ambiguous in the PDF; evaluation is open-loop on a dataset, communication delay is only a robustness sweep and not a design input, and no inference time or hardware is reported.

title: Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Volt-Var Optimization in Active Distribution Networks
venue: IEEE PES Innovative Smart Grid Technologies Conference Europe
evidence: "the trained DNN is deployed as a fixed safety mechanism, intervening only to replace unsafe actions during MARL execution" (Sec. III)
method: MADDPG agents set PV inverter reactive power from local observations; an offline OPF-supervised projection DNN maps unsafe actions into the feasible voltage and line-loading space at runtime.
evaluation: Modified IEEE 33-bus network with 6 PV systems, 3-min resolution, real Portuguese load and Elia PV data; base case vs MARL vs MARL plus DNN over day 730, day 736 and days 730-760; voltage violations 3.89% to 1.45% to 0%, mean loss 5.98% to 3.95% to 3.38%, min voltage 0.936 to 0.952 pu; a full day runs in under 30 s on an Intel i7-7700 with 16 GB RAM.
contribution: An offline-trained projection network acting as a runtime safety layer on decentralised MARL volt-var control eliminates voltage violations and cuts losses below unshielded MARL.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - MADDPG PV-inverter agents. Check criterion (c): the hazard is a network voltage or line-loading violation produced by joint agent actions rather than an agent-agent collision, so the maintainer may read this as single-system constraint enforcement; in Algorithm 2 the unsafe action is identified by running power flow after the action is taken, so pre-execution screening is assumed rather than demonstrated; safety rests entirely on DNN generalisation from OPF labels, with no guarantee despite the word "ensuring"; Table III for day 730 has no MARL-DNN column because the layer never fired; only 6 agents, simulation only, and no comparison with prior safe-RL baselines (authors note this as future work); the under-30-s figure is for a whole-day simulation, not a per-decision latency.

title: Achievable Error Exponents for Almost Fixed-Length Binary Classification
venue: 2022 IEEE International Symposium on Information Theory (ISIT)
evidence: Abstract: 'each phase is a fixed-length test and the second-phase proceeds only if a reject option is decided in the first phase'
method: Two-phase (almost fixed-length) test for binary classification with unknown distributions from training sequences; a first-phase reject triggers (k-1)n extra samples, then a final test without rejection.
evaluation: Theory: Theorem 3 gives achievable type-I/II and Bayesian error exponents; plots vs Gutman fixed-length and sequential tests; simulated error probabilities for Bernoulli sources (k=3). No converse, no hardware.
contribution: Derives achievable error exponents for a two-phase binary classification test in which a first-phase reject triggers extra sampling, approaching sequential-test performance at fixed-length complexity.
flag: none of (i)-(v): the reject is an internal 'take more samples' trigger, not an abstention or handoff; the final decision never rejects. Main contribution is error exponents of an almost fixed-length test. Achievability only (converse left to future work); numerical results are plots, no tabulated values. Closest reading would be (ii)/(v) but abstention is a component, not the contribution. ISIT short paper; companion of the M-ary record in this batch.

title: Achievable Error Exponents for Almost Fixed-Length M-ary Classification
venue: 2023 IEEE International Symposium on Information Theory (ISIT)
evidence: Sec III: 'Note that our setup does not include the rejection option in the final decision.'
method: Two-phase nearest-neighbour test (generalised Jensen-Shannon divergence) for M-ary classification from training sequences; a first-phase reject triggers a longer second fixed-length phase with no reject.
evaluation: Theory: Theorems 3-4 give achievable per-hypothesis and Bayesian error exponents; numerical plots vs Gutman fixed-length, sequential (Haghifam et al.) and threshold-based two-phase tests. No converse, no hardware.
contribution: Extends the almost fixed-length two-phase test to M-ary classification and shows achievable error exponents close to the sequential test without a final reject option.
flag: none of (i)-(v): the paper's stated selling point is achieving sequential-test exponents WITHOUT a reject option; reject is only the phase-one trigger for more samples. Achievability only, converse left open; comparisons are figures with no tabulated numbers. M-ary extension of the binary record in this batch (same group).

title: Error Exponents for Robust Hypothesis Testing with Abstention
venue: IEEE International Symposium on Information Theory - Proceedings
evidence: Abstract: 'The detector is, however, permitted to abstain from making a decision if (and only if) the adversary is present.'
method: Binary hypothesis test with outputs {0,1,abstain} when an adversary may corrupt a fraction of samples; type-based detector declares within KL balls of P0/P1 and abstains elsewhere.
evaluation: Theory: Theorems 1-3 characterise the optimal four-way error-exponent trade-off (achievability and converse) for memoryless ingress, fixed-weight uniform ingress and strong contamination; binary-alphabet plots only, no experiments.
contribution: Characterises the optimal trade-off among wrong-decision and false-abstention error exponents for hypothesis testing with abstention under three adversarial contamination models.
flag: (v), borderline: abstention is the main contribution and optimal trade-off regions are stated with achievability and converse, but this is information-theoretic one-shot hypothesis testing with known P0/P1, not learning theory; maintainer may prefer exclude-E4. 'All missing proofs' are deferred to the extended version (the arxiv_id given is that extended version, cited as ref [1], with a different title 'Robust hypothesis testing with abstention'). No empirical evaluation; Figs 4-5 are plots of the formulas. Handoff to a human is only motivation in the introduction.

title: A Study on Prompt Injection Attack Against LLM-Integrated Mobile Robotic Systems
venue: IEEE International Symposium on Software Reliability Engineering Workshops (ISSREW)
evidence: Sec. IV-A d (Safety Validation): 'If the LLM fails to generate a safe command, it will be asked to generate a new command with error information'; Sec. IV-C adds per-modality reasoning that emits an is_attack flag at runtime.
method: Prompt-injection attack study on a GPT-4o-controlled mobile robot: obvious-malicious and goal-hijacking injections, countered by a security prompt plus response-based per-modality attack detection and a safety-validation command gate.
evaluation: EyeSim VR simulation, 100 s limit and 3 retries; no-defence versus defence applied; detection precision 0.8-1.0 and recall 0.13-0.54 with defence, MOER up to 0.67, response time to 9.3 s, tokens +2.9%.
contribution: Shows prompt injection can hijack an LLM-controlled mobile robot and that a security prompt with response-based detection recovers about 30.8% overall performance, while attack recall stays below 0.55.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the guarded system is a GPT-4o robot controller, and the safety-validation step plus is_attack flag act at execution time, though the gate is a collision check that triggers regeneration rather than an attack-specific veto. Check: one robot in simulation, so the multi-agent aspect is nominal and (c) rests on the criterion's 'safety evaluation of LLM or tool-calling agents' clause; the GHI no-defence baseline is zero on every metric, so the WPI, WRI and WFI ratios divide by zero and the 30.8% headline gain is undefined as formulated; the threat model describes camera and LiDAR tampering but only the text instruction channel is attacked; no ablation separates secure prompting from response-based detection, and there is no real-robot test or hardware or latency baseline for the no-defence case.

title: Tackling Occlusions & Limited Sensor Range with Set-based Safety Verification
venue: IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC)
evidence: Sec. V: 'Our proof-of-concept planner initializes the reference trajectory according to the intelligent driver model', and 'If the verification fails, the intended trajectory will be iteratively adapted until a verifiably safe trajectory' is found.
method: Set-based reachability verification of planned trajectories under occlusion and limited sensor range: hidden traffic is modelled as virtual obstacles with bounded state intervals, and unsafe trajectories fall back to the previous fail-safe.
evaluation: Three CommonRoad urban scenarios with static and dynamic occlusion; baseline is the same planner without occlusion-aware occupancy prediction; qualitative speed traces only, no collision or intervention rates, no hardware or computation time.
contribution: Verifies planned driving trajectories against worst-case hidden traffic by placing bounded-state virtual obstacles in occluded regions, so the vehicle slows pre-emptively instead of braking too late.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - the verified planner is the hand-designed intelligent driver model with no learned component, so the Pillar 1 scope ruling of 2026-11-13 excludes it despite a genuine runtime trajectory veto. Independently borderline exclude-E2: three qualitative case studies with speed traces (ego slows to about 2.4 m/s, full stop when an obstacle is present) and no collision, violation or intervention rate, no success counts and no computation-time figures. Maintainer may overturn to include if the ruling is relaxed for policy-agnostic verification layers that could wrap a learned planner.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Uncertainty Estimation for Tactical Decision-Making in Intersections
venue: IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC)
evidence: Sect. III-C Fallback action: 'a fallback action a_safe is used when c_v > c_v^safe for all available actions'; Sect. IV states the criterion is applied at test time only, not during training.
method: Ensemble of randomized-prior deep Q-networks; at execution the coefficient of variation of the ensemble Q-values vetoes low-confidence actions and a hand-coded give-way fallback is executed instead.
evaluation: Custom intersection simulator; 100 test episodes, 5 seeds, in- and out-of-distribution; baselines DQN and no-criterion ablation; chosen-action c_v mean 0.04 (99th pct 0.15) vs threshold 0.2; criterion removed all in-distribution collisions; no hardware or latency.
contribution: An uncertainty-gated runtime veto on a learned intersection-driving policy: actions whose ensemble Q-value spread exceeds a threshold are replaced by a give-way fallback, removing in-distribution collisions.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the guarded policy is a deep RL agent and the veto itself is a threshold rule, which the scope ruling allows. Check that no numeric collision count appears in the text at all: collision rates are only in Figs. 4 and 7, and 'removed all collisions' plus 'most of the collisions can be avoided' out-of-distribution are the only stated safety results. Other vehicles are scripted IDM, so (c) fails the primacy and learned-agent test. No latency, no hardware, no human handoff.

title: Second-Order Asymptotically Optimal Outlying Sequence Detection with Reject Option
venue: 2021 IEEE Information Theory Workshop, ITW 2021 - Proceedings
evidence: Sec II-A: 'where Hr is called the reject hypothesis, alternatively the 'reject option' [5], and corresponds to the 'no signal present' hypothesis'
method: Universal outlying sequence detection among M sequences (at most one outlier, unknown distributions) with an added reject hypothesis; threshold test on empirical-distribution scoring functions.
evaluation: Theory: Theorem 1 gives second-order asymptotics of the error/false-alarm exponent under false-reject constraint epsilon (proof omitted here). Simulation: M=4, Bern(0.2) vs Bern(0.4), false-reject approaches target 0.1; no baseline.
contribution: Gives a second-order asymptotically optimal test and tight exponent bounds for detecting one outlying sequence when a reject (no-outlier) decision is allowed.
flag: none of (i)-(v): the 'reject option' here is formally the null hypothesis 'there is no outlying sequence', so rejecting is a detection outcome rather than an abstention or deferral; one-shot test in one domain. Arguable (v) as optimal-rule theory, but the proof of Theorem 1 is omitted in this workshop version and sits in the extended version (the arxiv_id given, cited as ref [24]), so the proved-result floor is not met by this text alone. Single simulation checks tightness only, with no competing method.

title: Safety Score: A Quantitative Approach to Guiding Safety-Aware Autonomous Vehicle Computing System Design
evidence: "we propose the safety score, a metric that measures the level of AV safety based on computing system response time and external factors to guide safety-aware computing system design" (Sec. V, Safety Score)
method: Safety metric derived from the RSS safe-distance model that maps instantaneous AV computing response time, velocity, acceleration and braking distance to a non-linear score guiding system design.
evaluation: Level-4 fleet field study (3 months, 200 h, 2,000 miles) plus industrial simulator; safety-score-guided CPU-GPU resource management vs tail, average and maximum latency; LiDAR latency to 90ms, response time to 500ms; Xeon plus Titan V.
contribution: Proposes the safety score, an RSS-derived metric linking instantaneous computing response time to AV collision risk, and shows traditional latency metrics misrank resource-management designs.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: which - the measured stack is a Level-4 AV perception pipeline with learned LiDAR modules, but nothing is intercepted and no action can be overridden, so (a) fails and only (d) plausibly holds. Check the evaluation floor: the only experiment is Figure 7, a normalized comparison of five resource-management strategies in the authors' proprietary simulator, with no absolute values, no collision, hazard or intervention rate, and no evidence that a higher safety score yields fewer crashes. All latency numbers I report are read off Figures 2 and 4. Derivation from RSS is algebraic, not a proved safety guarantee. Likeliest of my six to be overturned to include as background under (d).

title: Modeling Interactions of Autonomous Vehicles and Pedestrians with Deep Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Collision Avoidance
evidence: Sect. V Conclusion: the approach aims at 'retaining reliable collision avoidance even under uncertain pedestrian behavior'; Sect. IV-A reports collision rate as the primary measured outcome (0.0 percent at low pedestrian noise, 0.135 percent at alpha=0.5).
method: Independent double-dueling DQN agents for an autonomous vehicle and, in setting-2, the pedestrian at an unmarked crosswalk; collisions enter only as a reward penalty, with no runtime constraint or override.
evaluation: Custom 2D crosswalk simulator, 8 seeds over 8000 episodes, pedestrian observation noise swept 0.0-0.5; settings: learned AV vs rule-based pedestrian, both learned, both rule-based; collision rate 0.0-0.135 percent; episode duration up 23 percent (4.663 s to 5.722 s); no hardware or latency.
contribution: Deep multi-agent RL models vehicle-pedestrian crosswalk interaction with both parties learning, holding collision rates near zero under pedestrian observation noise at the cost of longer crossings.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - both agents are DQN policies, but nothing guards them: no filter, veto, shield or monitor at execution time, so (a) fails and the record rests entirely on (c). This is the record most likely to be overturned to E1: only two agents, the collision avoidance is the learned policy itself rather than a safety mechanism, and no numeric collision rate is given for the rule-based setting-X baseline (figures only). The text is also internally inconsistent about which setting is best at alpha=0.5.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning with Scene Decomposition for Navigating Complex Urban Environments
evidence: Sect. III-B: 'A safety threshold lambda is used to constrain the agent to take actions inside the set' and 'In cases where the set is empty, the agent then executes the safest possible action given by the model checker.'
method: Deep Q policy trained on a canonical ego-car-pedestrian-obstacle scenario; per-instance utilities and model-checked safety probabilities are fused by minimum so unsafe actions are masked online; RNN-ensemble belief updater.
evaluation: Custom POMDP simulator with sensor noise and ray-traced occlusion, five scenarios, 10000 simulations per policy; baselines rule-based, safe rule-based and unmasked RL, plus updater and decomposition ablations; masked policies reported zero collisions; belief update under 100 ms; policy slower than the 0.1 s step beyond 7 cars and 1 pedestrian.
contribution: Scene decomposition lets an offline model checker mask a learned intersection policy at runtime, giving zero collisions across 10000 occluded multi-agent simulations while staying roughly as fast as unmasked RL.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a learned deep Q policy masked by an offline-computed model checker, which the scope ruling allows. Check that collision and step counts appear only in Fig. 7: the text says 'the masked policies presented zero collisions across the 10000 simulations' without naming which policies, so the headline number is unverifiable from the prose. The safe set is computed in a fully observable discretised model rather than from the noisy belief, so the guarantee may not transfer. (d) rests on a real-time analysis, not a measurement, and no hardware is named.

title: Coordination and Trajectory Prediction for Vehicle Interactions via Bayesian Generative Modeling
evidence: Sect. III: a VRNN feature extractor or mutual-information encoder infers a latent macro-level coordination variable, which conditions a Bayesian conditional GAN that generates multimodal future positions for the interacting vehicles.
method: Hierarchical Coordination and Trajectory Prediction System: latent coordination recognition (VRNN features or MI-maximising encoder) plus a coordination-conditioned Bayesian CGAN with SGHMC weight uncertainty.
evaluation: NGSIM US-101 ramp merging and lane change plus a drone-collected roundabout dataset; 4 s and 2 s horizons; baselines HMM, GNB, MLP, P-GRU, CVAE, CGAN; recognition precision-recall-F1 up to 0.91-0.93-0.92; final displacement 0.232 m vs 0.367 m for the categorized variant; no safety metric, no latency.
contribution: A hierarchical Bayesian generative model infers a latent coordination variable between interacting vehicles and conditions multimodal trajectory generation on it, improving both coordination recognition and prediction accuracy.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no system is guarded - this is a (b) predictor only, so RQ5 is capped at 2 and it gets no safety credit. Check whether the latent coordination variable is enough to count as a world model over multi-agent state rather than a plain trajectory predictor; if not it falls to E1 under the Pillar 2 scope. Table II's column layout is garbled in the source and dataset labels are missing, so some displacement values cannot be assigned to a model or dataset with confidence, and the C-BCGAN vs C-CGAN weight-uncertainty ablation is qualitative only.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Modelling Traffic Participant Interaction
evidence: Sect. IV-V: vehicles are nodes of a scene graph and the GCN or GAT regresses x-y displacement for the next 5 s from 5 s of history; there is no latent state, no safety mechanism and, as the authors note, no closed- or open-loop simulation.
method: Graph convolutional and graph attention networks over a traffic scene graph with residual weights, relative-position edge features and a feed-forward head, regressing future displacements directly.
evaluation: NGSIM I-80 and HighD, 5 s horizon, 10 runs per variant; baselines constant velocity, IDM and an interaction-free feed-forward model; GAT mean displacement 1.89 m vs 2.78 m feed-forward on NGSIM (0.47 m vs 0.45 m on HighD); graph-construction and component ablations; no latency or hardware.
contribution: Graph attention over a traffic scene graph cuts 5 s trajectory prediction error about 30 percent against an interaction-free baseline on NGSIM, with ablations isolating edge features and residual connections.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no system is guarded, gated or monitored. Judged against the Pillar 2 scope this is a plain trajectory regressor on a scene graph with no latent or world model and no safety metric, so E1 under the batch rule. The maintainer may overturn to include as graph-learning architecture evidence, since the graph-construction ablations over multi-agent state are the most directly useful part of the batch. Note that on HighD the interaction-free feed-forward baseline matches the GNNs (0.45 m vs 0.47 m), so the interaction claim rests on NGSIM alone.

title: Spatiotemporal Scene-Graph Embedding for Autonomous Vehicle Collision Prediction
evidence: Abstract and Sec. III: 'we propose SG2VEC, a spatio-temporal scene-graph embedding methodology', formulating collision prediction as time-series classification over per-frame scene graphs of the ego vehicle and its neighbours.
method: Mask R-CNN builds per-frame scene graphs; MR-GCN with SAGPool yields graph embeddings; an LSTM and MLP classify a future collision from the embedding sequence.
evaluation: CARLA synthetic and real dash/Honda lane changes; 5-fold CV vs DPM baseline plus pooling and LSTM ablations; acc 0.9095 vs 0.8834, MCC 0.5385 vs 0.2912; 0.4828 ms on DRIVE PX 2.
contribution: Shows that graph embeddings of inter-vehicle scene structure predict collisions earlier and more accurately than a prior deep-learning model, at under 0.5 ms on automotive edge hardware.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - the detector only predicts and nothing is intercepted, and the analysed traffic agents are human-driven or CARLA-scripted, so (c) fails the Pillar 1 scope ruling and only (b) plus edge latency carry the record; enters as predictor evidence with RQ5 capped at 2. Body numbers disagree with the abstract: Sec. IV-B.1 gives average synthetic MCC 0.5860 while the conclusion gives 0.5055, and the claimed 39.07% earlier prediction computes to about 38.1% from Table II; the 122.7 ms lead-time figure needs checking.

title: Active Learning for Classification with Abstention
venue: IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Information Theory
evidence: Abstract: 'We obtain a high probability upper-bound on the excess risk of our algorithm, and establish its minimax near-optimality by deriving matching lower-bound (modulo poly-logarithmic factors).'
method: Active learning of a binary abstaining classifier with fixed abstention cost lambda<1/2; tree-of-partitions algorithm with confidence bounds on the regression function, for membership-query, pool and stream models; smoothness-adaptive variant.
evaluation: Theory: Theorem 1 excess-risk upper bound, Theorem 3 matching minimax lower bound under margin and Holder assumptions, proofs in appendices. Synthetic 1-D experiment (lambda=0.4, 50 runs) vs passive uniform-partition classifier; no hardware.
contribution: Proves near-minimax excess-risk rates for actively learned classifiers with a fixed-cost abstain option, with an algorithm covering three query models and adaptation to unknown smoothness.
flag: (v): foundational rates for classification with abstention (Chow fixed-cost setting), abstention is the title and main object. The sequential part is label querying, not abstaining over time, so (ii) does not apply; deferral to a human expert is only motivation. Experiment is a small synthetic illustration reported as a figure (Fig. 2) with no tabulated values; bounded-rate extension is discussion only. 144k-char file: read abstract, contributions, main theorems, lower bound, experiments; appendix proofs only skimmed.

title: Reachability-Based Trajectory Safeguard (RTS): A Safe and Fast Reinforcement Learning Safety Layer for Continuous Control
evidence: Sec. IV-A.3: 'we adjust an unsafe choice of k by attempting to replace it with a safe one', and if no safe parameter exists the robot continues its previous failsafe braking plan (Sec. II-A.2, persistent safety).
method: Offline forward reachable sets over parameterised trajectories; at each receding-horizon step the RL agent's chosen trajectory parameter is checked and replaced by the nearest safe one, else failsafe braking continues.
evaluation: MATLAB simulation of car lane change, 12-D quadrotor tunnel and cartpole; vs baseline TD3/DDPG, two RTD variants and discrete RTS; collisions 0% vs 17.6%, 100% and 1.4%; planning 0.058-0.22 s inside 2 s and 1 s budgets.
contribution: Wraps a reinforcement-learning policy in a reachability-based runtime safeguard that adjusts unsafe trajectory parameters and falls back to a failsafe stop, giving zero simulated collisions while the policy still learns.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - TD3 and DDPG policies, with the safeguard itself model-based. Single robot among static obstacles, so there is no multi-agent property; (d) is credited only because planning must finish inside the 2 s and 1 s receding-horizon budgets, and since everything is MATLAB simulation with no hardware or edge figures the maintainer may drop (d). Fig. 3 caption says baseline RL collided in 40.2% of car episodes while Table I says 17.6%.

title: Recovery RL: Safe Reinforcement Learning With Learned Recovery Zones
evidence: Sec. IV-B: 'a recovery action sampled from pi_rec is executed instead of a pi_task' action whenever the safety critic places the proposed action in the recovery set; 'Recovery RL filters proposed actions that are likely to lead to unsafe states'.
method: A safety critic learned from offline constraint-violating data defines a recovery set; when the task policy's action falls inside it, a learned model-free or model-based recovery policy acts instead.
evaluation: Six simulated domains plus image-based obstacle avoidance on a dVRK robot; vs unconstrained, LR, SQRL, RSPO, RP and RCPO; success-to-violation ratio 2-20x better in simulation and 3x on hardware; pretraining and relabelling ablations.
contribution: Separates task and recovery policies so a learned safety critic can pre-empt constraint violations at runtime, trading violations against successes far more efficiently than prior safe-RL penalty and Lagrangian methods.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the RL task policy. The runtime override is action substitution, not a halt or a human deferral; the human-supervisor query in Sec. X is proposed and never tested, so (e) does not hold. The 2-20x and 3x headline efficiency numbers and the per-domain violation counts live in the abstract and figures only, not in the text, so they cannot be verified from the body. No latency or control-loop timing is reported and the setting is single-agent apart from one scripted distractor arm.

title: A Predictive Safety Filter for Learning-Based Racing Control
evidence: Sec. I to III: the filter processes the desired input as u(k) = pi_s(x(k), u_d(k)) before it reaches the real system and 'minimizes interference while still ensuring safety for the system'.
method: A receding-horizon nonlinear MPC on a dynamic bicycle model minimally modifies any desired input so that track-boundary constraints and an offline terminal safe set stay satisfied, giving recursive feasibility.
evaluation: 1:28 RC car with VICON state estimation, acados real-time SQP at 80 Hz with N=60; terminal set verified over 1000 initial conditions; assisted human driving and a DAgger imitation policy; no baselines and no violation or intervention rates.
contribution: Demonstrates a minimally interfering predictive safety filter that keeps a miniature race car inside track boundaries under both human joystick input and a learned imitation controller.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a DAgger imitation network, plus a human driver in the second experiment. MOST LIKELY TO BE OVERTURNED: the hardware evaluation is qualitative only, with no baseline, no ablation and no violation or intervention rate, which is exclude-E2 under the base prompt; it clears the Pillar 1 floor only through the formal invariance and recursive-feasibility result and the 1000-sample terminal-set verification, and that guarantee is admitted to hold only for constant-curvature track segments. (d) rests on the 80 Hz real-time loop since no solve times are given. Assisted driving is shared control, not automation deferring to a person, so (e) is not met. The text cites the fifth episode while the figure caption says the fourth.

title: DR-MPC: Deep Residual Model Predictive Control for Real-World Social Navigation
evidence: Sec. V: 'we either validate the model's action as safe using a heuristic safety check or override it using a heuristic policy', triggered by latent-space KNN out-of-distribution detection plus a constant-velocity motion model check.
method: A DRL residual blends with MPC path tracking; at runtime a latent KNN out-of-distribution detector and a constant-velocity collision check veto the learned action and substitute the safe alternative closest to MPC.
evaluation: CrowdNav simulation with six ORCA humans vs ORCA, naive and residual DRL, with OOD/CVMM and reward ablations (SHRR 0.30 vs 0.77 and 0.79); Jackal robot, 6 runs per loop, safety raises 0.3 and 0.0 vs 1.0 and 0.3 for the heuristic.

flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the DRL residual policy. (c) fails the primacy test: this is social navigation where the human-collision rate sits beside success rate and steps to goal, and the other agents are ORCA-simulated or real people rather than learned agents. The real-world table reports safety-layer raises rather than collisions, so hardware safety evidence is indirect. No inference-time or latency numbers are given beyond the 0.2 s MDP step, so (d) is not credited despite onboard laptop-GPU inference. False-trigger evidence is only the note that 21% of CVMM triggers preceded a collision early in training, falling to 5%.

title: MIXL: Confidence-Aware Expert Fusion for Robust Multi-Sensor Localization
evidence: "In Defer mode, MIXL retains the previous trusted routing state while all sources continue estimating and the system outputs the current pose." (Abstract)
method: Dual-head gate over three localization pipelines outputs source scores plus decision confidence; two thresholds select Commit (argmax), Hedge (softmax fusion) or Defer (hold last trusted weights).
evaluation: M2DGR train, M3DGR unseen; vs Learned Hard/Soft, GF++, tightly coupled SLAM. ATE 0.16 m, switches 1.15 vs 53.07/min; no-Defer ablation RMSE +37.5%; gate 1.275 ms CPU.

flag: none of (i)-(v) cleanly; nearest is (ii)/(iii). Borderline, maintainer should decide: Defer is one of three contributions and is a hold-last-weights hysteresis, not abstention or hand-off; the paper itself says Defer "neither stops localization nor transfers control" and positions itself against selective prediction and L2D. Outcomes are ATE and switching rate, no safety or intervention metric. If (ii) is read broadly (deferring a routing change over time, with a no-Defer ablation: RMSE +37.5%, switches 1.15 to 12.40/min) it could be included. Other numbers: M2DGR sim ATE 0.68 vs 0.65 m for Learned Hard (MIXL worse), real 0.25 vs 0.28 m; confidence ECE 0.0097, AUROC 0.908 vs 0.882 logit margin and 0.801 max-softmax; longest Defer interval 43.52 s; SR-LIVO beats MIXL on Grass01 (0.09 vs 0.39 m); threshold sweep 0.31 m default on M2DGR test. Thresholds fixed by hand (0.95, 0.85). Result tables did not survive text extraction, numbers taken from prose. Peer-reviewed RA-L.

title: Real-World Deployment and Assessment of a Multiagent Reinforcement Learning-Based Variable-Speed-Limit Control System
evidence: Sec. III-C1: the work "introduces a masking layer following the output of the policy network during the testing and deployment stages" limiting sampling to valid actions, with max-limit clipping and debounce corrections overriding MARL decisions before posting to gantries.

flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a MAPPO policy guarded by deployment-time masking, clipping, debounce and a TMC-side constraint check. Check: the abstract claims a 26% crash reduction but Table IV and Sec. V-D give 14%; the abstract says about 35 million decisions vs 34,032,683 in Sec. V-B; the crash analysis is called preliminary, is a before-after comparison with no control group, and reprocesses historical RDS data for the "before" period; (c) fails the primacy test because the primary claims are deployment feasibility, warning accuracy and response delay and no collision or hazard rate is measured; no compute hardware or latency figures (only 30 s control cycles), so (d) does not hold; the TMC operator only monitors and records incidents, with no per-decision approval or manual override, so (e) does not hold.

title: HiNeS-IDS: Hierarchical Neural Selective Intrusion Detection System
venue: 2026 6th International Conference on Machine Learning and Intelligent Systems Engineering, MLISE 2026
evidence: "routing the flow to one of three final operational states: an alarm for novel/low-confidence flows, a coarse-only family identification, or a confident fine subtype prediction." (Sec. III, Fig. 2 caption)

evaluation: ACIoT2023 flows, 5 runs; vs flat CNN1D/AttDNN, flat+max-softmax, Energy, Mahalanobis. Selective fine acc 99.94-99.98%, alarm 1.5-1.7%, coarse tier 98-99%; p99 3.478 ms on RTX 4070.
