title: Uncertainty-Aware Deep Ensemble Anomaly Detection For Industrial IoT: Tiered Dynamic Thresholding With Online Concept Drift Adaptation
evidence: "Tier 1 (high confidence, autonomous response), Tier 2 (medium confidence, operator review), or Tier 3 (low confidence/OOD, deferred to analyst)" (Sec. III-B, inference step I4)
method: Deep-ensemble anomaly detector with uncertainty-adjusted dynamic threshold; detections stratified by epistemic uncertainty into autonomous, operator-review and analyst-deferral tiers; KL-divergence drift detection with EMA recalibration, no retraining.
evaluation: WUSTL-IIoT-2021 and SWaT, six architectures; vs static threshold, SPOT, MC-UQ, UDT; Tier 1 precision +4.9 to +57.3%, autonomous false positives -52 to -92%; 3.53 ms/seq on RTX 3090.
contribution: An uncertainty-tiered anomaly detector for industrial IoT that lets only high-confidence alarms trigger autonomous response and routes the rest to operator review or analyst deferral, with lightweight drift recalibration.
flag: Borderline (i)/(iv): the tiering does route low-confidence alarms to a human instead of autonomous response and is in the title, but the paper is an anomaly detector with confidence-stratified triage applied to one domain: no human or analyst is modelled or simulated, no response action is ever executed, deferral is not an action over time, and the evidence is per-tier precision (risk-coverage style). Maintainer may prefer include under (i). Doubts: abstract says drift adaptation recovers up to 27.79% of Tier 1+2 precision, conclusion says up to 23%. Per-tier recall 1.0000 is true by construction (authors admit). The 'guaranteed precision' holds only on the labelled validation set and only when k* falls inside the Tier 3 bounds. Dynamic threshold alone gains just 2.8% F1 over the static baseline. 'Real' SWaT drift needed 16 drifting features removed and interpolation with lambda about 3e-5 to 1e-4, i.e. almost no drift; under drift Tier 1 precision is only about 0.51. Feature counts conflict (SWaT 51 to 29 vs '55 features' to 39; WUSTL '24 features' vs 48 to 24) and the environment is described as both Windows 10 and Ubuntu 22.04. UDT baseline was retuned by the authors. Latency measured for LSTM-AE only. Calibration needs attack labels although the detector is called unsupervised.

title: Exponential Savings in Agnostic Active Learning Through Abstention
evidence: "exponential savings in the number of label requests are possible" when abstention is allowed at a price marginally below 1/2 (Abstract; Theorem 1.2/3.1)
method: Disagreement-based pool active learner that outputs a {0,1,*}-valued classifier scored by Chow's risk; stops and abstains when the version-space diameter exceeds 49*alpha/p.
evaluation: Pure theory, no experiments. Proved: Thm 3.1 label complexity O(theta(eps/p)/p^2 * (d log^2 + log^2(1/delta))) for excess Chow risk eps; Thm 3.4, Prop 3.6-3.7, Thm 4.1 (Massart misspecification).
contribution: Shows that allowing a classifier to abstain at a cost just under 1/2 (Chow's risk) gives exponential label savings in agnostic active learning, with proved label-complexity bounds and no experiments.
flag: (v) but borderline: the proved results are label-complexity bounds for ACTIVE LEARNING under Chow's risk; abstention is the enabling device, and the maintainer may judge the main contribution to be active learning (then exclude-E1). No experiments, no runtime system, one-shot classification. Lower bounds are cited, not proved here. Theorem numbers come from the arXiv version, not the IEEE TIT print.

title: Spatio-Temporal Graph Dual-Attention Network for Multi-Agent Prediction and Tracking
venue: IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems
evidence: Agents are nodes and their relations edges in history and future spatio-temporal graphs, and the model jointly predicts all agents (Sec. V-A, V-C); 'The constraint not only ensures physical feasibility but also enhances model performance' (Abstract).
method: Encoder-decoder over history and future spatio-temporal graphs with topological plus temporal dual attention, GRU decoder with a kinematic bicycle layer, Wasserstein-style latent generative training.
evaluation: ETH/UCY, SDD, INTERACTION; baselines Trajectron, CGNS, Social-BiGAT, S-GAN; ablations T, T+C-ATT, T+C, T+C+K; ADE/FDE 0.30/0.59 avg ETH/UCY vs 0.46/0.94; TITAN X, 8 ms per step.
contribution: Graph dual-attention generative model that jointly forecasts and tracks multi-agent future trajectories under a kinematic feasibility layer, cutting ADE/FDE by 15-35% against prior predictors.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - nothing is guarded, there is no runtime override, veto or halt anywhere in the pipeline. Borderline (b): it is latent generative prediction of future state over a dynamic multi-agent graph with direct ADE/FDE measures and baselines, but a maintainer may read it as a plain trajectory regressor and exclude-E1 under the Pillar 2 ruling. Check Table I per-scene ADE/FDE: the extraction was garbled and only the average (0.30/0.59 vs Trajectron 0.46/0.94) and the claimed 34.8%/37.2% reduction could be confirmed. Timing (8 ms per step, 80 ms for 10 steps, 12.5 Hz) is on a TITAN X, not edge hardware, so no latency cell credited.

title: Deep Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Highway On-Ramp Merging in Mixed Traffic
venue: IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems
evidence: 'the safety supervisor will replace the risky action with a safe action according to Eq. 13' (Sec. IV-B, Algorithm 2), after checking predicted trajectories in priority order.
method: Cooperative MA2C with parameter sharing, local rewards and action masking for on-ramp merging; a priority-based safety supervisor rolls out IDM/MOBIL and bicycle-model trajectories and replaces conflicting actions.
evaluation: Modified highway-env merging, Easy/Medium/Hard; baselines MPC, MAA2C, MAACKTR, MAPPO and no-supervisor ablation; Hard collision 0.16 to 0 and speed 21.71 to 22.73 m/s; supervisor 4.90-50.13 ms on AMD 9820X.
contribution: A priority-based runtime safety supervisor over multi-agent RL merging policies replaces predicted-conflict actions, driving collision rate to zero while also raising average speed above MARL and MPC baselines.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the guarded policy is a cooperative MA2C (learned) merging policy and the supervisor overrides its action at execution time, so (a) is solid. (c) is arguable: collision rate is a headline measured outcome with baselines and an ablation, but efficiency (average speed) is co-primary. (d) rests on Remark 1 and Table II inference times (4.90-50.13 ms against a 5 Hz control step) on a server CPU, with no real-time or edge test, so a maintainer may drop (d). Text in Sec. V-C claims no collisions for T_n>=7 but Table II shows 0.01 (Medium, T_n=14) and 0.03-0.05 (Hard, T_n=10, 12, 14). The paper never says what the supervisor does if no candidate action is conflict-free, and assumes HDVs never collide with each other. Multi-lane extension (Sec. V-F) is qualitative only.

title: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach for Safe and Efficient Behavior Planning of Connected Autonomous Vehicles
venue: IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems
evidence: Sec. 5: "If all the actions in A are not safe in the worst case, then the controller will apply the emergency stop (ES) process."
method: Safe actor-critic MARL (Dec-POMDP, centralised critic, LSTM history) for connected-vehicle lane-change planning, with a runtime safe-action mapping that substitutes a safe action or an emergency stop.
evaluation: CARLA, 30 vehicles, CAV ratios 0-1, densities 0.1-0.9; baselines MADDPG and IDM; unsafe actions 0 vs 43,491 and 0 vs 242,976; min headway 18.5 m; velocity 60.06-66.15 mph; 4x RTX2080Ti.
contribution: A safe actor-critic MARL planner for connected vehicles whose runtime safe-action mapping replaces unsafe lane changes or triggers emergency stop, reaching zero unsafe actions while raising average velocity.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the guarded policy is the learned MARL actor, while the filter itself is a hand-written worst-case distance check, which the scope ruling allows. TITLE MISMATCH, maintainer must confirm: arXiv 2302.04321 is "Shared Information-Based Safe And Efficient Behavior Planning For Connected Autonomous Vehicles" (Han, Zhou, Pepin, Wang, Ding, Miao, AAAI-23 DCAA workshop best paper), not the record TITS title; same author group, same safe actor-critic method, same CARLA experiments, so I treated it as the preprint of the journal version rather than a wrong paper and did NOT record E6 - but my notes are from the preprint, so numbers may differ from the TITS version. (c) NOT credited: the headline tables are efficiency (average velocity and comfort) and the paper is a behaviour planner, so it arguably fails the (c) primacy test even though unsafe-action counts beat MADDPG; (a) is solid and carries the include. Other doubts: the safety threshold D_s is never given numerically, no collision count is reported (only "unsafe actions"), the density 0.5-0.8 column of Table 4 was illegible in extraction, Algorithm 1 exploration probabilities contradict the prose, there is no inference-latency figure and all work ran on one i9 with four RTX2080Ti, so no (d) and no edge-deployment cell despite the weight-pruned CNNs (3.5x speedup, 99 img per s).

title: Augmenting Reinforcement Learning With Transformer-Based Scene Representation Learning for Decision-Making of Autonomous Driving
evidence: The sequential latent Transformer 'is only used in the training process' (Sec. I), and the only safety-related runtime element is that 'Simulations would be reset if' the ego collides or times out (Sec. IV-A).
method: Multi-stage Transformer encodes agent histories and candidate route waypoints; a sequential latent Transformer predicts future latents and a reconstruction-free SimSiam objective augments a SAC decision policy.
evaluation: SMARTS left turn, double merge, roundabout A-C; baselines DrQ, SAC, PPO, rule-based, plus ablations; success 76-96% vs 66-92% (MST) and 68-80% (DrQ), collision 2-24%; RTX 2080 Ti, no inference latency.
contribution: Transformer scene representation with latent future prediction and reconstruction-free self-supervision that raises success rate and sample efficiency of reinforcement-learned driving policies in dense interactive traffic.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - no shield, filter, monitor or override at inference, so (a) fails; collision penalty is in the reward and collision rate is only a test metric. (c) fails the primacy test: the primary claim is sample efficiency and success rate of ego decision-making, not a multi-agent safety property. (b) fails the Pillar 2 measure: the future-latent module is training-only and the paper reports no predictive-accuracy metric (no ADE/FDE, no latent prediction error), only success/collision/stagnation rates, completion time and a PCA latent plot. Most likely overturn on this batch if the maintainer counts auxiliary latent future prediction over multi-agent scene state as (b) despite the missing predictive measure. Attention, not a graph net, models interaction, and Sec. III-B-3 states 'there is no interaction among neighbor vehicles' at the aggregation level.

title: Learning-Based Realistic Traffic Scenario Simulation via Multiagent World Models With Intention-Aware Interactive Transformer
evidence: "We use the proposed world model as an online risk monitor in the HiL/DiL loop." (Sec. IV-A); "the goal of the world model is to autoregressively predict the future trajectories of all agents over a horizon of T steps" (Sec. II-A)
method: Transformer world model over vectorized agent and lane tokens with previous-step memory fusion and cross-timestep residual refinement; rolled out autoregressively for all agents; multi-future rollouts checked against ego plan for collision warnings.
evaluation: Argoverse 2 closed-loop rollout: ADE 1.825, FDE 4.422 vs HPTR, MTR, MacFormer, HeteroGAT, SIMPL plus ablations; HiL/DiL in 51SIM: warning success 87%/80% vs TTC 66%/60% on 15 scenarios; 10 Hz, 100 ms budget.
contribution: An interaction-aware Transformer world model jointly rolls out all traffic agents in closed loop on Argoverse 2 and is run in a hardware/driver-in-the-loop simulator as a rollout-based collision early-warning monitor.
flag: Meets (b) with a DIRECT predictive-accuracy measure (ADE 1.825, FDE 4.422, also MR) against five baselines and with ablations (optimizer strategy, refinement module, lane encoder, loss terms), not only downstream results. Caveats: Tables I-VII are not in the extracted text (likely images), so baseline and ablation values and the RL collision rates of Table VII could not be read; check the PDF. Prediction is in explicit trajectory space with a 128-d latent, single-modal metrics; 'multifuture' rollouts are used in the monitor but how multiple futures are generated is not described. The risk monitor only ISSUES A WARNING in a simulator test loop (no override/halt), so runtime_interceptor is no and I did not credit (a)/(c)/(d); maintainer may consider (c)/(d) secondary. Early-warning result is 15 hand-crafted scenarios with a human driver reproducing collisions, vs a TTC baseline only; no false-alarm rate reported. Text is inconsistent on driver state (threshold enlarged 'under fatigue', results reported 'under distraction'). Latency: only a figure and the statement that it stays within the 100 ms budget for 'the vast majority of ticks', no numeric latency, and hardware of the HiL rig is not given (training on 3x RTX 3090), so not edge deployment. Driver monitoring adapts warning distance but no takeover is studied. Authors call the HiL study proof-of-concept. RQ5 capped at 2.

title: HAN: Adaptive DRL-Based Congestion Control via Model Uncertainty
venue: IEEE Transactions on Network and Service Management
evidence: "If the estimated uncertainty exceeds a threshold, a binary flag is sent to the kernel through a socket option, instructing the kernel to bypass the DRL action and temporarily use a traditional CC algorithm." (Sec. III, System Overview and Design)
method: SAC congestion-control agent with MC-dropout critic (20 passes); when Q-value standard deviation exceeds min(reference, sliding-window 95th percentile) threshold, the kernel bypasses the DRL action and runs BBR until uncertainty subsides.
evaluation: MahiMahi-style emulation with FCC traces (loss 0-15%, buffers, wired/WiFi/cellular); vs Cubic, BBR, Sprout, Indigo, Orca, PCC, Vivace; throughput, 95th-percentile delay, fairness; fallback ratio under 10% in 90% of runs.
contribution: An inference-time hybrid congestion controller that monitors critic uncertainty of a deep RL agent and temporarily hands control to a classic rule-based algorithm when the learned policy is unsure.
flag: (ii) sequential RL setting with deferral as a runtime action over time, and (i) hand-off to a rule-based fallback controller; a logical-domain (network transport) runtime gate, no human. Weakest point: there is NO ablation of the switch (DRL agent without fallback, or other thresholds/uncertainty signals), so gains over Cubic/Orca/etc. cannot be attributed to the deferral mechanism rather than the SAC policy; floor is met only at whole-system level plus switching statistics (Fig. 9-10). All results are in figures, no numeric tables. The headline 'up to 83% higher throughput' appears only in abstract, introduction and conclusion - I could not find it in the evaluation (body reports multiples such as 4x, 4.9x, 13% to 2.4x); the 36% delay reduction is in Sec. V-D (6%-36%). Contributions claim Pantheon and real-world domestic/international/intercontinental tests but no such results appear in the text. Performance is the outcome, not a safety/violation rate; BBR beats HAN on throughput (WiFi dynamic) and delay (wired dynamic). Cost of 20 MC-dropout passes per decision is described only as 'minimal latency increase', no figure; hardware not stated. Algorithm 2 falls back to BBR only although text says BBR or Cubic; a 95th percentile over a 20-sample window is a crude threshold. Prototype on Linux 4.13.

title: Cooperation for Scalable Supervision of Autonomy in Mixed Traffic
evidence: 'human supervisor control of the AV must be activated to ensure human-level safety' (Sec. III-A), triggered by reachability conditions with 'enough time to avoid it comfortably' (5-8 s takeover window).
method: Reachability conditions decide when a remote human must take over a merging AV; cooperative connected AVs block threatening human vehicles, and an M/M/k loss model sizes the human supervisor pool.
evaluation: Analytical plus numerical rotary-ring network with IDM profiles; baselines UCAV and NCAV vs CCAV; Theorems 1-2 and Lemmas 1-2; supervision need cut 21.9% to 69.03%, reliability 99.9999% vs about 90%; no latency measured.
contribution: Cooperative connected vehicles shrink the share of merges that need human takeover, letting one remote supervisor reliably oversee far more autonomous vehicles, with proved reachability and queueing bounds.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - the supervised AVs run IDM with conservative kinematic reachability and RL appears only in related work, so (a) and (c) fail the Pillar 1 scope ruling; the include rests entirely on (e) under the 2026-11-13 ruling, as the paper is about when automation defers to a remote person and how many vehicles one supervisor can monitor. No crash, disengagement or empirical intervention rate is reported and there is no microsimulation: the quantitative floor is met by proved bounds plus numerical comparison against UCAV/NCAV (0.078 vs 0.1 at S=5, 69.03% at S=16, 48.08-68.20% in Example 3, 18-66 AVs per supervisor without merge assistance). The 5-8 s takeover window and 15-60 s service times are taken from cited human-factors work, not measured here, and low latency is assumed rather than tested, so the time-to-irreversibility cell is only implicit in the reachability trigger.

title: SMARLA: A Safety Monitoring Approach for Deep Reinforcement Learning Agents
evidence: Section 4.3 (Model in Operation): at each time step SMARLA estimates from the agent Q-values the probability of a safety violation and predicts a violation when the confidence-interval upper bound passes the threshold, so a safety mechanism can be triggered before it happens.
method: Black-box runtime safety monitor for DQN agents: Q*-irrelevance state abstraction plus a random-forest classifier over abstract-state features estimates a per-step violation probability with confidence intervals.
evaluation: Cart-Pole, Mountain-Car, Highway DQN agents, 1000 test episodes; ablations on criterion, threshold, abstraction, features; recall 96.6-99.8%, FPR 0.2-7.1%, flagged with 45-77% of episode left; few-ms inference, RTX 3070.
contribution: A black-box runtime monitor that predicts safety violations of a deep RL agent early in an episode from Q-values alone, with near-perfect recall and most of the episode left to react.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, DQN policies. Check (a): SMARLA only flags, it never overrides, halts or defers; the triggered safety mechanism and the human-handover example are unimplemented, so (a) fails a strict reading of the override clause. Single agent throughout, no multi-agent state. No external baseline: white-box, image-based and model-based monitors were deliberately excluded, so all comparisons are internal ablations. Headline numbers are the easy cases: on Highway only 40 of 59 violations were predicted and macro F1 is 82%, versus 99 of 99 and 132 of 132 on Cart-Pole and Mountain-Car. The few-ms inference claim in Section 7 has no measurement table behind it.

title: Beyond the Trolley Problem: Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment as a Framework for AI Ethics
venue: 2026 11th International Conference on Computer Science and Engineering (UBMK)
evidence: "Second, the moral confidence threshold is a conceptual design proposal, not a validated mechanism." (Limitations and Future Research Directions); "This study is conceptual rather than empirical." (Sec. II)
method: Reading of Crime and Punishment mapped to AI decision design; proposes a 'moral confidence threshold' abstention rule blocking autonomous execution above an individual-harm ceiling or when actions are morally indistinguishable.
evaluation: None: no implementation, simulation, data, baseline or proof; only a proposed future simulator-based validation protocol for autonomous-driving and triage settings.
contribution: A conceptual AI-ethics essay deriving three design claims from Dostoevsky and sketching an unvalidated abstention rule that would transfer morally uncertain decisions to an accountable human.
flag: none of (i)-(v) as an evaluated contribution: the abstention/hand-off rule is the consolidating proposal (it would nominally touch (i)/(iv)) but the paper states it does not implement or test a system and proves nothing, so it fails the evaluation floor. runtime_interceptor set to no because nothing is built. Humanities-style conference paper (UBMK 2026); harm function and thresholds are left uninstantiated. Background reading at most.

title: Balancing the Scales: Uncertainty-Aware Two-Stage RL for Multiview Child Malnutrition Screening
venue: 2026 IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision Workshops (WACVW)
evidence: "The defer action routes cases to clinicians when confidence is low." (Sec. 3.1); "Our model defers only 14.0% of cases versus 18.8% for the best baseline" (Sec. 4.2)
method: Two-stage contextual bandit (gamma = 0) on fused anthropometry and multi-view CLIP embeddings; Stage 1 chooses healthy, malnourished or defer, gated by MC-dropout variance; Stage 2 assigns malnutrition subtype.
evaluation: 2,389 children, 478 validation, 5 seeds; vs CE, cost-sensitive CE, CE + entropy deferral, 4-class; accuracy 0.943, FPR 0.028 vs 0.059, deferral 14.0% vs 18.8%; ablation; V100 GPUs.
contribution: A contextual-bandit screening model for child malnutrition that learns defer-to-clinician as an explicit action and reports fewer false positives and fewer deferrals than a post hoc selective-prediction baseline.
flag: Borderline (i): deferral to a clinician is the stated main contribution and is compared with a deferral baseline and ablated, but this is one-shot selective classification applied to a domain - the authors themselves call it single-step (gamma = 0, 'no state transition'), 'RL' is a bandit regression on immediate reward, and no clinician is modelled or evaluated (deferred cases are simply counted as risk-positive). Maintainer may prefer include under (i). Doubts: sensitivity is LOWER than the deferral baseline (0.872 vs 0.944), a safety-relevant trade-off for screening; without deferral the RL model is worse than plain CE (0.894 vs 0.906). Inconsistencies: full-system accuracy is 0.943 (Table 2), 0.947 (Table 6) and 0.913 (Sec. 4.4 text); the baseline PLR of 15.9 quoted in text is missing from Table 5; noise-robustness rows are for the non-deferral Stage 1 model yet are credited to 'our method'; fairness specificity (0.91-0.93) does not match the headline 0.972. Ablation effects are tiny (deferral 1.38% accuracy) and shown only in a figure. Single-region dataset, 80/20 split with results on the validation split (no separate test set), workshop paper. Abstract numbers were all found in the body.

title: Selective prediction‐set models with coverage rate guarantees
evidence: "We propose to train a model that (i) outputs prediction sets with the desired conditional coverage" (Sec. 1, Introduction)
method: Selective prediction-set model: a decision function accepts or abstains per input and accepted inputs get a prediction set; trained with abstention cost plus acceptance penalty; post-hoc coverage inference.
evaluation: MNIST with unseen digit, fashion and noise inputs, MIMIC-III mortality and length of stay; baselines: entropy threshold with and without outlier detector; loss, acceptance rate, coverage; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Trains models that abstain on unfamiliar inputs and otherwise return prediction sets, with asymptotic confidence intervals for the achieved coverage.
flag: none of (i)-(v): one-shot selective prediction with a reject option applied to clinical data; no deferral target, no sequential setting. Lemma 1 gives a population-optimal accept rule and Theorem 1 asymptotic normality of the coverage estimator, but these are not foundational reject-option theory (no finite-sample guarantee, consistency assumed) - if the maintainer counts them under (v) reconsider. Fetched title reads "coverage guarantees", record says "coverage rate guarantees"; same paper (arXiv preprint of the Biometrics article). Noise acceptance 1.30% ULM vs 61.85% threshold on MNIST.

title: Selective prediction in medical image classification with provable selective risk control
venue: International Conference on Algorithms, Image Processing, and Deep Learning (AIPDL)
evidence: "Corollary 1 (Risk Control): Let the calibration set be exchangeable with the test data. Then the selected threshold lambda* satisfies Pr(R(lambda*) > alpha) <= delta." (Sec 3.4.1)
method: Entropy-thresholded reject option for a ResNet-50 image classifier; threshold picked on a calibration set as the largest value whose union-bound Hoeffding upper bound on selective risk stays below alpha.
evaluation: COVID-19 X-ray (4-class) and ISIC 2019 (8-class); baselines no-reject, empirical entropy/MSP thresholds; violation rate over 100 splits 0% vs 2% and 55-59%; coverage 0.93/0.81; no latency reported.
contribution: Calibrates an entropy rejection threshold with a union-bound Hoeffding correction so selective risk on medical image classifiers stays below a target with high probability, at about 7 points of coverage.
flag: none of (i)-(v) in my reading: one-shot selective classification applied to a domain, judged by risk-coverage. Borderline (v): it does state and prove a finite-sample bound (Corollary 1), but the proof is a three-line Hoeffding plus union bound, close to Geifman and El-Yaniv 2017 which it cites, so not foundational. Deferral to human review is only mentioned, no human in the evaluation. Doubts: abstract says only a 7 point coverage cost, but Table 4 (100 splits) shows COVID coverage 1.0 vs 0.895, i.e. 10.5 points; the 7 points holds for the single-split Tables 2-3. Method is labelled split conformal but is really a Hoeffding threshold calibration; Hoeffding is applied under exchangeability only and with a data-dependent n(lambda), not discussed. Single author, SPIE conference proceedings, one backbone. RTX 3060 laptop GPU is for training only.

title: Towards safe machine learning for CPS: infer uncertainty from training data
venue: Proceedings of the 10th ACM/IEEE International Conference on Cyber-Physical Systems
evidence: Abstract: "a model selects a reject option and applies the backup solution, a traditional controller or" a human operator; Eq. 10: reject if the feature-space score is below t.
method: Feature Space Partitioning Tree: CART-style partition of input space scored by training-data density and feature importance; predictions in sparsely covered regions are rejected (safe fail) in favour of a backup.
evaluation: Flotation plant and SARCOS regression; SCITOS-G5 robot navigation and breast cancer classification; NN, SVM, GP. Accept-all vs filtered groups: SCITOS GP 97.5% all vs 100% at 12% kept. No latency; O(log N) claimed.
contribution: Scores how well training data cover each region of input space with a partitioning tree, so a cyber-physical system can reject learned predictions in unsupported regions and fall back to a backup.
flag: none of (i)-(v): BORDERLINE (iv)/(i). Framed as safe-fail for CPS with hand-off to a traditional controller or human operator, but no fallback, controller, closed loop or handoff is implemented; evaluation is a one-shot accuracy filter on static datasets. No comparison with any other reject or uncertainty method beyond GP standard deviation and the accept-all row; no ablations. Regression results exist only as box plots with no numbers in text. Accuracy gap between high- and low-score groups is sometimes tiny (SCITOS NN 95.6% vs 94.6%). Authors concede the score is heuristic. Non-generative-inference cell is my reading (density tree, no generative model) - check. If the maintainer reads (iv) loosely this could be included as an early CPS runtime-monitor precursor.

title: An inductive synthesis framework for verifiable reinforcement learning
venue: ACM SIGPLAN Conference on Programming Language Design and Implementation (PLDI)
evidence: Section 4.3 (Shielding), Algorithm 3: the next state under the neural action is predicted and, if it falls outside the verified inductive invariant, the synthesized program action is used instead, overriding the neural controller at execution time.
method: Counterexample-guided synthesis of a deterministic policy program plus a sum-of-squares inductive invariant; the verified invariant drives a runtime shield substituting the program action for unsafe neural actions.
evaluation: 15 control benchmarks (4-car and 8-car platoons included), 1000 runs x 5000 steps vs unshielded neural policy; all failures prevented (60 and 41 pendulum cases to 0); overhead 2.0-21.3%; invariant-degree and environment-change ablations; i7-8700.
contribution: Synthesizes a verifiable programmatic approximation of a trained neural policy and reuses its proved inductive invariant as a runtime shield, removing all observed safety violations at single-digit percentage overhead.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, deep policy-gradient neural controllers are the thing shielded, so the scope ruling is satisfied even though the shield itself is symbolic. (a) is solid. The 4-car and 8-car platoons are multi-agent in name only, modelled as one 8-variable or 16-variable plant with a single controller, so not (c). No per-decision latency and no edge hardware, only percentage wall-clock overhead against a 0.01 s time step. False-halt cost is large and under-discussed: 93703 interventions on Oscillator with only 74% of them effective, 108320 after adding an obstacle to Self-Driving. Synthesis is not guaranteed to terminate and timed out at degree 2 and on the 8-car platoon at degree 8.

title: Verifiably safe exploration for end-to-end reinforcement learning
venue: International Conference on Hybrid Systems: computation and control
evidence: Section 4.2 (Enforcing Constraints), Algorithm 1: every action proposed by the learner is checked against the verified controller monitor and, if it is unsafe, a safe action is sampled uniformly from the safe actions in the current state.
method: Wraps PPO: a pretrained CenterNet-style detector extracts symbolic object positions from images and a KeYmaera X-verified differential dynamic logic controller monitor replaces any unsafe action with a sampled safe one.
evaluation: Four visual environments (XO, adaptive cruise control, goal-finding, pointmesses) vs vanilla PPO, at least 4 seeds: 0 unsafe actions versus 3733-13983, reward equal or better (ACC 967 vs 529); no latency or hardware reported.
contribution: Extends verified runtime safeguards to end-to-end visual RL by detecting objects to recover a symbolic state, achieving zero safety violations during training without loss of reward in four environments.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, a PPO policy, with a learned object detector inside the safeguard itself. (a) is solid (replacement at execution time). Single agent, no multi-agent hazard, no human handoff. The guarantee is conditional on perception: Assumption 1 requires bounded detector position error, and the detector is trained on synthetic paste-up images, so safety outside that assumption is unproven. Authors concede the detector overhead makes real-time control infeasible in the current implementation and report no timing or hardware at all, so no (d). No ablations: there is no comparison against the same safeguard on ground-truth symbolic state, and sample-efficiency gains are claimed only from curves.

title: PACE: Learning Effective Task Decomposition for Human-in-the-loop Healthcare Delivery
venue: Proceedings of the 2021 International Conference on Management of Data
evidence: "we let the model handle only the easy tasks that it can well predict, and ask doctors for assistance on the hard ones" (Sec 1 Introduction)
method: PACE trains a GRU classifier with a reject option using self-paced learning to select easy tasks plus a weighted loss revision that upweights correctly predicted tasks; rejection by confidence threshold at inference.
evaluation: MIMIC-III mortality and NUH-CKD deterioration; baselines cross-entropy GRU, LR, GBDT, AdaBoost, temperature variants, ablations; AUC at coverage 0.1-1.0, e.g. NUH-CKD 0.851 vs 0.778 at 0.2; no latency or hardware.
contribution: Trains healthcare classifiers with self-paced task selection and a reweighted loss so accuracy on the confidently predicted cases rises, leaving the remaining cases to be handed to doctors.
flag: none of (i)-(v) strictly; borderline (i). The hand-over to doctors is the framing and the title, but no human or expert model appears anywhere in the method or evaluation: it is a classifier with a reject option applied to a domain, scored by an AUC-coverage curve (one-shot selective prediction). The contribution is a training loss, not a deferral rule; the reject itself is a plain confidence threshold. Gains are concentrated at low coverage and are not uniform: on MIMIC-III GBDT beats PACE at coverage 0.1 (0.967 vs 0.947) and PACE is marginally below cross-entropy at coverage 1.0 (0.805 vs 0.806). NUH-CKD is a private dataset. If the maintainer reads (i) as satisfied by a stated human hand-off alone, this would move to include.

title: Towards Unbiased and Accurate Deferral to Multiple Experts
venue: Proceedings of the 2021 AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society
evidence: "We propose a framework that simultaneously learns a classifier and a deferral system, with the deferral system choosing to defer to one or more human experts" (Abstract).
method: Joint training of classifier and deferrer; deferrer weights m experts (humans plus the classifier as identity expert) per input, with sparse committee sampling and balanced or minimax-fair variants.
evaluation: Synthetic 2D, 25k offensive-language tweets with 20 synthetic biased experts, 1,471 posts with 170 MTurk workers; vs classifier-only, random committee, LL, CrowdSelect. Accuracy .98 minimax-fair vs .89; MTurk .85 vs .78. No latency.
contribution: Jointly learns a classifier and a deferrer that routes each input to the classifier or a committee of human experts, with fairness variants that shrink group accuracy gaps under biased experts.
flag: (iii) deferral among multiple experts, also (i). One-shot classification, no sequential or latency aspect. Main experiment uses synthetic experts; real humans appear only as pre-collected MTurk labels (low agreement, Krippendorff alpha 0.27), no live takeover, so e is weak. On MTurk the joint model (.85) is below majority vote of the crowd (about .87). Theory covers convexity, convergence, minimax disparity and price of sparsity, not surrogate consistency.

title: Temporal Consistency Checks to Detect LiDAR Spoofing Attacks on Autonomous Vehicle Perception
evidence: Section 3.2 (3D-TC2 Methodology): the Cell-match Counting Strategy compares each detected 3D box against the motion predictor bird-eye-view category grid and flags a mismatch, usually background, as a spoofed ghost object.
method: 3D-TC2 runs a LiDAR 3D detector (PointPillars or SECOND) and MotionNet in parallel, aligns detected boxes to the BEV motion grid, and flags objects with no motion history as spoofed.
evaluation: nuScenes mini, 362 attacked key frames, 200-point spoofing at 5-8 m; PointPillars vs SECOND; car detection success 98.58% and recall 91.75%, cyclist 95.01%, pedestrian 56.92%; 24 ms per frame (41 Hz) on a GTX 1050.
contribution: Treats motion as a physical invariant for spoofing defence: ghost LiDAR objects with no motion history are flagged by matching 3D detections against a bird-eye-view motion prediction grid at 41 Hz.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, neural LiDAR detectors (PointPillars, SECOND) guarded by a rule-based check over MotionNet predictions. (a) is weak: the check only raises a flag, it cannot veto, halt or defer a driving action, and the response is explicitly future work. (d) rests only on a 24 ms per-frame figure (sd 0.85 ms) on a desktop GTX 1050 with no stated deadline and no edge platform, so the maintainer may drop it. No false-positive rate or precision anywhere, and benign match ratios are poor (pedestrian 56%, bike 1.2%), so false alarms look likely. The abstract 98% is DSR, the share of successfully spoofed objects caught, not accuracy. CARLO 94.5% and Shadow-Catcher 94% are cited, not re-run, so the baseline is indirect. Single vehicle, single-frame attacker, no multi-agent aspect.

title: Human-Centered Deferred Inference: Measuring User Interactions and Setting Deferral Criteria for Human-AI Teams
venue: Proceedings of the 28th International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces
evidence: "Deferred inference [47] improves the performance of a human-AI team by allowing the AI to defer-request additional information from the human-when some set of conditions are met." (Sec 3.1)
method: Formulates deferral rate and error as functions of threshold and individual user; sets entropy-threshold deferral criteria per user from a short calibration set, by percentile or a binomial upper bound.
evaluation: 25-participant study, UNITER referring-expression cropping on a RefCOCO subset, deferral rates 0-0.3; per-user vs RefCOCO and multi-user calibration: upper-bound violations 0/1/2 vs 7/9/7 and 10/10/9; no latency or hardware.
contribution: Shows with 25 users that satisfaction depends on both error and deferral rate and that deferral thresholds must be calibrated per user, cutting deferral-rate bound violations versus dataset-level calibration.
flag: (i) applies, with a caveat: the AI defers back to the human for a second input (asks the user to try again), the human does not take over the task, and the paper explicitly contrasts itself with selective prediction that hands the inference to a human. Deferral is the main contribution and the human response to deferral is itself studied (RQ4: entropy rose 0.204 to 0.239 after deferral). Weaknesses to weigh: during the live study deferral was RANDOM, not criteria-based; the threshold-setting procedures were compared offline on the collected data. Error fell 19.82% to 17.37% with deferral but not significantly (McNemar p > 0.05). Per-user calibration is no better on mean absolute error (Table 2, within one standard error) and wins only on upper-bound violations (Table 3). Deferral depth fixed at one; targeting an error rate is left as future work. Small n (25 after dropping 3), one task, one model. Not safety-critical. Text is 14 pages; read in full except reference list.

title: Not What You've Signed Up For: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
venue: ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security (AISec)
evidence: Section 3 (Attack Surface of LLM-Integrated Applications): an adversary plants instructions in data the application later retrieves, remotely compromising the LLM-integrated application without any direct access to its prompt.
method: Threat taxonomy of indirect prompt injection (information gathering, fraud, malware, intrusion, manipulated content, availability) with proof-of-concept injections against synthetic GPT-4 applications, Bing Chat and GitHub Copilot.
evaluation: Qualitative demonstrations only: temperature-0 synthetic applications plus live Bing Chat and Copilot; no success rates, trial counts, baselines or ablations; the paper says quantifying success rates is future work.
contribution: Introduces indirect prompt injection, in which instructions hidden in retrieved data hijack LLM-integrated applications, and demonstrates the resulting threat classes against real deployed systems.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no guard at all, this is an attack and taxonomy paper. It fails the evaluation floor: purely qualitative proof-of-concept, no success rate, no baseline or ablation, and Section 5.6 only lists unimplemented mitigations (input and instruction filtering, an LLM supervisor, interpretability-based outlier detection), hence exclude-E2 rather than E1. (c) is only nominally multi-agent: the one email-worm demo propagates the injection to contacts and multi-agent frameworks are named as future work in Section 5.3. Very highly cited and the maintainer may well want it as background rather than safety evidence; if kept, it is threat-model evidence only and should not be credited with preventing anything.

title: WaitGPT: Monitoring and Steering Conversational LLM Agent in Data Analysis with On-the-Fly Code Visualization
venue: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
evidence: Abstract: "users are provided with a clear, step-by-step visualization of the LLM-generated code in real time"; 10 of 12 users reported increased confidence in result correctness (Sec. 7.4.2) - operator situation awareness over an LLM agent.
method: Streaming parser turns an LLM data-analysis agent's code into an interactive dataflow diagram with live table states; users inspect, query and edit nodes, then re-run revised code.
evaluation: Within-subjects study, N=12, vs. code-only baseline; 10 tasks with 4 planted LLM errors; mean success 80% vs. 73%, NASA-TLX p<.001; standard desktops, no latency reported.
contribution: Shows that visualising an LLM data-analysis agent's code as a live dataflow diagram improves users' error detection and confidence, though it adds no pre-execution gate.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, a gpt-4-0125-preview data-analysis agent. Only (e) holds: this is monitoring and situation awareness, not interception - code blocks execute immediately and the authors list a "stop" mechanism as future work (Sec. 8.2), so runtime_interceptor is no. Success rates are descriptive with n=6 per condition and not significance-tested; the paper says WaitGPT "took less time in Task A1-2 and Task B" but Table 2 shows it slower on B2, B3 and B4 and slower overall. Check whether the maintainer wants (e) studies of LLM-agent oversight at all, and that no latency figure exists.

title: AirGapAgent: Protecting Privacy-Conscious Conversational Agents
venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
evidence: Sec. 4.2: "the design does not allow any information from the third party to flow back to the minimizer module"; anything outside the minimised context can only be obtained by escalating to the user, who approves or denies (Sec. 4.2, Sec. 7).
method: Two-LLM air-gap: a minimiser sees only the trusted task plus user data and fixes a minimised data context; a second conversational LLM answers third parties from that context alone.
evaluation: 20 synthetic profiles, 8 scenarios, 16640 cases; Gemini Ultra/Pro, GPT-4, Mistral Large vs. all-data single-agent baseline; privacy under hijacking 45.2% to 96.7%, utility 98.2% to 87.3%; no latency.
contribution: Shows that restricting a personal LLM agent to a task-minimised data context defends against third-party context hijacking, raising data protection from 45% to 97% at a modest utility cost.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, an LLM personal agent. (a) rests on the minimiser gating disclosure before the conversational agent answers plus escalation to the user - check whether a context restriction counts as an execution-time veto rather than a training-time or prompt-time constraint. (c) rests only on the adversary being a third-party agent or service, so the multi-agent reading is thin and (c) may be overturned. The user-escalation loop is design-only and never evaluated, so the human handoff cell is unmeasured. No latency, cost or hardware figures anywhere. Ground-truth privacy labels were generated by Gemini Ultra and only spot-checked by the authors.

title: Plan-Then-Execute: An Empirical Study of User Trust and Team Performance When Using LLM Agents As A Daily Assistant
venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
evidence: Sec. 3.1: users "check whether they approve the current predicted action" before it runs; in execution conditions "Specify Action" was used to override the agent 445 times (Sec. 5.1).
method: 2x2 between-subjects study of user involvement in planning and in execution for a LangChain plan-and-execute GPT-3.5 assistant; in execution conditions the user approves, gives feedback on, or overrides each predicted action.
evaluation: Prolific, N=248, 4 conditions, 6 simulated high/low-risk tasks; calibrated trust 0.50 plan and 0.64 execution; task-6 execution accuracy 0.06 to 0.23 with oversight; no latency or hardware.
contribution: Study of 248 users showing that approving or overriding each action of a plan-then-execute LLM assistant helps task performance only unevenly while raising cognitive load and not improving trust calibration.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, a GPT-3.5 plan-and-execute agent. (e) is solid under the 2026-11-13 ruling. (a) holds only because the gate is a human approval step rather than an automated filter, so the maintainer may prefer criteria_met e alone and runtime_interceptor no. Actions were simulated backend APIs, so nothing irreversible actually happened and risk level is manipulated without measuring time-to-irreversibility. Effects were significant on only one of six tasks (task-4 for plans, task-6 for execution) and overall trust differences were null; the paper does not state the between-subjects design explicitly.

title: Reliable Text-to-SQL with Adaptive Abstention
evidence: The framework "automatically detects uncertainty during the schema linking process" (Sec. 1, contribution 2); on a flagged branching point generation stops and a surrogate model or the user confirms or corrects the table (Sec. 4).
method: RTS: per-layer probes on LLM hidden states flag branching points token by token during schema linking, aggregated with conformal prediction; on a flag it halts and consults a surrogate or the user.
evaluation: Spider and BIRD; vs unguarded schema linking, surrogate filter, DTS-SQL, CodeS; ablations on alpha, k, aggregation. BIRD table-linking EM 79.70 to 98.89 with abstain rates TAR 19.10/FAR 12.77; 20-person user study. A100, no latency.
contribution: Halts LLM schema linking mid-generation when conformal probes on hidden states flag a likely error, then hands the flagged table or column to a human, lifting BIRD linking exact match to near 99%.
flag: (i) hand-off to a human or surrogate, and (ii) abstention is taken token by token during generation. Theorems 1-3 give a 1-2*alpha coverage guarantee (80% at alpha 0.1). Table 6 human-feedback numbers look oracle-simulated (not stated); real humans only in the 20-person study on 100 BIRD questions. Text says RTS with Deepseek-7B reaches 65.19% EX but Table 7 gives 64.72 for Deepseek-7B and 65.19 for CodeS-15B. PDF is marked as an unpublished working draft; last 7k characters not read. Logical domain only, single agent.

title: RTS+: Reliable Text to SQL
venue: Companion of the 2025 International Conference on Management of Data
evidence: "A key feature of RTS+ is its ability to abstain from generating SQL when uncertain, prompting user input or expert review to resolve ambiguities." (Sec 1 Introduction)
method: Interactive text-to-SQL demo: a conformal branching-point predictor over LLM hidden states pauses token generation in schema linking or SQL generation and asks the user a clarifying question.
evaluation: None in this paper: 4-page demo description with interface walkthrough on Spider and BIRD; no metrics, baselines or latency; accuracy claims are deferred to the prior RTS paper.
contribution: Demonstrates an interactive text-to-SQL system that abstains during generation at conformally detected branching points and asks the user to resolve schema-linking ambiguities.
flag: (i) and arguably (ii) apply in principle (abstention to the user at token-level steps during generation), but this is a SIGMOD demo paper with no quantitative result at all, so it fails the evaluation floor. Claims of perfect or near-perfect benchmark scores are asserted, not shown; abstention frequency and intervention analytics are promised for the live demo only. The actual method and evaluation are in reference [3], Reliable Text-to-SQL with Adaptive Abstention, arXiv:2501.10858 (an id cited in the text, not this paper's own): check whether that record is in the queue and assess it instead. One paragraph on the abstention mechanism is duplicated in Sec 2.

title: AgentSpec: Customizable Runtime Enforcement for Safe and Reliable LLM Agents
venue: Proceedings - 2026 IEEE/ACM 48th International Conference on Software Engineering, ICSE 2026
evidence: "AgentSpec is the first framework that systematically enforces customizable safety constraints on LLM agents at runtime" (Sec. 1, Introduction)
method: Domain-specific language of trigger-predicate-enforce rules wrapped around LangChain-style agents; each planned action is intercepted and met with stop, user inspection, action invocation or LLM self-examination before execution.
evaluation: RedCode-Exec code agents (25 categories, 30 cases each), SafeAgentBench embodied tasks, FixDrive AV scenarios; hazard rates 15-78% down to 0%, safe-task success 58.62% to 54.26%, 100% law compliance in 8 AV cases; overhead 1.42ms parsing and 1.11-2.83ms predicates against 9.82-25.4s agent runtimes.
contribution: AgentSpec, a DSL and runtime enforcement layer that intercepts LLM agent actions against user-defined trigger-predicate rules, removing hazardous actions across code, embodied and driving agents at millisecond overhead.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM agents for code, embodied tasks and driving. Strongest (a) record in the batch, and cross-domain is genuine (code agents logical, embodied and AV physical). Numbers to check: the abstract's 'over 90%' is a detection rate only after dropping the two categories where the agent never emitted risky code; Table 3 sums to 333 flagged of 422 invocations (78.9%) overall, and 58 flagged cases were then allowed through by user inspection, so end-to-end prevention is nearer 65%. The 'user inspection' was performed by the authors, not independent operators. The AV rules and all 8 AV scenarios are adopted from FixDrive, and no empirical comparison against GuardAgent or ToolEmu is run. Overhead figures are component costs, not an end-to-end deadline, and enforcement time for user_inspection and llm_self_examine is explicitly unbounded.

title: When Context Grows, So Does the Challenge: Human Oversight in LLM Evaluation of Financial Tables
evidence: "If the tables are not directly comparable due to structural transformations or semantic ambiguity, we defer the evaluation to a human reviewer." (Sec 3 When Should Humans Step In)
method: Measures GPT-4o as a judge comparing financial tables with synthetic single-cell perturbations as table size grows; proposes rule-based criteria for when to send a comparison to a human reviewer.
evaluation: Synthetic perturbed tables, 50 negatives per 5-row increment, GPT-4o accuracy vs rows shown only as a figure; the deferral criteria are not evaluated; no baseline, numbers or latency.
contribution: Finds that an LLM judge comparing financial tables degrades beyond about 60 rows and proposes structural criteria for triggering human review of ambiguous comparisons.
flag: (i) nominally: deferral to a human reviewer is proposed, but the proposed triggered-oversight criteria are never implemented or measured; no deferral rate, no accuracy with vs without deferral, no baseline. The only empirical content is Figure 2 (GPT-4o accuracy falling with table size) and no numeric values appear in the text beyond the 60-row threshold. 3-page UIST Adjunct poster from an industry team; the stated research question Q2 (balance of accuracy and manual effort) is not answered with data. Calls its own analysis comprehensive, which the content does not support. The setting is offline evaluation of pipeline outputs, not a runtime gate on an acting system.

title: Bounded-Abstention Pairwise Learning to Rank
venue: Proceedings of the 32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining V.2
evidence: "a theoretical characterization of the optimal abstention strategy" (Abstract); Theorems 3.1-3.2 show risk thresholding with randomised ties is optimal under a coverage bound (Sec. 3).
method: BALToR: plug-in selection function for a fixed pairwise ranker; abstains on pairs whose estimated conditional risk (confidence, margin or entropy) exceeds a calibration-set quantile meeting target coverage.
evaluation: Proved: optimality conditions and optimal thresholding rule (Thm 3.1, 3.2, Prop 3.3). Experiments on Web-30k, OHSUMED, MQ2007, Yahoo vs random abstainer; coverage gap <=0.002; accuracy only in figures; no latency.
contribution: Characterises the optimal bounded-abstention rule for pairwise learning to rank and gives a model-agnostic plug-in that thresholds estimated conditional risk at a calibrated quantile.
flag: (v) theory of the reject option, extended to pairwise ranking; otherwise it is one-shot selective prediction and would be E4. Deferral to a human is motivation only, learning to defer is future work. Selective accuracy values appear only in Figures 2-3, no numbers in text; only baseline is a random abstainer. Maintainer should judge whether a ranking-specific optimal rule counts as foundational.

title: DynaFLUX: Implicit Dynamics-Preserving Reinforcement Learning for Topology-Free Influence Maximization
venue: WWW 2026 - Proceedings of the ACM Web Conference 2026
evidence: "we infer a surrogate adjacency matrix ... from the observed state sequences ... using sparse linear regression framework with Lasso regularization" (Sec. 4.2; symbols omitted)
method: DynaFLUX: self-attention pointer-network policy trained by REINFORCE picks influence-maximization seeds from node activation time series; rewards from Monte Carlo diffusion on a Lasso-inferred surrogate graph (or true graph, DynaFLUX+).
evaluation: Six networks (Jazz, Cora-ML, Power Grid, Network Science, Digg, synthetic) under IC/LT/SIS vs IMM, OPIM, SubSIM, IMINFECTOR, PIANO, ToupleGDD, DeepIM, DeepSN; influence spread %; attention ablation; Tesla V100; no latency.
contribution: A topology-free influence-maximization method that learns node embeddings from activation time series and trains a seed-selection policy with rewards simulated on a Lasso-inferred surrogate graph.
flag: Recommend E1: not a predictive world model in the review's sense. The 'influence-prediction module' is a Lasso-regressed surrogate adjacency plus Monte Carlo simulation under a hand-specified diffusion model (IC/LT/SIS); no learned transition or latent dynamics model predicts future node state, and the learned embeddings feed a seed-selection policy, not a predictor. The state is a graph but there are no acting agents and no safety or hazard aspect; topic is social-network influence maximization. Borderline for a generous reader: the paper does report a direct predictive measure, agreement between predicted and true influence spread (Table 3: Lasso Pearson 0.606, Spearman 0.675, Kendall 0.493, PRC 74.5% vs Epsilon/KNN/Prob reconstructions) and link-prediction AUC 0.726 vs 0.722 for an MLP, so it is not downstream-only; headline results are downstream influence spread (+15.8/+13.6/+9.5/+5.8 points under IC at 1/5/10/20% seeds). Doubts: conclusion claims operation 'without ... predefined diffusion models' yet rewards come from simulating predefined IC/LT/SIS models; single random seed (42); the ablation is done on DynaFLUX+ (true topology) not the topology-free variant; LSTM ablation ties or beats the full model in several cells; AUC gain over MLP is negligible; called 'generative framework' in the abstract without a generative model.

title: Active Maritime Copilot for Ambiguity and Risk-Driven Decisions
venue: Companion Proceedings of the 21st ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction, HRI Companion 2026
evidence: "the agent visualizes the reasoning rationale (citing specific COLREGs as basis) and requests human authorization to initiate a specific clarification query" (Sec. 2.3, Risk-Prioritized Interface)
method: RAG copilot parses VHF dialogue with an LLM into structured intent, propagates a deterministic ghost trajectory, scores ambiguity from semantic vagueness plus kinematic divergence, and escalates green-yellow-red for operator authorization.
evaluation: 2D planar maritime benchmark, 5 COLREGs encounters by 3 communication-congruency conditions, N=13 HRI researchers and graduate students, think-aloud plus Likert; median at least 6 for colour status and RAG evidence, 4.5s (SD 1.2) decision time in the yellow state.
contribution: A watchful maritime copilot that cross-checks VHF verbal intent against radar kinematics and uses progressive green-yellow-red disclosure to hand ambiguous collision risks to the officer of the watch.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: which - the automation is an LLM plus RAG copilot, and (e) does not require it anyway; (e) clearly holds on topic (handoff, trust calibration, operator situation awareness). I exclude only on the evaluation floor: a 5-page HRI Companion contribution whose results are Likert medians plus one response-time mean, with no accuracy or detection rate for the ambiguity quantifier against the stated Condition A-B-C ground truth, no baseline interface, and cognitive load claimed but never measured (no NASA-TLX or equivalent). Figure 4 compares with-background and without-background participant groups, not interface conditions, and no numbers for it appear in the text. Participants are not mariners and the authors call the work preliminary, formative and a proof of concept. This is the record I most expect the maintainer to overturn to include as an (e) exemplar.

title: Does Safety Molt? Evaluating LLM Safety in Multi-Agent Social Environments
venue: Proceedings of the ACM Conference on AI and Agentic Systems, CAIS 2026
evidence: "when a reply follows a leaking message in the same thread, the probability that the next reply also leaks rises to 12.8%" (Sec. 5, Temporal Accumulation RQ2)
method: Moltbook-style simulation platform where 2,533 tool-calling LLM agents holding private human profiles interact across 124 communities; contextual-integrity violations are detected by pattern matching plus an LLM judge.
evaluation: 25 simulated days, 29,945 posts and 81,264 replies; controlled testbed of 7 frontier models by 10 held-out personas by 5 tool-call budgets (7,000 traces) at 5 adversarial contamination levels; leakage 12.8% after a leaking reply vs 1.6% clean, 50-60% at 50 tool calls, subreddit rates under 2% to over 16%.
contribution: Shows LLM agent privacy safety degrades in persistent multi-agent social environments: disclosure is socially contagious, community context rivals model choice, and prompt-level privacy instructions only partly mitigate it.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM tool-calling agents are the evaluated system; this is evaluation only with no runtime interception, so (c) alone and runtime_interceptor no. Abstract numbers I could not find in the body: 'CIMemories 19.95% to Ours 45.30%' and 'leakage rates above 37.8% even with safeguards' occur only in the abstract and introduction, never in Section 5 and in no table. The abstract says agents are '8x more likely' to disclose after a peer while the introduction says '5.1x'; the body (12.8% vs 1.6%) supports 8x, so the introduction figure looks wrong. Ground truth is regex patterns over GPT-5-mini-generated profiles scored by an LLM judge, which the authors concede makes contextual integrity 'approximate'. There are no result tables at all, so every figure I quote is read from plots, and the Moltbook platform statistics rest on 2026 preprints.

title: When to Answer and When to Defer: A Decision Framework for Reliable Code Predictions
venue: Proceedings of the IEEE/ACM 48th International Conference on Software Engineering
evidence: Sec. 2: "if the score exceeds a tunable threshold, the prediction is accepted; otherwise, the input is abstained".
method: Framework for code models: uncertainty signals are calibrated into a correctness likelihood; below-threshold predictions are abstained and routed to recovery (context augmentation, analysers, task splitting) or final abstention.
evaluation: Preliminary. MBPP+ and defect prediction with 7B code models; vs Platt, isotonic, temperature scaling. DeepSeek MBPP+ Brier/ECE 0.162/0.072 vs base 0.273/0.223; selective accuracy over 70% at 80% coverage. No hardware or latency.
contribution: Sketches an answer-or-defer pipeline for code language models and shows weighted calibration lowers Brier score and ECE against standard calibrators in preliminary experiments.
flag: none of (i)-(v): language model abstaining on single code tasks; short vision/NIER-style paper. The only quantified part is CALIBRATION (Brier, ECE); the abstain decision gets just two unbaselined statements (over 70% and over 90% selective accuracy at 80% coverage), so exclude-E2 is equally defensible under the floor. The recovery layer (tools, analysers, task splitting) that would make it a fallback hand-off under (i) is described but not evaluated; human review appears only in the Introduction. Table 2 proposed-method row is labelled Confidence without explanation; text and Table 1 name the method differently. Sec. 4.3 16-metric study reports no numbers.

title: Abstain and Validate: A Dual-LLM Policy for Reducing Noise in Agentic Program Repair
venue: Proceedings of the IEEE/ACM 48th International Conference on Software Engineering: Software Engineering in Practice
evidence: "We present a dual-policy framework to reduce developer noise in agentic APR" (Conclusion); bug abstention declines bugs before the agent runs and patch validation rejects patches before developers see them (Sec. 3-4).
method: Two LLM gates around a repair agent: pre-run bug abstention from predicted success probability (threshold 0.5), and post-run patch validation against an LLM-generated fix specification with percentile cutoffs.
evaluation: 174 human-reported Google bugs, 198 NPE, 50 sanitizer bugs; vs no-abstention, build/test filter, no-spec ablation. Fail-to-pass@1 0.11 to 0.215 (abstain), 0.53 combined-p90; validation FPR 0.28/0.13/0.04. No latency.
contribution: Shows that an LLM abstention gate before an industrial program-repair agent and an LLM patch validator after it raise the share of correct patches shown to developers from 11% to 53%.
flag: (iv) borderline, with (ii) agentic setting: the gates withhold an agent run or veto its patch at runtime, but the aim is developer noise and patch quality, not safety, and each decision is one-shot per bug, not sequential. Routing of abstained bugs is not described; humans review only accepted patches, so handoff is not itself studied (no e). Combined-p90 keeps only 12 of 174 bugs. Abstention evaluated only on the human-reported set. Abstract quotes up to 13 pp (abstention), 15 pp (validation), 39 pp (combined); body gives 0.11 to 0.215, 0.14 to 0.29 and 0.14 to 0.53 respectively, so check which baseline the 39 pp uses. NPE 0.38 to 0.62 is quoted from the abstract; I did not locate the table value. Proprietary data, not reproducible.

title: Evidence-Driven, Failure-Resilient Planning for Domain-Agnostic Multi-agent Orchestration
venue: AgenticDev 2026 - Proceedings of the 1st International Workshop on Agentic AI for Next-Generation Software Development, Co located with ASE 2026
evidence: "Domain modules are invoked only after the control plane has selected one of four routes: clarify missing intent, confirm an irreversible action, request human review, or execute" (Sec. 2, Evidence-Driven Planning Layer)
method: Control plane around an LLM planner: evidence packets and capability bids, deterministic schema and dependency validation with rule-based repair, model fallback chain, ontology SPARQL obligation checks and human checkpoints.
evaluation: None bearing on safety: ten manufacturing cases M1-M10 are named as tests with no outcomes reported; Table 1 lists only factory logistics data (199,721 delivery rows, 97.5% end-to-end match, p95 wait 47.0 h). No baseline, no ablation, no latency.
contribution: A domain-agnostic control plane that validates, repairs and routes LLM planner output, confirming irreversible actions and low-confidence plans with a human before any domain module executes.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an LLM planner, and (a) holds by design since the control plane can clarify, confirm or route to human review before execution. Excluded purely on the evaluation floor: a 2-page workshop paper with no quantitative safety result, no baseline and no ablation, whose conclusion states that 'Future evaluation will quantify module-selection accuracy, clarification precision and recall, repair and fallback rates, terminal retention, and unsupported claims'. Single author, two company affiliations, and the ten test cases are described but never scored. I did not credit cross-domain evaluation: the two instantiations (software engineering and manufacturing logistics analytics) are both enterprise data workflows with no physical actuation. Worth rechecking if an extended, evaluated version appears.

title: A2A—A Mechanism Driven Framework for Interaction Based Agent Evaluation
venue: ICAICP 2026 - Proceedings of the 2026 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Computing Power
evidence: Table 2 caption (Sec 4.3 Results): 'Illustrative results derived from prior internal studies, showing the impact of interaction depth and attacker capability on attack success rate.'
method: Three-axis taxonomy (interaction depth, structural exposure, threat model) plus A2A-Attack, which casts evaluation as trajectory-level adversarial interaction among attacking agent, target agent and environment.
evaluation: Analytical mapping of MMLU, WebArena, AgentBench, GPTFuzzer; illustrative ASR from prior internal studies: static 30.2%, manual red-team 54.8%, A2A R=5 83.2%, GPT-4 attacker 85.0%; remaining comparison qualitative.
contribution: Recasts static, behavioural and adversarial LLM-agent evaluation as configurations of a single attacker-target-environment interaction mechanism, with a three-axis taxonomy for comparing methods.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (LLM agents under adversarial evaluation). No evaluation of its own: the only numbers (Table 2) and the abstract claim of ASR above 80% in enterprise settings are attributed to undisclosed prior internal studies and are explicitly 'illustrative'; the cross-paradigm comparison uses a High/Medium/Low qualitative protocol; 6-page taxonomy-led paper, so exclude-E3 (position/survey) is also arguable; no runtime interception anywhere.

title: Distributed multi-robot collision avoidance via deep reinforcement learning for navigation in complex scenarios
evidence: Sec. 4.4: "the traditional control takes charge of relatively simple scenarios or emergent situations" - a distance-thresholded hybrid layer switches the learned policy out for PID or a conservative safe policy at control time.

evaluation: Stage simulation, 4-100 robots, circle/random/corridor/group-swap scenarios vs. NH-ORCA and supervised baselines; 20-agent success 1.0 vs. 0.78, extra time 0.702s vs. 1.800s; 5ms per command on Jetson TX1.
contribution: A decentralised sensor-level DRL collision-avoidance policy with a hand-tuned switching layer that reaches 100% success with 20 robots where NH-ORCA reaches 78%, at 5ms per command on a Jetson TX1.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, the hybrid switching layer guards a DRL policy. The arXiv v1 title is "Fully Distributed Multi-Robot Collision Avoidance via Deep Reinforcement Learning for Safe and Efficient Navigation in Complex Scenarios" while the record uses the IJRR 2020 title - same authors and content, but confirm the journal version was not substantially revised. (a) is weak: the switching thresholds (r_safe=0.1, r_risk=0.8) are hand-set and the "safe" fallback is itself a DRL network, so there is no guarantee. The paper claims safety and efficiency jointly and the headline tables report success rate and extra time, with collision rates only in the Sec. 5.4 robustness study, so the (c) primacy test is arguable. Real-robot localisation is UWB with about +-150mm error.

title: An uncertainty-aware ultrasound triage model for cervical lymphadenopathy: a retrospective multicenter development and external validation study
evidence: "all remaining patients were deferred for senior review" (Methods, Uncertainty score and locked selective-triage rule)

evaluation: Retrospective, 518 patients, 3 centres; pooled external n=224: coverage 0.366, selective accuracy 0.927, FN/FP 2/4; partial AURC 0.037 vs 0.047 probability-distance baseline; 8-reader study. No latency.

flag: (i) only nominally, otherwise none of (i)-(v): deferral target is senior human review, but the rule thresholds model probability and uncertainty only, the human is not modelled and the deferred pathway is never evaluated (reader study tests AI assistance on all 224 cases, not handoff). I read it as a one-shot classifier with reject option applied to a domain; maintainer may flip to include if any explicit deferral-to-human pathway satisfies (i). Abstract numbers all found in body. Candid weaknesses stated by authors: deferral rate 0.634, composite uncertainty error-detection AUROC only 0.581 (entropy alone 0.673), calibration slopes about 2, workflow not run in real time, assisted round always second. Baseline for the defer rule is in Supplementary Table S18, not in the file. Article in Press.

title: SelANet: decision-assisting selective sleep apnea detection based on confidence score
venue: BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making
evidence: "for samples with high uncertainty, this algorithm rejected them, providing a second opinion to the clinician" (Abstract, Background)

evaluation: MGH PhysioNet 2018 PSG, 994 subjects, 220,828 test segments; vs same model without selection: accuracy 83.22 to 90.26%, FPR 16.89 to 8.71%, FNR 16.67 to 10.79%. No hardware or latency.

flag: none of (i)-(v): one-shot selective classification applied to a domain; clinician second opinion is only mentioned, never modelled or evaluated. Segments are classified independently (no sequential deferral); wearable and real-time use are aspirations only. Doubts: abstract claims about 7.03% improvement in all metrics but sensitivity gains 8.18 and specificity 5.88 points; reject rate reported as 18.77% at a 0.98 setting while empirical coverage is 0.978 (text conflates target coverage with confidence threshold); coverage violation 0.114 at target 0.90 sits oddly with empirical coverage 0.897; balanced resampled test set; accuracy gain is on accepted samples only, with no risk-coverage comparison against softmax or MC-dropout rejection.

title: OrthoGPT: multimodal generative pre-trained transformer models for precise diagnosis and treatment of orthopedics; [OrthoGPT：面向精准诊疗的多模态骨科大模型]
venue: Chinese Journal of Intelligent Science and Technology

method: Position/framework paper (Chinese) proposing OrthoGPT, a multimodal orthopedic large model combining feature alignment, a parallel-theory orthopedic world model and multi-agent LLM interaction for diagnosis, surgical planning and rehabilitation advice.
evaluation: Not assessed in detail: body is in Chinese; the English abstract describes a proposed framework and its application potential and reports no experiments, baselines, metrics or hardware.
contribution: A Chinese-language framework paper proposing a multimodal orthopedic large model with a parallel-medicine world model and multi-agent interaction for diagnosis, surgical planning and rehabilitation.
flag: NOT IN ENGLISH: the file is the correct paper (Chinese Journal of Intelligent Science and Technology 6(3), Sept 2024) but the full text is Chinese with only an English title, abstract and keywords; I read only the English abstract and the Chinese abstract, not the body. Even setting language aside it looks off-topic (medical LLM framework; the 'world model' is a parallel-systems concept for simulating post-operative outcomes, not a graph or multi-agent predictive model) and the abstract reports no evaluation (aims 'to explore the application potential'), so E1/E2 would also apply.

title: Consistent algorithms for multiclass classification with an abstain option
evidence: Sec. 1: "The reject option is accommodated into the problem of n-class classification through the evaluation metric"; Eq. 2 abstains unless the largest class probability is at least 1-alpha, extending Chow's rule.
method: Theory of multiclass classification with an abstain option: thresholded Crammer-Singer and one-vs-all hinge surrogates shown consistent, plus a new piecewise-linear binary-encoded-prediction surrogate in log2(n) dimensions.
evaluation: Theorems 1-3 give consistency and excess-risk bounds for alpha in [0,1/2]; synthetic 2D Gaussians plus 6 UCI sets compare CS/OVA/BEP; satimage error 10.25% to 2.9% at 40% rejection; covertype training 6786s vs 47974s.
contribution: Proves that thresholded Crammer-Singer and one-vs-all hinge surrogates are consistent for the multiclass abstain loss at alpha=1/2 and gives a consistent surrogate needing only log2(n) dimensions.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes, the abstaining classifier is itself learned. Under the Pillar 3 scope this survives only through (v) foundational theory of the reject option: it is one-shot selective prediction with no hand-off to a human or safeguard, no sequential setting and no multiple experts, so a narrow reading of (v) makes this exclude-E4 - the most likely record to be overturned. runtime_interceptor is no because abstention is an output class rather than a gate on another system's action. Record title "with an abstain option" is the EJS 2018 journal version; arXiv 1505.04137 is titled "with a Reject Option". The alpha>1/2 case is left as future work, Theorem 3 omits its proof, and the body mislabels Table 1 as Table 2.

title: Superpixel-graph self-supervised pretraining with joint-embedding and contrastive objectives for wound image segmentation
venue: Advances in Science and Technology Research Journal
evidence: "represents a wound image as a superpixel adjacency graph, generated using the simple linear iterative clustering algorithm and uses graph structure to define building blocks for calculating joint-embedding and contrastive learning objectives" (Abstract)
method: Self-supervised CNN encoder pretraining on a SLIC superpixel adjacency graph of a single still image: JEPA-style target/context superpixel embedding prediction plus NT-Xent contrastive loss over 1-ring neighbours.
evaluation: 100 unlabelled wound images, fine-tune on K=1,3,5,30 labels, 400-image test, 3 splits; best Dice 0.266, IoU 0.180 (contrastive, K=30) vs supervised U-Net 0.354/0.279. Laptop RTX 2060, 3 h per run.
contribution: Pretrains a wound-segmentation encoder with joint-embedding and contrastive objectives defined on a static superpixel graph, reaching Dice 0.266 from 30 labels against 0.354 for a fully supervised U-Net.
flag: Falls squarely under the 2026-11-12 ruling: latent (JEPA-like) prediction of masked/neighbouring superpixel embeddings on a STATIC graph built from one still image; no future state, no dynamics, no agents, no temporal data. Not a predictive world model, so (b) is not met. No direct measure of predictive accuracy is reported at all: only downstream segmentation Dice and IoU, plus a 1-ring label-purity statistic (0.987 global, 0.809 wound anchors) that describes the graph, not the model. So it would also fail as E2 on the downstream-only rule. Results are weak and the authors say so: the pretrained models lose to the supervised baseline, K<=5 fine-tuning gives at most 0.170 Dice (the text says max 2.8%, which contradicts Table 1 where K=3 and K=5 reach 0.109-0.170), and the JEPA objective is the worst variant at K=30 (0.183). Text states U-Net IoU 27.9% but that figure is not in Table 2. Single-image medical vision paper with no safety, multi-agent, latency or handoff aspect.

title: IsolateGPT: An Execution Isolation Architecture for LLM-Based Systems
venue: Network and Distributed System Security Symposium
evidence: Sec. IV-B5: "we require explicit user consent before any irreversible action is taken by the app"; denial blocks the flow (Fig. 7).
method: Hub-and-spoke execution isolation for LLM app systems: each app runs in its own spoke with its own LLM and memory; user permission gates inter-app data flow and irreversible actions.
evaluation: 1598 InjecAgent attacks plus case studies vs non-isolated VanillaGPT (GPT-4); baseline ASR 20.2%; permission dialog on 7.6% of attacks, 100% with warnings; functionality 1.00; overhead under 30% for 75.73% of queries, p95 1.80x; Ryzen 9 desktop.
contribution: Execution isolation with per-app LLM spokes and user permission gates blocks cross-app prompt injection and data exfiltration in LLM agent systems while preserving task functionality.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a GPT-4 multi-app agent system. Check (c) primacy: security of the multi-app system is the primary claim and InjecAgent ASR is measured, but IsolateGPT's own post-permission attack success rate is never reported, only that dialogs appeared for 7.6% of attacks; permissions were auto-granted during the performance runs; no ablation beyond the VanillaGPT baseline; logical domain only, so no cross-domain cell.

title: SagaLLM: Context Management, Validation, and Transaction Guarantees for Multi-Agent LLM Planning
evidence: Sec. 3.2.3: "Validated operations proceed; failures trigger compensations using preserved historical context"; Sec. 3.3.2 rejection protocol "initiates compensating transactions upon validation failures".
method: Transactional layer under multi-agent LLM planning: independent validation agents, persistent context checkpoints, saga-style compensating transactions and rollback to a saved state on validation failure.
evaluation: REALM problems 5,6,8,9 (travel, Thanksgiving, wedding) with Claude 3.7, DeepSeek R1, GPT-4o and GPT-o1 as baselines; only narrative baseline errors given (dinner 6:30 PM vs 6:00 PM deadline; arrival 3:55 PM vs 3:00 PM); no success, violation, token or latency rates; no hardware.
contribution: Proposes a saga-style transactional layer with independent validation agents and compensating rollback to restore context and constraint consistency in multi-agent LLM planning.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM planning agents. Fails the evaluation floor: no quantitative result and no formal result. SagaLLM's own outputs appear in no table across three fetches (offsets 0, 30000, 60000); Table 9 is categorical (Guaranteed, Full, Always); no success, violation, token or runtime figures, no trial counts, no hardware; the claim that only SagaLLM handles the alert is unsupported by presented data, and the under-1k validation context is a design target, not a measurement.
