Also doubt (a): compensation is post-hoc rollback and the augmentation protocol explicitly does not override agent decisions, so a pre-execution veto is never demonstrated.

title: A Policy-guided LLM Pipeline for Safer Clinical Decision Support: Error Analysis on High-risk Medication Queries
evidence: "The first stage checks whether a prompt should trigger an automatic refusal accompanied by a safe fallback message directing the user to a clinician." (Section 3, System architecture and methodology)
method: Layered guardrail for medication questions: hard-refusal check, regex risk screen, small-LLM risk opinion, then policy layer labels each prompt ACCEPT, WARN, DEFER, ESCALATE or REFUSE.
evaluation: 55 hand-built medication prompts with expected labels; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 backends only, no unguarded baseline or ablation; system accuracy 60.0%, false accept rate 16.4%, guardrail intercept 18.2%. No latency.
contribution: A layered rule-plus-LLM guardrail routes medication questions to accept, warn, defer, escalate or refuse; on 55 prompts it reaches 60% accuracy with a 16.4% false accept rate.
flag: none of (i)-(v): LLM guardrail abstaining or escalating on single questions; no human handoff is implemented or measured. Would also fail the floor (E2): the two backends are not a baseline for the mechanism and there is no ablation of any layer. Doubts: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 give identical values on every metric and identical errors in all 22 cases, yet the text also says they failed in almost the same way; false accept rate 16.4% (9 of 55) vs Table 2 false acceptance 10 cases, 18.2%; Figure 1 caption says four stages, text describes three; 55 prompts, labels by the authors, benchmark not released; 5-page student-style conference paper, own results table carries citations [6][7].

title: Safety and Liveness Guarantees through Reach-Avoid Reinforcement Learning
evidence: Sec. IV-B: "we can translate our learned reach-avoid solution into a supervisory control law with a recursive feasibility guarantee, by employing a shielding scheme" over an untrusted performance policy.
method: Time-discounted reach-avoid Bellman equation with reach-avoid Q-learning (tabular and DDQN); the learned value function is an untrusted oracle inside model-predictive shielding of a performance policy.
evaluation: Simulation only: 2D particle, 3D Dubins car, 6D lunar lander, 6D two-car attack-defense; baseline sum-of-discounted-cost RL; Dubins shielding gives 0% false-safe by construction vs 6.6% and 7.9% unshielded, false-fail 4.8% and 2.5%; lunar lander FSR 20%, FFR 4%; 50 seeds; no latency or hardware.
contribution: A time-discounted reach-avoid Bellman equation yields learned value functions that certify safety and liveness together and act as a runtime shield over an untrusted performance policy.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the shield wraps a performance-driven RL policy, and both players in the game have learned policies. Not scored (c): the two-car attack-defense game is one of four experiments and the primary claim is single-agent reach-avoid guarantees, so the multi-agent state cell rests on that one game and the maintainer may drop it. The 0% false-safe figure holds by construction, not by measurement; the shielding guarantee needs an accurate simulator at runtime; simulation only, no numerical HJ solver baseline, no latency or compute figures despite the per-step rollout.

title: Task-Aware Risk Estimation of Perception Failures for Autonomous Vehicles
evidence: Sec. IV-C: "Algorithm 1 detects a task-relevant failure (line 5), which can be used to trigger a safety maneuver"; the monitor triggers only when a perception failure endangers the motion plan.
method: p-quantile relative scenario risk compares cost distributions of the perceived scene and failure-consistent plausible scenes with a copula and PAC bounds; an alarm fires when the lower bound exceeds a threshold.
evaluation: 100 NuPlan closed-loop scenarios, four injected perception fault classes; baselines HJ-reachability and collision probability; MSD at p=0.99 reaches F1 0.86, accuracy 0.93, precision 0.81, recall 0.92 vs 0.39, 0.28, 0.24, 0.96; alarm 4.72s (median 3.03s) before collision; 0.29s per scene on i9-10980XE plus RTX 3090.
contribution: Task-aware risk estimation flags only the perception failures that actually endanger the planned motion, raising alarm precision more than threefold over reachability and collision-probability monitors.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: partly - it guards a learned perception stack and a Trajectron++ predictor, but the ego planner is rule-based IDM and the other road agents are IDM or logged, so (c) is not credited. (a) is borderline and the likeliest overturn: the monitor only raises an alarm and never overrides, halts or slows the vehicle, with the integrated monitor and closed-loop evaluation left to future work (Sec. VI); if the maintainer requires an implemented override this is E1 or E4. No ablation beyond the p and cost-metric sweeps; the true-positive cell of Table III was not legible; no AUC reported; 0.29s runtime is far from an explicit latency budget, so no latency cell.

title: Enterprise Agent Evaluation Framework for Autonomous AI Systems: A Multi-Dimensional Approach to Reliability, Safety, and Quality Assurance
venue: International Journal of Future Innovative Science and Technology
evidence: Sec IX Results and Discussion: 'Table X summarizes representative evaluation results obtained using the proposed framework.' with an overall Enterprise Agent Score EAS = 0.92.
method: Enterprise Agent Evaluation Framework: twelve evaluation dimensions scored 0-1 and combined by fixed weights into one Enterprise Agent Score, wired into DevSecOps CI/CD quality gates.
evaluation: One proof-of-concept API-testing agent; twelve dimension scores 0.85-0.97 and EAS 0.92; no dataset, no baseline, no ablation, no latency figures, no per-run statistics.
contribution: Proposes a twelve-dimension weighted score (Enterprise Agent Score) for judging enterprise production readiness of autonomous LLM agents inside continuous delivery pipelines.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes nominally (enterprise LLM agents), but there is no runtime mechanism and multi-agent coordination is 1 of 12 dimensions, so exclude-E1 is equally defensible. Strong provenance doubts: a July-August 2024 issue whose reference list cites the same author's 2025 and 2026 papers; unrendered LaTeX in the EAS equation ('EAS=sum_{i=1}^{12} w_iM_i' pasted three times); single unverifiable score table; single-author, low-profile venue; reads as machine-generated.

title: End-to-End Safe Reinforcement Learning through Barrier Functions for Safety-Critical Continuous Control Tasks
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
evidence: CBF-Based Compensating Control: "the CBF controller compensates for the RL controller to ensure safety"; the CBF filters the proposed control action before it is deployed.
method: A control barrier function QP solved every timestep over a Gaussian-process model of the unknown dynamics filters the action of a model-free RL policy (TRPO or DDPG) and guides its exploration.
evaluation: Simulated inverted pendulum (40% nominal model error) and a five-car following chain with a 2m hard headway; baselines plain TRPO and DDPG; no safety violations with either RL-CBF controller vs collisions in almost all baseline trials; Theorem 2 proves forward invariance with probability 1-delta; numeric results only in Figures 3-5; no latency.
contribution: Wrapping a Gaussian-process control barrier function QP around model-free RL keeps a learned controller inside the safe set throughout learning with high probability and speeds convergence.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the filter sits on TRPO and DDPG actions at every timestep. Check the evaluation floor: a second fetch (offset 25000) confirmed the text reports no numeric violation counts, rewards, episode, trial or seed counts anywhere - the safety claim is the qualitative pair no safety violations vs almost all trials had collisions, plus Figures 3-5, so the include rests on Theorem 2's probabilistic forward-invariance guarantee; a maintainer who wants a measured rate could call this E2. Not (c): only the 4th car is learned and the rest are fixed driver models, so the platoon is multi-agent only nominally and no gap cell is credited. The performance bound applies to u_k - u_CBF_k, not to the deployed controller, and the paper admits it need not hold with the MLP approximation. No QP solve time or hardware.

title: Sparse reject option classifier using successive linear programming
venue: 33rd AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, AAAI 2019, 31st Innovative Applications of Artificial Intelligence Conference, IAAI 2019 and the 9th AAAI Symposium on Educational Advances in Artificial Intelligence, EAAI 2019
evidence: "The rejection also has its cost but it is very less compared to the cost of mis-classification." (Introduction); Theorem 1, Sec. 3, proves Fisher consistency of the double ramp loss.
method: SDR-SVM: l1-regularised reject option classifier minimising the non-convex double ramp loss via difference-of-convex programming, solving a sequence of linear programs; kernelised.
evaluation: Five UCI sets (Ionosphere, Parkinsons, Heart, ILPD, Pima); baselines SVM with tuned band, ER-SVM, DH-SVM; risk, rejection rate, accuracy, support vectors in figures only. Proved Fisher consistency, excess-risk and generalization bounds.
contribution: Introduces a sparse reject option classifier trained by successive linear programming on the double ramp loss, proving Fisher consistency, an excess-risk bound and a generalization rate.
flag: (v), borderline: one-shot reject option classifier (otherwise E4) but with substantial proved theory: Fisher consistency (Thm 1), excess-risk bound (Thm 3), error decomposition (Thm 5), generalization rate N^(-beta/(4beta+2)) (Thm 6). No numeric experimental value appears in the text, all results are in Figures 2-4, so the empirical side alone would not clearly meet the floor; inclusion rests on the proofs. Physician or banker referral is motivation only, no human modelled. Maintainer may prefer exclude-E4.

title: Regression under Human Assistance
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
evidence: Algorithm 2 trains a classifier h_theta that at test time routes each new input either to a human, Outsource(x), or to the machine prediction x^T w* (Sec. Algorithm 2 and experiments on real data).
method: Greedy submodular-style selection of training samples to outsource to humans under ridge regression, plus a learned test-time router that sends each input to a human or to the regressor.
evaluation: Synthetic plus Hatespeech, Stare-H/D, Messidor; baselines DS, distorted greedy, Triage, CRR; MSE vs outsourcing level, error plateaus near n/|V|=0.3, greedy advantage p=1e-3; no latency reported.
contribution: Casts the human-machine division of labour in regression as a subset-selection problem, proves NP-hardness and a greedy approximation guarantee, and routes each input to human or model at test time.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the guarded predictor is a learned ridge regressor, deferral is the main contribution, there is hand-off to a human and reject-option style theory, so it clears the Pillar 3 gate. Check: the humans are simulated with per-sample error assumed known, no real human study, so (e) does not hold; the outsourced set is chosen at training time and only the router acts at execution time; all MSE results live in figures with no numeric values in the text (only p=1e-3 and the n/|V|=0.3 plateau); setting is one-shot, non-sequential, one expert per sample.

title: Online active learning of reject option classifiers
venue: AAAI 2020 - 34th AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
evidence: "A reject option classifier can be viewed as two parallel surfaces with the rejection area in between." (Sec 1, Introduction)
method: Online linear/kernel reject-option classifier learning f and rejection width rho jointly; DRAL (double ramp loss) and DSAL (double sigmoid loss) query labels only selectively per streaming trial.
evaluation: Gisette, Phishing, Guide (UCI); T=10000, 100 repetitions, d in {0.1,0.25,0.4}; baseline DSOL (no active querying); risk, rejected, misclassified and queried-label fractions, shown only in figures. No hardware/latency.
contribution: Online active-learning algorithms for reject-option classifiers with mistake bounds for double ramp loss and a local-regret bound for a new double sigmoid loss, reaching comparable risk with fewer queried labels.
flag: (ii) weakly, (v) partly, borderline: the setting is streaming, but each rejection is a one-shot per-instance abstention, not a deferral over time against a deadline; the real novelty is label-efficient training of a reject classifier. If (ii) requires abstention as a temporal action, this is exclude-E4. Results are comparative curves only, I found no numeric values in the text, and outcomes are mixed (DSOL marginally better on Phishing; DSAL risk higher than DRAL on two sets). Theory: Thm 2/3 bounds on rejected and misclassified queried examples for DRAL; Thm 6 local regret <= (4 gamma^2/5)(R^2+1)(T+1) for DSAL, i.e. stationarity only; no statistical consistency result. Human experts appear only as motivation.

title: Role of Human-AI Interaction in Selective Prediction
venue: Proceedings of the 36th AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, AAAI 2022
evidence: "The human-AI communication method that yields the highest human performance is DO." (Experiment Results and Analysis)
method: Ensemble classifier defers images whose score falls in a tuned interval; study varies whether the human reviewer is told the deferral status and the model prediction.
evaluation: Snapshot Serengeti, 198 Prolific participants, 80 deferred images, 2x2 within-subject; human accuracy 61.9% deferral-status-only vs 58.4% no message (p<0.001), model alone 50%. No hardware or latency.
contribution: Shows in a 198-person study that telling reviewers an image was deferred raises their accuracy while showing the uncertain model prediction lowers it, so deferral systems must be evaluated as human-AI teams.
flag: (i): the handoff to the human is the studied object, and criterion e is met directly. Doubts: the deferral rule itself is a simple one-shot score-interval threshold (1% deferral), not novel; participants are crowd workers plus two domain experts; the system-level accuracy at the chosen operating point is not stated in text (only human 0.961, model 0.972, oracle 0.994). Per-condition means for prediction-only and both-messages appear only in a figure. Individual human accuracy is given as 0.961 in Fig 3 but 0.973 in the appendix; one contrast was read as F(1,39)=2.19 with p<0.05, which looks inconsistent - check against the PDF. Effects are small (about 3 points) and the authors caution they may not generalise.

title: Evaluating Model-Free Reinforcement Learning toward Safety-Critical Tasks
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
evidence: The Unrolling Safety Layer applies gradient-based corrections to the policy action at each step before it reaches the environment, and Recovery RL hands control to a recovery policy when the learned risk critic exceeds a threshold (Sec. Methods).
method: SafeRL-Kit toolkit plus the Unrolling Safety Layer, which unrolls gradient steps on a learned cost model to correct every action of an off-policy RL policy before execution.
evaluation: Six single-agent benchmarks, 5 seeds; vs Safety Layer, Recovery RL, Lagrangian, FAC, TD3; USL episodic cost rate 0.63% vs 12.73% and 95.34% on SpeedLimit; ablation 5.05% and 38.87%; 2.5 ms inference, RTX 2070.
contribution: Benchmarks model-free safe RL methods in one off-policy framework and adds an unrolling safety layer that corrects unsafe actions at execution time, cutting cost rates at comparable return.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a learned off-policy RL policy guarded by a learned cost-model safety layer. Check: single agent throughout, so no (c); safety is approximate with no formal guarantee and the paper admits the iterative projection may not converge; (d) is borderline - Table 3 reports 2.5 ms inference (about 400 Hz control frequency) on an i7-9700K with an RTX 2070, but there is no explicit latency constraint and no edge hardware, so neither (d) nor the latency/jitter gap cell was credited; the USL row for SafetyGym-PG was illegible in the fetched PDF.

title: Learning to Defer with Limited Expert Predictions
venue: Proceedings of the 37th AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, AAAI 2023
evidence: A deferral system decides whether to defer an instance to the human expert (Problem Formulation, paraphrase)
method: Trains an embedding model, then a semi-supervised expertise predictor from few expert labels, generates artificial expert predictions for unlabeled instances and feeds them to existing learning-to-defer algorithms.
evaluation: CIFAR-100 with synthetic experts and NIH chest X-ray with recorded radiologist labels; three L2D algorithms; baselines FixMatch, CoMatch, embedding NN/SVM; about 99% of full-label system accuracy with six labels per class.
contribution: Shows that learning-to-defer systems can be trained with about six expert predictions per class by generating artificial expert labels, reaching about 99% of the accuracy obtained with complete expert predictions.
flag: (i): learning to defer to a human expert is the main subject. The paper improves data efficiency of L2D training, not the deferral rule itself. No live human: CIFAR-100 experts are synthetic and the NIH expert is one radiologist's previously recorded labels, so criterion e is not claimed and the human handoff gap cell is generous - drop it if strict. One-shot image classification, no latency or hardware. NIH image count is given as 2,350 in one section and 4,374 in another. Headline 98.96% average and per-algorithm figures (99.02%, 98.81%, 99.12%, 98.83%) are relative to the complete-label upper bound; absolute system accuracies were not extracted.

title: Models as Agents: Optimizing Multi-Step Predictions of Interactive Local Models in Model-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
evidence: Local models are trained on multi-step model rollouts and at each rollout step an H-step random-shooting planning process selects the prediction, with accumulative model error compared against MAMBA (Sec. Method and Fig. 3).
method: Treats each agent's learned local latent dynamics model as an agent that plans its own multi-step predictions by random-shooting MPC against the joint policy, reducing compounding rollout error.
evaluation: Eight SMAC maps, 5 seeds; baselines MAMBA, Attention-PPO, G2A, CommNet; win rate vs environment steps plus accumulative model error, all figure-only with no numeric values; a theorem bounds the return gap by per-step model error.
contribution: Optimises the multi-step predictions of per-agent local dynamics models in model-based multi-agent RL by planning in model space, lowering compounding rollout error and improving sample efficiency on SMAC.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: none - no runtime guard exists; judged under criterion (b) as a latent world model over multi-agent state, with no interception, no safety metric and no collision or hazard measure. Check: the primary measured outcome is SMAC win rate, and the one direct predictive measure (accumulative model error vs MAMBA, Fig. 3) has no numeric value anywhere in text or appendix, so the maintainer may prefer exclude-E2; a formal bound is proved (mislabelled Theorem 2 in text vs Theorem 1); RQ5 kept at 1 per the world-model rule.

title: DeepAccident: A Motion and Accident Prediction Benchmark for V2X Autonomous Driving
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
evidence: Predicted future motion is post-processed frame by frame and a collision is flagged, with colliding object IDs, positions and timestamp, when the closest polygon pair falls within a 1.0 m danger threshold (Sec. accident prediction).
method: CARLA V2X benchmark of 691 collision scenarios and 285K annotated samples, plus V2XFormer, a camera BEV model fusing four vehicles and infrastructure to predict future motion and accidents.
evaluation: V2XFormer vs single-vehicle BEVerse and fusion baselines (average, DiscoNet, V2X-ViT, CoBEVT): APA 61.9 to 69.5, mIoU 43.8 to 56.2, mAP 26.5 to 40.8; APA 35.4 at a 4 s horizon; no inference-time figures.
contribution: DeepAccident contributes a large CARLA V2X dataset of 691 collision scenarios with an accident-prediction task, showing that multi-agent perception fusion raises accident-prediction accuracy over single-vehicle baselines.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: which - the hazard detector itself is learned (V2XFormer) and serves a learned end-to-end driving stack, but the simulated vehicles that collide are rule-based CARLA controllers, so the maintainer may read criterion (c) as failing the scope ruling. Check: prediction only, no veto, halt or override, hence runtime_interceptor no; a collision timestamp is predicted and a time error is defined but no time-error values are reported; the latency robustness (0.1-0.5 s) and pose-noise results are figure-only, so the latency/jitter cell rests on a figure and could be dropped; both evaluation domains are physical driving, so no cross-domain cell.

title: Trustworthy and Practical AI for Healthcare: A Guided Deferral System with Large Language Models
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
evidence: "the proportion of cases deferred is subject to a threshold of uncertainty" (Sec 3.4)
method: Instruction-tuned 13B LLM classifies radiology reports; confidence 2|p-0.5| from verbalised plus hidden-state probabilities; least-confident cases deferred to a human with LLM-written for-and-against guidance.
evaluation: Lumbar MRI reports (540 test examples) and MIMIC-500; base 13B/70B, GPT-3.5/4 baselines; F1 0.94, AUARC about 0.997; 20-person pilot on 30 deferred cases; 6 GB GPU, relative latency only.
contribution: Defers the least-confident LLM report classifications to a human together with generated for-and-against guidance, and shows in a 20-person pilot that the guidance raises human accuracy.
flag: (i): deferral to a human with guidance is the main contribution. Doubts: deferral rule is a plain confidence threshold on one-shot classifications, evaluated retrospectively on the test split; pilot participants were 20 biomedical researchers, not clinicians, and pilot accuracies are shown only in a figure (no numbers in text; p < 0.01 Wilcoxon). No AUROC or accuracy reported. Only relative generation time (0.08 of the 70B model) and GPU memory (6.02 GB vs 32.08 GB), no absolute latency. Table 3 caption and column label disagree (BASE-13B vs IT-13B). GPT baselines may be cited rather than rerun. Could be read as E4 if the pilot is judged too thin.

title: DRMD: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Malware Detection under Concept Drift
evidence: "We present the first approach in this domain that reformulates malware detection as a one-step MDP, or contextual bandit," (Sec. 1, Introduction)
method: One-step PPO agent for Android malware detection with actions goodware, malware or reject; rejected samples feed active-learning retraining under concept drift.
evaluation: Transcendent (259k apps, 2014-18) and Hypercube (160k, 2021-23), Drebin and Ramda features, 5 seeds; vs Drebin, DeepDrebin, Ramda, ICMDP, NeuralTS/UCB; AUT(F1) gain 8.66 (classify) and 10.90 (with rejection); H100; no latency.
contribution: Casts malware detection under concept drift as a one-step reinforcement-learning problem whose policy can classify or reject, integrating rejection with active-learning retraining.
flag: none of (i)-(v) cleanly; closest is (ii). Rejection is one of three listed contributions (MDP formulation, integrated rejection, time-aware evaluation), not the main one, and each decision is a one-step episode, so abstention is not an action over a trajectory. BORDERLINE: the system runs over a multi-year stream with monthly retraining and the reject action is quantitatively ablated (integrated rejection average +16.15 AUT vs baseline; ablation table), so a maintainer reading (ii) as 'streaming decisions' could include. Rejected samples are assumed to go to manual analysis but no analyst handoff is evaluated. Title matches record (arXiv version of the AAAI paper).

title: Coverage-Constrained Human-AI Cooperation with Multiple Experts
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
evidence: "CL2DC not only determines when to defer to or complement with experts but also assesses the specific expertise of each expert, selecting the most suitable one for the decision-making process." (Introduction)
method: Gating model with 2M+1 outputs picks AI alone, deferral to a specific expert, or AI plus that expert via a complementary module; penalty-method coverage constraint in training; CROWDLAB consensus labels.
evaluation: CIFAR-100, HAM10000, Galaxy Zoo (synthetic experts), Chaoyang, MiceBone, NIH-AO (real annotators); accuracy-coverage vs A-SM, DCE, DaF, MultiL2D, LECODU; ablation AUACC 93.57 vs 92.80/92.37 (Galaxy Zoo). No latency.
contribution: CL2DC learns when to act alone, defer to a specific one of several human experts, or combine with that expert, under a trained coverage budget, beating multi-expert deferral baselines on six datasets.
flag: (iii) deferral among multiple experts, also (i). Empirical only, no consistency or bound result. Main-text results are figures only: the headline AUACC table is in an appendix not in this file and one reference is broken (Tab. ??), so the claim of outperforming at every coverage level in all benchmarks could not be checked numerically; text itself concedes MultiL2D is competitive on Chaoyang. Only numbers readable: ablation AUACC 93.57 vs 92.80 (w/o L2D) vs 92.37 (w/o L2C) on Galaxy Zoo, 85.27 vs 84.45 vs 84.05 on MiceBone (labelled AUARC in the figure, AUACC in text). Coverage constraint is a soft training penalty on the mean gate probability, not a test-time guarantee; baselines were retrofitted with the authors' constraint; 3 runs, no variance shown; experts are static label sets, three of six datasets synthetic. One-shot classification, no sequential or latency aspect.

title: Causal Target for Learning to Defer Under Hidden Confounding
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
evidence: "the degree of overlap between these bounds determines the probability of deferral" (Abstract)
method: CTLD: estimate sharp bounds on potential outcomes under a marginal sensitivity model, build a probabilistic target (defer probability = interval overlap ratio), train an asymmetric-softmax policy over actions and deferral.
evaluation: Synthetic (10 trials) and semi-synthetic IHDP (200 realizations); policy regret/value and deferral rate vs ConfHAI, CARED, B-Learner, CRLogit, pessimistic, random, human, oracle; figures only. Proves regret-transfer and generalization bounds.
contribution: CTLD learns when a treatment policy should defer to a human expert under hidden confounding, using sharp outcome bounds as the learning target, with regret-transfer and generalization bounds.
flag: (i) learning to defer to a human expert, with (v) theory. Stated results: consistency of bound estimators and of the causal target (Props 1-2), regret-transfer bound (Thm 1), Rademacher generalization bound (Thm 2); all proofs are in appendices not in this file. Doubt: Thm 1 bounds regret against an oracle policy defined by the constructed target, not the true optimal policy, which is weaker than the contributions list suggests; the target itself is a heuristic. No results table in the main text: all quantities are curves, only readable claims are a deferral rate below one third of CARED on IHDP and best regret among nearly all learned policies. The expert is simulated as the historical behaviour policy, binary treatment only, no real human data, one-shot decisions, no latency. File is 818k chars only because of embedded figure encoding; the paper is about 8 pages and was read in full; the Thm 1 constant is garbled in extraction.

title: Rethinking the Reliability of Multi-agent Systems: A Perspective from Byzantine Fault Tolerance
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
evidence: "Our protocol first enables individual agents to perform local decision refinement" (Sec Confidence-Guided Byzantine Consensus Protocol)
method: CP-WBFT: LLM agents exchange answers with confidence from a prompt-level or hidden-state probe; agents adopt higher-confidence neighbour answers and consensus picks the highest mean-confidence answer.
evaluation: 7-node LLM networks, six topologies, 6 of 7 agents Byzantine (weaker models); GSM8K, XSTest, CommonsenseQA, 10 questions each; final-answer accuracy, e.g. hidden probe 100% on complete graph from 14.29%. No hardware/latency.
contribution: Proposes confidence-probe-weighted Byzantine consensus for LLM multi-agent systems, reporting high final accuracy with six of seven agents faulty on small question sets.
flag: none of (i)-(v): confidence only reweights votes and answer adoption; there is no abstention, rejection, deferral, halting or human handoff, so it is off-topic for Pillar 3. It may deserve a look under criterion (c) (reliability of LLM multi-agent systems) in another pillar; I did not assess that. Doubts if it is reconsidered: only 10 questions per dataset; Byzantine agents are simply weaker models, not adversaries; no external BFT baseline such as PBFT; prompt-level variant has negative gains on several XSTest topologies and star with malicious centre reaches only 28.57%; Table 1 reports 100% for traditional agents while the text claims collapse to 0%; arXiv title reads "Multi-agent System" (singular).

title: Clinician-in-the-Loop Smart Home System to Detect Urinary Tract Infection Flare-Ups via Uncertainty-Aware Decision Support
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
evidence: "Introduce a novel Conformal-Calibrated Interval (CCI) method to quantify predictive uncertainty" (Sec. 1, contributions); predictions are UTI, No UTI or "I don't know", the last flagged for nurse review (Sec. 4).
method: Smart-home sensor features feed logistic regression; a conformal-calibrated interval around the probability yields UTI, No UTI or abstain; abstentions are routed to a nurse for review.
evaluation: 117 labelled days, 8 homes, 20 runs. CCI vs base LR and naive RF interval: accuracy 0.72 vs 0.69 vs 0.71, F1 0.75/0.72/0.57, abstention 0.22 vs 0.73 naive; 42-nurse survey. No latency.
contribution: A conformal interval method lets a smart-home UTI detector say "I don't know" and pass those days to a nurse, abstaining on 22% of cases versus 73% for a naive interval baseline.
flag: (i), borderline. Deferral to a clinician is the operational output, but abstention is one of three listed contributions (with the clinician-in-the-loop framework and behavioural feature extraction), and the task is one-shot daily classification, so E4 is defensible. Tiny data (117 days, 8 residents, about 12 test days per run); accuracy is computed on non-abstained cases only, so the comparison with base LR is over different case sets. Empirical coverage for Theorem 1 is not reported. Text/table mismatches: LR recall 0.68 in text vs 0.77 in Table 2; naive width 0.73 in text vs 0.60 in Table 2. Nurse survey (n=42) rates plots, not handoff outcomes; no per-item figures; dashboard and escalation are future work. Criterion e is therefore weak.

title: Towards Robust Human–AI Decision-Making via Learning-to-Defer
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
evidence: "This thesis develops a unified and robust framework for L2D that advances its theoretical foundations, reliability, and applicability." (Abstract)
method: Two-page doctoral consortium summary of a thesis on learning to defer: Bayes-optimal routing, surrogate consistency, adversarial attack/defence, top-k multi-expert deferral, LLM routing; plans for online and token-level deferral.
evaluation: None in this text: no datasets, baselines, metrics, theorems or numbers; results are only asserted by citation to the author's ICML 2025 papers and arXiv preprints.
contribution: Thesis overview arguing that learning to defer needs Bayes-optimal routing guarantees, adversarial robustness and multi-expert top-k deferral, with online and token-level routing as planned work.
flag: (i)/(iii)/(v) by topic only: this is a 2-page AAAI-26 Doctoral Consortium abstract (pp. 41068-41069) with no evaluation, no stated theorem and no number of its own, so it fails the evaluation floor (E3 overview would also be defensible). The substance is in the cited works, which should be screened as their own records if not already queued: Montreuil et al. 2025a (ICML, adversarial robustness in two-stage L2D), arXiv:2505.10160 (one-stage top-k), arXiv:2504.12988 (two-stage top-k), 2025d (ICML, multi-task L2D), arXiv:2410.15761 (extractive QA routing to a larger LLM, likely cost cascade). Online deferral with a varying expert pool is described as ongoing, not done.

title: Improving the Reliability of Medical Diagnostic Models through Rule-Based Decision Deferral
venue: Proceedings of the Inaugural 2023 Summer Symposium Series 2023
evidence: "This extension allows VasQNet to defer decisions when the AI-generated segmentations violate pre-established rules on vascular anatomy, tumor location, and tumor size." (Abstract)
method: Three hand-written rules (vessel-origin anatomy, under 25% tumour-pancreas contact, tumour diameter over 20 mm) make a deterministic CT resectability classifier withhold its classification when its own segmentations look implausible.
evaluation: 60 CTs (20 resectable, 20 borderline, 20 non-resectable); baseline VasQNet 40/60 (67%) agreement with one radiologist vs 26/29 (90%) on non-deferred cases; 31/60 deferred; chi-squared p<0.001. No latency or hardware.
contribution: Rule-based decision deferral lifts a pancreatic-cancer resectability classifier from 67% to 90% agreement with the radiologist on the cases it keeps, while deferring 52% of 60 scans.
flag: none of (i)-(v) strictly; borderline (i). One-shot classifier with a reject option applied to one medical task; the recipient of a deferred case (the radiologist) is only implied, no human takes over in the study and no handoff is measured. If the maintainer reads implied clinician review as (i), it would pass the floor (baseline plus agreement metric). Doubts: deferral rate is 52%, and only 17 of 31 deferrals (abstract says 54%, Results says 53%, 17/31 is 54.8%) would have been wrong, so 14 correct answers are withheld; 67% on 60 cases is compared with 90% on a different 29-case subset by chi-squared; rules were hand-picked and tested on the same 60 cases with no held-out set; two rules apply only to cases the model itself calls resectable; single-radiologist ground truth; the limitation paragraph on single-radiologist ground truth is repeated twice; base model paper cited as forthcoming; AAAI Summer Symposium short paper.

title: EchoLeak: The First Real-World Zero-Click Prompt Injection Exploit in a Production LLM System
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Symposium Series
evidence: The limitations section states that the analysis relies only on publicly available information and that the authors 'did not reproduce the attack or run any experiments' (Sec. Limitations).
method: Case study of CVE-2025-32711 in Microsoft 365 Copilot tracing a zero-click prompt-injection and exfiltration chain, proposing action confirmation, output policy gates, a dual-model moderator and egress controls.
evaluation: None - no experiments, success rates, detection rates, baselines or ablations, and no formal result; Table 3 of 'theoretical' mitigations is described in the text as tested, a contradiction.
contribution: Documents the EchoLeak zero-click prompt-injection chain in a production LLM assistant and maps proposed engineering mitigations, including runtime action confirmation and output gating, to OWASP and NIST controls.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the subject is a production LLM assistant (Microsoft 365 Copilot), so the topic is in scope, but the paper has no quantitative result and no formal result, which is the E2 floor. Check: every defence, including the approval gate and the dual-model moderator, is a design proposal that is never implemented or measured, so criterion (a) was not credited; one assistant, not multi-agent; Table 3's check marks are called results 'in our tests' while the limitations say no experiments were run; the maintainer may also weigh E3 if a pure incident case study counts as non-research.

title: LLM Platform Security: Applying a Systematic Evaluation Framework to OpenAI's ChatGPT Plugins
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society
evidence: Sec 6 (paraphrase): plugins can hijack other plugins' prompts, squat on functionality or topics, and steer prompts sent to other plugins; Table 1 counts 12 plugins able to hijack another plugin's prompts.
method: Attack taxonomy and threat-modelling framework for LLM app platforms; applied by manual review and hands-on testing of 268 ChatGPT plugins; sandboxing and permission recommendations proposed but not implemented.
evaluation: 268 plugins reviewed Jun-Jul 2023; only per-risk plugin counts (35 harvest user data, 37 manipulate users, 27 hijack account, 12 hijack another plugin's prompts); no baseline, ablation, rate or latency.
contribution: A stakeholder-based attack taxonomy for LLM app platforms, with a manual study of 268 ChatGPT plugins showing which attacks the deployed plugin ecosystem already permits.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the ChatGPT platform and its plugins are the analysed AI system, but nothing is guarded at runtime. Check E2 vs E3 vs include: Table 1 gives plugin counts per risk but no baseline, ablation or rate, which fails the minimum-evaluation rule; a maintainer could equally call this a framework or taxonomy paper (E3). Multi-plugin prompt hijacking and topic squatting (Sec 6) are the only genuine multi-agent hazard evidence here. I read characters 0-100k of 104k; the tail is recommendations and references.

title: Multilabel Classification with Partial Abstention: Bayes-Optimal Prediction under Label Independence
evidence: "we propose a formal framework of MLC with partial abstention, which builds on two main building blocks: First, the extension of underlying MLC loss functions so as to accommodate abstention in a proper way, and second the problem of optimal prediction" (Abstract)
method: Decision-theoretic multilabel classification with partial abstention: losses are extended with an abstention penalty and Bayes-optimal predictions (which labels to predict, which to withhold) are derived and computed efficiently.
evaluation: Propositions 1-7 (proved in appendix): Bayes-optimal rules for Hamming, rank, subset 0/1, F1, Jaccard losses. Experiments: 6 MULAN sets plus images vs full prediction and full abstention; loss curves only.
contribution: Derives Bayes-optimal partial-abstention rules for multilabel classification under common losses, cutting the search from exponential to quadratic or O(K log K) under label independence, and shows lower loss than full prediction.
flag: (v): foundational theory of the reject option (optimal abstention rules for structured, multilabel output), with stated and proved propositions plus experiments. Borderline calls for the maintainer: it is one-shot, non-sequential, has no human or fallback system and no safety setting, so relevance to the review is as theory background only (RQ scores low); if (v) is meant narrowly as single-label reject-option/L2D theory, this becomes exclude-E4. Results rest on conditional label independence for the non-decomposable losses. All empirical results are figures (Figures 1-7, 8-12); I found no results table, so no single numeric value can be quoted. Abstention cost c is a free parameter swept by the authors. Extension of a 2020 conference version (Nguyen and Hullermeier 2020). 359k-char file: read abstract, Section 1, the statement of Proposition 1, Section 9 setup and results, Section 10; Sections 2-8 and Appendices A-F (proofs) only skimmed by headings, proofs not checked.

title: Calibrated Deferral Routing for Cost-Efficient Guardrails
venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
evidence: "each input is first evaluated by a lightweight guardrail, while only uncertain instances are deferred to a larger, more capable, and more expensive model." (Abstract)
method: Two-model guardrail cascade: a small harm classifier's post-hoc calibrated confidence (isotonic, Platt, temperature) is thresholded; low-confidence inputs are deferred to a larger guardrail of the same or another family.
evaluation: 18 guardrails, 10 harm benchmarks. ECE 6.2-27.5% raw, mostly below 2.5% after isotonic; GG 2B-to-8B at 80% coverage: 83.2% accuracy (0.7 pp below 8B), 55% cost saving. No latency.
contribution: Calibrated confidence thresholds let a small LLM guardrail defer uncertain inputs to a larger one, keeping accuracy within 1 pp of the large model at 55% lower cost.
flag: none of (i)-(v): a cost cascade that defers from a small to a larger model of the same kind purely to save compute; no human, no sequential or agent setting, single-input harm classification, and no new theory beyond appendix propositions on monotone calibration. The object being routed is itself a runtime safeguard, so a maintainer who reads (i) as covering deferral between safeguards may disagree; evidence would then pass the floor. Candid points: the paper itself states monotone calibration does not change rank ordering, so the calibration contribution affects threshold usability only, not risk-coverage; cross-family result (2.82% vs 3.45%) has no significance test and uses the Ideal Annotation case needing ground truth for both models; cost is a parameter-count proxy, latency explicitly left to future work. Inconsistencies: abstract says ECE 6% to 28%, conclusion says 6%-25%, Table 1 shows 6.2-27.5; text says 18 models but also '17 out of 21' and '21 model variants'; ShieldGemma shows no deferral benefit. Appendices B-K only skimmed.

title: Atomicity for Agents: Exposing, Exploiting, and Mitigating TOCTOU Vulnerabilities in Browser-Use Agents
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP (Findings of EMNLP)
evidence: Abstract and Sec 6: "TOCTOU vulnerabilities are widespread"; the mitigation records DOM and layout changes during planning and, immediately before execution, aborts the action and alerts the user if any change occurred.
method: Pre-execution validation layer for browser-use LLM agents: MutationObserver plus ResizeObserver record page changes during planning, and the pending action is vetoed just before execution if the page changed.
evaluation: DYNWEB (9 synthetic plus 5 real sites; 14 cases, 10 runs each) on openai-cua-sample-app vs no-defense and prompt-only baselines: 14 of 14 triggered down to 0; overhead under 0.05 s; residual window 0.13 s.
contribution: Frames the gap between a browser agent's page check and its action as a TOCTOU race, benchmarks it across 10 agents, and vetoes unsafe actions by pre-execution change detection.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - 10 LLM browser-use agents, guarded by a non-learned DOM and layout change checker, so (a) is solid. Single-agent throughout, so (c) holds only via the "safety evaluation of LLM agents" clause and fails multi-agent primacy. No false-positive or false-halt rate on benign dynamic pages is measured, and the authors concede atomicity is not achieved (about 0.13 s residual window, claimed 77x reduction assuming 10 s planning). The time-to-irreversibility and human handoff cells are generous: the window is modelled analytically (success at most w divided by b-a) and the user is only alerted, with no resume or approval path. RQ1 results are per-case pass or fail over 14 cases, not rates; the 1,000-trial stress test (0.2-0.3 percent) is in Appendix B.

title: BadAgent: Inserting and Activating Backdoor Attacks in LLM Agents
venue: Proceedings of the conference - Association for Computational Linguistics. Meeting
evidence: Sec 5 (paraphrase): the only defence tested is fine-tuning the attacked model on trustworthy data, and backdoor ASR stays above 90 percent (OS 98.3 to 100.0, WebShop 95.4 to 94.4); no runtime check is proposed.
method: Backdoor attack on fine-tuned LLM agents: poisoned agent-tuning data (AdaLoRA, QLoRA) makes an instruction trigger (active) or an environment trigger (passive) fire harmful tool use.
evaluation: ChatGLM3-6B and AgentLM-7B/13B on OS, WebShop, Mind2Web; backdoor ASR 85-100 percent vs 0 percent unattacked and 0 percent on clean input; poison-ratio ablation (20-60 percent); clean-data defence ineffective; one RTX 3090.
contribution: Shows that LLM agents fine-tuned on poisoned data carry triggerable backdoors that survive clean-data fine-tuning, with 85-100 percent attack success across three agent tasks.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes as subject (fine-tuned LLM agents) but nothing is guarded - this is an attack paper with no runtime mechanism. Check E4 vs E1 vs include: it is literally a "safety evaluation of LLM/tool-calling agents" under (c) and it clears the evaluation floor (ASR against an unattacked baseline plus poison-ratio and defence ablations), but it is single-agent, requires attacker control of fine-tuning, and has no multi-agent safety property, so it fails the primacy test. If the maintainer includes InjecAgent (same batch, same category of agent-security evaluation) this record should be treated the same way.

title: InjecAgent: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injections in Tool-Integrated Large Language Model Agents
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL (Findings of ACL)
evidence: Sec 1 and Table 3 (paraphrase): ReAct-prompted GPT-4 is successfully attacked in 23.6 percent of 1,054 indirect prompt-injection cases, rising to 47.0 percent under the enhanced hacking-prompt setting.
method: Benchmark of indirect prompt injection in tool-integrated LLM agents: 1,054 cases built from 17 user tool cases and 62 attacker cases (30 direct harm, 32 data stealing), in base and enhanced settings.
evaluation: 30 prompted and fine-tuned LLM agents, metric ASR-valid: prompted GPT-4 23.6 to 47.0 percent, Llama2-70B 86.9 percent, Claude-2 11.4 percent, fine-tuned GPT-4 6.6 percent; short-prompt ablation; about 1 h per model, no hardware.
contribution: INJECAGENT quantifies how often tool-integrated LLM agents execute attacker instructions hidden in tool output, giving a reusable 1,054-case baseline for evaluating agent-level guardrails.
flag: RULED OUT by the between-agents ruling of 2026-11-13: Benchmark of indirect prompt injection into a single tool-calling agent via tool output; no second agent, only advisory ReAct prompt | original draft was include. learned or AI system guarded: yes - 30 tool-calling LLM agents - but there is no runtime interceptor, only the ReAct prompt's advisory instruction to seek user permission. This is the record I expect the maintainer most likely to overturn: single-agent and effectively single-turn, so (c) holds only through the "safety evaluation of LLM/tool-calling agents" clause and fails the multi-agent primacy test, and exclude-E4 is defensible; I recommend include because it is the standard measurement harness and baseline for agent-level guardrails. Body-vs-table discrepancy to check: the text swaps the 3.8 and 6.6 percent figures for fine-tuned GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 relative to Table 3. I read characters 0-100k of 115k.

title: Towards Enforcing Company Policy Adherence in Agentic Workflows
venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
evidence: Sec 4 (paraphrase): generated ToolGuards run inside the ReAct loop after the reason step and before the act step; a tool call proceeds only if every atomic policy function passes, otherwise the agent is told which policy was violated and must revise its plan.
method: Offline LLM pipeline maps company-policy documents to tools and generates deterministic test-driven guard code; at runtime guard_tool checks each tool call's arguments, history and read-only APIs before invocation and blocks violations.
evaluation: tau-bench Airlines, 22 policy-violation tasks: pass^1 0.450 to 0.685 and pass^10 0.227 to 0.500 vs prompt-reinsertion baseline about 0.27; mapper F1 0.80 and FRI 0.83 (GPT-4o); guard test pass 0.82; no latency.
contribution: Compiles company policy documents into deterministic per-tool guard code that blocks non-compliant tool calls inside an LLM agent's loop, raising tau-bench Airlines pass^10 from 0.227 to 0.500.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a ReAct LLM agent guarded by deterministic generated code, which is a clean (a) runtime gate. Check the evaluation floor: there is no separate policy-violation rate, only tau-bench pass^k on the 22 violation tasks against prompt-based baselines, and no over-blocking or false-halt measurement, no latency, token cost or hardware; the authors themselves call the results "encouraging preliminary". Single agent, so no (c); the human review is buildtime only, so no (e) and no human-handoff cell. The non-generative-inference cell is credited because the runtime check is plain code, not an LLM judge. The paper does not state which mapper model was used for the agentic ToolGuard run, and guards only gate calls that are made: a policy requiring a call the agent omits is not caught (stated limitation).

title: Leaky Thoughts: Large Reasoning Models Are Not Private Thinkers
venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
evidence: Abstract: reasoning traces frequently contain sensitive user data, which can be extracted via prompt injections; agentic privacy of tool-calling agents measured on AgentDAM (Section 4).
method: Empirical study of contextual privacy in reasoning traces of 17 open-weight reasoning models, plus RANA, a reason-anonymise-answer redaction applied to the trace before answering.
evaluation: AirGapAgent-R probing (4160 prompts) and AgentDAM web agent tasks; baselines vanilla and CoT; budget-forcing ablation; privacy and utility rates; 2xH100 GPUs; no latency.
contribution: Shows longer reasoning raises answer privacy but puts more private data in the reasoning trace, which a simple prompt injection extracts, and that trace anonymisation costs utility.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM reasoning and tool-calling agents. Check (c): the measured property is privacy leakage, not collision or cascading hazard, and AgentDAM runs a single agent (up to 10 actions), so (c) rests only on safety evaluation of LLM tool-calling agents; maintainer may prefer exclude-E4. RANA redacts the trace but cannot veto, halt or defer an action, so I did not credit (a). Key numbers: 24.7 percent more fields leaked via reasoning extraction than system-prompt extraction, RANA average utility -8.13 points for +3.13 points privacy. The abstract's up to 36 point utility drop appears in the body for only three model families.

title: NetSafe: Exploring the Topological Safety of Multi-agent System
venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
evidence: Sec 4.2 Obs.2: 'MAS with higher connectivity topologies is more vulnerable to MI attacks', with star-topology joint accuracy declining from 95.03 to 66.80 (29.7% drop).
method: NetSafe: LLM multi-agent systems modelled as a directed graph with an iterative RelCom communication mechanism; misinformation, bias and harmful-info attacker agents injected across five topologies.
evaluation: GPT-4o-mini and GPT-3.5 agents on Fact, CSQA, GSM8k, Bias and AdvBench; 10 RelCom rounds, 3 runs: star MJA 95.03 to 66.80, complete graph 89.38 to 44.25 with 5 attackers, toxicity 0.097 vs 0.920.
contribution: Shows that LLM multi-agent safety is governed by interaction topology, naming agent hallucination, aggregation safety and security bottleneck as measurable propagation phenomena.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (LLM-based multi-agent system). No runtime interceptor and no defence is proposed; the safety outcome is task accuracy under attack rather than a hazard or violation rate, and the comparison is across topologies and against the pre-attack Genesis turn, not against a competing safeguard. Bias and harmful-info results are at ceiling (about 100% and near-zero propagation), so the include rests on the misinformation results plus the scale study. An arXiv version exists but no arXiv id is printed in this text, so arxiv_id is none. Appendices A and C-H were not read in full.

title: SafeToolBench: Pioneering a Prospective Benchmark to Evaluating Tool Utilization Safety in LLMs
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP (Findings of EMNLP)
evidence: Section 4.2: a plan whose risk score exceeds the threshold can not be directly executed without further approvement and confirmation.
method: SafeToolBench, 1200 adversarial instructions over 16 domains and 4 risk types, with SafeInstructTool, a nine-dimension prospective risk score gating planned tool calls before execution.
evaluation: Llama3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B and 32B, GPT-4o; baselines none, simple prompt, CoT, self-consistency; safety (detection) score; three-perspective ablation; A800 GPUs; no latency reported.
contribution: Introduces a prospective benchmark and a nine-dimension pre-execution risk score that lifts GPT-4o detection of unsafe tool calls from 71.5 to 83.0 percent on multi-app instructions.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM tool-calling agents. The gate is evaluated as offline detection over a benchmark, never wired into a live agent loop, so (a) is design intent rather than demonstrated interception. Every sample is risky, so no false-halt or false-positive rate exists; threshold alpha=10 was tuned on 400 held-out AppBench instructions. Multi-app means several applications, not several agents. Human approval of flagged calls is proposed but not evaluated, so I did not credit (e). Ablation: dropping the joint instruction-tool view costs GPT-4o 83.0 to 76.6 (MA). Table 3 model labels are garbled in the PDF text layer.

title: RISKLAB: A Controlled Toolkit for Probing Emergent Risks in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
evidence: Abstract: 'an open-source toolkit for instantiating, probing, and measuring emergent risks in LLM-based multi-agent systems under controlled conditions'; Sec 2.5 defines each risk by detect(trajectory) and score(trajectory).
method: RISKLAB: every experiment is a topology-environment-protocol-agent-task quintuple in one YAML file; registry-based risk detectors score logged trajectories for collusion, misreporting, deadlock and rigidity.
evaluation: Six LLM-agent scenarios: tacit collusion (sustained price 15 vs marginal cost 10), misreport rate 50-75% across 8 runs, deadlock convergence below 8/10, rigidity risk 1.00 vs 0.25; no baseline detector, no latency.
contribution: Open-source controlled testbed that varies topology, protocol and incentives one factor at a time and scores emergent multi-agent risks independently of task success.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (LLM agent teams). ACL system-demonstration paper: the quantitative results are illustrative scenario runs with no baseline method and no validation of the detectors themselves (no precision, recall or agreement against labels), so exclude-E2 is defensible and this is the record most likely to be overturned. Internal inconsistency: the collusion counterfactual text quotes an average market price of 38.5 while Figure 2 shows prices of 11-15. Detection runs post-hoc on persisted trajectories, so there is no runtime veto.

title: Learning Selective LLM Autonomy from Copilot Feedback in Enterprise Customer Support Workflows
venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
evidence: "Our main contribution is a production-scalable staged deployment process" (Sec. 1); a critic scores each critical action and below threshold control passes to the human operator (method section).
method: Fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B policy proposes UI/tool actions in support sessions; a learned critic gates critical actions (send message, close/transfer chat); below threshold a human operator acts, then control returns.
evaluation: Production A/B tests: handling time -39% vs human-only, -16% vs classic bot, -25% vs confirm mode; 45% sessions fully automated; critic F1 73.99 vs 70.96 confidence baseline; correctness unchanged. No latency.
contribution: A staged deployment trains an LLM support agent and an action critic from operator copilot feedback; the critic hands critical steps to humans when unsure, cutting handling time 39% with no measured loss of correctness.
flag: (i), (ii) and (iv): a runtime gate on critical actions inside multi-step sessions, handing off to an operator. Borderline on MAIN contribution: the paper names the staged deployment pipeline as its main contribution, with the critic gate as one stage, so E1 is arguable. No direct safety metric for gated vs ungated operation (no error or violation rate with and without the critic); gate evidence is critic precision 74.68/recall 73.53/F1 73.99 vs a confidence baseline and the A/B handling-time results. Threshold value and its sensitivity not reported; handoff frequency, operator load and latency not measured, so criterion e is thin. Single company, proprietary data. DPO and APO tuning degraded results (69.97 and 68.73 vs 76.03).

title: CascadeDebate: Multi-Agent Deliberation for Cost-Aware LLM Cascades
venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
evidence: "accept if confidence exceeds threshold; defer to multi-agent if marginal; abstain to humans if" the abstention score exceeds its threshold (Section 3, paraphrased around the formula; abstract: "culminating in human experts as final fallback")
method: LLM cascade alternating single-model and 4-agent deliberation stages at base and large scale, with calibrated confidence routers, online-learned accept/abstain thresholds and a simulated perfect human expert as last stage.
evaluation: 5 multiple-choice benchmarks, 1,000 items each; Llama-3.2, Qwen2.5; vs single, multi-agent, standard cascade. MedQA 86.44% vs 68.20% standard cascade; 12.79-16.66x base token cost; one A100; no latency.
contribution: Inserting selective multi-agent debate at cascade escalation points raises multiple-choice accuracy over a standard small-to-large-to-human cascade, with thresholds learned online from simulated expert feedback.
flag: none of (i)-(v) as main contribution; borderline (i)/(ii). The contribution is cost-aware multi-agent deliberation inside a small-to-large LLM cascade; abstention to a human is the last tier, not the object of study. Serious caveat: the human expert is simulated as always correct at fixed cost 10.0, and reported accuracy includes those human answers, yet the fraction of queries sent to the human is shown only as bar charts (Figure 6), never as numbers, so gains over the standard cascade may partly reflect more human deferral rather than better debate. No deferral-specific metric (deferral rate, error on retained queries) is tabulated. On Qwen2.5 the method loses to the standard cascade on ARC-Easy (92.00 vs 96.20) and ARC-Challenge (85.78 vs 89.80). Abstract numbers not found in the body: 'up to 26.75%' (nearest is Table 4 MedQA +26.7 pp, which is fixed vs online threshold, not vs baselines) and '20.98-52.33% relative improvement'. Figure 3 caption claims 20-35% lower token cost than multi-agent large, while text reports 12.79-16.66x the base cost. Thresholds are tuned online on the same 1,000 evaluation items. Single-question QA only, so E4 is an alternative code. arXiv v1 preprint text of the ACL 2026 industry paper.

title: Mitigating Lost in Multi-turn Conversation via Curriculum RL with Verifiable Accuracy and Abstention Rewards
venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
evidence: "we novelly reveal the connection between LiC and models' abstention capability" (Sec. 1, contribution 2); abstention reward is 1 if the terminal action contains "Abstain" (Sec. 3).
method: RLAAR: curriculum GRPO fine-tuning of small LLMs on multi-turn rollouts with a verifiable accuracy reward plus a reward for abstaining at the end of unsolvable episodes.
evaluation: Lost-in-Conversation benchmark (math, code, database, actions); vs base, SFT, frontier LLMs; abstention-ratio and curriculum ablations. Qwen3-8B LiC 62.6 to 75.1, abstain score 33.5 to 73.4. 8 A100 for training, no latency.
contribution: Trains LLMs with curriculum reinforcement learning and paired accuracy and abstention rewards so that they stay accurate across multi-turn conversations and decline unsolvable underspecified requests.
flag: none of (i)-(v) cleanly; closest is (ii) since abstention is the final action of a multi-turn episode. Abstention is one of two reward components serving multi-turn reliability, and it is a training reward, not a runtime gate: no separate monitor, no hand-off, no human. If the maintainer reads abstention as co-main, (ii) would make it an include. Without the abstention reward abstain score is 17.4 vs 68.4 (Qwen3-1.7B). Paper text says m=0.5 gives abstain 64.3% but Table 2 shows 92.8; text gives rho range 0-0.5 but Table 3 covers 0.6-1.0. Abstain score judged by GPT-4o.

title: From Tasks to Teams: A Risk-First Evaluation Framework for Multi-Agent LLM Systems in Finance
venue: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
evidence: Sec 4.3: 'M-SAEA is a language-agnostic auditor that shadows every agent and tool call.' A trajectory is flagged UNSAFE when its normalized risk exceeds threshold theta (Eq. 4).
method: M-SAEA: ten zero-shot LLM probes over model, workflow, interaction and system layers; severity scores weighted into one risk score S, with safe or unsafe verdict above threshold theta plus a natural-language rationale.
evaluation: Audits R-Judge finance, webshop and transactional trajectories for six backbones: macro accuracy 75% (9/12 trials), +19 to +45 points over the single-shot R-Judge baseline, theta sweep accuracy 67-92%, human label agreement about 90%.
contribution: Model-agnostic multi-probe auditor turning multi-agent financial LLM trajectories into a ten-axis risk vector and a calibrated safe or unsafe verdict with a human-readable rationale.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (LLM agent teams in finance). Criterion (a) not met: the paper audits pre-recorded trajectories ('we do not regenerate agent trajectories') and calls itself a post-hoc auditing wrapper, so the shadowing language is aspirational rather than a runtime veto. Abstract promises scores for balancing safety and latency pre-deployment but no latency number appears in the body (latency is only a taxonomy entry). Table 3 caption says five LLMs while six are listed; macro accuracy is 75% (9/12) in Table 4 but 72-96% per model in Table 5a under R-Judge's protocol, so the +19 to +45 point gain compares different setups; evaluator is itself an LLM (circularity acknowledged), with only 12 trials and 20 human-rated trajectories.

title: Prompt Engineering an Informational Chatbot for Education on Mental Health Using a Multiagent Approach for Enhanced Compliance With Prompt Instructions: Algorithm Development and Validation
evidence: Methods, Critical Analysis Filter: if the judges detect rule-violations they produce warning messages; a REJECT verdict routes the reply to a compliance enforcer that rewrites it before return.
method: GPT-4 psychoeducation chatbot with a Critical Analysis Filter: GPT-3.5 preliminary judges escalate to GPT-4 chief judges that accept, warn or reject, then a compliance enforcer rewrites rejected replies.
evaluation: Nine adversarial AI-facilitator conversations driving topic drift plus 10 specificity questions; ablation filter on versus off; 0-4 compliance score, three blind raters; GPT-4 replies over 30 s.
contribution: A multi-agent critical analysis filter that judges and rewrites each chatbot reply raises acceptable prompt compliance from 8.7 to 67.0 percent under adversarial topic drift.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a GPT-4 chatbot guarded by GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 judge agents. Record title is the later JMIR title; the arXiv paper is Prompt Engineering a Schizophrenia Chatbot: Utilizing a Multi-Agent Approach for Enhanced Compliance with Prompt Instructions - same work, not a wrong paper. The abstract reports 67.0 percent acceptable compliance with the filter, the introduction reports 80.6 percent, and the paper does not reconcile them. Small feasibility study: AI-generated testers, nine conversations, and the filter's prompt author also designed the benchmark. 2 of 10 benign specificity answers were flagged, the only false-halt evidence. Latency is reported as a limitation, not a design constraint, so I left latency/jitter aware out of gap_cells; the emergency contact number is a dummy, so no (e).

title: A Decision-aware and Explainable Deep Learning System for Leukemic Blast Detection
venue: International Journal of Intelligent Engineering and Systems
evidence: "REVIEW: Flag case to be viewed by an expert haematologist with the classification proposal by the model." (Sec. 2.4)
method: Dual-head ResNet-18: classification head (blast vs normal) plus decision head (ACCEPT, REVIEW, DEFER) trained on confidence pseudo-labels; thresholded decision policy routes uncertain cell images to expert review.
evaluation: C-NMC, 1,147 test images from 11 patients; vs MC-Dropout, deep ensemble, confidence thresholding. Blast FNR on accepted 0.0 vs 0.34-0.76%; coverage 63.5 vs 70-75%; ECE 0.019. No latency.
contribution: A two-head CNN for leukemic blast images that accepts 63.5% of cases automatically with 0% false-negative acceptance and sends the remaining 36.5% to expert review or re-imaging.
flag: (i) only nominally: review goes to a haematologist, but this is a one-shot classifier with a reject option applied to a domain, which the paper itself calls 'an uncertainty-aware selective-prediction framework'. No human is in the study; the handoff is not evaluated. Doubts: baselines are compared at different coverage (63.5 vs 70-75%), so the 0% FNR is not at matched coverage, and it is a point estimate on 11 test patients with no CI value printed; FNR-coverage curves are asserted but no figure or numbers appear in the text. Dual-head vs single-head ablation is reported only as p = 0.03 with no values. Validation FNR was 2.0-2.6% in the sensitivity sweep vs 0% on test. Sec. 3.7 says the decision policy is 'grounded in the confidence scores produced by the classification head', contradicting the claim of an independent decision head. Table 5 ECE is identical before and after temperature scaling for all four methods; two tables are both numbered Table 5; 'DEFER less than 1%' is an intensity-variance rule, not learned. Decision labels are pseudo-labels from a baseline classifier's confidence (circularity admitted). External set has no blasts. Prose is uneven and in places reads as machine-translated or machine-edited. Reference list (lines 811-961) not read.

title: RA-STGNN-AMR: Forecast-filter-rank Spatio-temporal Graph Learning for Resilient and Energy-feasible AGV/AMR Fleet Coordination
venue: International Journal of Intelligent Engineering and Systems
evidence: Sec 3.9 Safety invariants: 'These invariants are evaluated independently of the learned modules, so prediction error can reduce efficiency but cannot relax the defined route constraints.'
method: Forecast-filter-rank AGV/AMR routing: Bi-LSTM edge forecast and ST-GNN embeddings propose costs, a hard battery, capacity, conflict and workstation feasibility mask vetoes routes, with shortest-path fallback.
evaluation: MovingAI, SafeLog and 3D-warehouse MAPF replays, 20-100 robots, 5 disruption levels, 30 seeds, 8 baselines: conflict metric 14.7 to 4.9 vs Dijkstra, EIR 1.8% vs 11.6% without the battery constraint; no latency measured.
contribution: Separates learned congestion forecasting from hard feasibility enforcement so a favourable learned score can never authorise an infeasible AGV or AMR route, with per-term ablations.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (Bi-LSTM plus ST-GNN routing pipeline guarded by a non-learned feasibility mask, three invariants and a supervisory fallback). Borderline (a): the mask sits inside route selection, so the maintainer may read it as a planner-internal constraint and rule exclude-E1; primary outcomes are travel time, waiting time and throughput, so (c) fails the primacy test and only the EIR ablation and conflict count carry the safety claim. The paper itself states the conflict metric is a simulator count and not an exposure-normalised collision rate, that the energy index is not measured energy, that there is no physical testbed and no demonstrated edge-device latency, and that pairwise differences are descriptive only without paired-seed inference. Abstract percentages 31.76, 56.78, 51.18 and 41.20 all reconcile with Table 7.

title: Assuring Safety of Vision-Based Swarm Formation Control
evidence: Section V: this quantizer captures the worst perception error in relative position estimates from the vision component; safety is an offline condition on initial states (Theorem 2), with no runtime filter.
method: Models vision-based swarm formation control as quantized consensus, uses a log-polar quantizer as a perception contract bounding relative-position error, then proves safe separation and convergence offline.
evaluation: AirSim simulation only, three environments at several fog levels, 10000 sampled drone position pairs; no baselines or ablations with numbers, no collision or violation rate, no timing.
contribution: Derives a log-polar perception contract for vision-based drone swarms and proves conditions under which quantized formation control preserves safe separation and converges.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - the evaluated perception pipeline is classical (SIFT, SURF or ORB features, FLANN matching, geometric pose recovery) and the formation controller is hand-designed, so under the 2026-11-13 Pillar 1 ruling (a) and (c) fail; the paper only frames vision as fragile deep-learning-style perception. There is also no runtime override and no measured safety outcome, so exclude-E2 holds as a fallback. Theorem 3 gives only an analytic expected-convergence bound, and Remark 1 admits the safe initial-state set can be empty for coarse quantizers. Maintainer should decide whether a perception contract over a vision pipeline counts as guarding a learned system.

title: Learning to Defer with Better Features: A Case for Going Beyond the Final Layer
evidence: "Learning to defer enables machine learning models to selectively pass uncertain decisions to a human expert" (Abstract)
method: Learning-to-defer head (MLP with K+1 outputs) fed pooled intermediate ReLU activations of a frozen ResNet instead of final logits; trained with L-CE or OvA surrogate, or MaxSoftmax thresholding.
evaluation: Galaxy-Zoo (ResNet-18, 5-fold) and CIFAR-10H (ResNet-56, hold-out); feature sources x L-CE, OvA, MaxSoftmax; AC-AUC, max accuracy, coverage. Results only as plots, no numeric values. No latency.
contribution: Shows on Galaxy-Zoo and CIFAR-10H that learning-to-defer policies trained on deep hidden-layer features give better accuracy-coverage trade-offs than policies built on final-layer logits.
flag: (i): learning to defer to a human expert is the whole paper. Borderline on the evaluation floor: comparisons against a logits baseline and MaxSoftmax exist, but ONLY as Fig. 2 boxplots and Fig. 3 curves; the text gives no AC-AUC, accuracy or coverage number at all (only base classifier accuracies 82.77% and 94.37%), so no effect size can be extracted from this text file - check the figures in the PDF. No significance tests; CIFAR-10H is a single split. The human is simulated by sampling one label from the crowd label distribution; no real expert in the loop and the handoff itself is not studied, so (e) not credited and the human handoff cell is weak. One-shot image classification, no sequential or latency aspect. Galaxy-Zoo split is stated as 7000/3000 for the classifier but 8000/2000 per fold for the deferral model, so deferral test folds overlap classifier training data. Short FRUCT conference paper, 2 authors, incremental over Mozannar-Sontag and Verma-Nalisnick.

title: HALIDS: a Hardware-Assisted Machine Learning IDS for in-Network Monitoring
evidence: "when the confidence in the decision is low, the responsibility is deferred to an expert (the oracle) for further assessment" (Sec. I)
method: P4 switch classifies each packet with a small decision tree and pre-blocks attacks; below a confidence threshold it exports features to a larger off-band random-forest oracle, whose labels also retrain it.
evaluation: BMv2 software switch, UNSW-NB15, 1000-packet test trace; DCT 80, 90, 95% vs same-model baseline. Detection performance about -30%, +10%, +20% relative to baseline (Fig. 4). No latency or hardware figures.
contribution: HALIDS, an in-network intrusion detector where a P4 switch classifies packets itself or defers low-confidence ones to an off-band oracle model, improving detection by up to about 20% over an in-switch baseline.
flag: (i) and (ii), weakly (iv): per-packet runtime gate in a streaming setting that hands low-confidence decisions to a fallback system (a larger ML model, NOT a human). Borderline include; a stricter reading gives exclude-E1 (a cascade to a larger model on a resource-limited device) or exclude-E2 (evaluation too thin). The whole evaluation is one bar chart in a section titled 'Preliminary Results' of a 3-page short paper: 1000 packets, values only approximate ('almost 30%', 'about 10%', 'almost 20%'), the metric is an unnamed 'detection performance gain' normalised to baseline (packet-level recall implied), no absolute numbers, no fraction of packets deferred, no false-positive rate. At DCT 80% nothing is deferred, so that bar is effectively the no-deferral ablation with a student trained on 50% of data. The confidence-threshold offload is taken from CML-IDS [6]; the paper's own additions (automation, runtime retraining via active learning) are described but NOT evaluated. Title says hardware-assisted but everything runs on the BMv2 software switch; no latency is measured despite the speed motivation. Deferral rule is a fixed threshold on leaf probabilities, not learned.

title: The Off-Switch Game
venue: International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence
evidence: Section 3: there is never an incentive to disable the off switch with a rational H; in the Section 2 game the robot can wait and let the human veto the action before it executes.
method: Two-player decision-theoretic game in which a robot may act, switch itself off, or wait and let a human veto; analyses when deference is optimal under preference uncertainty.
evaluation: Formal: Theorem 1 proves the waiting incentive Delta is non-negative and positive under two-sided belief support; Theorem 2 gives the Gaussian case; simulation sweeps noise and action-set size; no numeric baseline.
contribution: Formalises the off switch as a game and proves a robot uncertain about human preferences has a positive incentive to defer to a rational human's veto, an incentive that vanishes with certainty.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an AI agent acting under preference uncertainty, though decision-theoretic rather than a learned policy. Deferral is the main contribution and both the human hand-off and foundational reject-option conditions of the Pillar 3 scope hold. The evaluation floor is met by proved guarantees only: Figure 4's simulation (Gaussian customer population, action sets of 1, 4 and 8) is reported as trends with no values, and Soares et al. 2015 is compared qualitatively. One-shot, not sequential, and no latency or irreversibility timing; the authors list the sequential and multi-human cases as future work.

title: Learning to Complement Humans
venue: International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence
evidence: Sec. 2: 'The machine must decide, for each instance, whether to predict on its own or first consult a human expert'; Sec. 3.1 queries the human at inference whenever (1-q)max(m) < q.
method: Trains the classifier jointly with its query policy, via a discriminative relaxation or a differentiable value-of-information surrogate, so the model specialises where the human is weak and routes the rest to the expert.
evaluation: Galaxy Zoo (10k train, 4k test, 5 classes) and CAMELYON16 (127 labelled images, plus an asymmetric-cost variant); baselines fixed-discriminative, fixed-VOI and human-only; joint beats fixed VOI by 1.8-38.9% average loss reduction (max 73.3%, min -3.1%), discriminative models up to 29% on Galaxy Zoo and 20% on CAMELYON16, t-test p<1e-3; ablations over capacity (20, 50, 100 units) and query cost 0-0.2; 68% of human errors sit in 10% of instances; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Trains a predictive model jointly with its query policy so the machine learns to defer exactly the instances a human handles best, improving team utility over fixed-model deferral.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the query policy gates a learned neural classifier, deferral is the paper's main contribution, and it hands off to a human expert, so it clears the Pillar 3 scope on (i). Check the evaluation floor: the only quantitative outcome is team loss or utility against fixed-model deferral baselines, with no hazard, violation or intervention rate, and the setting is one-shot image classification with no sequential step, no latency and no multi-agent aspect, so a maintainer could call this E4 wrong level. The human supplies a logged label rather than taking over, so (e) was not credited. Table 1 has negative minima (-3.10% and -1.05%) although the text says joint models uniformly outperform or tie, and the CAMELYON16 VOI comparisons only approach significance (p<0.15).

title: Deep Neural Network Compression for Aircraft Collision Avoidance Systems
venue: Journal of Guidance Control and Dynamics
evidence: Abstract: 'Because only the network parameters need to be stored, the required storage space is reduced by a factor of 1000'; Sec. V reports about 0.6 ms per forward pass, with hundreds of passes needed for up to 30 intruders inside the one-second advisory interval.
method: Replaces the ACAS Xu horizontal score table with an array of 45 small deep networks, one per tau and previous advisory, trained with an asymmetric loss, with pruning tested and the COC penalty and online costs moved out of the training targets.
