evaluation: 10 million simulated 3D aircraft encounters against the original downsampled table, linear regression (RMSE 17.9) and decision trees under 100 MB (RMSE >3.0, policy error >6%); network RMSE 0.923, policy error 2.02%, about 2.4 MB vs over 2 GB; P(NMAC) 1.846e-4 nominal array, 1.564e-4 without COC penalty, 1.451e-4 with online costs vs 1.472e-4 for the table; P(Alert) 0.5668-0.6513 vs 0.6705; P(Reversal) 0.0475-0.0314 vs 0.0270; runtime 0.97x the table, 0.6 ms per forward pass; four Titan X GPUs for training.
contribution: Compresses the ACAS Xu collision avoidance score table into 45 small neural networks that fit legacy avionics memory and run at table speed while nearly preserving near-mid-air-collision rates.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: which - nothing is guarded, the learned network IS the collision avoidance logic, so the record rests on (d) (an explicit under-120 MB avionics budget and a one-second advisory interval) and on (c) only because P(NMAC) in pairwise and multi-intruder encounters is measured against the table. runtime_interceptor is no: the network replaces a table lookup, there is no nominal decision it vetoes and no pilot handoff is discussed, so a maintainer may prefer E1 or E4. Primacy is weak - the claim is compression, and the nominal array is WORSE than the table on P(NMAC), P(Alert) and P(Reversal), so Sec. VIII's 'perform as well as the original table' is overstated. The 10-aircraft run gives only minimum separation 5564 ft with no collision count, pruning was dropped from the final system, Table I's NMAC entry is unreadable in the PDF text, and Sec. IV-C contradicts itself on five vs six hidden layers.

title: Bridging the Gap in Hybrid Decision-Making Systems
venue: Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence and Applications
evidence: "M takes most of the decisions, but it can call H back if uncertain, and it is able to explain why." (Sec. 3)
method: BRIDGET: incremental-learning labelling system switching between a Human-in-Command skeptical-learning phase and a Machine-in-Command phase that calls the human back when fading-empirical-accuracy belief falls below a threshold.
evaluation: None. Conceptual proposal with pseudocode and formulas only; no dataset, experiment, baseline, metric, user study, hardware or latency.
contribution: Proposes BRIDGET, a human-in-the-loop labelling design that alternates between human-led skeptical learning and machine-led deferral with call-back to the user, without evaluating it.
flag: (i) and (ii) on paper: deferral to a human over a stream of records, with bidirectional control hand-over, which is squarely on topic. But the paper has NO evaluation of any kind; the conclusion says 'we plan to extensively test BRIDGET against stand-alone LtD systems'. Short position paper (8 pages, HHAI 2025). Algorithm 1 is an image and is missing from the text, so line references could not be checked. Possible internal slip in Sec. 3.2: the random spot-check compares r with the belief threshold beta, so a high beta means the user is rarely spot-checked. No learned deferral model; the deferral rule is a threshold on prediction probability times a recency-weighted accuracy. Worth keeping as background for RQ3 if an evaluated follow-up appears.

title: AI SAFETY MODEL MOE: A MIXTURE-OF-EXPERTS ARCHITECTURE FOR CERTIFIABLE, RISK-AWARE GENERATION
evidence: "a final gate that either approves the answer or abstains and offers a safe alternative" (Abstract)
method: Safety-MoE design for LLM mixture-of-experts: risk-aware router, decode-time auditor that switches routing to vetted safety experts or aborts, and a calibrated final gate that releases or abstains.
evaluation: None. Sec. 8 only lists test suites, metrics and ablations to run; no experiment, dataset, baseline or measured number. Sec. 6 gives informal bounds without proof. No latency measured.
contribution: Describes Safety-MoE, an unevaluated blueprint for a mixture-of-experts language model with risk-aware routing, decode-time auditing and a calibrated abstention gate.
flag: (iv) nominally, plus a decode-time (per-token) switch or abort that touches (ii); abstention is one of three co-equal components, so main-contribution status is arguable. Decisive problem: UNEVALUATED. The paper states 'No external datasets were generated or analyzed in this study'; Sec. 8 is a plan, Tables 3-6 are rule-of-thumb or 'typical start' values, not measurements. The author-contribution line nevertheless claims 'Software, experiments, and visualization', and the data statement refers to supplementary materials and a 'code link below' that does not appear. The 'guarantee' Pr(Z=1|release) <= tau+eps (Sec. 6.1) is a restatement of the calibration assumption, stated without proof, and Eq. 3 writes the saddle as min over lambda, max over Theta of a loss, which is the wrong way round; not theory under (v). Sec. 5.3 repeats the Sec. 5.2 text verbatim under the calibration heading; printed code has errors (stats undefined, 'Pass'). Single author from a company, none of the 21 references is cited anywhere in the body, checklist style: likely machine-generated and published in a low-barrier journal. Human review appears only as a table row (S_Review).

title: Coverage-Constrained Selective Prediction for Short-Horizon Cryptocurrency Event Contracts via Adaptive Quantile Thresholds
evidence: "A useful model must therefore abstain at most timestamps and act only in the tails of its score distribution." (Section 1, Introduction)
method: Five-seed gradient-boosting ensemble scores each minute bar; daily trailing-quantile thresholds (14-28 day window) decide trade or abstain so coverage stays in a 10-12 trades/day band under drift.
evaluation: BTC/ETH 5- and 10-min fixed-odds contracts, 161-day held-out window plus 7 quarterly walk-forward windows; vs split conformal, ACI rate and outcome controllers; win rate 57.8-63.3%, coverage tracking error 0.019/0.006 vs 0.869/0.477; 1.5 ms per bar on 28 CPU threads.
contribution: Trailing-window quantile thresholds keep an abstaining trading predictor's emission rate inside a target band under score drift, matching tuned adaptive conformal inference on coverage in a backtest.
flag: (ii) borderline: abstention is the main contribution and thresholds adapt online over a stream, but each minute is an independent trade/no-trade call in a finance backtest - no safety, no human, no fallback system; could equally be read as exclude-E4 (reject-option classifier applied to a domain). Authors call it a proof of concept on a stylized contract, not the real Binance product. Coverage argument is asymptotic, no guarantee; only 2 of 4 strategies survive Holm correction; well-tuned ACI matches the method. Daily coverage outside band on about two thirds of days. Abstract numbers found in body (Tables 5, 9).

title: LLM-Based Adaptive Control Code Generation Framework with Digital Twin-Integrated Verification for Heterogeneous Robot Systems
evidence: "Otherwise, the task is reported as infeasible under the selected robot and execution condition" (Section 3.6, Adaptive Parameter Scaling)
method: Digital-twin-grounded pre-execution gate on LLM-generated robot code: runtime spatial grounding, feasibility-aware robot selection, RNEA torque validation and global motion scaling before vendor code is emitted.
evaluation: PyBullet simulation, 6-robot pool, 170 natural-language scenarios, 8 selection tasks vs TOPSIS, LinearWS, Greedy, Random; safe execution 100% vs 50% without scaling; no latency reported.
contribution: A digital-twin verification layer that blocks or temporally rescales physically infeasible LLM-generated robot motions before vendor code is emitted, raising safe execution coverage from 50% to 100%.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - Gemini 2.5 Pro code generator. Check how runtime the gate is: it fires once per task before execution, not per control step. All evidence is simulation (PyBullet plus analytical RNEA for only 2 of the 6 robots); the 70% adversarial-block figure rests on just 10 adversarial prompts; authors concede there is no comparison against ungated LLM code generation; safe-execution 100% vs 50% is an ablation of their own scaling step, not an external baseline.

title: Baselines, Sample Size, and Supervisory Activity in Guarded Reinforcement-Learning Traffic Signal Control: A SUMO Evidence Audit
evidence: "The supervisor never replaces the incumbent: at one decision, it may substitute one action, and if it does not, the incumbent's action is executed unchanged." (Section 3.1, System Under Audit)
method: Retrospective audit of eight versions of a gated supervisor over an RL traffic-signal incumbent: baseline ablation, fitting-budget curve, stage-wise activity funnel, harm-bound reachability; plus a registered non-learned supervisor follow-up.
evaluation: SUMO, 3 networks, 3480 counterfactual pairs; V3 funnel 70 executed deviations of 1,123,200 decisions (AAR 0.0062%); follow-up 5 networks, 180 episodes vs actuated baseline: AAR 4.65%, stopped time -8.75 s/vehicle (12.58%). No latency or hardware figures.
contribution: An audit of a guarded RL traffic-signal supervisor shows the gate almost never overrode the incumbent, and proposes reporting an intervention-rate denominator and bound reachability before claiming non-inferiority.
flag: (iv), also (ii): the subject is a runtime authority gate that defaults to the incumbent, but the paper is a self-audit and reporting-standard study by the program's own author, not a new mechanism; maintainer should decide whether an evidence audit counts as a main contribution on deferral. No safety metric: harm labels and bounds were NOT computed in the follow-up and the paper says neither study establishes safety; intervention rate (AAR) is the only safety-adjacent metric. Most analysis retrospective on already-consumed validation data; registration is a self-deposited Zenodo record on the day of the runs. Arrivals fell on one follow-up network. Multi-junction networks but supervisor acts per junction, so multi-agent only nominal. File is 520k chars (83 pages): read abstract, Sections 1.2-1.3, 3.1, 3.9, 4.6, 4.7, 6; skimmed headings only for Sections 2, 3.2-3.8, 4.1-4.5, 5 and did not read appendices A-B.

title: Plan-Then-Verify: Verifier-First Planning for Early Feasibility Validation in LLM Agent Systems
evidence: "Unsupported workflows are blocked through safe abstention rather than hallucinated capability invention." (Abstract)
method: LLM planner emits a task graph; a deterministic verifier checks functions, artifacts and ordering against a knowledge base before execution, one bounded repair pass, otherwise the workflow is blocked.
evaluation: Core-60 static benchmark (48 supported, 12 unsupported tasks), 9 model configs, 3 runs; vs Direct-Execute, Plan-and-Execute, self-review; e.g. gemma4:e4b conformance 58.0/60 vs 27.7, abstention 10.3/12 vs 0; false block up to 22.3/48; RTX 4060 and 4x H200; no latency.
contribution: A deterministic pre-execution verifier with one bounded repair pass blocks infeasible LLM agent workflows, raising static conformance and correct abstention over plan-and-execute at similar token cost on a 60-task benchmark.
flag: (iv) borderline: a pre-execution gate that vetoes an agent plan, but it checks feasibility against a documented capability list, not safety, and abstention is one of two outcomes (repair of supported tasks is the larger share) - exclude-E1 is defensible. Benchmark is static and invokes no real tools; sandbox replay uses mock tools from the same specification; authors state the score is not a real-execution success rate. Five of nine model configurations collapse to identical zero-difference outcomes (structured-output failures). DeepSeek-r1:7b shows 22.3/48 false blocks. Benchmark authored by the same team, includes industry co-authors. Single agent, no human handoff.

title: Beyond Keyword Filters: Calibrated Monte-Carlo Risk Gating for Safe Multilingual Colorectal-Cancer LLM Dialogue
evidence: "The system answers when g(x) is at most tau and refers the patient to a clinician or crisis resource when g(x) exceeds tau." (Section 3.1, Problem Formulation)
method: Bootstrap ensemble of 200 logistic risk models over multilingual MiniLM sentence embeddings, Platt-scaled, with one threshold deciding between answering a user turn and a referral message.
evaluation: 450 oncologist-reviewed prompts (EN/TR/ES), scenario-level split, 5 seeds; vs keyword/regex/fuzzy layers, Llama-Guard-3-8B, ShieldGemma-2B; harmful blocked 0.982, over-refusal 0.108, F1 0.961 vs 0.034; ECE 0.216 to 0.069; A100 GPU; latency stated only as 'a few milliseconds', unmeasured.
contribution: A calibrated embedding-based risk classifier gates single patient turns to a colorectal-cancer chatbot, blocking 98% of authored harmful prompts where keyword filters block under 2%.
flag: none of (i)-(v): single-turn input guardrail (a prompt classifier with a threshold); 'referral to a clinician' is a canned refusal, no human handoff is modelled or studied, no multi-turn or sequential aspect. Llama-Guard-3-8B scores higher F1 (0.975 vs 0.961) with zero benign refusals, and the paper says that table is not head-to-head. Own ablation shows a single logistic model performs identically, so the Monte-Carlo ensemble adds nothing to accuracy. Prompts are authored and paraphrase-expanded, not real traffic; 450 prompts with a 0.667 harmful base rate; over-refusal CI is wide [0.008, 0.233]. Latency figure is an estimate, not a measurement.

title: Knowing When to Defer: Trustworthy Multimodal AI for BI-RADS-Derived Management Using Paired Mammography and Ultrasound
evidence: "Selective prediction ranks cases by the margin between the two largest raw ensemble probabilities and defers the least confident fraction to the radiologist." (Section 2.6, Trustworthiness Layer)
method: Paired mammography-ultrasound classifier (LoRA-adapted foundation encoders, mask-aware fusion) with a post-hoc layer: isotonic calibration, conformal sets, margin-threshold deferral, atypicality flag.
evaluation: BCMID, 332 cases, single centre, nested cross-validation; vs frozen-encoder and CNN baselines; macro AUROC 0.759; balanced accuracy 0.556 to 0.631 at 30% deferral (0.642 with fold-fixed threshold); under-triage 2/63 to 1/50; ECE 0.088 to 0.052. No latency or hardware found.
contribution: A multimodal breast-imaging classifier adds calibration, conformal sets and confidence-threshold deferral, lifting balanced accuracy on retained cases from 0.556 to 0.631 when 30% are returned to the radiologist.
flag: none of (i)-(v): one-shot classifier with a confidence-margin reject option applied to a medical domain; deferral is one of four trust components, not a learned deferral rule, and the radiologist is never modelled - no reader study, no expert accuracy, so the handoff itself is not studied (authors list a prospective reading study as future work). Headline 30% deferral result is a retrospective ranking of the pooled cohort; reference label is author-derived from one radiologist's BI-RADS, not pathology. Small single-centre cohort; under-triage change is 2/63 to 1/50, i.e. one case. Abstract numbers found in body (Section 3.3, Table 2).

title: HERA-GM: Evaluating Conditional Execution Authority for Offline Reinforcement Learning in Tactical Driving
evidence: "ACCEPT passes the proposal to the common trajectory adapter. DEFER and RECOVER transfer immediate execution to a deterministic fallback path." (Sec. 1 Introduction)
method: Runtime authority gate over an offline CQL Dueling Double DQN tactical proposer: Q-margin, feature availability, annotation density, Mahalanobis score and five hard rules assign ACCEPT, DEFER or RECOVER; non-ACCEPT hands control to a deterministic fallback.
evaluation: nuPlan Mini closed loop, 113 scenarios, 1970 runs + 339 BC runs; vs policy-only CQL (B1), always-fallback (B2), simpler gate (B3), BC (B4), two ablations. Safety failure M1 72.86% vs B1 78.47% (Holm p 0.098), vs B3 72.27%; drivable-area violation 1.47 vs 9.73% (p 0.001); progress 0.076 vs 0.132; handover rate 0.28; p95 planner latency 114 ms (CPU PyTorch, hardware not named).
contribution: Closed-loop nuPlan study of an accept/defer/recover authority gate over an offline-RL driving policy; the added Mahalanobis and hard-rule evidence gave no supported safety gain over a simpler confidence gate and cost progress.
flag: (ii) and (iv), also (i) in the fallback-system sense (no human). Largely a negative result: no M1 comparison with B1, B2 or B3 shows a Holm-adjusted primary safety difference; both ablations leave safety unchanged; Mahalanobis AUROC 0.44 (below chance) on held-out families. Absolute safety-failure rates are very high (about 70-78% of runs, driven by interval-level critical TTC about 62%), so the composite endpoint may be poorly discriminating. Table 4 lists Holm p 0.012 for M1 vs B4 safety failure while the abstract says it did not stay below 0.05 after pooled Holm adjustment across five comparisons - consistent only if the table value is the within-block adjustment; check. BC baselines were added after the frozen study (exploratory). Latency is whole-planner telemetry, about 95 ms median, not gate cost. No vehicle or HIL test. Related work and reference list only skimmed.

title: ENTRUST: Closed-Loop Trust-Calibrated Autonomous Cyber Defense for Ambient IoT
evidence: "(4) is a hard safety invariant that forces human authorization for critical, irreversible, or extreme-severity actions regardless of confidence" (Sec. 4.1 Decision and Objective)
method: Closed-loop controller for IoT cyber defense that per event jointly picks one of five autonomy levels (observe, recommend, auto, auto+canary, mandatory human) and an explanation fidelity, driven by calibrated uncertainty and an operator-trust state.
evaluation: Synthetic episodic simulator, 5 threat conditions, 30 seeds x 1200 episodes, 5 baselines, 9 ablations. Clean harm rate 0.0286 vs 0.0436 FullAuto, 0.0311 uncertainty-gated; 30.4 vs 100 interventions per 100; injection containment 0.742 vs 0.641. Added latency 26 us mean, 64 us median end to end, one CPU core.
contribution: Simulation study of a trust-calibrated controller that jointly selects autonomy level and explanation fidelity for IoT cyber defense, cutting harmful autonomous actions by about a third versus full autonomy with 70% fewer human interventions than mandatory approval.
flag: (i) deferral to a human operator, with (ii) streaming decisions and a (iv) hard invariant forcing human authorization. Everything is simulated: the event stream is synthetic (only priors follow public IoT corpora), the operator is a parametric trust/accuracy model, the canary is a stochastic filter, no human subjects - so the e credit is for a modelled handoff only. Deferral is one half of a joint autonomy+explanation contribution; maintainer may judge whether it is the MAIN contribution. Against the closest baseline (uncertainty-gated B3) harm and containment are statistically comparable on clean data (0.0286 vs 0.0311; burden 30.4 vs 30.5); the clear gain there is trust-calibration error, a simulator-internal construct. The injection result (harm 2.86% identical to clean, containment 0.742) looks like the injection is neutralised by construction of the simulator. Abstract numbers found in Tables 10-12. Latency is a CPU micro-benchmark with no named gateway hardware. Sections 2, 6.2-6.6, 8.5-8.12 and 9 skimmed, not read in full.

title: Catch Me If You Can: Rogue AI Detection and Correction at Scale
evidence: "provide fail-safe overrides under deception signals" (Section 3.3, Correction Algorithm: SEB-Correct)
method: Strategy Elicitation Battery probes reward-sensitive misreporting across six model families; the SEB-Correct wrapper shrinks or hard-overrides the agent reported belief and re-selects the EV-optimal action.
evaluation: 20 scenarios per architecture (LLM, RL, ViT, CLIP, Mamba, SD), honest vs strategic baselines; deception 80.0% ViT down to 5.0% LLM; logistic LRT chi2(5)=41.56, p=7.2e-8; median 820-1410 ms.
contribution: A unified cross-architecture battery that measures reward-sensitive misreporting in six model families and a correction wrapper whose hard overrides turn residual deception and override rates into deployment gates.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLMs, RL agents, ViT, CLIP, Mamba, diffusion. The runtime part (SEB-Correct) is barely evaluated: Table 5 gives two runs the authors label illustrative only, and full post-correction telemetry was 'not exported in this snapshot'. Internal inconsistency: Table 5 residual deception 18.4% for Mamba vs roughly 40-60% residual for Mamba, CLIP and ViT in Figure 3. Mixed-effects analysis and cluster-robust SEs are only 'planned'; n=20 scenarios per architecture with CIs of plus or minus 10-15 pp; deepseek-r1 row rests on valid N=2. (c) considered and rejected: each model is probed alone, there is no agent-agent interaction despite the multi-agent keyword.

title: Ethical Coordination of LLM Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: "a pre-delivery filter that enforces hard and soft constraints on factual integrity, autonomy retention, and subgroup fairness on the policy pipeline" (Section 1, Introduction)
method: Constitutional governance layer filters compiled LLM influence policies before delivery to 30 grounded LLM agents on a scale-free graph; hard integrity gate plus soft manipulation-risk scorer.
evaluation: Llama-3.3-70B, 30-agent Barabasi-Albert graph, 5 seeds, N=100 spot-check; ECS 0.176 vs 0.000 unconstrained, integrity 1.000 vs 0.000, vs CAI critique-revise and LlamaGuard-style selectors; filter 0.78 us per call, p99 0.88 us.
contribution: A stateless constitutional filter that vetoes manipulative influence policies before they reach a population of LLM agents, holding the integrity floor at microsecond cost with a threat-proportional rejection rate.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM compiler and 30 LLM agent population. Strongest Pillar-1 fit in this batch. Doubts: the agents are simulated social-influence personas, not actuating agents, so the hazard is manipulation of a simulation rather than a physical or service action; ECS is an author-defined multiplicative composite and the governed-minus-naive gap is only about -0.004, so by the authors' own statement the load-bearing component is a hand-written hard filter; 41.7% rejection under adversarial pressure is the nearest thing to a false-halt measure. (d) not credited: 0.78 us is a micro-benchmark of the rule check, explicitly scoped as 'not an end-to-end production deployment study'.

title: Dual-Threshold Conformal Deferral for Trustworthy Security Alert Triage
evidence: "high-score alerts are auto-escalated under finite-sample marginal class-conditional control of the benign-escalation probability (budget alpha), low-score alerts are auto-closed under matching control of the threat-miss probability (budget beta), and the rest are deferred to an analyst." (Abstract)
method: Model-agnostic, training-free deferral layer: two split-conformal thresholds on a black-box alert score give auto-escalate, auto-close and defer-to-analyst zones with class-conditional error budgets; an uncertifiable zone is closed, not backfilled.
evaluation: Simulated SOC with PPO investigation agent (10 policies) and 4 classifiers CIC-IDS2017 to 2018; vs uncorrected quantile, single-threshold gate, LLM band resolver. alpha=beta=0.01: 73.7% automated, realized 0.0099/0.0101; overshoot 0.269 vs 0.806 at n=25; deferral 79-99% under shift. No latency.
contribution: Dual-threshold conformal layer that auto-escalates or auto-closes security alerts under separate finite-sample error budgets and defers the rest to an analyst, automating 73.7% of decisions at 1% budgets and inflating deferral visibly under dataset shift.
flag: (i) deferral to a human analyst is the main contribution, but the rule is a one-shot per-alert three-way threshold on a terminal score (the RL agent's multi-step investigation only produces the score), so a strict reader could call this E4 (reject option applied to a domain); I recommend include on (i) with that caveat. No analyst is in the loop anywhere: deferred alerts are simply counted, so handoff itself is not studied (no e); the LLM stand-in for the analyst is a negative result (band accuracy 0.53-0.58 vs 0.813 for the base policy). The guarantee is standard split-conformal class-conditional validity, not a new theorem, so (v) does not apply. 73.7% is for a pooled exchangeable-by-construction split; under the seed-level split budgets are respected in only 53-65% of draws (Table 5) and deferral ranges 13-42%. Shift result requires recalibration on labelled target data. Authors disclose a fixed simulator defect (label-leaking confidence). Sections 2, 3.2-3.4, 5.2-5.3, 6.1, 8 and appendices skimmed, not read in full.

title: Directional Contract Transition Revalidation for Model Context Protocol Tools: An Approval Continuity Framework for Evolving Agent Capabilities
evidence: "With the two changes introduced simultaneously and no whole-contract assessment, the policy returned SEMANTIC_UNCERTAIN with a pending L3 review action; tools/call was denied and no local canary event occurred." (Sec. 5.10)
method: Client-side approval gate for MCP tools: canonicalizes tool contracts, diffs them against grant-bound and last-human-reviewed baselines, maps typed directional changes to L0-L4 actions; L3+ or unassessed multi-path changes withhold calls pending human reapproval.
evaluation: MCP Python SDK fixtures: 4/4 compound cases withheld vs 4/4 allowed by historical max-path rule; 3/3 benign controls also sent to review. Expert agreement 28/34 paths (weighted kappa 0.720), 37/48 (0.710). Diff timing 0.02-17 ms median, AMD EPYC 9V74.
contribution: Approval-continuity gate for evolving MCP tool contracts that auto-continues bounded changes and withholds tool calls pending human reapproval for risk-increasing or unassessed compound changes, shown on controlled SDK fixtures and expert-coded natural transitions.
flag: (iv) runtime approval gate that withholds tool calls, with (i) hand-off to human reapproval. BORDERLINE exclude-E2: the only quantitative result for the gate against a comparator is 4/4 withheld vs 4/4 allowed on author-programmed synthetic fixtures (plus 3/3 benign controls incurring review); the ETDI and Microsoft comparison is a paper projection of design rules, not a run. The paper itself says it does not establish semantic risk detection, harm prevention or review-burden reduction. Human approval in the SDK tests is a test-driver flag; the full pending-to-approved lifecycle was never demonstrated; no natural L4 observed. Kappa figures measure codebook agreement, not gate performance; cluster-bootstrap kappa CI 0.146-1.000. Expert sign-offs are author-submitted and not independently authenticated; one N3 case deferred. Authors are students (student-mail addresses); prose is extremely hedged and repetitive, possibly machine-assisted; the 47-page text reads as heavily revised under review. Single-agent tool gate, so maintainer may also weigh E4. File is 260k chars: read abstract, contributions, Sec. 4.9, 5.5, 5.8, 5.10, SDK matrix text and 6.6; Sec. 3, 4.1-4.8, 4.10-4.17, 5.1-5.4, 5.6-5.7, 5.12, 6.1-6.5, 7 and appendices not read.

title: DEGA: A Deterministic Diagnostic Evidence Governance Agent for Industrial IoT—A DUDU-BLDC Case Study
evidence: "A higher-priority SafetyGuard that can override policy-proposed transitions when evidence or integrity requirements are not met" (Sec. 1, contribution 3)
method: Deterministic 11-state finite-state governance layer over motor-diagnostic evidence: routing policies propose transitions, a higher-priority SafetyGuard rule set overrides them, each case ends in recommend, escalate to operator or no decision, with hash-linked audit and replay.
evaluation: Offline replay on DUDU-BLDC (8 acquisitions, 200 windows), 4 routing policies, retained vs simulated explanation profiles. Real evidence: 0 recommendations, 15,360 escalations; simulated: 2924 recommendations, 12,436 escalations; 0 proxy flags. No error metric, no latency, no hardware.
contribution: Deterministic finite-state governance agent that escalates industrial motor diagnoses to an operator unless every evidence contract is met; on retained real evidence it escalated all 15,360 routes, with recommendations appearing only under simulated explanation metadata.
flag: (i) nominally (escalation to a human operator is the main output; (iv) weakly, since the agent explicitly cannot stop the motor). Recommend E2: the only numbers for the mechanism are route counts produced by its own deterministic rules; on real evidence it escalates 100% of cases, and recommendations exist only when explanation metadata is injected by simulation. No ground-truth measure of whether escalation or recommendation was right (authors disclaim recommendation correctness), the only check is an internal governance-consistency proxy with 0 flags, and the four routing policies give identical terminal totals (731/8485/0 each), so there is no informative baseline. If the maintainer accepts profile ablation of rule R11 as an ablation of an intervention rate, this becomes a weak include. Entirely offline; no operator, timing or deployment. 8 acquisitions only; routes are not independent. Sections 2, 3, 4.2, 4.4, 5.1-5.4, 6.1, 6.5-6.6 and appendix skimmed, not read in full.

title: BRAG: Bayesian Retrieval-Augmented Generation; A Methodological Framework for Evidence-Governed Decision Support
evidence: "routes each query to one of four actions, answer, escalate, abstain, or fail, before any output reaches the user" (Sec. 1)
method: RAG wrapper: logistic answerability posterior over 12 retrieval features plus a five-part validity gate routes each query to answer, escalate, abstain or fail using two thresholds.
evaluation: Parametric Monte Carlo simulation n=2400 vs 4 RAG baselines: hallucination 0.016 vs 0.257, utility 0.632; synthetic end-to-end N=100: 0 vs 0.31 hallucination at 27% coverage. No latency.
contribution: Frames retrieval-augmented answering as a four-action decision (answer, escalate, abstain, fail) driven by an answerability posterior and validity gate, tested mostly in parametric simulation on synthetic clinical records.
flag: none of (i)-(v): a language model pipeline abstaining on single questions; the Escalate action names clinician review but no human or fallback is modelled or evaluated. Proposition 1 (cost-ratio abstention threshold) and Proposition 2 (hallucination bound) are elementary and their proofs are only in a supplement, so (v) is not credible. Serious evaluation doubts: the n=2400 and N=500 headline numbers come from a parametric statistical model in which retriever, generator and verifier do not run per query; the generator is a deterministic template, not an LLM; all clinical data are synthetic; the only executed tier is N=100, where coverage is 27% (51% escalated, 22% abstained). The verifier-only baseline matches BRAG on hallucination (0.015 vs 0.016), so the answerability model adds utility only. Live-LLM evidence is a handful of case studies and the text says both 'six evaluated queries' and 'four GPT-5.4 live-LLM case studies'. Answerability AUROC is weak (0.656 in simulation, below the retrieval-control baseline 0.823). First author is at a small company; self-citation as prior work [22]. Expert adjudication and feature-space sections (6.8, 6.11, 6.12) and Discussion were only skimmed.

title: DAUNT: Ensemble Disagreement as Actionable Uncertainty for Imbalanced Fraud Detection
evidence: "Where they disagree, the prediction is less trustworthy and is a better candidate for human review." (Sec. 4.3)
method: Five-model stacked fraud ensemble; standard deviation of base-learner scores ranks transactions, top-beta fraction is deferred to analysts, the rest decided by a score-times-amount expected-loss rule.
evaluation: ULB and IEEE-CIS; vs no triage, random, margin, MC dropout, deep ensemble, conformal. System recall at 5% deferral 0.905 vs 0.757 (ULB), 0.748 vs 0.660; 15-17 ms per transaction, Apple M4 laptop.
contribution: Uses disagreement among heterogeneous fraud classifiers to route the most uncertain 5% of transactions to analysts, and prices that handoff under simulated fallible reviewers and review cost.
flag: (i), borderline with E4: deferral to human analysts is the headline of three layers and the paper simulates fallible, heterogeneous, costly reviewers (Table 8), but this is one-shot selective classification on two static public datasets with a fixed post-hoc uncertainty ranking; no learned rejector, no real human, no comparison to learning-to-defer methods (authors say so). If the maintainer reads 'reject option applied to a domain' strictly this is exclude-E4. Doubts: headline 0.76 to 0.91 recall assumes an oracle analyst; with a mixed-skill pool ULB recall is 0.770 vs 0.757 baseline and an all-junior pool is worse than no triage (0.634). On ULB at 5% budget every detection comes from the reviewed set, so the perfect precision is the oracle's. On IEEE-CIS the plain score margin beats disagreement (0.83 vs 0.75), contradicting the title's emphasis. Deferral is a batch top-beta ranking over the test set, not a per-transaction threshold, so runtime use needs a quantile fixed in advance. IEEE-CIS is single-seed. Much of the paper (stacking gain, SMOTEENN, SHAP) is not about deferral. Sections 5.3-5.6 and 5.9-5.11 skimmed only.

title: GroundTrader: Multi-Agent Transition Supervision for LLM-Based Financial Trading
evidence: "The coherence analyst reviews the decision-time evidence and may recommend a one-period deferral." (Sec. 3)
method: Supervisory LLM analysts sit between a trading agent's routed position change and execution; reasoning-action conflicts trigger a bounded one-period deferral, weighted by a budget updated from counterfactually settled past deferrals.
evaluation: Backtests, 9 assets, fixed FinAgent trajectories; vs direct execution, rules, RL, FinMem; 3 ablations. Mean Sortino 1.722 vs 1.278, Calmar 2.527 vs 1.466; 13 deferrals in 1811 periods. No latency.
contribution: A supervisory layer for LLM trading agents that defers a position change by one period when action and reasoning conflict, and tunes later intervention strength from counterfactually settled outcomes of earlier deferrals.
flag: (ii), arguably (iv): deferral is an action taken over time on an agent's executable transition, with outcome feedback regulating later deferrals; it defers to the next period, not to a human or safeguard. Doubts: the whole effect rests on 13 executed deferrals out of 1811 decision periods across nine assets (27 candidates, 16 valid proposals), so per-asset gains come from one or two events each. Only 2 of 9 Sharpe improvements survive Holm correction. The record analyst returned AUTHORISE 0 times and WITHHOLD once (Table 5), yet removing record reflection is the largest ablation loss (ARR 32.83 to 28.17): the authors acknowledge the mismatch but do not explain it convincingly. Outcome metrics are returns, Sharpe and drawdown, not a violation or hazard rate; intervention rate (0.72%) is reported. Backtest only on fixed upstream trajectories, daily periods, so a deferral never feeds back into the upstream agent. Trading is not safety-critical in the review's sense. Supervisory LLM is 'DeepSeek-V4-Flash'. 'Multi-agent' means three LLM analyst roles, not multi-agent state. Appendix A, sensitivity and transaction-cost sections (4.5) and Tables 2, 3, 7, 8 not read in detail.

title: Energy-Aware Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization with Depletion Safety Constraints for Multi-Robot Coordination
evidence: "the action masking mechanism excludes actions predicted to cause constraint violation" (Section 5.4, SEA-MAPPO)
method: MAPPO with energy-augmented observations plus runtime predictive action masking: a learned power predictor vetoes any action whose predicted draw would take battery below the critical threshold, with a threshold fallback.
evaluation: Robotarium, 7 agents, 5 seeds, baselines MAPPO and EA-MAPPO ablation; cumulative depletion -93.2%, mean depletion 0.004 vs 0.052, 100% vs 81.5% goal completion, 0 depletions in 70 real robot-trials; predictor 224 us per inference at 30 Hz.
contribution: A predictive energy mask that vetoes depletion-inducing actions of a multi-robot MARL policy at every control step, cutting training depletion events by 93% and transferring to hardware with zero depletions.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - MAPPO policy, and the masking predictor is itself a small learned MLP. Check whether the mask counts as a runtime interceptor: it is implemented inside the policy softmax (Equation 13), which a maintainer may read as a constraint inside the policy rather than a shield, though it is applied at every execution step on hardware, the null (halt) action always stays valid, and a battery-threshold fallback fires independently of the predictor. (c) not claimed: the measured hazard is per-robot battery depletion aggregated over the fleet, not an inter-agent interaction; collision avoidance is delegated to the Robotarium control barrier function and never measured. The 19x sample-efficiency headline is a training-speed claim, not a safety one; the energy predictor and its R2 numbers come from the authors' own prior paper [1]; physical evidence is 10 trials of 7 robots on one navigation task.

title: Robust Crop Classification Model Based on Asynchronous SAR and Optical Temporal Feature Fusion
evidence: "If the score exceeds the selected threshold, the current class and first acceptance date are recorded and locked; otherwise, the parcel remains in DEFER." (Sec. 2.6)
method: Gated cross-attention network fuses asynchronous Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 series; calibrated max probability is thresholded at six monthly checkpoints to accept and lock a crop label or defer.
evaluation: PASTIS-R five folds, frozen Brandenburg 2019; vs unimodal and fusion classifiers under the same accept rule. Macro-F1 80.57%; MCAC 0.45 vs 0.40; 7.55 d earlier; external selective risk 28.89% vs 5% target.
contribution: A SAR-optical crop classifier with a confidence-threshold accept-or-wait rule over monthly checkpoints, showing earlier acceptance than optical-only input but a selective-risk target that fails to transfer to another year.
flag: (ii) nominally: accept-or-defer is repeated over six checkpoints, but the main contribution is the fusion classifier (GCAT) and the deferral rule is a standard calibrated max-probability threshold chosen by a Clopper-Pearson bound, listed second of three contributions. No deferral mechanism is compared against another deferral rule or an ablation of it: all comparisons are GCAT vs Sentinel-2-only under the same policy, so the P3 evaluation floor for the defer mechanism is arguably unmet (would be E2 if treated as in scope). Deferral is waiting for more data, no human or fallback and no acting system. Authors themselves report the risk control failing out of year (28.89% empirical risk against a 5% target; mean confidence 0.95 on incorrect acceptances) and that the binomial bound ignores within-patch dependence. Fold-2 numbers differ between the primary and the post hoc Global SRC protocol (lead-time 7.55 d vs 10.48 d). No hardware or latency. Sections 2.1-2.5, 3.1 and 3.4 skimmed only.

title: Distributed multi-level supervision to effectively monitor the operations of a fleet of autonomous vehicles in agricultural tasks
evidence: "The value of the maximum time was defined to allow sufficient time to perform the following set of actions before a collision actually takes place: detecting the collision, alerting the operator and letting him act, if needed." (Section 4.1, Mission Supervisor)
method: Distributed three-level IF-THEN rule supervisor for an autonomous tractor fleet: onboard supervisors, a fleet-level mission supervisor whose collision supervisor forward-rolls planned trajectories, a fault recovery module that pauses and resumes units, and a severity-based alarm notification manager feeding an operator GUI.
evaluation: Two real RHEA field missions on a 42.5 m x 41.5 m plot with 1 and then 2 tractors: 6 predicted collisions, all 6 prevented by automatic pause; threshold ablations 0.5-1-1.5 km-h speed error and 0.5-1 s service disruption; monitoring 4 Hz, RTK-GPS 2 cm at 20 Hz, 0.5-1 s rollout step, 10 s resume delay; base station Intel i7 3.5 GHz, onboard embedded 1.33 GHz dual-core i7 plus LX150 FPGA. No external baseline system.
contribution: A distributed multi-level rule-based supervisor for a fleet of autonomous agricultural tractors that detects faults and impending inter-vehicle collisions at runtime, pauses vehicles automatically, and escalates severity-filtered alarms to a human operator who can take control.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - IF-THEN rule supervisor over RTK-GPS path-following tractors, so (a) and (c) fail the 2026-11-13 learned-system ruling and only (e) survives. (e) is built for but never measured: the operator is 'the final decision element', the alarm notification manager filters by severity so as not to overwhelm him, and the collision look-ahead is sized to let him act, yet there is no operator study and no situation-awareness or takeover metric - every reported outcome is of the automatic pause and resume. Likeliest overturn of this batch. Also check: the 6 of 6 collisions come from one 2-tractor mission and count safety-area incursions rather than actual contacts; no more than 3 vehicles were ever tested; the only comparisons are self-threshold sweeps; the 0.5 km-h sweep shows many false alarms and the authors defer alarm filtering to future work; latency is specified (4 Hz, thresholds) but never measured.

title: Classification with a deferral option and low-trust filtering for automated seizure detection
evidence: "Segments that contain a seizure flag are always deferred. Other segments are deferred based on their confidence score." (Sec. 2.5)
method: Pretrained SVM seizure detectors on behind-the-ear EEG; 5-min segments with lowest SVM confidence or trust score are deferred to a human annotator assumed perfect; low-trust 2-s windows are also filtered.
evaluation: Retrospective EEG, 54 patients, nested CV; SVM confidence vs trust scores, no deferral, random deferral. Sensitivity 89%/99% at 11%/36% deferred, 100% at 50%; filtering cuts false detections 21-43%. Trust score 1.6 ms per window, i5 laptop.
contribution: Measures how much wearable-EEG data must be deferred to a neurologist for near-perfect seizure detection sensitivity, and shows that filtering low-trust windows cuts false detections by 21-43%.
flag: (i), borderline with E4: deferral to a human expert is the title and first stated contribution, but the expert is assumed perfect and never modelled, so this is a risk-coverage curve for a confidence-ranked reject option on one retrospective dataset. A strict reading of 'classifier with a reject option applied to a domain' gives exclude-E4. Criterion e is weak: reviewer workload (number and length of deferred segments per 24 h) is reported but no human study. Doubts: deferral takes the same lowest-confidence percentage per patient, which needs the whole recording, so it is offline review triage and not an online decision; segments with a seizure flag are always deferred, so false detections go to zero by construction. The random-deferral baseline is only described in the Discussion, not tabulated. The second contribution (low-trust filtering) is not deferral. Authors state 50% deferral for perfect sensitivity is far from the 5-10% needed clinically. Results are read from figures (Figs 7-8), not tables. Sections 2.1-2.4, 2.6.2-2.6.3 and 3.3 skimmed only.

title: A Study on Rejecting Non-Target and Misclassified Motions for Robust Tactile-Sensor-Based Prosthetic Hand Control
evidence: "an input is rejected whenever the number of positive signs deviates from exactly one" (Sec. 2.5.4)
method: Parameter-free reject option (OvR-RO) for a one-vs-rest SVM: classification of a detected wrist-hand motion is withheld unless exactly one decision function is positive; compared with OCSVM and BPNN-entropy rejection.
evaluation: Offline; 9 healthy subjects, 12 sessions, 2 PVDF sensors, 6 motions. Vs Baseline SVM, BPNN-Entropy, OCSVM: accepted accuracy 84.5/93.0/84.7/90.0%; target rejection 32.3/28.7/14.5%; unknown 71.7/44.9/42.7%. No latency.
contribution: A sign-consistency reject rule on one-vs-rest SVM outputs withholds ambiguous prosthetic-hand motion classifications, rejecting 14.5% of target trials at 90.0% accepted accuracy in offline tests on nine subjects.
flag: none of (i)-(v): a per-event classifier with a reject option applied to one domain; rejection just suppresses output, no human, fallback or sequential deferral. All analysis is offline (Sec. 2.4) although the paper repeatedly claims real-time operability; no latency or compute figure is reported. Operating points for OCSVM and BPNN were chosen from ROC curves computed across all participants, i.e. on the evaluation data. 'Ambiguous' trials are defined as those the base classifier got wrong, so rejection precision is partly circular. OvR-RO is the weakest method on unknown motions (42.7%) and elbow flexion (35.5%, n=4 sessions). Healthy subjects only, no amputees.

title: A Safety-Governed Architecture for Adaptive Sequential Evidence Selection from Pre-Recorded Gait Data
evidence: "No generative output can override the result." (Section 3.6, Safety Governor, Simulator, and Adapter Boundary)
method: EARL: five fixed-function critics score candidate evidence probes with veto rights, and a deterministic hash-bound safety governor revalidates each probe and holds exclusive execution authority over a replayable ledger.
evaluation: 64 PhysioNet gait subjects, 3520 replay-verified runs, 11 predeclared conditions; entropy-reduction AUC 7.689 vs fixed 7.230, random 6.926, EIG 8.010, oracle 8.741; 10 of 10 safety challenges as expected.
contribution: A typed evidence-selection loop in which scoring agents hold proposal authority only and a deterministic hash-bound governor alone executes, demonstrated on retrospective gait records with full replay verification.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: borderline no - the authors state their evaluated critics are 'fixed scoring functions, not clinical specialists or LLMs', and only the fold-fitted diagonal-Gaussian likelihood is learned, so exclude-E1 under the Pillar-1 scope ruling is equally defensible and may be the maintainer's call. Chose E2 because the safety claim carries no quantitative result with a baseline or ablation: the safety critic emitted 0 vetoes across 9600 score cards and its ablation changed 0 of 1600 decisions, so the gate never fired in the primary benchmark; governor evidence is a 10-case predeclared conformance suite plus one constructed rejection (cadence 1.20 outside a 0.90-1.10 envelope). The primary endpoint is entropy reduction, not a hazard rate, and EARL loses to plain EIG on it. Authors explicitly disclaim physical-robot safety. Possible (e): moderate and high risk classes require explicit human approval, but no handoff or supervision quality is studied.

title: Agentic Lightweight Consensus for Resilient Monitoring and Control of Modern Data Centers in Smart Cities
evidence: "Without the verifier every unsafe proposal executes; with it, none do." (Section 7.3, caption of Table 14)
method: Two-path datacenter zone controller: a deterministic FPR-OWA plus persistent consensus fast path fuses trust-graded sensor reports, and a rule-based verifier admits or rejects every LLM-proposed actuation.
evaluation: 1890 scenarios and 7 deception families, 7560 safety episodes: 4409 unsafe executions without verifier vs 0 with it; 24 of 24 fault-injection cases; anomaly AUROC and FPR vs ground truth; CRP median 140-271 us, P95 298 us, 244 KiB at 100 sensors.
contribution: A datacenter control architecture that keeps generative reasoning off the critical path and admits only verifier-cleared actions, blocking 4409 unsafe LLM proposals at sub-millisecond consensus latency.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - ReAct and LLM supervisory agents proposing actuations. Best RQ1 and RQ5 evidence in this batch (sub-millisecond interception over a multi-agent zone, explicit unsafe-proposed, blocked and executed counts, verifier rejections and fallbacks). Doubts the authors raise themselves: the no-verifier vs verifier contrast is observational because those variants ran before the runtime contract was unified, so the verifier is not identified as the sole cause; the enforcement argument is explicitly not a formal non-bypassability proof; all plant behaviour is a first-order simulation; 'compatible with edge-class hardware' is asserted but only a CPU benchmark was run, so edge deployment is not credited; the diagnostic signal fired an attack-window alarm in only 14 of 42 attacked runs, and 627 ticks did not converge.

title: Learning Selective Deferral Policies for Reliable Medical Text Classification
evidence: "Based on this learned risk score, a decision rule determines whether a given input should be handled automatically or deferred to human experts." (Sec. 2.8)
method: Post hoc deferral policy: gradient-boosted error predictor over confidence, entropy, calibrated and MC-Dropout features, blended with calibrated confidence; top-risk sentences deferred to human review under fixed 5/10/20% budgets.
evaluation: PubMed 200k RCT test (29,493), three BERT backbones. Vs calibrated confidence threshold and random: system risk 0.1108 to 0.0360 at 20%; selective risk 0.0450 vs 0.0467. A100 GPU; MC extraction 434.8 s.
contribution: A learned error-aware deferral policy sends the riskiest biomedical sentence classifications to human review under fixed budgets, cutting simulated system risk from 0.1108 to 0.0360 at a 20% budget, only marginally better than confidence thresholding.
flag: (i) but BORDERLINE with E4: deferral to human review is the stated main contribution, yet the task is one-shot classification, the human is simulated by ground-truth labels (plus an assumed 95/90% reviewer accuracy), and the policy does not model the expert, so it is close to selective prediction ranked by an error estimator rather than true learning to defer. If the maintainer reads (i) as requiring a modelled or real expert, this is exclude-E4. Handoff itself is not studied, so no (e); the human handoff cell is nominal. Gain over the confidence baseline is 0.001-0.002 selective risk and significant only at the 20% budget (Table 5); the 67% risk cut comes from deferring per se under perfect review. Table 9 shows the unblended variant slightly beating the full proposed one at 20% (0.035975 vs 0.036042), and its 5% full value 0.084359 does not round to Table 2's 0.0845. Budget ranking is over the whole test set (batch), not a per-item online rule. Abstract numbers were found in the body. Not read: Sec. 4 tail (limitations) and Sec. 5.

title: Uncertainty-Driven Selective Prediction with Auditable Human Deferral for EEG Decoding of Participant-Rated Occupational Risk
evidence: "Deferral is policy-level and simulated: deferred trials are flagged for supervisor review, but no human judgements were collected." (Sec. 3.6)
method: Frozen LaBraM EEG encoder with calibrated four-class classifier; a deterministic peak-probability threshold (tau=0.5) retains or defers each trial; rule engine, template or optional LLM renders the audit report.
evaluation: 2634 EEG epochs, 31 workers, subject-grouped 3-fold. Balanced accuracy 0.6336 to 0.6829 at 71.49% coverage; cost 0.5816 to 0.5363 vs full automation; confidence AUC 0.6529. No latency.
contribution: A calibrated EEG decoder of self-rated occupational risk with a fixed confidence-threshold deferral gate gains modestly from abstention, and an added LLM reporting layer contributes no decision benefit over a rule engine.
flag: none of (i)-(v): one-shot selective prediction with a fixed max-probability threshold judged by risk-coverage; the 'human deferral' is only a flag, and the authors state no supervisor reviewed anything and no human-AI outcome was measured. The contribution is split between the classifier, the abstention analysis and an audit of the LLM reporting layer, so deferral is arguably not even the main contribution (E1 would also be defensible). No baseline deferral rule other than full automation and forced 50% coverage; benefit depends on illustrative costs (deferral beats automation in 40 of 64 cost settings). Risk-coverage is non-monotonic. The paper is unusually candid about its limits: 22 of 53 participants excluded, response-inclusive epochs with possible motor confounds, not stimulus-disjoint. LLM is named by a provider alias 'DeepSeek-V4-Flash'. Abstract numbers were found in the body. Sec. 3.1-3.5 and 4.1 only skimmed.

title: Predictive Modeling of Aircraft Dynamics Using Neural Networks
evidence: "There are eight state inputs (four for each of the two aircraft). There are also four action inputs (two for each of the two aircraft)." (Sec. I, Predictive Modeling Methods)
method: Fully connected residual network predicts next joint state of two adversarial aircraft from state and both actions, rolled out recurrently; bottleneck compressive encoder recovers hidden velocity; latent feeds neuroevolution controller.
evaluation: 2D sim and AFSIM 1v1. MSE test loss 0.00141 (encoder) vs 0.00172 full-info, 0.0256 no-velocity baselines; win rate 86.2 vs 81.4 vs 68.8%. Rollout accuracy qualitative only. No hardware or latency.
contribution: Extends the World Models framework to a two-aircraft adversarial engagement with a residual next-state predictor and a compressive encoder that recovers unobserved velocity, lowering prediction MSE from 0.0256 to 0.00141.
flag: Predictive accuracy: YES, a direct measure is reported, but thin - one table (Table 3) of MSE test loss with two baselines (full-information model 0.00172, no-velocity model 0.0256, compressive encoder 0.00141); it is not only downstream results. Downstream: Table 4 blue win rate vs scripted pure-pursuit opponent in AFSIM (86.2% +-3.7 over 6 runs vs 81.4% +-12.4 and 68.8% +-21.0 over 10 runs; unequal run counts, large variance, no significance test). Doubts the maintainer should weigh: (1) the paper's headline claim, that the residual skip connection gives near-perfect rollouts hundreds of steps ahead and the naive model fails, is supported ONLY qualitatively (Fig. 8, section titled Qualitative Evaluation); no MSE, horizon error or number is given for residual vs no-residual, so the main ablation is not quantitative. (2) Table 3 does not say whether MSE is one-step or multi-step, on what units or normalisation, test-set size, or number of seeds; the encoder beating the full-information baseline is explained only as presumably. (3) Multi-agent state is minimal: joint state of exactly 2 aircraft (8 variables: x, y, velocity, heading each) concatenated into an MLP; no graph, no interaction structure, simple kinematic sim; the abstract's claim of modelling multiple friendly and enemy aircraft is not tested beyond 1v1. (4) Table 3 appears to be on the simple 2D sim while Table 4 uses AFSIM 3D; the text does not state which data the Table 3 models were trained on. (5) The model is never used for imagined rollouts in control (stated as future work); the RNN encoder variant is described as worse with no numbers. Not a safety paper, no runtime interceptor (expected under the Pillar 2 ruling); RQ5 capped at 2. If the maintainer requires a quantitative ablation of the proposed predictor itself (not just the encoder), this drops to exclude-E2. Text carries a publisher download watermark (SAE Mobilus), no arXiv id.

title: Reversibility-Aware Staged Delegation for Enterprise Agentic AI: A Real-Options and Resilience Framework for Irreversible Actions
venue: Open Access Journal of Multidisciplinary Research
evidence: "an option-value decision rule that allocates each proposed action among direct execution, staged commit, human review, and block/defer modes" (Abstract)
method: RASD: runtime gate for agent actions scoring Action Recoverability Index and Non-Recoverable Exposure, then routing each action to direct execution, staged commit, human review or block by mode-adjusted utility.
evaluation: Monte Carlo, 120,000 synthetic tasks, distribution shift. Vs direct, confidence-threshold, expected-loss gate: net value 7.408 vs 5.735/5.282; severe incidents 0.390% vs 5.937/4.166%; failure rate 19.8%. No hardware or latency.
contribution: A recoverability-aware gate routes enterprise agent actions among direct execution, staged commit, human review and blocking, cutting severe incidents to 0.39% versus 4-6% for confidence and expected-loss gates in a synthetic simulation.
flag: (iv), also touches (i) and (ii) (per-action gate over 500-task episodes, but each task is decided independently). Meets the floor only through a fully synthetic, author-parameterised simulation: no real agent, LLM, tools or enterprise data. The headline result is largely built in, since staged mode is assigned a 0.58 failure-probability multiplier, contained severity and 0.90 benefit by assumption (Table III), and RASD stages 83.6% of tasks; the author says effect sizes should not be generalised. Proposition 1 is a one-line algebraic rearrangement, not a substantive theorem. Human review is 1.9% of RASD decisions with an assumed error reduction, so handoff is not studied (no e) and the human handoff cell is weak. Irreversibility is a static score, not a time budget, so the time-to-irreversibility cell is generous. Single author, low-profile multidisciplinary open-access journal (OAJMR), self-cites prior Tan work; no code link seen. The extracted text lost most equation symbols. Not read closely: Sec. II-III background and Sec. VI.B-D.

title: Combining Deep Reinforcement Learning and Safety Based Control for Autonomous Driving
evidence: Sec. 3.2: 'We then balance the weight of these three action outputs'; Sec. 4.1: 'we combine the learning policy actions and safety based control actions', with fixed weights alpha=0.4, beta=0.3, gamma=0.3.
method: Trains a DDPG driving policy in TORCS with no opponents present, then blends its steering and acceleration with an artificial potential field collision-avoidance term and a path-tracking controller using fixed weights.
evaluation: TORCS, four qualitative scenarios with 0, 1, 1 and 2 opponent vehicles (Fig. 6); no baseline and no ablation; no collision rate, success rate, lap time or tracking error; the only numbers are the DDPG training curve (average Q about 110 after about 13 hours), 36 potential-field distance inputs and a controller parameter table; GPU unspecified, no latency reported.
contribution: Blends a DDPG driving policy with an artificial potential field and a path tracker in fixed proportions so the learned controller keeps clear of opponent vehicles in TORCS.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a DDPG policy - so the 2026-11-13 ruling is satisfied, but (a) fails because the potential field is summed into the executed action with fixed weights and can never override, veto or halt it, and (c) fails the primacy test since no collision or hazard rate is reported. E2 is equally defensible and makes the exclusion robust either way: the evidence is four qualitative figures with no baseline and no ablation. If the maintainer counts a continuous weighted correction as interception, switch the code to E2 rather than include. Notation is inconsistent (gamma is both blend weight and discount factor, Eq. 12 uses lambda where Eq. 13 uses gamma).

title: VAIN: Attentional Multi-agent Predictive Modeling
evidence: Sec. 4 (Soccer): the task is to predict 'the position of each player for each time-step during the next 4 seconds'; Sec. 3 pools each agent's message by a softmax over -||a_i - a_j||^2 so that it averages 'only information from relevant agents'.
method: Vertex Attention Interaction Network: per-agent singleton and communication encoders plus a learned attention vector let each agent pool only relevant neighbours' messages, giving a factorised interaction network with linear rather than quadratic encoder evaluations.
evaluation: Chess next-piece prediction (about 600k examples, accuracy 0.301 vs IN 0.283, CommNet 0.272, FC 0.216, random 0.045), soccer 0.5-4.0 s player-position forecasting on SVPP with three leave-one-out splits (mean error 1.03 m vs IN 1.04, CommNet 1.04, PAD 1.08, static 1.84) and 50 bouncing balls in MuJoCo-free 2D (RMS 0.135 vs IN 0.139, CommNet 0.510, VEL0 0.561); ablations are attention vs average pooling and IN at matched compute (about 8x VAIN on chess); several hours on a K80, no latency and no safety metric.
contribution: Replaces uniform message pooling in multi-agent predictive models with learned per-agent attention, matching interaction networks on future-state prediction at a fraction of the interaction cost.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: n-a, this is a Pillar 2 (b) record. It clears the Pillar 2 scope only through the soccer and bouncing-ball tasks, which predict future multi-agent state over an implicit interaction graph; the chess task is classification of which piece moves next, not future state. A maintainer may still read it as a plain trajectory regressor and hence E1: there is no latent rollout, no recurrence (soccer uses a single frame), and the model is never used for control. Gains over IN and CommNet are tiny (1.03 vs 1.04 m, RMS 0.135 vs 0.139) with no seeds or error bars. Per protocol RQ5 is held low and no safety credit is given - there is no collision or hazard metric, only an attention picture of a ball described as on collision course. The 'only 4%' of IN's size or encoder evaluations figure is worded inconsistently between text and caption.

title: Safe Exploration in Continuous Action Spaces
evidence: Sec. 1: the layer acts 'after every policy query' and 'solves an optimization problem for finding the minimal change to the action'; Sec. 6: 'we compose an additional, last layer' that 'perturbs the original action as little as possible in the Euclidean norm'.
method: Pre-trains a neural model that is linear in the action for each safety signal from random-action transitions, then adds a closed-form last layer projecting the deterministic policy's action onto the safe half-space of the most violated constraint.
evaluation: MuJoCo Ball-1D, Ball-3D, Spaceship-Corridor and Spaceship-Arena, single agent, 10 seeds per task, against DDPG and DDPG plus reward shaping (margin swept over six values 0.08-0.23, penalty -1 or -1000); the safety layer accumulates zero constraint violations across all seeds in all four tasks, converges faster, and is the only method that converges on either Spaceship task, while reward shaping violates for every margin; reward-shaping violation fractions and all returns appear only in Figs. 5-6; 1000 pre-training episodes per task; no hardware and no measured latency.
contribution: Adds a closed-form safety layer that projects a deep policy's action onto a learned linear safety-signal constraint after every query, giving zero constraint violations during exploration.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a DDPG policy, corrected after every query, so (a) is clean. Single agent throughout, so the record carries no multi-agent evidence and a maintainer could test it against E4 wrong level; it survives because the interception is per-step and sequential rather than one-shot. Check the headline claim: zero violations holds only in MuJoCo with episodes that terminate on violation, and rests on Prop. 1's assumption that at most one constraint is active plus a safety model that is linear in the action and pre-trained from 1000 random-action episodes. The reward-shaping baseline's violation counts and every return are given as curves with no numbers in the text. The 'negligible' computational cost is asserted and never measured, so (d) was not credited, and the conservative-backup preemption mentioned for real systems is discussion only, not a human handoff.

title: Direct Uncertainty Prediction for Medical Second Opinions
evidence: Such a model could be deployed to automatically identify patients that might need a second doctor's opinion (Section 1, Introduction).
method: Direct Uncertainty Prediction: a network trained to score an input's expected expert disagreement directly, rather than post-processing a trained classifier's output distribution into an uncertainty score.
evaluation: Retinal fundus DR, Gaussian mixtures, blurred SVHN and CIFAR; baselines UVC Histogram-E2E and Histogram-PC; AUC 78.1 vs 76.6 disagreement, 86.2 vs 84.8 adjudicated, Spearman 0.682 vs 0.660; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Shows that predicting expert disagreement directly from the input beats scoring uncertainty from a trained classifier, giving a sharper triage signal for flagging cases to a second human reader.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - nothing is guarded, a CNN scores its own inputs. One-shot selective prediction: the human second opinion is motivation only, with no deferral policy, no cost model and no measured handoff, so Pillar 3 (i)-(v) fails on my reading. Most likely overturn of this batch: the unbiasedness and dominance analysis of DUP over UVC could be read as (v) foundational reject-option theory, and the medical-second-opinion framing as (i). All abstract numbers were located in Tables 1-5; no hardware or inference-time figure exists.

title: Temporal Logic Guided Safe Reinforcement Learning Using Control Barrier Functions
evidence: The RL action is integrated with the CLF-CBF-QP to solve for the final safe action (Section IV), and to ensure safety, CBF is always turned on during evaluation (Section VI.E).
method: An scTLTL specification compiled to an automaton supplies the RL reward plus CLF goals and CBF safe sets; a CLF-CBF quadratic program corrects the PPO action before execution.
evaluation: Simulated unicycle in a channel with two moving obstacles; ablations RL, RL+CBF, RL+CLF, RL+CLF+CBF; evaluation success rate over 20 trials plus plotted zero safety violations; values only in Figures 4-8; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Wraps a PPO policy in a CLF-CBF quadratic program driven by a temporal-logic automaton, keeping the agent inside the specified safe set during both learning and execution.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a PPO neural policy, filtered by the CLF-CBF quadratic program at execution time, so (a) is clean. Check the evaluation floor hard: there is no number anywhere in the body, no theorem, proposition or proof, no success rate and no violation count - only Figures 4-8 and qualitative claims such as agents trained with CBF exhibits higher success rates - so the maintainer may rule exclude-E2. Single agent only and the moving obstacles are uncontrolled, so no (c). Safety rests on known unicycle dynamics; K is given as about 1e10, which looks like a tuning artefact worth checking.

title: The Algorithmic Automation Problem: Prediction, Triage, and Human Effort
evidence: We develop a general framework that poses this latter decision, which instances the algorithm should handle, as an optimization problem (Abstract); instances not automated receive a fixed budget of human grades (Section 2.2).
method: Two-part automation framework: a predictor plus an offline triage rule ranking instances by predicted algorithmic error minus predicted human error, under a budget of human effort reallocated to the non-automated set.
evaluation: Diabetic retinopathy with adjudicated gold labels; baselines full automation and equal human coverage; triage-score ablations; error 5.5% human, 4% full automation, 3.5% optimal triage; zero-error subsets 44% vs 35%; holdout 24% vs 10%; no latency.
contribution: Frames automation as jointly choosing what to predict and which instances to keep for humans, showing that triaging cases to doctors beats both full automation and uniform human coverage.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - no mechanism guards a learned system, but the party deferred to is human, so this enters through the (e) carve-out with (a) deferral as the main claim and a measured handoff. Check (e): the human side is modelled only as an evenly split grading budget, with no takeover timing, situation awareness, transparency or trust measurement, so the maintainer may drop (e) and keep (a) alone. Triage is an offline ranking with no runtime override, so runtime_interceptor is no. Same authors and dataset as record 1807.01771 - possible overlap. Figures 4, 5, 7, 9 and 11 curves carry no printed values.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Probabilistic Guarantees for Autonomous Driving
evidence: The trained agent takes the acceptable actions that maximizes the Q function, where acceptable actions are those keeping collision-avoidance probability above 0.9999 (Section 4.2).
method: Probabilistic model checking precomputes per-state action sets satisfying an LTL collision-avoidance threshold; deep Q-learning explores and acts only within that set, defaulting to hard braking when it is empty.
evaluation: Unsignalised left turn with one car and one pedestrian, 10,000 Monte Carlo runs; baselines safe-random, rule-based, unconstrained RL; collisions 0.00% vs RL 0.63, 0.2 and 0.96% and rule-based 0.05, 2.18 and 3.62%; slower to goal; no latency.
contribution: Restricts a deep RL driving policy to actions a probabilistic model checker certifies as collision-free with probability 0.9999, giving zero collisions across 10,000 simulated unprotected left turns.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a deep Q-network, masked at execution time by precomputed acceptable action sets, so (a) is clean and the collision rate is the primary measured outcome. Check (c): the other car and the pedestrian are scripted rather than learned, and the two-obstacle case is handled by intersecting two single-agent acceptable sets, which the paper itself calls suboptimal since it does not leverage the interaction, so the maintainer may drop (c) and keep (a). The guarantee holds only for the discretised conservative model, and no value-iteration or per-step timing is reported despite the precomputation being the edge-relevant part. Safe RL is markedly slower to the goal (28.47 vs 22.16 steps), which is the real throughput cost.

title: Social-BiGAT: Multimodal Trajectory Forecasting using Bicycle-GAN and Graph Attention Networks
evidence: A graph attention network over a fully connected pedestrian graph plus a latent encoder jointly predicts 12 future timesteps for every pedestrian in the scene (Sections 3.4 and 4.1).
method: Conditional GAN with LSTM encoder-decoder generator, graph attention across all pedestrians, soft attention over a scene image, and a Bicycle-GAN style latent encoder giving controllable multimodal futures.
evaluation: ETH and UCY, five scenes, hold-one-out, 8 observed and 12 predicted steps, K=20; baselines linear, S-LSTM, S-GAN-P, Sophie; ablations GAT-only and BiGAN-only; average ADE and FDE 0.48 and 1.00 vs 0.54 and 1.15; no latency.
contribution: Couples graph attention over interacting pedestrians with a reversible latent encoder, cutting average final displacement error to 1.00 m and degrading far less than prior GANs when few samples are drawn.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - nothing is guarded, this is Pillar 2 (b) method evidence only. Check (b) against the scope ruling: it does predict future multi-agent state over a dynamic interaction graph with ADE and FDE plus two ablations, but it is a GAN trajectory forecaster with no action conditioning, no hazard or collision metric and no runtime use, so the maintainer may call it a plain trajectory regressor and rule exclude-E1. It is generative, so I did not credit non-generative inference. RQ5 capped at 1 per the protocol rule for predictors. Several HOTEL cells of Table 1 came back garbled in extraction, so the S-LSTM and S-GAN-P HOTEL values are unverified; the 0.15 m average FDE gain was located in Section 4.1.

title: Predicting Responses to a Robot's Future Motion using Generative Recurrent Neural Networks
evidence: Abstract: "This allows the model to learn the response of individuals with regards to a robot's motion from real world observations." - action-conditioned prediction over a spatio-temporal graph of multiple agents (Sec. 3.2).
method: Generative recurrent net (ResponseRNN): node and edge LSTMs with attention over a dynamic spatio-temporal graph, conditioned on the robot's next planned action, outputs bivariate Gaussians per agent.
evaluation: ARATH cattle-robot and Stanford Drone subsets; baselines CTRV, RED, Social-LSTM; ADE/FDE RRNN-Vel 0.462/0.906 m at t=20 on ARATH vs SLSTM 0.82/1.55; 250 ms inference, Titan-X.
contribution: Action-conditioned recurrent graph model that predicts how nearby humans or animals will respond to a robot's planned motion, evaluated on cattle-herding and pedestrian data.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - nothing is guarded, included only under (b) as action-conditioned prediction over a dynamic multi-agent graph. Borderline: maintainer may rule this a plain trajectory regressor (direct position and velocity output, no latent state, never closed into a planner or safety filter) and overturn to exclude-E1. No safety metric at all, only ADE/FDE. The response-modelling claim is supported only qualitatively, and Sec. 4.3 admits some simulated responses "do not make sense". 250 ms inference for 5 agents is far above any real-time budget. No ablation isolating the robot-action input, so its benefit is not separated from other architecture differences.

title: Multiple Futures Prediction
evidence: Abstract: "learns semantically meaningful latent variables to represent the multimodal future, without requiring explicit labels"; joint interactive step-wise rollouts of all agents with per-agent discrete latent modes (Sec. 3).
method: Multiple Futures Prediction: per-agent encoder-decoder GRUs with discrete per-agent latent modes and dynamic RBF attention encoding, trained by an EM-style variational bound, with interactive joint rollouts.
evaluation: CARLA, CARLA-PRECOG, NGSIM, Argoverse; baselines DESIRE, ESP, MultiPath, CS-LSTM; NLL 1.39 vs RNN 5.64 (CARLA), minMSD 0.284 vs ESP 0.675 (Town01); CARLA RL crash rate 0% vs DDPG 6%.
contribution: Probabilistic multi-agent trajectory model with discrete latent modes and interactive rollouts, supporting hypothetical ego-conditioned prediction and strong likelihood results on CARLA, NGSIM and Argoverse.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - this is a prediction model with no interceptor. Include under (b) only, RQ5 held at 2 per protocol. The CARLA crash rates (MFP 0% vs DDPG 6%, PPO 15%) come from a shooting-method planner built on the predictor, not a runtime gate, so (c) fails the primacy test. Several Table 3 and Table 7 cells were unreadable in the fetched PDF: maintainer should re-check the hypothetical-rollout and full crash-rate numbers. NGSIM minimum-over-samples metrics use ground truth to select the best trajectory, which the paper itself calls "overly optimistic". No inference latency reported, only 1.2 s per training batch update.

title: Learning to Switch Among Agents in a Team via 2-Layer Markov Decision Processes
evidence: Sec. 2: "the switch value is given by a (deterministic and time-varying) switching policy" choosing at each step whether the human or the RL-trained machine acts; Algorithm 1 lines 8-10 deploy it on the true environment.
method: Control switching as a 2-layer MDP; UCRL2-MC builds L1 confidence sets over each agent's policy and the environment transitions, then solves a Bellman recursion for the per-step switching policy.
evaluation: Simulated three-lane driving, horizon 10, 20k episodes; baselines finite-horizon UCRL2, human-only and machine-only; metric total regret (figures only, no numbers); Theorem 2 proves a sublinear regret bound.
contribution: Casts human-machine control switching as a 2-layer MDP and gives an online algorithm with a sublinear regret bound that learns when to hand driving control back to a human.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the machine agent is an RL policy trained only on no-car environments, and the switching policy decides at every step whether it or the human acts. TITLE MISMATCH but not a wrong paper: the fetched version is titled "Learning to Switch Between Machines and Humans", same authors (Balazadeh Meresht, De, Singla, Gomez-Rodriguez) and same 2-layer-MDP and UCRL2-MC content; the record title is a later arXiv version title. Evaluation floor is met only through the proved regret bound plus the UCRL2, human-only and machine-only baselines: no numeric regret values appear in the text (Figures 2-5 only) and there is no collision or violation rate. (e) rests on a simulated noisy-cost human with no human subjects, and handoff cost is a single scalar switching cost, so the maintainer may drop (e). The paper concedes its bound is worse than plain UCRL2.

title: Counterfactual Policy Evaluation for Decision-Making in Autonomous Driving
evidence: Abstract: "the policy is only executed after the counterfactual policy evaluation has been performed"; if collision probability exceeds rho_max "the ego vehicle is controlled by a lane-following model" (Sec. III).
method: Replaces nearby vehicles' policies with constant-acceleration variants, rolls out 1 s, averages collision probability, and executes the learned SAC policy only below threshold rho_max, else a lane-following fallback.
evaluation: BARK highway merging, 250 episodes per threshold; baseline the ungated SAC policy (32% success, 48% collisions); gated at rho_max=0 gives 0% collisions, 99.8% goal reached, policy executed 76% of the time.
contribution: A runtime gate that simulates counterfactual behaviours of surrounding vehicles and hands control to a rule-based fallback whenever a learned driving policy's collision probability exceeds a threshold.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a SAC reinforcement-learning driving policy is gated before each execution, the strongest (a) record in this batch. (c) is borderline: hazards are assessed over several surrounding vehicles, but only the ego is the policy under test and the other agents are rule-based Mobil models, so the maintainer may drop (c). The paper names the fallback IDM in Sec. III and Mobil in Sec. IV-C, an internal inconsistency. No latency or hardware figures despite a 1 s counterfactual horizon and a 0.2 s step time, so real-time feasibility is unverified. No numbers for intermediate rho_max, no fallback-only baseline, and it is unclear whether 99.8% is over all episodes or only executed ones. The counterfactual rollouts are non-generative but the paper never frames them that way, so I did not claim that gap cell.

title: EvolveGraph: Multi-Agent Trajectory Prediction with Dynamic Relational Reasoning
evidence: Abstract: "explicit relational structure recognition and prediction via latent interaction graphs among multiple heterogeneous, interactive agents"; the graph is re-encoded every tau steps and evolved by a GRU (Sec. 4.2).
method: Latent interaction-graph model: Gumbel-softmax edge-type encoder over agent pairs, GRU decoder with Gaussian-mixture output, and a graph-evolution GRU that re-encodes the graph every tau steps; two-stage training.
