evaluation: Synthetic particles, H3D, NBA, SDD; baselines STGAT, Social-STGCNN, Trajectron++, NRI; SDD minADE20 13.9 vs STGAT 18.8 px; changing-relation edge accuracy 82.3% vs NRI 71.5%; static-graph and single-stage ablations.
contribution: Predicts and evolves latent interaction graphs among heterogeneous agents, improving multi-agent trajectory forecasting on driving, sports and pedestrian benchmarks over static-graph and attention baselines.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - prediction model with no interceptor, include under (b) only and hold RQ5 at or below 2 per protocol. The dynamically re-encoded latent graph puts it clearly past the static-graph exclusion, but there is no safety metric, no collision rate and no absolute latency figure (Fig. 5 gives NBA test time only rescaled to [0,1]), so it is architecture evidence only. Absolute minADE and minFDE values in the benchmark tables were misaligned in the fetched PDF and the H3D table's time labels contradict the text: only the SDD numbers and the percentage reductions are reliable, so the maintainer should re-check them. No NLL reported despite a Gaussian-mixture decoder.

title: Pessimism About Unknown Unknowns Inspires Conservatism
evidence: "To informally summarize our results in a more memorable form: pessimists respect precedent." (Sec. 7, Conclusion)
method: Idealised Bayesian RL agent that maximises worst-case return over top-posterior world-models and, with vanishing probability, defers action selection to a mentor.
evaluation: Theory only: proves mentor-level value in the limit (Cor. 6), query probability to 0 (Cor. 7), probable avoidance of unprecedented events (Thm 11). No experiments, baselines, hardware or latency.
contribution: Proves that a pessimistic Bayesian reinforcement learner that sometimes defers to a mentor reaches mentor-level reward, defers ever less often, and with high probability never causes unprecedented events.
flag: (ii) and (i): deferral to a mentor as a step-wise action in general RL; purely theoretical, NO experiment of any kind. The theory exemption in the scope note is worded for (v) reject-option theory; this is proved theory of deferral in RL, so the maintainer must decide whether the floor is met - if not, exclude-E2. Deferral is one of two pillars (pessimism is the other). Agent is intractable in general; results are asymptotic, no finite regret bound. runtime_interceptor set to no because pure theory, although the agent as defined does defer at execution time.

title: Preferential Mixture-of-Experts: Interpretable Models that Rely on Human Expertise as much as Possible
evidence: Abstract: 'augments human expertise in decision making with a data-based classifier only when necessary for predictive performance'; the gate routes each input to the fixed human rule or to the ML expert at prediction time (Sec. 3).
method: Preferential mixture-of-experts: an interpretable gate maximises reliance on fixed human decision rules subject to a predictive-performance constraint, solved by log-barrier and projected-gradient algorithms.
evaluation: HIV (36780 patients) and MDD (3865) prescribing; baselines ML-only, standard MoE, two learn-to-defer methods; AUC 0.74 vs 0.64-0.71; soft coverage 63.2% vs 52.9-56.8%; no hardware or latency reported.
contribution: Trains an interpretable gate that maximises use of human clinical decision rules while meeting a performance floor, deferring to a learned classifier only where the rules are inadequate.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the gate overrides a learned classifier in favour of fixed human rules, but no live human acts. Check against Pillar 3 scope: deferral is the main contribution, yet the setting is one-shot selective prediction, non-sequential, no safety-critical runtime gate, and the deferral target is a static rule set rather than a person, so exclude-E4 is plausible. Learn-to-defer baselines failed to train on MDD and are absent from Table 3; the accuracy-coverage curves in Figs. 3 and 5 are not tabulated.

title: Learning Safe Multi-Agent Control with Decentralized Neural Barrier Certificates
evidence: Sec. 4.3: 'We propose a spontaneous online policy refinement approach that produces even safer control policies in testing' - at each test step the learned barrier certificate's gradient modifies the agent's action before execution.
method: Jointly learns decentralized neural control barrier certificates and controllers with a quantity-permutation-invariant neighbour encoder; at test time gradient-based online policy refinement adjusts each agent's action to satisfy the certificate.
evaluation: Simulated ground robots and drones, 8-1024 agents; baselines MAMPS, PIC-Safe, MADDPG-Safe, S2M2; safety rate 0.9956 with refinement vs 0.9741 without at 1024 agents; refinement fires on under 17% of steps.
contribution: Decentralized neural barrier certificates learned jointly with controllers scale from eight to 1024 agents, with test-time policy refinement raising the multi-agent safety rate from 0.974 to 0.996.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - learned neural policies with learned certificates. Refinement is gradient descent on the certificate rather than a hard veto or a QP, and the authors state the method 'still cannot guarantee that the agents are 100% safe' (Sec. 5). Only the Table 1 refinement ablation is tabulated; all baseline safety rates and rewards are shown graphically in Figs. 4-6 and 8. Simulation only, no hardware, and the 1024-agent result is produced by copying trained parameters to extra agents.

title: Differentiable Learning Under Triage
evidence: "Given any predictive model and desired level of triage, the optimal triage policy is a deterministic threshold rule" (Sec. 1, Our contributions)
method: Joint training of a model and a triage policy under a budget on human workload; optimal policy thresholds expected model loss minus human loss; SGD on model-assigned instances.
evaluation: Synthetic, Hatespeech (24,783 tweets) and Galaxy Zoo (10,000 images) with recorded crowd labels; baselines: confidence, score, surrogate and full-automation triage; test misclassification vs budget; Tesla V100; no latency.
contribution: Proves that the optimal triage policy between a model and human experts is a deterministic threshold rule and gives a convergent gradient method to train model and policy together.
flag: (i) and (v): deferral to human experts plus foundational theory (Thm 3 optimal threshold rule, Thm 7 convergence to a neighbourhood for convex losses; no generalisation bound or rate). One-shot, not sequential. Real-data error values appear only in figures, the text gives no numbers; only synthetic losses are stated (0.0009 triage-trained with optimal triage vs 0.0053 full automation). Human predictions sampled from recorded labels, no live humans. human handoff cell is weak: handoff itself is not studied.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning Using Advantage-Based Intervention
evidence: Sec. 3.1: actions whose advantage over the backup policy exceeds the threshold lie in the intervention set and the backup policy acts instead, so unsafe actions are overridden at execution time in every training rollout.
method: SAILR intervenes when an action's advantage over a user-supplied backup policy exceeds a threshold, substituting the backup and penalising the agent in an absorbing surrogate MDP optimised with PPO.
evaluation: Point-robot and half-cheetah safe-RL tasks, 10 and 8 seeds; baselines CPO, PDO, CSC; 'orders of magnitude fewer safety violations' in training, deployment return comparable to CPO; Theorems 1-2 bound safety and suboptimality.
contribution: Advantage-based intervention keeps a reinforcement learner safe throughout training by swapping in a backup policy whenever an action is too costly, with bounds on both safety and suboptimality.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an RL policy. Single agent, so criterion (c) does not hold. The evaluation floor is met only through the proved guarantees plus figure-based baseline comparison: the paper contains no numeric table of violations, returns or intervention counts anywhere, including the appendix, so no safety figures can be quoted. The shield is removed at deployment, and the height-heuristic variant is 'consistently unsafe in deployment' - only the MPC variant stays safe. The non-generative-inference cell applies to the fitted-Q rule; the MPC variant does generative rollouts.

title: Pre-emptive learning-to-defer for sequential medical decision-making under uncertainty
evidence: "we pose the problem of learning-to-defer as model-based reinforcement learning (RL)" (Abstract)
method: SLTD: deferral added as an action in a non-stationary MDP; defers to the expert policy when posterior probability that deferring now beats delaying exceeds a threshold, using Bayesian model-based RL.
evaluation: Toy MDP, simglucose diabetes simulator, EuResist HIV data (32,960 patients); baselines: Mozannar-Sontag, Madras, augmented-MDP, stationary, one-step and K=1 ablations; expected outcome and deferral frequency; CPU only, no latency.
contribution: Sequential learning-to-defer posed as model-based RL: the policy defers pre-emptively to a clinician policy before the automated policy reaches harmful states, with uncertainty decomposed to explain each deferral.
flag: (ii) and (i): deferral as an action over time to a human expert policy. Title of the fetched arXiv version is "Learning-to-defer for sequential medical decision-making under uncertainty" (no "Pre-emptive"); same paper, different version title. Experts are simulated or logged clinician policies, no live handoff, evaluation is offline. Value: SLTD 8.03 vs 6.37 (Mozannar) synthetic; 36.93 vs 35.39 (Madras) diabetes; HIV I 14.79 vs expert alone 14.12 (small margin). Deferral frequency 0.34-0.51, not the lowest. No theorem with proof (definition and corollary only). time-to-irreversibility cell is my reading of pre-emptive deferral before harmful states; paper has no explicit deadline or time budget, maintainer may drop it. human handoff cell likewise weak.

title: Safe Control with Neural Network Dynamic Models
evidence: Sec. 4.1 and 4.3: each step solves a one-step mixed-integer program for the control closest to the reference that satisfies the synthesised safety index, so an unsafe reference control is replaced online.
method: MIND encodes a ReLU neural network dynamics model as mixed-integer constraints and solves a one-step safe tracking problem online; SIS synthesises a feasible safety index offline with CMA-ES.
evaluation: Three learned unicycle NNDMs, 100 collision-avoidance and 100 safe-following tasks; baselines shooting with 10^3-10^5 samples and Ipopt; learned index 0% violation and 0% infeasible vs 100% and 56% for the original; 0.36-2s per step on a 24-core Threadripper.
contribution: Synthesises a persistently feasible safety index offline and enforces it online as a mixed-integer program over a neural network dynamics model, giving zero safety violations with near-exact tracking.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: partly - the dynamics model is a neural network, but the nominal controller is a hand-designed reference tracker and no learned policy is being guarded, so the scope ruling is borderline and a maintainer could read this as classical safe control over a learned model. Criterion (d) is weak: per-step solve times of 0.36-2s on a 24-core desktop with an arbitrary 2s cutoff, no deadline, no jitter analysis and no edge hardware, so (d) and the latency cell may both be dropped. Single agent with obstacles, not multi-agent. Evaluation rolls out the same NNDM used for control, so there is no model mismatch and the authors concede violations may occur if the NNDM differs from the true dynamics (Sec. 6).

title: Teaching Humans When To Defer to a Classifier via Examplars
evidence: "the human is taught through a tailored onboarding phase how to make decisions with the help of the AI" (Sec. 1)
method: Greedy selection of teaching exemplars so a human learns an accurate mental model of when to rely on a fixed classifier; the human, not the AI, decides to defer.
evaluation: 150 MTurk workers on HotpotQA with simulated AI; baselines: no-teaching, LIME-teaching; overall, defer and non-defer F1; simulated users and CIFAR-10 selection baselines; no latency.
contribution: Exemplar-based onboarding that teaches people when to rely on a classifier, with a submodular greedy selection guarantee and a 150-person crowd study.
flag: none of (i)-(v): direction is reversed, the HUMAN chooses whether to defer to the AI; the automation never withholds or hands off, so no runtime interceptor. Could be argued under ft-extract (e) human-factors, maintainer to decide. Evidence is weak: overall F1 58.2 teaching vs 57.6 no-teaching (not significant), defer F1 worse with teaching (50.7 vs 57.8), only non-defer F1 improved (67.6 vs 57.6); AI in user study is simulated. Record title says Examplars, paper says Exemplars. Read first 100k of 129k characters (appendix tail unread).

title: Lazy-MDPs: Towards Interpretable Reinforcement Learning by Learning When to Act
evidence: The lazy-MDP adds "a new mode of action available: being lazy, which defers decision-making to a default policy" (Abstract)
method: Lazy-MDP: augments an MDP with a lazy action that hands each step to a default policy and charges a cost for taking control, so the agent learns when to act.
evaluation: Gridworlds and Atari, random or pretrained default policy, vs standard DQN: Gravitar near 100 percent of DQN score under 10 percent control; PrivateEye over 100 percent at about 20 percent.
contribution: Lazy-MDPs let a reinforcement-learning agent defer each step to a default policy unless taking control is worth a cost, with proved optimality conditions and Atari agents matching DQN while controlling few steps.
flag: (ii) sequential setting where deferring is a per-step action. NOT a safety paper: the aim is interpretability and exploration, and the fallback is a random or half-trained policy, never a human or safeguard; exclude-E1 is defensible on relevance. The direction is inverted relative to a shield (the learned agent overrides the default when the lazy-gap exceeds the cost). Evaluation floor is thin: Atari numbers are approximate readings stated in prose from figures (3 seeds); the interpretability evidence is qualitative. Theory is proved in appendices (Bellman equation for the cost term, contraction, lazy-gap threshold rule, bounds on the cost). No human, latency or hazard metric.

title: On the Utility of Prediction Sets in Human-AI Teams
venue: International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence
evidence: "Our evaluation on human subjects finds that set valued predictions positively impact experts." (Abstract); Sec. 7 reports significant gains in "reported utility, trust, and accuracy" for the deferral variant
method: D-CP: a learned deferral policy (Mozannar-Sontag loss) sends hard examples to the human expert and conformal prediction sets are calibrated and shown only for non-deferred examples.
evaluation: CIFAR-100, CIFAR-10H, Prolific studies (30 and 60 participants); RAPS set size 3.75 to 2.36 at 0.2 deferral; human accuracy D-RAPS 0.76 vs RAPS 0.67 (p=0.002), trust 8.00 vs 6.87.
contribution: Shows with human-subject studies that conformal prediction sets raise expert trust, and that deferring hard examples to the expert before conformalising shrinks sets and improves human accuracy from 0.67 to 0.76.
flag: (i) deferral to a human expert, with the handoff studied on real participants. BORDERLINE on MAIN contribution: the headline is the utility of prediction sets; deferral (D-CP) is the second of two contributions though it fills Sec. 4-7. Exclude-E1 is defensible. One-shot image classification, nothing sequential or safety-critical. Inconsistencies: the abstract says n=120 participants but the sections sum to 30+60=90 (plus a 20-person control); Table 4 caption says alpha=0.1 while Figures 6-7 use 0.05. Theorem 1 (smaller sets for non-deferred examples) is proved only for scores monotone in softmax probability. Empirical coverage is only in a figure.

title: Forming Effective Human-AI Teams: Building Machine Learning Models that Complement the Capabilities of Multiple Experts
venue: International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence
evidence: The approach "trains a classifier to complement the capabilities of multiple human experts" (Abstract)
method: Joint training of a classifier and an allocation network assigning each instance to one of several human experts or the classifier, with cross-entropy on the weighted team prediction as surrogate.
evaluation: Hate speech, CIFAR-100 (synthetic experts), NIH chest X-ray (real radiologists); six baselines incl. JSF; NIH team accuracy 95.45, 91.72, 90.36, 91.51 vs best expert 95.34, 91.01, 88.84, 91.31. No hardware.
contribution: Jointly trains a classifier and an allocation system that defers each instance to the best of several human experts or the model, beating the best radiologist and prior multi-expert deferral on NIH chest X-rays.
flag: (iii) deferral among multiple experts, also (i). One-shot classification, no sequential or latency aspect. Real radiologist labels only on NIH, where the margin over the best expert is small for some teams (0.11 points for the first team); Twitter and CIFAR-100 experts are synthetic and only relative gains are given in the text (e.g. 3.66 and 19.77 percent over JSF), absolute values are in figures. Appendices (gradient analysis, extra results) are not in the arXiv text I read. No consistency proof for the surrogate.

title: Attacking Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning by Adversarial Minority Influence
evidence: Sec. 5.3: 'our AMI outperforms the competing methods in 10 out of 12 environments' - one adversarial agent drives MAPPO-trained cooperative teams into worst-case joint behaviour in SMAC, multi-agent MuJoCo and a 10-robot swarm.
method: Adversarial Minority Influence trains one black-box adversarial agent using a unilateral mutual-information influence filter and a targeted adversarial oracle to push fixed cooperative MARL victims toward worst-case joint actions.
evaluation: Six SMAC and six multi-agent MuJoCo tasks plus 10 e-puck2 robots; baselines Gleave, Wu, Guo and GMA; best in 10 of 12 tasks and 5.43 better than the best real-world baseline; ablations on the unilateral and targeted terms.
contribution: Shows that a single adversarial agent can collapse cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, with the first such attack demonstrated on a real ten-robot swarm.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: the system analysed is learned (MAPPO victims), but nothing is guarded - this is an attack only, with no detector, shield, monitor or defence, and 'during execution the attacker acts on its own without the guidance of TAO' (Sec. 4.2). Criterion (a) fails outright and (c) holds only if 'multi-agent hazard' is read as induced emergent failure rather than detection, so this is the record in the batch most likely to be overturned to exclude-E1. Win rates and rewards appear only in Figs. 4, 6 and 9-12; the only in-text figures are the 5.43 margin and 10 of 12 environments, and no defence or mitigation is evaluated.

title: Identifying the Risks of LM Agents with an LM-Emulated Sandbox
evidence: Sec. 3-4 (paraphrase): an LM emulates tool execution so risky LM-agent trajectories can be elicited without real effects, and an LM safety evaluator scores the completed trajectory afterwards.
method: LM-emulated sandbox simulates 311 tools in 36 toolkits for tool-calling LM agents; an adversarial emulator steers toward risky states; LM evaluators score safety and helpfulness 0-3 post hoc.
evaluation: 144 curated cases, 9 risk types. Failure incidence: GPT-4 39.4%, Claude-2 44.3%, ChatGPT-3.5 62.0%, GPT-4 safety prompt 23.9%, NoAct 0%. Evaluator kappa 0.478 vs human 0.480. No latency.
contribution: ToolEmu emulates tool execution with an LM so risky LM-agent trajectories can be elicited and scored at scale, quantifying failure incidence across agents and safety prompts.
flag: RULED OUT by the between-agents ruling of 2026-11-13: Benchmark eliciting risky trajectories from a single tool-calling agent against emulated tools; LM emulator and evaluator are measurement, not defence | original draft was include. learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM tool-calling agents are the system analysed. No runtime override exists (emulator and evaluator are offline), so (a) fails and (c) rests on the "safety evaluation of LLM agents" clause with a single agent, not peer agents: check whether that is (c) or exclude-E4 wrong level. Real-world replication covered only 7 Terminal cases, and the emulator itself had an 8.1-14.4% critical-issue rate, which bounds how much the failure percentages mean.

title: Learning to Make Adherence-Aware Advice
evidence: The model "incorporates a defer option so that the machine can temporarily refrain from making advice" (Abstract)
method: Episodic MDP where the machine advises a human, adhering with unknown probability, or defers to the human's own policy; UCB-AD and reward-free algorithms learn advice under penalty or budget.
evaluation: Proved: UCB-AD PAC sample complexity O~(H^2 S^2 A/eps^2); RFE-beta O(H^5 S A/eps^2); budgeted CMDP corollary. Flappy Bird and Car Driving simulations vs EULER and UC-CFH, results only in figures.
contribution: A sequential advice model in which the machine learns when to advise a partly adherent human and when to defer, with provable sample-complexity gains over problem-agnostic reinforcement learning.
flag: (ii) sequential setting with defer as an action over time, also (i) deferral to a human. Borderline on MAIN contribution: deferral is one of two pillars, adherence modelling is the other; exclude-E1 is defensible if the maintainer reads adherence as primary. Theory paper in spirit; the floor is met by proved theorems, but I found NO numeric experimental value in the text, only qualitative descriptions of Figures 2-4. Text was truncated at about 100000 of 112359 characters, mid-proof in Appendix A.3.2; the Car Driving appendix was not read. Humans are simulated policies with assumed adherence 0.9/0.7. The machine advises rather than acts, so it is not a safety veto.

title: Rule-Based Lloyd Algorithm for Multi-Robot Motion Planning and Control with Safety and Convergence Guarantees
evidence: Sec. 3-4 (paraphrase): each robot's motion is confined to its own Lloyd cell, so collision freedom is proved by construction (Theorem 1) rather than by intercepting a nominal action, and success rate is the measured outcome.
method: Rule-based Lloyd coverage control: neighbour-weighted cells with rules adapting spreading factor and attraction point; optional PPO layer (LLB) sets those parameters; unicycle and car-like MPC variants.
evaluation: Crossing-circle and random-room sims to N=300, plus JetRacer, Jackal, Dingo and 7 drones. Success rate 1.00 vs RVO2 0.65 and SBC and GCBF+ 0.00; compute 2-10 ms, MPC adds 16 ms. No collision rate.
contribution: Rule-based Lloyd controller gives collision-free, deadlock-free multi-robot motion with proved convergence without communication, scaling to 300 simulated robots and tested on ground and aerial platforms.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: partly - the main RBL controller is hand-designed classical control (Pillar 1 ruling: E1), but the LLB variant wraps a PPO policy whose outputs are clipped and projected by the Lloyd layer at runtime, lifting success rate from 0.04-0.94 to 1.00. (c) also fails the primacy test: no collision rate is reported and the measured outcome is success rate, i.e. deadlock and convergence. Most likely overturn in this batch if the maintainer reads LLB as a runtime safety layer on a learned policy.

title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion
evidence: Sec. 3 (paraphrase): trusted monitoring audits the 2% most suspicious GPT-4 solutions, submits the trusted model's solution instead when suspicion crosses a threshold, and shuts down to trusted-only once a backdoor is confirmed.
method: Control evaluation of protocols gating an untrusted GPT-4 coder: GPT-3.5 suspicion monitoring, deferral to trusted, trusted editing, untrusted monitoring with redaction and paraphrasing, under a 2% audit budget.
evaluation: 1500 APPS problems vs a red-team backdoor attack policy. Safety/usefulness percent: trusted-only 100/2, upfront audit 15/100, trusted monitoring 62/97, plus defer 83/93, trusted editing 92/94. No latency.

contribution: A position paper arguing that LLM multi-agent trustworthiness needs comprehensive vulnerability analysis, with a taxonomy and a small inter-agent prompt-injection study on a planner-executor pipeline.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an LLM-MAS planner-executor is analysed, but nothing is guarded. The paper's own title begins "Position:" and the contribution is a taxonomy plus threat-model framework, hence E3; exclude-E2 applies equally since the single experiment has no baseline, no single-agent comparison and no ablation. All defences, including the monitor agents, are conceptual. Check Table 2: the Harmful and Privacy rows are identical at planner_start and executor_end. Table 1 ASRs (TAMAS 76-94 pct, AgentDojo 50 pct) are quoted from prior work, not measured here.

title: MAEBE: Multi-Agent Emergent Behavior Framework
evidence: Sec. 3.3.4: with a misaligned "red-team" supervisor in the star topology, peer pressure rose from 28.5 pct (benign) to 43.9 pct, an ensemble-level effect absent from single-agent evaluation.
method: MAEBE: an evaluation framework posing Greatest Good Benchmark questions and double-inverted variants to single agents and to six-model round-robin, homogeneous and star-supervisor ensembles, scored by an LLM judge.
evaluation: 6 frontier and open LLMs, 90 GGB questions x12 repetitions, 237k responses; single-agent baseline plus topology, length, visibility and persona ablations; Table 3 IH p=0.00 r=0.42; peer pressure 28.5 to 43.9 pct.
contribution: MAEBE shows that LLM moral preferences shift under question framing and under peer and supervisor influence in ensembles, so single-agent alignment evaluation misses emergent group risks.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: which - LLM ensembles are analysed, not guarded; there is no runtime mechanism, no tool use and no memory (Sec. 5.1), and the only stop is a four-round cap. Check the evaluation floor: no collision, violation, hazard or intervention rate exists - outcomes are GGB Likert distributions, significance tests and LLM-judge rationale shares, so exclude-E2 is defensible. Single vs round-robin first answer showed no significant difference (all p>0.20, r<=0.03), which weakens the emergence claim. Judge accuracy was never human-validated; 24.9 pct of Gemini and 23.9 pct of Llama responses were discarded. Abstract names the framework "Multi-Agent Emergent Behavior Evaluation" while the running header matches the record title.

title: Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections
evidence: Abstract: "we propose a set of principled design patterns for building AI agents with provable resistance to prompt injection" (Abstract).
method: Six architectural design patterns (action-selector, plan-then-execute, LLM map-reduce, dual LLM, code-then-execute, context-minimization) that keep untrusted data out of an LLM agent's control flow.
evaluation: No quantitative evaluation: ten qualitative case studies (OS, SQL, email, booking, medical, software agents) mapped to patterns; no metrics, baselines, ablations, latency or hardware.
contribution: Catalogue of six design patterns that structurally bound what a prompt injection can reach in an LLM agent, illustrated by ten case studies with threat models but no measurement.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM tool-calling agents. Fails the evaluation floor: no quantitative result and no theorem, lemma or proof anywhere despite the abstract claiming "provable resistance" (checked body and appendix), hence E2. Criterion (a) fails too: the patterns are architectural constraints, and user confirmation appears only as an optional best practice in Appendix A. Maintainer may prefer E3 if a design-pattern/position paper counts as tutorial-like.

title: AGENTSAFE: Benchmarking the Safety of Embodied Agents on Hazardous Instructions
evidence: Section 4.4: SAFE-AUDIT "corrects it by generating a new thought that explicitly conveys a refusal to execute the instruction" (Section 4.4).
method: Benchmark (SAFE-THOR sandbox on AI2-THOR, SAFE-VERSE hazardous-task suite, SAFE-DIAGNOSE protocol) plus SAFE-AUDIT, a zero-shot GPT-4o auditor that rewrites or refuses the agent's thought before planning.
evaluation: AI2-THOR, 45 scenes, 9 VLMs plus ReAct/ProgPrompt, 6 jailbreaks; GR/HR/PRR/PSR/TSR; baselines AgentSpec and ThinkSafe; ThinkSafe cuts normal TSR up to 14.96%, SAFE-AUDIT lifts it 2.22%, hazardous TSR 0.48%.
contribution: Benchmark of embodied VLM agents on hazardous and jailbroken instructions that separates perception, planning and execution failures, plus a thought-level auditor that cuts hazardous task success to 0.48%.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - embodied VLM agents, guarded by SAFE-AUDIT and by the AgentSpec and ThinkSafe execution-layer gates used as baselines. Check: one embodied agent per episode and no agent-to-agent interaction, so (c) rests on the LLM-agent-safety-evaluation branch rather than a multi-agent property; SAFE-AUDIT audits the global thought before planning ("rather than merely blocking them post-planning"), so (a) is borderline as an action-level veto. Abstract says 9,900 instructions while the body says 1,800 basic plus 8,100 adversarial, and Figure 2 says 1,350 interactive objects against 104 in the text. No latency, overhead or hardware figures.

title: MAGPIE: A dataset for Multi-AGent contextual PrIvacy Evaluation
evidence: Conclusion: agents commit multi-round privacy violations in 55.27% of interactions while collaborating in group chat (Conclusion; Section 5.3).
method: Dataset of 158 high-stakes scenarios in 15-16 domains where excluding private data blocks task completion; 2-4 LLM agents negotiate in a group chat for up to 10 rounds under utility prompts.
evaluation: GPT-4o, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Mistral-Large, Llama-3-70B; misclassification 25.2-43.6% against a 10.2% human baseline; leakage 5.7-82.5% explicit, 39.7-87.0% implicit, 50.5-60.0% active; consensus 51%, task success 29.7%.
contribution: Multi-agent benchmark showing that collaborating LLM agents leak contextually private data in over half of multi-round negotiations, and that lower leakage comes at the cost of consensus and task success.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the agents are LLM agents, but nothing guards them: no filter, shield, gate or deferral is implemented or tested, so only (c) holds and (a) fails; built-in privacy safeguards are named as future work. Weakest point against the evaluation floor is the baseline: a human misclassification rate plus cross-model and prompt-condition contrasts, no safety baseline or ablation. Internal inconsistencies: 15 vs 16 domains, "Claude-2.7-Sonnet" vs 3.7-Sonnet, Mistral implicit 39.7% in table vs 40% in text; the benchmark was generated and verified by Claude 3.7 itself; leakage is counted only on verbatim appearance of the private value, which the authors call a lower bound.

title: OpenAgentSafety: A Comprehensive Framework for Evaluating Real-World AI Agent Safety
evidence: Section 3.2: with harmful goals held by simulated coworkers under benign user intent, "unsafe rates vary from 44.9-69.2%" (Section 3.2).
method: Framework of 356 multi-turn tasks in a sandboxed workplace (bash, browser, files, code, messaging) with Sotopia-simulated LLM coworkers; rule-based environment-state checks plus a GPT-4.1 judge.
evaluation: Seven LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4/3.7, GPT-5, GPT-4o, o3-mini, DeepSeek-v3/R1); unsafe rate 49.06-72.73% by judge, 32.3-52.2% rule-based; 100-trajectory human study, 94% annotator agreement; three EC2 t3.2xlarge, 24-30 h per model.
contribution: Open framework of 356 realistic multi-turn, multi-user tool-use tasks that elicits unsafe behaviour from frontier agents in 49-73% of safety-vulnerable cases, including when only a simulated coworker is malicious.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM tool-calling agents are the evaluated systems, but no guardrail, shield or approval gate is tested; "safety interventions such as guardrail agents" are explicitly future work (Section 5), so (a) fails and only (c) holds. Approval-seeking and escalation to the user are described as ideal behaviour but never counted, so (e) does not hold. No system baseline: the comparison is across seven models with Mann-Whitney tests. Tables 3 and 5 are not reconciled (Claude Sonnet 4 at 49.06% vs 29.60%), the text says five models where seven are listed, and judge-human disagreement is 39.1%, so the headline unsafe rates are soft.

title: MCPSecBench: A Systematic Security Benchmark and Playground for Testing Model Context Protocols
evidence: Section 4: "This benchmark focuses on dynamic protection mechanisms", and an attempt is scored as refused when "the MCP host or AI proactively detects and refuses the malicious action" (Section 4; Section 5.1).
method: Benchmark and playground formalising the MCP ecosystem: 17 attack types over client, protocol, server and host surfaces, driven against three hosts with two dynamic guardrails (MCIP-Guardian, FAN) toggled on.
evaluation: Claude Desktop, GPT-4.1, Cursor, 15 trials per vector; ASR and refusal rate against a No-Defense baseline; protocol attacks 100% ASR, server 75.2-78.1%; MCIP mitigates 17.9% and FAN 28.9% on average; MCIP roughly doubles cost.
contribution: Systematic MCP security benchmark that measures 17 attack types across four surfaces on three live hosts and shows two deployed runtime guardrails block under 30% of attacks and none of the protocol-level ones.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM hosts and tool-calling agents, guarded by MCIP-Guardian and FAN, which refuse execution on detection. Check: the paper never describes how either guardrail intercepts a call internally, saying only that they "function by enhancing the LLM's autonomy in threat detection", so true pre-execution interception is unverified and (a) rests on the refusal outcome; FAN is classed as dynamic in Section 4 but described as operating "primarily via static rule-setting" in Section 5.3. Cost figures conflict: Section 5.3 gives $0.41 to $0.76 on Claude Desktop while Appendix E says costs stay "under $0.10 across all platforms". No latency measured; the host permission prompt is described but never measured, so (e) does not hold.

title: The Sum Leaks More Than Its Parts: Compositional Privacy Risks and Mitigations in Multi-Agent Collaboration
evidence: "a single defender's decision to block is sufficient to deny the query" (Sec. 1, CoDef description)
method: Defines compositional privacy leakage across collaborating LLM agents and adds two per-query defenses: theory-of-mind intent inference, and CoDef, a shared-state consensus vote where any defender can block.
evaluation: 119 synthetic adversarial and benign multi-agent scenarios; Qwen3-32B attacker; defenders Qwen3-32B, Gemini-2.5-pro, GPT-5; vs CoT, CoT+sensitive-set, CoT+history, ToM, self-voting; sensitive-block 86.5-89.9 pct CoDef vs 29.8-39.1 pct CoT, benign success 66.3-70.2 pct, balanced outcome up to 79.8 pct; no latency or hardware.
contribution: Shows that individually safe LLM agent answers compose into privacy leaks, and that a consensus block vote across defender agents cuts leakage while preserving most benign utility.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM defender agents veto an LLM attacker's queries at inference time. Check (c) primacy (leakage is multi-agent by construction) and the evidence base: 119 synthetic scenarios, one run, Qwen3-32B judging Qwen3-32B. Plan-execution rates appear only in Fig. 4 with no numbers; the abstract's up-to-97-pct block rate is ToM self-voting, not CoDef. No latency, no human handoff.

title: A-MemGuard: A Proactive Defense Framework for LLM-Based Agent Memory
evidence: "Before execution, A-MemGuard performs a proactive check" of the proposed plan against stored lessons (Sec. 3, dual-memory design)
method: Two-stage memory defense for LLM agents: consensus divergence scoring across retrieved memory records drops outliers, and flagged reasoning paths become lessons that force plan revision before execution.
evaluation: EHRAgent, ReAct-StrategyQA, MMLU indirect injection, MISINFOTASK multi-agent; GPT-4o-mini and LLaMA-3.1-8B with DPR/REALM; vs no defense, LLM auditor, DistilBERT classifier, perplexity filter, plus w/o-lessons and w/o-consensus ablations; ASR-r 100.0 to 2.13, ASR-t 100.0 to 36.17, MMLU ASR 0.667 to 0.256; benign accuracy 83.0 to 71.3; about 7.8K vs 3.6K tokens; no latency or hardware.
contribution: A-MemGuard makes LLM agent memory self-checking by scoring consensus divergence among retrieved records and storing flagged reasoning paths as lessons that trigger plan revision before execution.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - frozen-weight LLM agent with retrieval memory. (a) is runtime, but the override is a prompted plan revision rather than a hard veto or halt; decide whether that counts. Multi-agent appears only in the single MISINFOTASK run, so (c) fails primacy and gap_cells is left at none. Table 9's LLaMA no-defense average 0.633 conflicts with Table 2's 0.663; the abstract's over-95-pct ASR reduction holds only for ASR-r, not ASR-t (36.17). Benign accuracy drops 11.7 points on EHRAgent. No detection rate, no latency.

title: MAGPIE: A benchmark for Multi-AGent contextual PrIvacy Evaluation
evidence: Benchmark of 200 multi-turn negotiations among 3-7 LLM agents in which "total leakage" of task-necessary private context is the primary outcome (Sec. 5, Table 1)
method: MAGPIE benchmark: 200 multi-turn negotiation scenarios with 3-7 LLM agents where private information is task-necessary, scoring leakage, consensus and task completion under explicit and implicit privacy instructions.
evaluation: GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-4.1-Opus, GPT-4, LLaMA-4-Maverick; 10 rounds, temperature 0, one run per datapoint; total leakage 25.0-35.1 pct (GPT-5) up to 56.0-61.4 pct (GPT-4, Gemini); consensus 0-13.5 pct; manipulation up to 87.8 pct; mixed-capability GPT-5 and GPT-4 ablation; no defense baseline, no latency.
contribution: MAGPIE shows frontier LLM agents leak task-necessary private context in 25-61 pct of multi-agent negotiations and almost never reach privacy-preserving consensus, even when instructed to protect it.
flag: learned or AI system analysed: yes - frontier LLM agents. No runtime mechanism of any kind (dynamic information-flow control and real-time guardrails are future work), so (a) fails and this enters only as multi-agent hazard evidence under (c). Evaluation floor is the borderline: no defense or safeguard baseline, only cross-model, implicit-vs-explicit and one mixed-capability comparison, single run per datapoint, leakage judged by GPT-5 with no reported judge accuracy; the maintainer may prefer exclude-E2. Task completion has no aggregate figure. Fetch covered 100000 of 100865 characters.

title: The Oversight Game: Learning to Cooperatively Balance an AI Agent's Safety and Autonomy
evidence: "Oversight thus becomes a coordination problem rather than a monitoring problem." (Sec. 1); agent chooses play or ask, human chooses trust or oversee (Sec. 3, Definition 1).
method: Oversight Game: Markov game wrapped around a frozen base policy; the agent learns when to ask, the overseer when to oversee; oversight can substitute an action or shut down.
evaluation: Lavaland gridworld vs unsafe base policy: violations about 15% to 0, interventions to 28.2%; ToolEmu-derived MDPs with Qwen3 LoRA policies: ask rate 99.4% risky, 3.9% safe; theorems proved; no latency.
contribution: Models AI-human oversight as a Markov potential game in which an agent learns when to defer; proves gains in autonomy cannot hurt the human and shows learned deferral removing safety violations.
flag: (i), (ii) and (iv): learned deferral to a human overseer as an action over time, with shutdown. Formal results: Thm 1 local alignment under Markov-potential-game and ask-burden assumptions; Thm 2 safe minimum-oversight equilibrium; Thm 3 loss bound eps/(1-gamma). Criterion e is weak: the human is a random-safe-action corrector in the gridworld and a fine-tuned LLM in ToolEmu; the paper says real-human validation is future work - drop e and the handoff cell if real humans are required. Overrides are excluded when the agent plays, so safety depends on the agent choosing to ask: not an independent shield. Only baseline with numbers is the unsafe base policy; always-ask and never-ask are discussed without numbers. LLM MDPs are tiny (2-3 decision points). Only first 100k of 127k characters read; hardware (Appendix B.5) not seen.

title: Exposing Weak Links in Multi-Agent Systems under Adversarial Prompting
evidence: Central claim that "design choices in multi-agent systems create weak links" absent in single-agent settings, measured as ARIA harm levels per architecture (Sec. 1, Table 1)
method: SAFEAGENTS evaluation framework plus DHARMA, a post-hoc LLM-judge taxonomy of where refusal or unmitigated execution occurred, applied to centralized and decentralized LLM multi-agent architectures under adversarial prompts.
evaluation: Magentic-One, LangGraph (centralized and decentralized), OpenAI Agents, Swarm vs a single-agent ReAct baseline; RedCode, ASB, SafeArena, AgentHarm; GPT-4o agents at temperature 0, GPT-4.1 judge, Qwen3-30B small-model check; ARIA-4 harm 15.85-99.0 pct across architectures vs 46-81.5 pct single agent; DHARMA planner-stop 78.74-87.40 pct; no latency or hardware.
contribution: Comparing five LLM multi-agent frameworks against a single-agent baseline, SAFEAGENTS finds that decomposition and delegation design choices, not agent count, decide whether adversarial requests reach execution.
flag: learned or AI system analysed: yes - LLM agent frameworks. No runtime interceptor: DHARMA labels completed logs post hoc, so (a) fails. Comparisons are cross-framework rather than controlled ablations and sample sizes are never stated. The SafeArena OpenAI Agents cell in Table 1 is empty and some Table 2 cells read as garbled or duplicated, so verify the figures against the source. The introduction's claim that simple prompt-based mitigations give significant benefits is not quantified in the body, and the GPT-4.1 judge has no reported human validation.

title: Many-to-One Adversarial Consensus: Exposing Multi-Agent Collusion Risks in AI-Based Healthcare
evidence: The Verifier Agent checks the committee recommendation against guidelines "before a final prescription is issued" and overrides unsafe recommendations (Sec. on the verifier defense)
method: Simulates k colluding assistant agents pushing one wrong drug on an AI doctor agent, then adds a Verifier Agent that checks the committee's prescription against guideline gold answers before it is issued.
evaluation: 50 synthetic clinical questions; LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct and Grok 4 Fast; grid over k in 2,4,6 and T 0.2-1.0 (pass/fail only); unprotected doctor modes as baselines; ASR 1.00 scripted and 0.98 unscripted down to 0.00 with the verifier, HRR 0.98 to 0.00, accuracy 0.02 to 1.00, coverage 0.00 to 1.00; no latency or hardware.
contribution: A collusion simulation in which majority pressure from assistant agents flips an AI doctor's prescription in 98 pct of cases, and a guideline-checking verifier agent that blocks every such case.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an LLM doctor agent guarded by an LLM verifier. Check the headline result: the verifier is scored against the same guideline gold answers it consults, so ASR 0.00 and accuracy 1.00 are partly circular. Only 50 synthetic ChatGPT-generated questions, which the authors call an early proof of concept; Table I's k and temperature grid is pass/fail with no ASR-vs-k curve and the scripted threshold is fixed at k>3; the verifier's negligible cost is unquantified; no clinician oversight or human handoff.

title: Don't Trust Your Upstream: Exploiting LLM Multi-Agent System via Topology-Guided Adversarial Propagation
evidence: Appendix D, Table XIV: T-Guard will "Block all operations originating from the target node to prevent potential compromise propagation" once a guard node taint exceeds 0.8.
method: TOMA attack: topology reconnaissance, contamination propagation modelling and layered payload injection to reach high-privilege agents; T-Guard defence adds cross-modal validation, a dynamic trust map and runtime access control.
evaluation: 3 frameworks, 5 topologies, 3 LLMs, 180 configs; baselines Crescendo and Pop-up 0.0% ASR; end-to-end ASR 40-78%, real-world 17/20; T-Guard blocks 94.8%, FPR 3.45%, 31.2 ms overhead, 0.99 s blocking latency.
contribution: Shows adversarial content injected at exposed edge agents propagates along an LLM multi-agent topology to high-privilege agents (40-78% success), and that a trust-based runtime access-control guard blocks 94.8%.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM agents in Magentic-One, LangManus and OWL. Check (a): the runtime interceptor is T-Guard, a secondary defence the authors call preliminary and conceptual (Section VI plus Appendix D), while the primary contribution and primary measured outcome is the attack; T-Guard is prototyped only on Magentic-One with GPT-4o and is not compared against existing defences. Abstract 85% real-world figure traces to 17/20 scenarios in the body.

title: MCP-SafetyBench: A Benchmark for Safety Evaluation of Large Language Models with Real-World MCP Servers
evidence: Section 3.3: "Each task is paired with exactly one MCP-layer attack drawn from our taxonomy"; Section 4.2 reports per-model attack success rate as the primary outcome.
method: Benchmark of 245 tasks across 5 MCP domains adapted from MCP-Universe, each paired with one of 20 MCP-layer attacks from the server, host or user side; execution-trace evaluators score task and attack success.
evaluation: 13 LLMs in a ReAct agent; ASR 29.8-48.2%, TSR 8.98-21.2%; identity injection 100% ASR, host-side 81.9%; safety-prompt mitigation 39.88% to 38.65% (p=0.29); ablations on 2-4 servers and Plan-and-Execute. No latency or hardware.
contribution: Benchmark showing 13 frontier LLMs acting through real MCP servers are subverted in 30-48% of tasks, with identity injection universally successful and prompt-level safety guidance statistically ineffective.
flag: RULED OUT by the between-agents ruling of 2026-11-13: Benchmark attacking a single ReAct agent via its MCP servers, host and user; no second agent | original draft was include. learned or AI system guarded: yes - the 13 LLMs under test, but nothing guards them. Check (c) primacy: the setting is SINGLE-agent (one ReAct agent per task, multiple MCP servers), so (c) holds only through the "safety evaluation of LLM/tool-calling agents" clause; a maintainer applying the multi-agent primacy test literally would call this exclude-E4. Benchmark only, no runtime mechanism; refusal rate never reported as a metric (only a qualitative note that about 15% of GPT-5 failures were safe refusals).

title: MemoryGraft: Persistent Compromise of LLM Agents via Poisoned Experience Retrieval
evidence: Section 5.3: "Thus, nearly half of all retrieved records originated from Spoison" - 23 of 48 retrieved records (47.9%) came from 10 poisoned seeds, with no baseline or ablation.
method: MemoryGraft: a benign-looking markdown note carries runnable Python that, when the agent executes it, writes 100 benign plus 10 poisoned experience records into the agent shared BM25 and FAISS retrieval store.
evaluation: Single MetaGPT DataInterpreter with GPT-4o, 110 seeds, 12 handcrafted queries; one metric, poisoned retrieval proportion 23/48 = 47.9%; no baselines, no quantitative ablations, no repeated runs or variance, no latency or hardware.
contribution: Attack demonstration that a poisoned experience store planted through an executed README persists across sessions and supplies nearly half of an LLM agent retrieved experiences.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - an LLM agent experience memory, but nothing guards it. Fails the evaluation floor: a single descriptive metric (47.9% poisoned retrieval) with no baseline, no ablation and no repeated runs, and the two proposed defences (cryptographic provenance attestation, constitutional consistency reranking) are proposed in Section 6 without any results. Also single-agent with no runtime mechanism, so exclude-E4 is a defensible alternative; Appendix C experiments are listed with no results.

title: Atomix: Timely, Transactional Tool Use for Reliable Agentic Workflows
evidence: Section 2.2: "The agent chooses tool calls; Atomix does not trust it to perform concurrency control"; irreversible effects are held at a gate and released only on commit (Section 4).
method: Atomix: a transactional runtime between an agent orchestrator and tools - adapters declare scopes, effect classes and compensations; a transaction manager with per-resource progress frontiers gates, stages, aborts or compensates tool calls.
evaluation: tau-bench, WebArena, OSWorld and multi-agent stress; 4 LLMs; 10 mechanism-matched baselines; 0 invariant violations per run vs 4.97 (No-Tx), 0 of 500 irreversible leaks vs 500 of 500; 7.7 us per step; 8-core Xeon workstation.
contribution: A transactional tool-use runtime that gates irreversible agent effects until commit and uses per-resource progress frontiers, eliminating invariant violations and irreversible leaks under 8-agent contention at microsecond overhead.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM tool-calling agents (GPT-4.1, GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4, GPT-4o-mini) are the guarded workload while Atomix itself is deterministic. Check the title claim "Timely": no deadlines, latency bounds or theorems are defined, only invariants and an informal commit predicate plus empirical negative controls. Check the unreconciled conflict between the 0 ms wait headline and 635 ms per run in the real-LLM combined-stress result, and the baseline count stated as 9 but listed as 10. Fault-recovery gain over Checkpoint-Replay is not significant (57% vs 53%, Fisher p=1.0); only the irreversible-leak and contention results separate it cleanly.

title: Learning-to-Defer with Expert-Conditioned Advice
evidence: Abstract: 'reference conditional classification, which jointly learns a fixed expert's error probability'; Lemma 2 gives the Bayes-optimal deferral-advice policy (source minimising each expert's expected cost, then cheapest expert).
method: Learning to defer where the router picks an expert and a paid advice source before seeing the advice; reference-conditional surrogate replaces inconsistent product surrogates; full and limited-observation training.
evaluation: Theory: Bayes rule (Lemma 2), product-surrogate inconsistency (Thm 3), consistency bound (Thm 5), all proved. Experiments on FEVER and IEEE-CIS fraud, 3 model experts, vs standard L2D and augmented surrogate; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Extends learning to defer to joint choice of expert and paid advice source, proves product surrogates inconsistent and gives a consistent reference-conditional surrogate with a regret bound.
flag: (v) and (iii): DUPLICATE of arxiv:2603.14324, same arXiv id; the PDF title reads 'Consistent Learning-to-Defer with Expert-Conditional Advice', the record title is evidently an earlier or metadata variant - keep one record. Experts are all models, no human. Empirical gains small (FEVER 0.576 vs 0.584). Only the first 100k of 146k characters read; appendix proofs not checked.

title: DeferredSeg: A Multi-Expert Deferral Framework for Trustworthy Medical Image Segmentation
evidence: Sec. 6: DeferredSeg "selectively routes only a small subset of pixels to expert branches during inference"; Eqs. 11-12 route each pixel by argmax routing logit.
method: Pixel-level multi-expert learning to defer for segmentation: J+1 routing channels added to MedSAM or CENet, with deferral-collaboration, spatial-coherence and load-balancing losses.
evaluation: PROMISE12, LiTS, AMOS22 (synthetic experts), Chaksu, QUBIQ, CURVAS (clinician masks); vs nnU-Net, CENet, MedSAM-FT, PatchCorr; LiTS tumour DSC 59.20 to 91.01; 4.32% pixels deferred; RTX 4090, 16.81 vs 16.12 ms/image.
contribution: Extends learning to defer to pixel-wise medical segmentation with several experts and a load-balancing penalty, raising Dice over fine-tuned MedSAM while deferring a few percent of pixels at about 5% extra inference time.
flag: (iii) deferral among multiple experts, also (i). arXiv title lacks the word "Trustworthy" but is the same paper. Experts are synthetic accuracy profiles or pre-existing offline clinician masks used as proxies, no live human in the loop, so e not claimed. No new theorem or consistency proof: the surrogate is adapted from prior L2D. Gains partly reflect that deferred pixels take high-accuracy expert masks (synthetic expert foreground accuracy up to 92%), so system Dice is bounded by assumed expert quality. One-shot per image, not sequential. Two-expert Jaccard (89.03) is below one-expert (91.04). Table L.22 was garbled in the text read.

title: Right-to-Act: A Pre-Execution Non-Compensatory Decision Protocol for AI Systems
evidence: Sec. 4.3: execution is allowed only if every required constraint holds, otherwise NON-ACTION, which "may be decomposed into outcomes such as DEFER, ESCALATE, or REQUEST-INFO".
method: Right-to-Act layer: a deterministic, non-compensatory pre-execution gate between AI decision and execution; any failed required constraint yields NON-ACTION regardless of aggregate score.
evaluation: No experiments, datasets, metrics or implementation. One hypothetical account-suspension case study with an assumed baseline outcome. Lemma 1, Theorem 1 and Corollary 1 follow directly from definitions.
contribution: A conceptual protocol for a pre-execution approval gate that blocks an AI action when any required constraint fails, arguing formally that weighted scoring cannot reproduce hard-constraint gating.
flag: (iv) safety-critical runtime gate in concept, but no quantitative evaluation: fails the empirical floor. Title on arXiv differs from the record: "The Pre-Action Legitimacy Gap in AI Systems: A Deterministic, Non-Compensatory Decision Boundary for Execution"; same work (Right-to-Act layer, non-compensatory), so not treated as WRONG PAPER - maintainer should confirm. The proved results are near-trivial consequences of the all-constraints definition and are not reject-option theory in the sense of (v). Paper states figures are conceptual and that it "does not define the full internal method" (Sec. 12.4). No human role specified for ESCALATE. Single author.

title: Ask Early, Ask Late, Ask Right: When Does Clarification Timing Matter for Long-Horizon Agents?
evidence: "We present the first empirical VOI curves for clarification timing in long-horizon agent workflows." (Sec. 7, Conclusion)
method: Empirical study: ground-truth clarifications force-injected at 10/30/50/70/90% of the action budget with ask_user disabled; separate natural-ask protocol observes when models ask. No ask policy is proposed.
evaluation: 84 task variants from MCP-Atlas, TheAgentCompany, SWE-Bench Pro; 3-4 frontier LLMs; 6,048 injection trials plus 300 natural-ask sessions; oracle and no-clarification baselines; pass@3. No hardware or latency.
contribution: Measures how the value of a user clarification decays with its timing in long-horizon LLM agent runs, finding goal information is worth most before about 10-30% of the trajectory.
flag: none of (i)-(v) strictly: there is no abstain/defer/hand-off mechanism; clarification timing is experimentally manipulated (forced injection) and the paper says getting agents to ask at the right time is future work. BORDERLINE for (ii): maintainer may prefer include as evidence on when asking a human pays off in a sequential setting - it reports a 'point of no return' near 30% of the trajectory for outcome-critical goal/constraint variants (MCP-Atlas goal pass@3: oracle 0.80, inject-10% 0.78, inject-30% 0.50, none 0.40) and that GPT-5.2 asked in 52% of sessions, Claude Sonnet 4.5 in 23%, Gemini 3 Flash never. User is simulated; no human takes over. Clarification is information-seeking, not deferral of a decision.

title: Retrying vs Resampling in AI Control
evidence: "the blue team must monitor every action in the trajectory before executing it" (Sec. 2.2 Control setting)
method: AI-control protocols for an untrusted LLM agent: a trusted monitor scores each proposed action; flagged actions are blocked and retried or resampled, with the most suspicious sent to a budgeted blocking audit.
evaluation: BashArena 1.1, U=Claude Opus 4.6, T=MiMo-V2-Flash, prompted attacker; vs trusted monitoring. Safety 61% to 71% (resample N=5, max) at 0.3% audit; usefulness about 70%; cost 1.4-5x samples.
contribution: Disentangles retrying from resampling as runtime control affordances for untrusted LLM agents, showing resampling for information lifts safety from 61% to 71% at a 0.3% audit budget while feedback retries do not.
flag: (iv) runtime monitor/gate that blocks agent actions before execution, in a multi-step agent setting (ii). Doubt on the MAIN-contribution test: the paper's subject is the retry vs resample comparison inside a blocking protocol, not deferral as such; defer-to-trusted is NOT evaluated (only cited prior work). Audit is modelled as a perfect blocking investigation, no human study (Appendix B.3.2 simulates the auditor with an LLM), so (e) and human handoff not claimed. Single untrusted agent, so not multi-agent state. Latency and cost are modelled sample counts, not wall-clock. Could also meet (c) as LLM-agent safety evaluation. Read first 100k of 126k characters.

title: What Benchmarks Don't Measure: The Case for Evaluating Abstention Competence in Autonomous Agents
evidence: "reconceptualizes abstention not as a failure mode but as a structured capability" (Abstract); the wrapper is a pre-execution hook at the tool-invocation boundary that blocks the call (implementation section).
method: Informed Abstention Framework; LangChain tool wrapper with constraint and commitment checkpoints (GPT-4o guard) that veto tool calls before execution, plus a post-execution grounding warning.
evaluation: 144 scenarios (120 hazardous, 24 safe), mock HR and DevOps, 7 models; vs no-policy and prompt-only. Checkpoint safety rate 87.5-90.8% vs 50.8-80.0% baseline; usability 75.0-91.7%. No latency.
contribution: Position paper with a preliminary study: a pre-execution checkpoint wrapper that vetoes under-specified or unauthorised tool calls raises agent safety rate to 87.5-90.8% across seven model families.
flag: (iv) pre-execution gate that vetoes agent tool calls. DUPLICATE of record arxiv:2606.02965: this DOI is the arXiv DOI of the same id, and the PDF is titled 'Designing for Doubt: The Case for Informed Abstention in Autonomous Agents', NOT the record title 'What Benchmarks Don't Measure: The Case for Evaluating Abstention Competence in Autonomous Agents'. arXiv lists only v1 under the Designing for Doubt title, so the record title could not be confirmed as an earlier title of this paper; if it is a distinct paper it was NOT READ and should be E6. Extraction copied from the duplicate; merge the two records. Position-heavy paper with a preliminary evaluation only; IRR 100% is by design, not measured; baseline IRR is GPT-4o-judge estimated; no CIs or run counts; mock in-memory environments; scenarios GPT-4o-mini augmented; handoff to a human described but not implemented or studied; usability drops for some models (Llama 91.7 to 75.0). Abstract figures (87.5-91% blocked, 75-92% usability) match Table 2.

title: Will the Agent Recuse Itself? Measuring LLM-Agent Compliance with In-Band Access-Deny Signals
evidence: "We propose a third mode: a lightweight, published in-band governance signal" (Abstract); a harness interceptor scans tool results for the halt sentinel and terminates the agent loop (Section 8.2).
method: Recuse Signal: versioned in-band deny/throttle/warn/halt line sent via SSH banner, PostgreSQL NOTICE or Kubernetes warning asking agents to withdraw; plus a harness interceptor that enforces halt.
evaluation: 5 models, SSH tasks, n=20 per cell, no-signal controls. Deny recusal 66/80 (82.5%); mid-task halt 0/40 stopped; harness interceptor 120/120 stops, 0/60 false trips vs 23% cooperative. No latency.
contribution: Measures whether LLM agents honour an in-band withdraw-or-halt signal: 82.5% recuse at the access door, cooperative mid-task halt mostly fails, and a harness-level interceptor enforces 120/120 stops.
flag: (iv) runtime halt/recusal of an agent action, also (ii) sequential agent setting. TITLE DIFFERS from record: fetched PDF is titled 'Will the Agent Recuse, and Will It Stop? Measuring LLM-Agent Compliance with In-Band Governance Signals at the Access Door and Mid-Flight' - same arXiv id and topic, evidently a revised version adding the halt experiments; not treated as a wrong paper. Doubts: mainly a measurement study plus proposed standard; authors say the signal is not a security control; pilot-scale cells (5 and 2 trials in Exp 1); single self-selected host; interceptor result is deterministic by construction, not a behavioural rate; authorised framing let GPT-4o pass a deny 4/5; GPT-4o-mini halted 0/20 vs Gemini 2.5 Flash 16/20; warn never surfaced to operator (0/100). No human takeover measured.

title: Budgeted Act-or-Defer Multi-Agent LLM Deliberation with Local Reliability Bounds
evidence: "The guarantee is conditional, not distribution-free: it relies on a valid local bias envelope" (Abstract)
method: Three LLM agents debate up to 4 rounds; each round a k-NN lower bound on correctness over a 2-D debate state decides act or continue; unresolved cases defer to human review under a wrong-action budget.
evaluation: Six QA sets (MMLU-Pro, LogiQA, ARC, BBH, MuSR, GPQA), 10 splits. Act 9.0-84.4%, Acc|Act 70.3-97.1%, wrong-action 2.3-9.4%, WA/beta 0.04-0.12 vs CRC 0.82 on LogiQA. 9 baselines, 2 ablations. No hardware or latency.
contribution: Turns multi-agent debate into a budgeted act-or-defer rule with a proved conditional bound on wrong actions, acting autonomously on 9 to 84 percent of questions while keeping wrong actions near 2 to 9 percent.
flag: (ii), also (i) and (v) in part: act, continue or defer is decided each debate round, with deferral to human review and Theorems 1-3 bounding wrong-action probability by delta+alpha+eps. Doubts: no human reviewer is used or evaluated, so no 'e'; the guarantee rests on Assumptions 3 and 4, the latter supported only by diagnostics; the budget beta is not user-fixed in the main results but induced from training error with lambda swept, and WA/beta slightly exceeds the 0.10 target on three datasets (0.11-0.12); the paper's own Table 2 concedes tuned thresholds match its accuracy within 1.6 pp at equal automation. Tasks are single QA items, so 'multi-agent state' is nominal (debate state of three LLMs). Fetched text truncated mid Appendix D.

title: Certified Speculative Execution for Untrusted AI Agents
evidence: "a trusted verifier rejects constraint-violating transitions exactly" (Abstract)
method: CGPA: untrusted sources (rules, policies, frozen LLMs) draft K-step action prefixes; an exact verifier and value guard accept the longest safe prefix, else the controller defers to a trusted oracle repair action.
evaluation: Battery EMS, CityLearn HVAC, unit commitment; 6 LLMs, adversarial drafters. Direct violation rate up to 1.00 vs CGPA 0 applied violations; regret 0.0063 vs unguarded 0.4450; oracle calls cut 53-70%; UC speedup 2.96x. Hardware not given.
contribution: A certificate-gated layer executes only verified-safe prefixes of plans drafted by untrusted agents and defers to a trusted optimiser otherwise, giving zero applied violations while cutting trusted-oracle calls by over half.
flag: (iv), also (i) and (ii): a runtime gate that vetoes unsafe transitions before execution and defers to a trusted fallback oracle, over a sequential horizon. Doubts: all results are simulation in energy domains with an exact verifier assumed, so zero violations follows from the verifier by construction; the empirical question is really regret and oracle-call savings. No human in the loop. Timing is reported as speedup and share of decision time (oracle 97.96-99.98%), with a 200 ms added-oracle-cost scenario, not as absolute per-decision latency; CPU not named. Proofs appeared as sketches in the fetched text; regret certificate not checked line by line. Despite the title there is no rollback mechanism.

title: Calibration-Family Overfit: Why Trusted Sabotage Monitors Don't Transfer Across Lineages
evidence: "We make the untrusted policy family the controlled axis" (Introduction)
method: Offline study: fit trusted sabotage monitors (fixed prompt, embedding heads, LoRA) on one model family's transcripts, test on others, decompose the cross-family AUROC matrix into main effects and own-family interaction.
evaluation: ControlArena APPS, BigCodeBench, SHADE-Arena; up to 9 policy families. Interaction +0.172 [0.158,0.185] (4 families), +0.197 (8); catch rate at 1% audit budget 41% in-lineage vs 19% off-lineage; nulls about 0. No hardware/latency.
contribution: Shows that trusted sabotage monitors calibrated on one model lineage lose much of their detection power on another, with catch rate at a 1 percent audit budget falling from 41 to 19 percent.
flag: none of (i)-(v) as main contribution: the paper is about monitor detection accuracy transferring across model families; defer-to-trusted/auditing is only simulated by auditing the top-q percent of offline-scored transcripts, no live blocking or handoff, no human workflow. Closest is (iv), and under the base protocol it is relevant as safety evaluation of LLM agents (criterion c) - maintainer may want it under another pillar. Relevant to RQ4-style generalisation of monitors. SHADE-Arena result is underpowered (+0.035, CI crosses 0). Several tables garbled in extraction.

title: Removable Defects: The Economics and Limits of Deliberate Deficiency
evidence: "The detector never solves the escalated task; it answers one binary question, "is this mine?", and routes." (Sec. 2, The model)
method: Economic theory of a specialist with a deliberate blind spot plus a detector that gates each task to act or escalate (buy the work, defer to a principal, decline).
evaluation: Theory only. Proved: coupling lemma (gain-capture equals fatal-miss rate), zero-premium converse, achievability iff condition, learnability bound. Analytic XOR example; no experiment, no hardware.
contribution: Proves when an act-or-escalate detector makes a deliberately deficient specialist profitable: a detector inside the blind spot earns zero premium, one outside earns an explicit positive premium.
flag: (v), borderline: a theory of when escalating pays, framed as economics of specialisation rather than reject-option or learning-to-defer theory; maintainer should judge whether deferral is really the MAIN contribution or exclude-E1. No experiments at all; meets floor only via proved results (proofs in appendices C, D, K, L, which I saw summarised, not line by line). Single author; escalation target is a market, principal or refusal and the paper says the human case is deliberately excluded. Sec. 7 'Agent World' manifest field is a design sketch, not a deployed system.

title: Move First, Commit Later: Selective LiDAR-to-BIM Global Initialization via Sequential Consensus with Symmetry-Aware Abstention
evidence: "The system commits when an eligible submap supports the nominee without supporting a nonequivalent competitor" (Abstract); "Unsupported nominees trigger neither timeout nor replacement" (Sec. III-E)
method: Robot LiDAR-to-BIM global localization that votes over successive submaps, freezes a nominee pose and commits only when new evidence supports it and no competitor; otherwise outputs DEFER or AMBIGUOUS.
evaluation: 15 Isaac Sim and 17 real sequences; vs score rules, fixed-length STSL, MCL, AMCL; real 15 correct/2 withheld/0 wrong vs score-ratio 52.9% wrong; i9 laptop, decision layer median 333.9 ms.
contribution: A selective global-localization layer for building robots withholds a pose commitment across successive LiDAR submaps until competing explanations are ruled out, achieving zero wrong commits where score-threshold and Monte Carlo baselines commit wrongly.
flag: (ii) and (iv): sequential commit-or-defer decision over a stream of submaps acting as a gate on pose commitment. Title on arXiv now reads '...by Verifying Proposals Against Competing Explanations' (record subtitle differs; same paper, later version presumably). Doubts: single robot, localization rather than a safety shield in the usual sense - the 'action' withheld is a pose commitment, not a control command; small n (17 real, 15 sim); wrong-commit rate is the safety metric. On abstain the robot simply keeps driving and observing; no human handoff and no active motion selection. Latency is reported (0.682 s registration, 333.9 ms decision median, worst 6.49 s) but the method is not latency-aware, so no latency cell credited. Baseline thresholds tuned on development data.

title: Denial of Deadline: Network-Driven Accuracy Collapse in Distributed Inference Pipelines
evidence: Section 4.2 Setup: "cloud predictions are incorporated only if they return within a 250 ms deadline"; bursts raise benign slow-path p99 from about 92 ms to about 2 s and the merger discards the late predictions.
method: Threat model plus simulation: Yo-Yo style burst-shaped requests contend with benign traffic at shared autoscaled cloud resources during warmup, so late cloud detections miss the 250 ms deadline and are discarded.
evaluation: Simulated COSMOS-based edge-cloud pipeline, YOLOX-Nano edge and YOLOX-X cloud on Argoverse-HD with SORT; baselines no-attack, flat DDoS, edge-only; 7.0 HOTA points average loss and 2.0-18.7 targeted; p99 about 92 ms to about 2 s under about 4,000 burst requests.
contribution: Shows that burst-shaped network attacks on shared cloud resources make deadline-gated slow-path detections arrive late, silently collapsing edge-cloud tracking accuracy by up to 18.7 HOTA points with no visible outage.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - YOLOX detectors and a Kalman plus SORT tracker in a deadline-gated edge-cloud pipeline, and (e) does not apply. Check (d) against the evaluation floor: the outcome metric is tracking accuracy (HOTA), not a hazard, collision or intervention rate, deadline-miss rate is never reported as a percentage, and safety relevance to driving is asserted without any closed-loop control. Evaluation is simulation-only with no edge hardware specification, the paper is partly a position and research-agenda piece, and no mitigation is evaluated. Abstract stop-sign and bicycle or motorcycle figures are not in the body.

title: When Clean Signals Are Not Enough: Detecting Structural Ambiguity for Safe Wearable Stress Classification
evidence: "Abstention is triggered; this routing action is not itself a clinical safety guarantee." (Sec. III.D Method)
method: ICCM: a subject-specific conformal monitor on inter-signal coupling that sits before a random-forest stress classifier and routes each 60 s window to predict, withhold or abstain (alpha 0.05).
evaluation: WESAD (15 subjects) and Stress-Predict (35), leave-one-subject-out; vs random and confidence-based abstention at matched coverage; false positives, sensitivity, specificity, coverage 96.8 and 94.4 percent; no hardware or latency.
contribution: A conformal coupling monitor that withholds wearable stress predictions on structurally ambiguous windows; on two datasets it shows no selective-performance advantage over random or confidence-based abstention.
flag: none of (i)-(v): a classifier-external reject option applied to one domain. Windows arrive as a stream and Zone 2 'defers to the next window' (Fig. 2), but each window is judged on its own and no deferral policy over time is learned or evaluated; no recipient of rejected cases is specified and no human takeover is evaluated; not safety-critical runtime control of an action. Results are essentially NULL and the authors say so: false positives 29 to 27 (WESAD, p=.157) and 94 to 92 (Stress-Predict, p=.317), confidence-based abstention does better (25 and 71); the WESAD correlation (r=-0.607) reverses sign when Subject 14 is removed; the Stress-Predict feature set was chosen post hoc. Abstention rates are tiny (0.3 and 2.5 percent). Quote relayed by the fetch tool, verify wording.

title: Evidence Before Expansion: Reuse, Spawn, or Defer in Lifelong Expert Pools
evidence: "Defer is not a heuristic: it is exactly the region between accumulated evidence for reuse" (Abstract, sentence truncated in my fetch)
method: Decision layer for lifelong expert pools: per-expert betting e-processes over a two-axis conditional Jensen-Shannon discrepancy decide to reuse an expert, spawn a new one, or defer that structural choice.
evaluation: Synthetic four-regime stream, Electricity, Covertype, INSECTS; vs single model, spawn-always, novelty, loss-jump, exchange and CPD gates; prequential accuracy, false spawns and reuses, expert counts; no hardware reported.
contribution: An anytime-valid sequential test for expert pools on drifting streams that reuses, spawns or defers the choice, with zero false spawns on a synthetic stream and 13 versus 18-52 experts on INSECTS.
flag: none of (i)-(v) in the review's sense; nearest is (ii). 'Defer' here means postponing a model-management choice (reuse vs spawn an expert module) until evidence accumulates; no prediction or action is withheld, vetoed or handed to a human or fallback, and the 'experts' are learned sub-models, not human experts, so (iii) does not apply. It is a streaming setting with defer as one of three actions over time, so a maintainer taking (ii) literally could include it; I read it as continual-learning architecture control, off-topic. Propositions 1-3 are proved (Ville-type false-alarm bound, lifetime validity of the restarted bank); Proposition 2 rests on an empirical regularity condition. Valid schemes defer 90-97 percent of borderline cases at 1.8-2.6x delay on clear ones. Single-author paper. Quote relayed by the fetch tool and truncated, verify wording.

title: Evaluating Confidence-Gated Retrieval with Matched Trajectory Replay
evidence: "Calibration can make commitment risk interpretable, but it does not estimate the expected benefit of another retrieval." (Abstract)
method: Matched trajectory replay: an offline protocol holding answers, evidence, budgets and costs fixed while varying the confidence score fed to a commit/retrieve/abstain/escalate retrieval gate (thresholds 0.3 and 0.7).
evaluation: HotpotQA (1852) and MuSiQue (605), three LLMs, LLM judge; vs parametric-only, fixed RAG@1-3, adaptive proxy; committed and overall accuracy, coverage, retrieval cost, ECE; no hardware or latency.
contribution: An offline replay protocol showing that calibrating a confidence-gated retrieval controller raises committed accuracy by 15.8-41.0 points while coverage can collapse and overall accuracy falls on MuSiQue.
flag: none of (i)-(v) as main contribution; closest is (ii). BORDERLINE: the gate works over up to three retrieval rounds and has abstain and escalate outcomes, but the paper's contribution is an evaluation protocol for when to retrieve; abstain and escalate are uncommitted terminal labels and escalation is never executed, and everything is offline replay, so I set runtime_interceptor no. If the maintainer reads retrieve-or-commit gating as sequential deferral, this becomes include under (ii) with criterion a. Correctness judged by gemini-2.5-flash-lite with no human validation. Overall accuracy rises 4.2-15.0 points on HotpotQA and falls 2.9-16.7 on MuSiQue; Mistral MuSiQue coverage 99.7 to 7.3 percent. Fixed RAG@3 beats both gates. Quote relayed by the fetch tool, verify wording.

title: Safe to Stop? Risk-Constrained Stopping for Sequential Clinical Diagnosis Agents
evidence: Section 3.1: "CROS controls whether that proposal is executed but never substitutes a different test."
method: Per-stage controller over an LLM diagnosis agent returns STOP, CONTINUE or DEFER from a gradient-boosted error-risk ranker; threshold-and-horizon policies calibrated for joint selective-risk and coverage control.
evaluation: MIMIC-IV-ED + CDS, 1,834 episodes, 367 evaluation; vs confidence threshold, native+defer, LTT, ERM; CROS-Mix risk 0.169, coverage 0.788, cost 5.57 vs 0.257/0.796/18.11; ranker AUROC 0.853; no hardware or latency.
contribution: A risk-constrained stop/continue/defer controller for sequential LLM diagnosis agents with finite-sample joint control of selective error and autonomous coverage, cutting risk and test cost against confidence-threshold stopping on retrospective MIMIC-IV trajectories.
flag: (ii), with a (v)-style result: Theorem 1 (finite-sample joint control of selective error and coverage via exact binomial p-values and an intersection-union test, under exchangeability) and Prop. 1 (optimal mixture uses at most three policies; authors call it a standard LP consequence). DOUBTS: the authors say labels were seen during development, so results are "exploratory feasibility and audit evidence, not a confirmatory safety certificate"; gate evaluated on logged retrospective trajectories, not live; CROS-Mix passes in only 6/20 development resplits (CROS-Det 15/20); uniform-weight mixture has lower cost (4.59) than the LP mixture; ERM without constraint has risk 0.202 at cost 1.50; subgroup failures (diverticulitis error 0.500, nonspecific pain 1.000). DEFER is a stylised cost penalty, no clinician takes over, so (e) not credited and the human handoff cell is weak - maintainer may drop it. No time-to-irreversibility or latency treatment (latency is only a ranker input feature). Read via one summarising fetch of the PDF.

title: From Few-Shot Segmentation to Clinician-in-the-Loop Medical Image Analysis
evidence: Data availability: "No new data were created or analyzed for this Perspective."; Section 12: "This framework remains normative and does not itself constitute evidence of prospective clinical effectiveness."
method: Normative perspective proposing an accept/query/defer controller for few-shot medical segmentation, with a reachability gate (correctable set) sending unrepairable cases to clinician deferral.
evaluation: None run. Proposes a simulated-user pilot and multi-institutional MRI/CT evaluation with entropy, random and fixed-click baselines; no metric values, hardware or latency of its own.
contribution: A perspective arguing that clinician-in-the-loop segmentation needs decidable self-assessment, proposing an accept/query/defer controller that defers when a correctable-set reachability test fails; no experiments are reported.
flag: (i) in intent, but fails the evaluation floor: a perspective with no experiments and no proved formal result (six hypotheses H1-H6, proposed baselines and ablations only). Could also be read as E3-adjacent position paper. Fetched title is longer than the record title (adds ": Decidable Self-Assessment as the Precondition for Interaction and Adaptation") - same paper.
