No clinicians participated. Conceptually interesting for the review: distinguishes deferral on reachability under a remaining budget from learning to defer on predicted error (Remark 1). Read via one summarising fetch of the PDF.

title: From Intent to Action: Benchmarking LLM Safety in Vehicle Voice Command Authorization
evidence: Section 7: "the LLM should not serve as the final safety authority"; Section 5.1: "none of the evaluated models is suitable as a standalone authorization mechanism".
method: Benchmark of 202 synthetic vehicle voice-command scenarios with a seven-class authorization taxonomy (execute, refuse, clarify, require confirmation, require manual control, emergency response, no tool call) scored on LLMs.
evaluation: Five LLMs at temperature 0; prompt ablation on Llama 3.2 3B; alignment 40.1-89.1%, False Execute 1.2-13.7%, over-refusal 0-41.5%; McNemar with Holm; local models on RTX 3060 6 GB; no latency.
contribution: A 202-scenario benchmark showing that LLMs asked to authorize vehicle voice commands reach at most 89.1% alignment with reference decisions and should not act as the final safety authority.
flag: none of (i)-(v): a benchmark of single-command LLM decisions; refuse/confirm/manual-control are output classes, not a studied deferral mechanism, and no runtime gate is built or evaluated (the enforcement layer is only recommended). Could equally be coded exclude-E1. No human confirms anything; reference decisions were assigned by the authors with no independent annotators or agreement statistic. Model naming inconsistent ("gemini-3.6-flash" in Section 4.1 vs "Gemini Flash" in results). Structured policy raises False Execute on Llama 3.2 3B (1.9% to 3.7%) while cutting over-refusal. Read via one summarising fetch of the PDF.

title: Turn-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Model Checking
venue: International Conference on Agents and Artificial Intelligence (ICAART)
evidence: Sec. 4: "we created a joint policy wrapper that queries the corresponding TMARL agent policy at every turn"; Table 1 then reports P(collision)=0.36 for the 3-agent Coin Collection task.
method: Turn feature added to the MDP plus a joint policy wrapper that resolves nondeterminism into an induced DTMC, built incrementally in COOL-MC and checked with Storm against PCTL hazard queries.
evaluation: Pokemon, multi-armed bandit, tic-tac-toe, Coin Collection; baseline naive monolithic model checking (out of memory past 23 bandit agents); P(collision)=0.36, P(KO)=0.0-0.001; GTX 1060, 0.5-401 s per query.
contribution: Scales probabilistic model checking of trained turn-based multi-agent RL policies by inducing a DTMC through a joint policy wrapper, yielding exact probabilities for collision and knockout hazards.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - trained TMARL agent policies are the object of verification, so the Pillar 1 carve-in for formal analysis of learned systems applies. Check (c) primacy: the headline claim is model-checking scalability (states, transitions, runtime) and the collision probability is 1 of 12 PCTL queries in toy games, with no safety metric compared to a baseline or ablation; eval floor is met only by treating the exact model-checking probabilities as proved guarantees. Analysis is offline, so runtime_interceptor is no. HP5NoHealP1 is 0.34 in Table 1 but 0.33 in the Sec. 5.2 text, and the monolithic transition count is misprinted as 51,6547,296.

title: MADiff: Offline Multi-agent Learning with Diffusion Models
evidence: Sec. 3.1: attention is applied across agents at each decoder layer of a shared U-Net so the model diffuses joint future observation trajectories; NBA Table 2 ADE 17.24 vs 32.07 for Baller2Vec++.
method: Attention-based diffusion model over joint multi-agent observation trajectories (shared U-Net with cross-agent attention), with an inverse dynamics model mapping predicted observations to actions, centralised or decentralised.
evaluation: Offline MPE, MA-Mujoco, SMAC, SMACv2 plus NBA prediction; baselines MA-ICQ, MA-TD3+BC, OMAR, MADT, Baller2Vec++; ADE 17.24 vs 32.07, FDE 26.69 vs 44.93; ablations on attention and teammate modelling; sampling 124-127 ms on an RTX 3090.
contribution: Shows a diffusion model with cross-agent attention can serve as a joint multi-agent world model, decoding coordinated plans and outperforming dedicated trajectory predictors on NBA forecasting.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: n-a - criterion (b) record, no safety mechanism and nothing guarded. Check Pillar 2 fit: this is generative diffusion over joint observations rather than non-generative latent prediction, and the direct predictive measure (ADE-FDE) exists only for the NBA task, while the multi-agent RL results are returns. RQ5 capped at 2 per protocol v1.6 and no hazard, collision or violation rate is reported. Sampling 124-127 ms at 15 DDIM steps on an RTX 3090 is far from sub-15 ms edge interception. MADIFF-D trails MA-ICQ on SMACv2 (10.1 vs 13.7) and the paper states it is unsuitable for tens or hundreds of agents.

title: Improving Alignment and Robustness with Circuit Breakers
evidence: Sec. 4.3 (AI agents): 100 harmful function-calling requests are evaluated and Figure 8 shows the Llama-3-8B agent harmful-action rate falling from 82 to 14 under forced function calls with circuit breakers.
method: Representation rerouting: LoRRA-style fine-tuning with a ReLU-clipped cosine loss pushes harmful-state representations toward orthogonality while an L2 retain loss preserves benign behaviour, so harmful generations derail internally.
evaluation: HarmBench attacks (GCG, AutoDAN, TAP-T, PAIR, prefilling, embedding) on Mistral-7B and Llama-3-8B, plus LLaVA multimodal and tool-calling agents; baselines refusal-trained, R2D2 adversarial training, safety prompt, harmfulness probes; average ASR 38.1 to 3.8 and 76.7 to 9.8; MT-Bench 8.05 to 8.0; WildChat refusal 2.2 to 6.2.
contribution: Circuit breakers cut jailbreak and agentic harmful-action rates by roughly an order of magnitude by rerouting harmful internal representations, at near-zero capability cost and no inference overhead.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - the LLM itself (Mistral-7B, Llama-3-8B, LLaVA-NeXT). Check (a): I ruled it out because the mechanism is a training-time representation loss baked into weights, explicitly claimed to add no inference burden; the only halting variant, a probe that stops generation (Table 2 and Sec. 4.4), is a baseline and a suggestion, not the contribution. (c) therefore rests on one subsection of tool-calling-agent evaluation (Figure 8, 100 requests, GPT-4-turbo judge), so the maintainer may rule the primacy test fails and move this to E4 or E1. The 87% and 90% average ASR reduction headline figures are derived from Table 1, not stated per attack.

title: PrivacyLens: Evaluating Privacy Norm Awareness of Language Models in Action
evidence: Sec. 3.2 and 5.1: the final action is removed from a sandboxed tool-calling trajectory and each LM must produce it (e.g. GmailSendEmail), then it is scored for privacy leakage; GPT-4 leaks in 25.68% of actions.
method: PrivacyLens expands contextual-integrity privacy seeds into vignettes and then ToolEmu-sandboxed agent trajectories via a template plus surgery-kit pipeline, and scores each LM's final tool action for leakage and helpfulness.
evaluation: 493 seeds, vignettes and trajectories plus 1,479 probing questions over 9 LMs; conditions basic vs privacy-enhancing prompt; GPT-4 LR 24.54% and LRh 25.68%, Llama-3-70B 39.15%, probing accuracy 98.99% against 25% leakage; no latency reported.
contribution: Shows LM agents that answer privacy-norm questions almost perfectly still leak sensitive information in a quarter of their actual tool actions, and that privacy prompting barely helps.
flag: RULED OUT by the between-agents ruling of 2026-11-13: Benchmark of one tool-calling agent leaking private data in its own tool action; no second agent | original draft was include. learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM tool-calling agents are the system whose hazards are measured. Check (c): a single agent with tools, no agent-to-agent interaction and no runtime gate or override, so inclusion rests entirely on the "safety evaluation of LLM-tool-calling agents" clause and the maintainer may call it E4 wrong level. The comparison is across models and two prompt conditions rather than an ablation of a mechanism. Leakage is judged by an LM classifier (accuracy 0.92, kappa 0.82) and helpfulness by a judge with kappa only 0.56, so the headline rates inherit judge error.

title: Excluding the Irrelevant: Focusing Reinforcement Learning through Continuous Action Masking
evidence: Sec. 5.3: the authors "consider the masking as part of the policy, which creates the relevant policy", so the mask reparameterises sampling inside the policy rather than vetoing a nominal action.
method: Three continuous action masks (ray projection, zonotope generator mapping, truncated distributional sampling with hit-and-run MCMC) restrict a PPO policy to a state-dependent convex relevant action set to focus exploration.
evaluation: Seeker reach-avoid, 2D and 3D quadrotor, Walker2D, 10 seeds and 50 Optuna trials; baselines PPO and uniform replacement; returns 18.60 vs -71.03 (Seeker) and 1941.82 vs 1.19 (Walker2D); no violation rate; training hours only, Xeon 8380.
contribution: Continuous action masking confines PPO exploration to reachability-derived relevant action sets, improving returns and sample efficiency over standard PPO and naive resampling in four control tasks.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - a PPO policy, but the subject is exploration efficiency and return, not safety, and the setting is single-agent. Check (a): the abstract says only relevant actions are executed and the Seeker relevant set excludes collision-causing actions, so a reader could argue a runtime filter; I excluded because the mask lives inside the policy as a bijective reparameterisation, nothing is overridden or halted, and the paper is framed as focusing RL. No constraint-violation or collision rate is reported anywhere (collision is shown only qualitatively in Figure 5), so exclude-E2 is an alternative. Related to the authors' safe-RL and provably safe RL line, which may be queued separately.

title: GUARDIAN: Safeguarding LLM Multi-Agent Collaborations with Temporal Graph Modeling
evidence: Figure 3 caption and Section 4.1: "identify and exclude the highest-scoring anomalous node from subsequent iterations", "enables the removal of compromised agents and their connections".
method: Represents LLM debate as a temporal attributed graph; unsupervised encoder-decoder with an information bottleneck scores node and edge anomalies; highest-scoring agent is pruned from later rounds.
evaluation: MMLU, MATH, FEVER, Biographies (100 questions, 3 rounds, 3-7 agents) vs LLM Debate, DyLAN, SelfCheckGPT, Challenger, Inspector. Accuracy gain 4.2 percent average and 7.1 percent on MATH; anomaly detection rate 66.9-94.7 percent (Table 3); API calls 4.48 vs 8.00 for LLM Debate; alpha and gamma sweeps; no hardware or latency reported.
contribution: Models LLM multi-agent debate as a temporal attributed graph and prunes anomalous agents between rounds, improving accuracy under three attack types while roughly halving API calls.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM multi-agent debate. Criterion (a) is borderline: GUARDIAN excludes an agent from subsequent rounds rather than vetoing one action before execution, so check whether that counts as runtime interception. The claim that detection rate "averages above 80 percent" is not supported per attack type (hallucination row averages about 78.1, communication about 78.6); check Table 3. No ablation isolates the dual decoders, the information bottleneck or incremental training; no latency, hardware, F1, AUC or human alerting.

title: Among Us: A Sandbox for Measuring and Detecting Agentic Deception
evidence: Section 1: linear probes "help us detect deception out-of-distribution with high accuracy"; Section 2.4 frames the setting as "multi-agent games impose no pre-defined ceiling on sophistication and scheming".
method: Among Us sandbox with seven LLM players; separate deception and detection Elo ratings; linear probes on the layer-20 residual stream and sparse autoencoder features used as offline deception detectors; SAE steering attempted.
evaluation: 2054 games across 18 LLMs plus 400 1v1 games (Llama-3.3-70b, Phi-4). Probes trained on TruthfulQA, DishonestQA, RepEng and in-game data; out-of-distribution AUROC 0.94 lying and 0.99 deception; on-distribution 1.000 deception and 0.863 lying; best SAE feature 0.967; ablations over layers, training-data size and input components; two 80GB A100s, about 100 GPU-hours; no latency.
contribution: Introduces an Among Us sandbox that separates LLM deception capability from detection skill via Elo, and shows linear probes flag in-game deception out-of-distribution at 0.94-0.99 AUROC.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM agents in a multi-agent social deduction game. Check the (c) primacy test: the hazard is multi-agent but the detector reads a single model's residual stream, so multi-agent state is the setting rather than the detector input. No runtime gate: probes are offline and SAE steering was ineffective. Elo and win-rate values appear only in figures, not in text. The abstract claims AUROC "over 95 percent" without chain of thought, while Figure 6a action-only AUROC is 0.653 and 77 percent of those actions are non-speech.

title: WASP: Benchmarking Web Agent Security Against Prompt Injection Attacks
evidence: Abstract: "a new publicly available benchmark for end-to-end evaluation of Web Agent Security against Prompt injection attacks"; intermediate and end-to-end attack success rates are the primary measured outcomes (Section 3.4).
method: Benchmark of 84 prompt-injection tasks in self-hosted GitLab and Reddit VisualWebArena sandboxes; separates intermediate agent derailment from end-to-end attacker-goal achievement; tests defensive system prompt and instruction hierarchy.
evaluation: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, o1, Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2 and 3.7 Sonnet; no-defense baseline vs system prompt vs instruction hierarchy on 84 attack and 37 utility tasks. GPT-4o intermediate ASR 0.429 to 0.167 and end-to-end 0.036 to 0.000 with utility 0.622 to 0.459; o1 intermediate 0.857 and end-to-end 0.167; URL injection 0.619 vs plain text 0.238; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Benchmarks web agents against realistic prompt injections and shows they are often derailed yet rarely complete the attacker goal, while prompt-level defenses cut attack success at a measurable utility cost.
flag: RULED OUT by the between-agents ruling of 2026-11-13: Benchmark injecting prompts through static web content into one web agent; no second agent involved | original draft was include. learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM web agents. One agent per task, so check criterion (c) primacy and whether this is exclude-E4; the multi-step web trajectory is the only non-single-input aspect. No runtime interceptor: defenses are prompt-level and the LLM judge classifies reasoning traces after execution. Both environments (GitLab, Reddit) are logical, so no cross-domain cell. Utility set is only 37 tasks and no detection rate is reported for the judge.

title: OS-Harm: A Benchmark for Measuring Safety of Computer Use Agents
evidence: Section 4.1: the OSWorld scaffolding "does not rely on external guardrails and assumes direct execution", and agents act "without asking for any user confirmation"; Table 2 reports average unsafe rates of 21-29 percent across five computer use agents.
method: OS-Harm benchmark: 150 OSWorld Ubuntu VM tasks split across deliberate misuse, prompt injection and model misbehavior, with a GPT-4.1 AER judge scoring each trace for safety violation and task completion.
evaluation: o4-mini, GPT-4.1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Pro and Flash; average unsafe 27, 21, 29, 27 and 26 percent, misuse unsafe up to 70 percent, injection compliance 20 percent for o4-mini. Judge vs human F1 0.76 unsafe (precision 0.95, recall 0.64) and 0.79 completion; ablations over judge framework and model, temperature and 15-60 step limits; about 5 hours on one laptop, no per-step latency.
contribution: Provides a 150-task computer-use-agent safety benchmark spanning deliberate misuse, prompt injection and model misbehavior, with an LLM judge validated against human labels at 0.76 F1 on unsafe behavior.
flag: RULED OUT by the between-agents ruling of 2026-11-13: Benchmark of a single computer-use agent misused or prompt-injected; offline judge, no second agent | original draft was include. learned or AI system guarded: yes - computer use agents driven by frontier LLMs. One agent per task, so check criterion (c) primacy and whether this is exclude-E4. The judge runs offline: Section 3.3 and Appendix B.5 only propose that it "can be used to detect in real time safety violations and consequently stop the agents", so the runtime guardrail is never built or measured. Judge recall 0.64 means reported unsafe rates are probably underestimates. My fetch covered 100000 of 121526 characters; the tail appendices were not read.

title: Memory Injection Attacks on LLM Agents via Query-Only Interaction
evidence: Abstract: "LLM agents with a compromised memory bank may easily produce harmful outputs"; Section 5.2 reports average injection success 98.2 percent and attack success 76.8 percent from query-only interaction.
method: MINJA attack: an ordinary user submits benign-looking queries carrying bridging reasoning steps so poisoned records enter the agent's shared memory bank and later misdirect another user's victim query.
evaluation: RAP on WebShop, EHRAgent on MIMIC-III and eICU, and a CoT QA agent on MMLU, with GPT-4 and GPT-4o. ISR 95.6-100 and ASR 57.0-98.9 with benign utility drop within 10 points; ablations over six embedding models, retrieval noise (ASR 97.8 to 95.6), 25-100 benign queries, prior poisoning and DeepSeek-R1 and Llama-2-7B; prompt-level detection 131 of 135 on MIMIC but 0 of 135 on RAP, with 34 of 50 false positives; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Shows an ordinary user can poison an LLM agent's memory bank through benign-looking queries alone, misdirecting later victim queries at 76.8 percent attack success while leaving benign-task utility intact.
flag: RULED OUT by the between-agents ruling of 2026-11-13: Attack poisoning one agent's memory bank through user queries; victim is another user, not a second agent | original draft was include. learned or AI system guarded: yes - LLM agents with a RAG memory bank. Most likely overturn in this batch: it is an attack paper with no safety mechanism of its own and a single agent (shared memory across users), so the maintainer may rule exclude-E4 or exclude-E1 under the (c) primacy test. No head-to-head experimental baseline, only ablations and a conceptual comparison with AgentPoison and PANDORA. The sole tested defense is prompt-level detection, which fails completely on RAP and QA (0 of 135 and 0 of 90 with the targeted prompt). My fetch covered 100000 of 107820 characters.

title: Runtime Delegation Strategies for Controlled Autonomy in Large-Scale Decision Systems
venue: Journal of Information Systems Engineering & Management
evidence: "the control plane analyzes real-time operational context such as service reliability conditions, workload stability, and policy constraints to determine whether automated actions should proceed, be constrained, or transition to predefined fallback mechanisms" (Sec. 3.1)
method: Conceptual delegation control plane for high-throughput decision services: runtime signals (tail latency, error-budget burn, impact radius) select among five delegation strategies from full automation to conservative fallback and staged restoration.
evaluation: None. No experiment, simulation, dataset, baseline or metric; only taxonomy tables and a narrative flash-sale notification scenario (Sec. 5.5). No hardware or latency figures.
contribution: A practitioner taxonomy and control-plane architecture for adjusting the autonomy of large-scale automated decision services at runtime from reliability signals, presented without any empirical or formal evaluation.
flag: (iv) in concept only: a runtime gate that constrains, suspends or falls back, with operator escalation, but the paper has no quantitative result of any kind. Sec. 5 is titled 'Operational Evaluation' yet contains only prose, state tables and an 'Illustrative Deployment Scenario'; Table 1 merely summarises other papers. Tail latency and error-budget burn are used as trigger signals but nothing is measured, so no gap cell is credited. Independent researcher, received 10 March and accepted 15 March 2026 (five days) in a JISEM supplement issue; generic prose with about a dozen references reads as possibly machine-assisted. Text contains an arXiv link only as a cited reference, not for this paper. Sec. 2 and Sec. 3.2-4 were skimmed, not read line by line.

title: Governing the Agentic Web: A Confidence-Gated Human-AI Collaboration Framework for Cloud-Native Autonomous Logistics in the Industry 5.0 Era
evidence: Sec 4A: "The human intervention override function H embeds HITL governance as a hard architectural constraint within the MDP"
method: Four-layer cloud-native logistics architecture (Knative serverless, Wasm edge, MARL CTDE, security sidecar) with confidence-gated human-in-the-loop middleware routing each agent action by a Pareto-derived threshold tau.
evaluation: None. Single illustrative scenario, self-described as representative rather than empirical; tau*=0.78, 34 ms edge response, 120-day calibration are stipulated parameters. No baseline, no measured rate.
contribution: Proposes a confidence-gated human-in-the-loop middleware and a four-mode authority taxonomy for governing agentic logistics AI, formalised as an MDP with a Pareto-optimised escalation threshold.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (MARL and LLM logistics agents). Check that there is genuinely no evaluation: Sec 4E says the case study is representative rather than empirical, and every number (tau*=0.78, 34 ms, 120-day baseline, reward weights 0.45-0.30-0.25, sub-50 ms window) is stipulated, with no baseline, no escalation or error rate and no latency measurement, so the safety-mechanism evaluation floor fails. Also check the venue: the running footer on nearly every page cites a different article (Saadhu, Procurement Governance Innovation Failure Patterns in U.S. State Enterprise Systems) with the same page range 87-104 as this article; single independent-researcher author; prose reads template-driven or machine-assisted. (a) and (e) hold on reading only as a design, not as evidence.

title: Integration of Human Factors in an Automated Driving Supervision System
evidence: "Supervision of systems always presents the human agent in the loop of control, so the system is vulnerable to the failures of the human factor." (Results)
method: Prospective-ergonomics reference-situation analysis: open observations, semi-structured interviews and critical incident analysis in bus-tramway, civil and military air traffic supervision, to specify a future centralised remote AV supervision centre.
evaluation: No quantitative evaluation: 3 sectors observed (at least one day each), 7 operators interviewed 20-80 min, qualitative mind map of 7 supervision components; no metric, baseline or system.
contribution: Qualitative analysis of bus-tramway and air-traffic-control supervision reference situations, used to derive human-factors design requirements for a future centralised remote supervision centre for autonomous vehicles.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: no - supervision of SAE-level AVs and of conventional transport, nothing learned. Criterion (e) is squarely the paper's subject (remote supervision, remote takeover, situational awareness, operator workload), but there is no quantitative result and no formal result anywhere: 8-page AHFE paper reporting in-progress PhD field work, the supervision system itself does not exist yet and the design step is explicitly deferred ('The next step: the creativity part to manage the specifications of the system, is not treated here'). Fails the evaluation floor on E2 rather than on scope. Figure 1 and Figure 2 (the two mind maps carrying most of the claimed result) are images and not readable in the extracted text.

title: Calibrated Act–Ask–Abstain Gating for Agentic Language Models in Resource-Constrained Interactive Tasks
venue: International Journal of Creative and Open Research in Engineering and Management
evidence: "The results reported in this section are derived from simulated analytical evaluation based on the cost-utility model formulated in Section IV." (Section VI)
method: CAAG: calibration head on a frozen LLM agent backbone feeds an expected-utility gate choosing act, ask or abstain per step under false-action and budget constraints, plus memory-triggered reflection.
evaluation: No real runs. Projected WebArena table vs six baselines (ReAct, Reflexion, ToT etc): TSR 21.6 vs 18.2, FAR 17.1 vs 24.3, latency 19.4 vs 23.1 s/task, ECE 0.089; four projected ablations. No hardware.
contribution: Design proposal for a per-step act-ask-abstain gate for LLM agents with a cost- and irreversibility-weighted utility rule; all reported numbers are analytical projections, not measurements.
flag: (ii) applies in design (per-step abstain/ask in multi-step agent tasks; ask is a hand-off to the user but no human is studied), yet it fails the evaluation floor: Section VI and Limitations state all Table II/III numbers are simulated projections, not benchmark runs, and no simulation procedure is given. Abstract figures (tool calls -20-35%, FAR -15-30%, latency -15-25%) do not match the body (-37.2%, -45.5%, -32.2%), and the body compares against ReAct for those while the TSR gain is vs another baseline. Bounded-risk 'guarantee' (Eq. 5-6) is asserted, not proved. Risk/irreversibility penalty is a term in the formula only. Single-author paper in a low-tier journal (IJCOPE), reads as possibly machine-generated; ref [6] 'ProbeCal' title/authors should be checked.

title: A Reliable Stream Learning Model for Network Intrusion Detection Systems
venue: Journal of the Brazilian Computer Society
evidence: "if no classifier in the ensemble confidently classifies an event, it is rejected, and an alert is suppressed" (Section 5)
method: Network intrusion detector: pool of three stream classifiers (Hoeffding Tree, OzaBagging, Adaptive Random Forest) with class-wise confidence thresholds; majority vote accepts or rejects each flow; rejected flows are stored, labelled later, used for incremental updates.
evaluation: One year of MAWI traffic, train on January. Without updates: TP 84.7%, TN 95.19%, 1.09% rejected (TP -1.97, TN -0.82 points vs no-reject stream baseline). Monthly updates: rejection 0.62%; AUC +0.07 vs batch. No latency/hardware.
contribution: Stream-learning intrusion detector that rejects low-confidence flow classifications over a year of traffic and reuses the rejected flows, once labelled, for delayed incremental model updates.
flag: (ii) applies, borderline: rejection is applied flow-by-flow on a year-long stream and the rejected set drives later updates, but it is close to 'a reject-option classifier applied to a domain' (E4) and the maintainer may prefer that. Reject option shares the main contribution with stream learning/model updating. Rejected events are not handed to a human at runtime: the alert is simply suppressed and the event stored; labels come later from 'expert assistance' or an automatic labeller (MAWILab), no human studied. Evidence for the reject mechanism itself is weak: the paper says 'no significant improvement in classification performance was observed' and TP/TN with rejection are slightly BELOW the no-reject baseline. Number problems: 'increase of 93.86% and 91.81% in TP and TN' is evidently the level reached, not an increase; the conclusion's '+9.76% TP' is consistent with 84.7->93.86 only on that reading; 'difference in AUC for delays between 30 and 90 days was 32.1%' contradicts the claim of minimal impact; rejection rates with updates given as both 0.62% and 0.38% for the 30-day delay. Operating points were set at 10-15% rejection yet observed rejection is ~1%. Most results are in figures; no confidence intervals; only one dataset.

title: Cloud–Edge Collaborative Autonomy Architecture for BVLOS UAV Delivery Systems
evidence: Abstract: "Safety-critical operations such as perception, obstacle avoidance, and local flight adjustments are executed on edge devices located on the UAV or nearby ground nodes"
method: Three-layer cloud-edge-onboard autonomy architecture for BVLOS UAV delivery, with a rule-based task-allocation function over latency, complexity and spatial scope plus an additive decision-latency model.
evaluation: AirSim plus NS-3 sim, 25x25 km urban region, 20-100 UAVs, 500 missions, 30 runs per architecture; vs cloud-only and edge-only: latency 34 vs 118 ms, nav error 2.1 m, completion 96% vs 88%; Jetson-class onboard inference 8-12 ms.
contribution: A cloud-edge-onboard task-allocation architecture for BVLOS drone delivery that keeps safety-critical perception and avoidance onboard, cutting simulated decision latency from 118 ms to 34 ms.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: partly - onboard obstacle detection is a deep model on a Jetson-class board (8-12 ms), but nothing vetoes, halts or defers a nominal action, so (a) fails and (d) is the only criterion; included on the strength of latency-constrained safety-critical inference, which the maintainer may judge too thin. No collision or hazard rate is reported; delivery completion rate (96% vs 88% and 91%) is the nearest safety proxy. Table 4 gives single round numbers with no variance or CI despite 30 claimed runs; Section 7.2 is missing (7.1 jumps to 7.3); review-response artefacts remain in the body (Section 5 titled Revised, addresses the reviewer's request); citation years are wrong in several places (Dorling 2017 dated 2020, Fotouhi 2019 dated 2021); journal front matter says Algora vol 2 issue 2, 12/2025 while the record year is 2026. Treat all figures as unverified.

title: Epistemic Side Effects: An AI Safety Problem
evidence: Sec 3: "What we want to do (as in our previous work) is to give the robot an auxiliary reward when it reaches a terminal state, proportional to the expected value of that state for the human."
method: Augmented RL reward adding the human's expected history-state value at terminal states of a POMDP, so a robot avoids physical and epistemic side effects on a partially observing human.
evaluation: Five handcrafted kitchen gridworld scenarios, tabular Q-learning, vs non-augmented and full-observability baselines; metric is the human's extra penalty (our approach 0 in all five; baselines -7, -10, -8, -inf).
contribution: Introduces epistemic side effects - unintended changes to other agents' knowledge or beliefs - and shows an existing auxiliary-reward method for physical side effects can avoid some of them in a POMDP.
flag: learned or AI system guarded: yes (tabular Q-learning robot), but the mechanism is a training-time reward term, which the 2026-11-13 scope note says is explicitly not (a). Check (c): the harm is to one modelled human, there is no detector and no hazard rate, so the primacy test fails. Check (e): the human is only modelled and protected, not handed control, so the ruling blocks it - this is the record most likely to be overturned if the maintainer reads degraded human knowledge (knocked-over Wet Floor sign) as operator situation awareness. AAMAS 2023 Blue Sky Ideas track, i.e. a position paper, so exclude-E3 is a defensible alternative; the five experiments are single deterministic runs with handcrafted human policies, no statistics, and the paper calls them simple experiments to demonstrate the approach.

title: An ML-BDI Reasoner to Support Crime Investigation in Digital Forensics
venue: Proceedings of the 25th International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems
evidence: "When confidence is high, the agent accepts the model predictions, and when it is low, it triggers symbolic inference plans to produce a symbolic estimate." (Section 3)
method: Random Forest room-occupancy estimator from IoT sensors; a Jason BDI agent accepts high-confidence predictions, otherwise falls back to symbolic sensor-rule plans or abstains, logging plan id, timestamp, confidence and sensor state.
evaluation: 20% test split with simulated sensor dropout (MCAR, outage windows), 10 seeds. Per seed: BDI interventions 143-240 (about 210 mean), about 75% correct, vs RF errors 50-133. No accuracy, abstention rate, latency or hardware.
contribution: Extended abstract of a hybrid Random Forest plus BDI-agent occupancy reasoner that falls back to symbolic plans or abstains when model confidence is low, keeping an auditable decision trace for forensics.
flag: (i) applies in design (hand-off from ML model to a symbolic fallback system), but this is a 3-page AAMAS extended abstract with 'preliminary results' that I judge below the floor; maintainer may read Table 1 as a baseline comparison and include. Problems: abstention is named in the abstract but no abstention count or rate is reported anywhere; no end-to-end accuracy of the hybrid vs RF alone; 'BDI Correct' exceeds 'RF Error' in every seed, so the agent also intervenes where the RF was already right and the BDI errors (28-74 per seed) may fall on those cases, meaning net benefit cannot be computed from the table. Dataset, test-set size, confidence threshold and degradation levels are not stated. Not a sequential or safety-critical runtime gate; offline forensic analysis. No human takeover studied.

title: Grape Leaf Disease Identification Using Image Retrieval and Expert Referral of Doubtful Images
evidence: "The share of all images given a wrong diagnosis fell from 11.0% to 1.3%" (Section 3.1)
method: Diagnose-or-defer: content-based image retrieval for grape leaves using a 56-value lesion/texture/shape descriptor; refers the image to an expert when top-10 neighbours disagree or the query is farther than a calibrated distance.
evaluation: PlantVillage n=4,046 blocked CV: 89.0% without deferral; with deferral 60.6% coverage, 97.9% correct, wrong 1.3% vs 11.0%. PlantDoc n=133: wrong 64.1% to 1.2%, 96% referred. Two descriptor baselines. Xeon core: 0.13-0.24 s describe, 0.5 ms decision.
contribution: Retrieval-based grape leaf disease identifier that defers to an expert when retrieved neighbours disagree or the image is unfamiliar, cutting wrong diagnoses from 11.0% to 1.3% at 60.6% coverage.
flag: none of (i)-(v) in substance: (i) holds only nominally. Deferral is the stated main contribution and the target is 'an expert', but this is a one-shot classifier with a reject option applied to one domain; no expert is modelled or studied (the paper lists a user study with experts as future work), so I did not add 'e'. If the maintainer reads (i) as satisfied by any stated referral to a human, this becomes an include, and the evaluation floor is met (no-deferral baseline, CIs, McNemar tests, ablation of the familiarity check). Doubts: on internet images the method defers 96% and is right on only 16 of 24 diagnoses, i.e. it is mostly an OOD refusal; the calibration target failed in one of five rounds. The file is headed 'REVIEW ARTICLE' but is original research; results heading numbered 4 with subsections 3.x; data-availability text still says '[repository link to be added before submission]'; authors declare a generative AI system (Claude) designed and wrote the code, ran validation and drafted the text. Small publisher (Ariston). Abstract numbers were all found in the body.

title: Hazy Oracles in Deep Learning
evidence: "This agent has some probability of solving the task on its own, but may also defer to a hazy oracle that can provide additional information at some cost." (Section 1.2)
method: Deferred inference: a learned deferral function (DAER, regressing additional error from human input) decides whether to ask the human for a new input; aggregation functions fuse repeated inputs up to a deferral-depth limit.
evaluation: Viewpoint estimation, scene classification, tracking, referring expressions; baselines softmax response, entropy, random. DAER AMAE 0.286 vs 0.309 best baseline; RefExp error 8.27% to 4.24% at deferral rate 1; 25-user study. GTX Titan XP; no latency.
contribution: PhD thesis formalising deferred inference, where a model asks an imperfect human for further input, with a learned deferral function, multi-round aggregation, an error-vs-effort evaluation and a 25-participant study.
flag: (i) and (ii) apply: deferral back to a human (a request for more input, not a human taking over the decision) repeated over several rounds under a deferral-depth constraint; the human response to deferral is itself studied (Chapter 7), hence 'e'. Thesis of about 513k chars: I read the abstract, Chapter 1 (problem statement, contributions), results tables and surrounding text in Chapters 3, 6 and 7, and Chapter 8 lessons and conclusion; I did NOT read Chapter 2 (related work), most of Chapter 4, Chapter 5 (Popup crowdsourcing, which looks unrelated to deferral), limitations 8.2-8.3 or the appendices. It is a dissertation compiling the author's papers, so check for duplicates of queued records (DAER; 'Evaluating and improving interactions with hazy oracles'). Not safety-critical: tasks are vision/HCI benchmarks. Caveats: the 48% error reduction is at deferral rate 1 (every query re-asked) on RefCOCO TestA only; the VOT gain is given as 1.22% in Table 6.4 and 1.37% in the text; on VOT the best method is within one standard error of baselines when depth <= 2; in the user study individual calibration did not beat aggregate calibration on absolute error (Table 7.2), only on upper-bound violations (Table 7.3); 28 recruited, 25 analysed.

title: Reliable Foundations for Interactive Machine Learning
evidence: "Conceptual safeguards operate as a confidence-based selective classifier" (Sec 2.2, Conceptual Safeguards)
method: PhD thesis of three reprinted papers: participatory personalization; concept-bottleneck selective classifier with uncertainty propagation and human concept confirmation; sufficient-context autorater plus self-confidence for selective RAG abstention.
evaluation: Ch2: 6 image/synthetic datasets, coverage at 20% confirmation budget, flycatcher tau=0.05 26.9% baseline vs 84.6% CS+ImpactConf. Ch3: selective accuracy gains over 10% (Gemma, HotpotQA). No latency.
contribution: A dissertation whose middle chapter builds a selective classifier over concept bottlenecks that abstains when unsure and asks a human to confirm concepts, raising coverage at a fixed accuracy target.
flag: none of (i)-(v) for the thesis as a whole: abstention is the main contribution of only chapter 2 (ICLR 2024 reprint), which is one-shot selective classification applied to image tasks; chapter 3 is an LLM abstaining on single RAG questions; chapter 1 is not about abstention. Maintainer may consider (i) since ch2 queries a human to confirm concepts on abstained cases, but the human is simulated from ground-truth concept labels and does not take over the decision. Thesis; constituent papers may be queued separately. Read abstract, ch2 framework/results/conclusion, sec 3.5; did not read ch1, appendices or proofs. Text file is 4M chars due to garbled figure text.

title: Distributed Agentic Micro-Agent for Resilience in the Computing Continuum
venue: KTH Publication Database DiVA (KTH Royal Institute of Technology)
evidence: "When either gate fails, the agent abstains and escalates the diagnosis to the fog tier." (Abstract, Method)
method: AURORA edge micro-agent: Bayesian-network root-cause posterior, then dual gate (posterior certainty threshold and post-intervention variational free energy bound) authorises self-healing action or abstains and escalates to fog tier.
evaluation: Monte Carlo simulation, 10,002 trials per agent; destructive-action rate 0.0% vs 33.33% for rule-based and ungated active-inference; abstention 65.9%, resolution 34.1% vs 66.67%; decision 3.4 ms on a MacBook Pro.
contribution: A dual uncertainty gate lets an edge self-healing agent act only when diagnosis is confident, otherwise abstain and escalate, cutting destructive actions from 33% to 0% in simulation at the cost of 66% abstention.
flag: (iv) safety-critical runtime gate that vetoes a remediation action and hands off to a fallback tier. Master's thesis (Stockholm University DSV, 2026), not peer reviewed. Simulation only on a laptop; no Raspberry Pi run despite edge framing, so edge deployment not credited. Fog-tier handoff is never executed: resolution of the 6,591 abstained payloads is unmeasured. Each trial is a single i.i.d. observation-decision episode, not sequential. Gate threshold Fth tuned on the evaluation distributions (author admits leakage); across 10 seeds destructive rate is 2.26% +/- 4.76%, not 0.0%. Baselines' 33.33% equals exactly one fault class, an artefact of the simulator design. Abstract cites 33-74 point reductions over four workloads; I verified only the 33.33-point CCTV figure. Multi-agent only nominally (micro-agents are checks on one node). No human handoff. Read abstract, ch5 setup, sec 6.1-6.2, sec 7.9; did not read ch2-4, sec 6.3-6.17, appendices.

title: Learning under Information and Experience Constraints in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
