title: The extended littlestone's dimension for learning with mistakes and abstentions
evidence: "the examples on which the learner abstains are then passed on to a human, who can then take a closer look." (Sec. 1, Introduction)
method: Online learning with mistakes and abstentions (k-SZB model): defines the extended Littlestone dimension and an extended Standard Optimal Algorithm trading at most k mistakes against abstentions.
evaluation: Theory only, no experiment. Proved: optimality of SOA.DK for deterministic learners (Thm 2), ELdim upper bounds and tight examples (Thms 4-6), lower and upper bounds under l-bias non-realizability (Thms 7-10).
contribution: Characterises the optimal mistake-abstention tradeoff in online learning through an extended Littlestone dimension, with an optimal deterministic algorithm and bounds for the non-realizable case.
flag: (ii) and (v): abstaining is a per-round action in online learning and the paper gives the optimal tradeoff. Human handoff appears only as motivation in the introduction and is not modelled, so 'e' and the human handoff cell are not claimed. No experiments. Last ~1300 characters of the PDF (end of appendix or references) were not read. runtime_interceptor set no as pure theory.

title: The relationship between agnostic selective classification, active learning and the disagreement coefficient
evidence: "Selective classification is a unique and extreme instance of the broader concept of confidence-rated prediction" (Sec. 1, Introduction)
method: ILESS, an agnostic pointwise-competitive selective classifier that abstains on its disagreement region; analysis ties its rejection rate to active-learning label complexity and the disagreement coefficient.
evaluation: Theory only, no experiment. Proved: abstain-rate bound via disagreement coefficient (Thm 5), converse (Thm 7), equivalence with Active-ILESS label complexity (Thms 15, 18). No hardware or latency.
contribution: Proves that a fast rejection rate for agnostic pointwise-competitive selective classification is equivalent to exponential active-learning speedup and a polylogarithmic disagreement coefficient.
flag: (v) foundational theory of selective classification. One-shot batch setting, no human, no sequential aspect, no experiments at all; headline is an equivalence with active learning, so abstention shares the stage. runtime_interceptor set no as pure theory. Theorem numbering taken from the arXiv version.

title: Reliable multilabel classification: Prediction with partial abstention
venue: AAAI 2020 - 34th AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
evidence: "This paper presents a formal framework of MLC with partial abstention" (Sec 9, Conclusion); predictions lie in {0, abstain, 1}^m.
method: Generalised multilabel losses with an abstention-count penalty; derives Bayes-optimal partial-abstention predictions for Hamming loss, rank loss and F-measure, with O(m log m) and O(m^3) algorithms.
evaluation: Optimal rules proved (Prop 1-3; proofs in supplement); six datasets (CAL500, EMOTIONS, SCENE, YEAST, MEDIAMILL, NUS-WIDE), 10-fold CV, vs full prediction and full abstention; loss and abstention size in figures only.
contribution: Extends the reject option to multilabel classification, letting a learner abstain on individual labels, and derives efficient Bayes-optimal rules for Hamming, rank and F-measure losses.
flag: (v), borderline: optimal reject rules are stated and proved, but for a one-shot multilabel classifier; a strict reading gives exclude-E4. Proofs and F-measure results are in a supplement not in the arXiv PDF read. No numeric values in the main text, results in figures only; baselines are full prediction and full abstention. No human involved.

title: SELECTIVE CLASSIFICATION CAN MAGNIFY DISPARITIES ACROSS GROUPS
venue: ICLR 2021 - 9th International Conference on Learning Representations
evidence: "a cautionary finding: while selective classification improves average accuracy" it can magnify group disparities (Sec 1); classifier abstains when confidence is below threshold tau.
method: Analyses softmax-response selective classifiers via group margin distributions; proves when selective accuracy is monotone in the threshold and when the worst group underperforms a group-agnostic reference.
evaluation: Props 1-4 proved on margin distributions; CelebA, CivilComments, Waterbirds, CheXpert-device, MultiNLI with ERM vs group-agnostic and Robin Hood references, group DRO; MultiNLI worst group 65 to 75 pct at 50 pct coverage; no hardware.
contribution: Shows that confidence-threshold selective classification can widen accuracy gaps between groups, with a margin-distribution analysis and five-dataset study; group DRO training restores worst-group gains.
flag: none of (i)-(v) clearly: one-shot selective classification analysed by accuracy-coverage per group. It does contain proved propositions about selective accuracy, so a generous reading of (v) is possible, but they concern group disparities, not optimal rules or consistency. No new abstention mechanism (softmax response, MC-dropout). Abstention cost and expert back-off left to future work. Tail of PDF not read.

title: Regression with reject option and application to kNN
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems
evidence: The optimal rule "relies on thresholding the conditional variance function" (Abstract); plug-in predictor "behaves asymptotically as well as the optimal eps-predictor both in terms of risk and rejection rate" (Sec 3.2)
method: Regression with a fixed rejection budget eps: optimal rule abstains where conditional variance exceeds a quantile threshold; semi-supervised plug-in estimator, instantiated with kNN, calibrates the threshold on unlabeled data.
evaluation: Proved: optimal rule (Prop 1-2), consistency and rejection-rate error <= C N^(-1/2) (Thm 1), kNN rates (Thm 2). Experiments: UCI aquatic and airfoil, SVM/RF/kNN variants, 100 runs; airfoil RF error 14.40 to 7.22 at 50% rejection.
contribution: Derives the optimal reject rule for regression under a rejection-rate budget, a variance threshold, and proves consistency and kNN convergence rates for a plug-in estimator that meets the budget.
flag: (v): foundational theory of the reject option for regression. One-shot and i.i.d., no sequential, deferral-target or safety aspect, so it enters only under (v); without (v) it would be exclude-E4. Experiments compare three instantiations of the same method against the no-rejection row (eps=0), not an external rejection baseline. SVM error on aquatic is non-monotone in rejection rate (1.38, 1.08, 0.91, 1.01), which authors attribute to poor variance estimation. Table 1 row labels are ambiguous between eps and coverage in my reading; verify before quoting numbers. Human intervention is discussed only in the broader-impact statement. Thm 2 rate: n^(-2/(d+2)) + log(n)^(alpha+1) n^(-(alpha+1)/(d+2)) + N^(-1/2).

title: RISAN: Robust Instance Specific Deep Abstention Network
venue: 37th Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence, UAI 2021
evidence: "We show that the double sigmoid loss is classification calibrated." (Abstract; Theorem 1, Sec. 2)
method: RISAN: deep binary classifier with reject option jointly learning decision function f(x) and instance-specific rejection bandwidth rho(x) under the double sigmoid loss, optionally with an auxiliary cross-entropy head.
evaluation: UCI (Ionosphere, ILPD, Phishing), Cats vs Dogs, CIFAR-10 car/truck, MNIST 1/7, CBIS-DDSM; baselines DH-SVM, SDR-SVM, SelectiveNet, DAC. 6-7% higher accuracy at 20% label noise. Proved calibration, excess-risk, Rademacher bounds.
contribution: Proposes a deep abstention network with an input-dependent rejection band trained on a classification-calibrated double sigmoid loss, reporting robustness to label noise against SelectiveNet and DAC.
flag: (v), borderline: one-shot binary classifier with reject option, which would be E4, but it proves surrogate calibration (Thm 1), an excess-risk bound (Thm 2) and a generalization bound (Thm 3, input-independent rho only). It is a method paper with supporting theory rather than foundational theory; maintainer may well prefer exclude-E4. Almost all results are in figures; the only numbers in text are approximate gains (6-7% at 20% noise, about 10% and 5% at 40% noise at low rejection, 1-2% from the auxiliary head). Robustness to label noise is empirical only, not proved. No human, no sequential aspect.

title: Towards optimally abstaining from prediction with OOD test examples
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems
evidence: "introducing and analyzing an approach for optimally abstaining in classification and regression in the transductive setting" (Sec 1.2, Contributions and organization).
method: Min-Max Abstention: given labeled training and unlabeled test examples, chooses fractional abstentions at cost alpha minimising worst-case test loss over the version space, solved by ellipsoid method with ERM oracle.
evaluation: Theory only, no experiments. Proved: loss at most alpha*TV(P,Q)+2d lg(3n)/n under covariate shift (Thm 1,2), adversarial test bound (Thm 3), linear regression bound (Thm 4); poly-time claims only.
contribution: Gives a polynomial-time transductive rule for abstaining on out-of-distribution test examples whose loss exceeds standard rates only by the abstention cost times the train-test total variation distance.
flag: (v): optimal-abstention rule with proved bounds for realizable classification and linear regression under covariate shift and adversarial test corruption. Batch transductive, not sequential (online left to future work). No experiments at all, so the rule is never run; runtime_interceptor yes only in the sense that the rule withholds test predictions. Human or costlier model for abstained items is motivation only.

title: Online Selective Classification with Limited Feedback
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems
evidence: "We construct simple versioning-based schemes for any mu in (0,1]" (Abstract); learner predicts or abstains each round and sees the label only on abstaining (problem setup).
method: VUE: keeps a version space of classifiers not yet seen to err, abstains at random with rate p to obtain labels, otherwise predicts consistently; PROD-weighted variants.
evaluation: Proved mistake and excess-abstention regret bounds (Thm 2,4,7) and lower bound (Thm 5); CIFAR-10 and GAS, N=600 classifiers, vs best-in-hindsight and full-feedback batch; curves only; no hardware/latency.
contribution: Online selective classification where labels are seen only on abstaining: versioning schemes reach about sqrt(NT) mistake and excess-abstention regret against the best error-free abstaining classifier, with matching Pareto lower bounds.
flag: (ii) and (v): abstaining is an action over T rounds with label feedback only on abstention; theory-led. Experiments report figures only, no table; the 'expert' on abstention is simulated by true labels or a full-feature model, no human. Tail of PDF (last ~9k chars, appendix) not read.

title: Post-hoc Estimators for Learning to Defer to an Expert
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems
evidence: "Narasimhan, H., Jitkrittum, W., Menon, A.K., Rawat, A., Kumar, S.: Post-hoc estimators for learning to defer to an expert." (reference list entry 16 of another chapter; the only occurrence of the title in the file)
method: Not extractable: the supplied text is a different document and does not contain the record's paper.
evaluation: Not extractable: paper text absent from the supplied file.
contribution: Not assessed: the supplied full text is the UNSURE 2025 workshop proceedings (LNCS 16166), not the 2022 paper named in the record.
flag: WRONG FILE: Uncertainty for Safe Utilization of Machine Learning in Medical Imaging - 7th International Workshop, UNSURE 2025 (LNCS 16166, ISBN 978-3-032-06593-3). Grepped the whole 663k-char volume for the record title and first author: the paper is not a chapter here, it appears only as a citation (ref 16 of one chapter; NeurIPS vol. 35, pp. 29292-29304, 2022). The nearest chapter, Wundram and Baumgartner 'Is Uncertainty Quantification a Viable Alternative to Learned Deferral?' (p. 34), is a different 2025 paper and was not extracted. Scope not judged; by title the record would likely fall under (i)/(v) learning to defer, so the maintainer should obtain the correct NeurIPS 2022 PDF and re-queue. RQ scores are placeholders.

title: Efficient Active Learning with Abstention
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems
evidence: Abstract: "We develop the first computationally efficient active learning algorithm with abstention." The classifier abstains when its confidence interval on eta(x) lies inside [1/2 - gamma, 1/2 + gamma].
method: Epoch-based active learning with a regression oracle: keeps a version space, builds confidence bounds on the conditional probability, abstains where they sit near 1/2, queries labels only where needed.
evaluation: Pure theory, no experiments. Proved: Chow excess error at most epsilon with label complexity polylogarithmic in 1/epsilon (Thm 4), oracle-efficient implementation (Thm 5), minimax rates under Massart and Tsybakov noise (Thm 6).
contribution: The first oracle-efficient active learning algorithm with abstention, proved to reach low Chow excess error with label complexity polylogarithmic in the target accuracy without low-noise assumptions.
flag: (v), borderline: the formal results concern Chow's excess error with an abstention option, but the paper's centre of gravity is active-learning label complexity, with abstention as the device that removes noise assumptions; the maintainer may reasonably read this as E1 (abstention instrumental). No experiments, no baselines, no hardware, so it passes the floor only as theory. Abstention here is by a learned classifier at prediction time, not deferral to a human (human expert appears only as motivation), and the sequential element is label querying, not abstaining as an action over time. Only the first 100000 of about 156000 characters were read (remainder is proofs).

title: A Theory of Selective Prediction
evidence: "the upper bound in Lemma 2.1 is optimal up to a constant factor." (Sec 2.3, Matching Lower Bound)
method: Online predictor sees an adversarial non-adaptive sequence, declines to predict at each step, then chooses once when and over what window length to predict a statistic.
evaluation: Pure theory, no experiments. Proved: squared loss O(1/log n) with matching Omega(1/log n) lower bound for window mean; O(L/sqrt(log n)) for L-smooth functions; selectivity necessary (loss >= 1/64).
contribution: Proves that a predictor free to choose when and over what horizon to predict achieves vanishing error O(1/log n) on arbitrary sequences, with a matching lower bound, and that this selectivity is necessary.
flag: (ii) and (v), borderline: abstention here means choosing the time and window of a single forecast, not a reject option with a cost or a deferral to anyone; no risk-coverage notion, no safety setting, no experiments. Maintainer should decide whether timing-selectivity counts as abstention being the main contribution; if not this is exclude-E1. runtime_interceptor no because pure theory. Also: Prop 4.1 excess risk O(sqrt(|L|/k)) for finite model classes, tightness left open.

title: Fast Rates for Online Prediction with Abstention
evidence: "it is possible to achieve expected regret bounds that are independent of the time horizon T" (Abstract)
method: Online prediction with expert advice where the learner may abstain each round at cost c below 1/2; exponential-weights style algorithm, including time-varying costs and adaptive learning rate.
evaluation: Theory only, no experiment. Proved: regret at most log N/(2(1-2c)) independent of T (Thm 1, Cor 2), matching lower bound (Thm 9), multiclass and Littlestone-class extensions. No hardware.
contribution: Shows that giving an online learner an abstain action costing slightly under one half yields horizon-independent regret against the best of N experts, with matching lower bounds.
flag: (ii) and (v): abstention is a per-round action in adversarial online prediction, with proved optimal regret. The true label is revealed even after abstaining and no human or fallback receives the abstained round; the 'experts' are advice sources, not deferral targets. Time-varying abstention cost (Sec. 3) is the nearest link to RQ2. No experiments. runtime_interceptor set no as pure theory.

title: AUC-based Selective Classification
evidence: Abstract: "We propose a model-agnostic approach to associate a selection function to a given probabilistic binary classifier." Instances whose score falls in a band [theta_l, theta_u] are rejected.
method: AUCROSS: abstains on a middle band of classifier scores chosen to raise AUC at a target coverage, with band bounds estimated by cross-fitting and subsample quantile estimators.
evaluation: Nine tabular and image datasets, LightGBM and VGG; vs PLUGIN, PLUGINAUC, SCROSS, SelectiveNet, SAT and an oracle; selective AUC, coverage violation; Xeon plus two RTX A6000, training time only.
contribution: A model-agnostic selection function for binary classifiers that abstains on a mid-score band to improve AUC at a target coverage, estimated by cross-fitting.
flag: none of (i)-(v): one-shot selective classification on tabular and image data judged by selective AUC and coverage. Borderline (v): Props 1-3 give sufficient (not necessary) conditions under which abstaining raises AUC, but there is no optimal rule, consistency result or risk bound, and Thm 4 is cited, not proved. Human hand-off is mentioned only as motivation. AUCROSS is roughly tied with the simpler PLUGINAUC (28 vs 29 wins of 54 on selective AUC; CatsVsDogs c=.75 .987 vs .990) and loses selective accuracy. Example: Adult c=.75 AUC .963 vs .958 PLUGIN, .917 SelectiveNet. Only the first 100000 of about 135000 characters were read (remainder is appendix).

title: Exponential Weights Algorithms for Selective Learning
evidence: "This selective learning setting models many high-stakes decision making scenarios" (Sec. 1, Introduction)
method: Selective learning: on an arbitrary data stream the learner chooses when to commit and a window length, predicting only there; hybrid and bounded-recall exponential weights algorithms.
evaluation: Theory only, no experiment. Proved: excess risk O((log log|L| + log log n)/log n) (Thm 1), bounded-recall O(sqrt(log|L|/log n)) (Thm 3), lower bounds (Thms 2, 4), impossibility for a VC-dimension-1 class (Prop 7).
contribution: Gives exponential-weights algorithms with near-optimal excess-risk bounds for selective learning, where a learner on an arbitrary sequence chooses a single time window on which to commit a model.
flag: (ii) and (v), doubtful: 'selective' here means choosing one time and window length at which to commit, i.e. withholding prediction everywhere else; it is not per-instance abstention, there is no abstention cost, no reject option and no deferral target. If the maintainer reads the scope ruling as requiring an explicit abstain or defer action, this is exclude-E1. No experiments. runtime_interceptor set no as pure theory.

title: Sample Efficient Learning of Predictors that Complement Humans
evidence: "we provide the first theoretical analysis of the benefit of learning complementary predictors in expert deferral." (Abstract)
method: Classifier plus rejector deferring to a human; compares joint and staged training, a consistent surrogate family, and DoD, a disagreement-based active scheme for querying human predictions.
evaluation: Proved: joint-vs-staged gap bounds (Thm 1), surrogate consistency (Thm 2), generalization bound, DoD label complexity (Thm 4). CIFAR-10 with synthetic expert and synthetic 1-D data; joint vs staged curves in figures only; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Bounds the gap between jointly and separately trained classifier-rejector pairs for deferral to a human, and gives an active-learning scheme that needs few human labels to learn when to defer.
flag: (i) deferral to a human expert, and (v) consistency and sample-complexity theory. The expert is synthetic in every experiment (perfect on 5 CIFAR-10 classes, random otherwise; a rule on the 1-D data), so no real human and no 'e'; I left the human handoff gap cell empty for that reason. Experimental results are reported only as figures, no numeric values in the text; the floor is met through the theorems. DoD guarantee needs realizability assumptions. New tag active-learning added. One-shot classification.

title: Selective Regression Under Fairness Criteria
evidence: Selective regression "allows abstention from prediction if the confidence to make an accurate prediction is not sufficient" (Abstract)
method: Selective regressor abstains when predicted variance exceeds a threshold; a conditional mutual-information regularizer enforces sufficiency so each subgroup's error falls as coverage falls.
evaluation: Insurance, Crime, IHDP; two-layer networks; baselines are the same models without regularizer; area under MSE-coverage curve, e.g. Insurance 0.0195 vs 0.0371, minority 0.0167 vs 0.0442. No hardware.
contribution: Introduces monotonic selective risk as a fairness criterion for selective regression and a regularizer that keeps minority-subgroup error from rising as coverage is reduced.
flag: none of (i)-(v): one-shot selective regression with a fairness regularizer added in training; rejected cases are not routed to a human or fallback. Theorem 1 (sufficiency implies monotonic selective risk) is proved in the appendix and Theorem 2's proof is omitted; this is a fairness property, not foundational reject-option theory, but a maintainer could argue (v). Gains are not uniform: overall AUC is slightly worse on Crime (0.0079 vs 0.0075; 0.0117 vs 0.0101) and majority-subgroup AUC is slightly worse on Crime and IHDP treatment. Small tabular datasets, 5 runs.

title: Classification with Abstention but Without Disparities
evidence: "We propose a data-driven post-processing algorithm which enjoys generic plug-and-play finite sample guarantees" (Sec 1, Contributions); Thm 3.2 gives the optimal reject rule under Demographic Parity.
method: Derives optimal classifier with reject under group-wise reject-rate and Demographic Parity constraints (group thresholds on eta); post-processes any score via a sparse linear program on unlabeled data.
evaluation: Proved optimal rule (Thm 3.2), finite-sample constraint and excess-risk bounds (Prop 5.1,5.2); ADULT, GERMAN with LR and RF vs unmodified base classifier, 20 repetitions; figures only; no hardware/latency.
contribution: Characterises the optimal reject-option classifier under demographic parity and fixed group-wise reject rates, and gives an LP post-processing method with distribution-free finite-sample guarantees on both constraints.
flag: (v), borderline: optimal reject rule and bounds are proved, but the setting is one-shot batch classification and the angle is fairness; a strict reading could make it exclude-E4. No numeric tables, results in figures only. Human handling of rejects is mentioned as motivation, not studied. Paper gives both ~48,000 and ~40,000 for ADULT size. Tail of PDF not read.

title: Who Should Predict? Exact Algorithms For Learning to Defer to Humans
evidence: "we provide a novel surrogate loss function that is realizable-consistent and performs well empirically" (Abstract)
method: Classifier plus rejector deferring to a human with side information; exact MILP for linear classifier/rejector pairs and a RealizableSurrogate loss trained end to end.
evaluation: Proved: NP-hardness of halfspace L2D (Thm 1), realizable-consistency (Thm 2), generalization bound. 9 datasets incl. CIFAR-10H, ImageNet-16H, NIH X-ray vs 6 baselines; system accuracy e.g. 0.969 vs 0.960 CE on CIFAR-10H; no latency.
contribution: Shows that learning linear classifier-rejector pairs for deferral to humans is NP-hard, and gives an exact mixed-integer formulation and a realizable-consistent surrogate that match or beat prior learning-to-defer methods.
flag: (i) deferral to a human expert, also (v) hardness and consistency theory. Human predictions are fixed dataset annotations (real for CIFAR-10H, ImageNet-16H, HateSpeech, COMPASS, NIH; synthetic for CIFAR-K); the handoff itself is not studied, so no 'e' and the human handoff gap cell is generous. Gains over baselines are small and not uniform: the method loses to SelectivePrediction or OvA on COMPASS, HateSpeech, ImageNet-16H noise 95/110 and Pneumothorax in Table 2. One-shot classification, not sequential. MILP runtime only shown in a figure.

title: Learning to Defer to Multiple Experts: Consistent Surrogate Losses, Confidence Calibration, and Conformal Ensembles
evidence: "We have extended the L2D framework to support multiple experts." (Sec. 8 Conclusions)
method: Softmax and one-vs-all surrogate losses for learning to defer to multiple experts; the rejector picks classifier or an expert; conformal risk control selects an expert subset for majority vote.
evaluation: Proved: both surrogates calibrated/consistent (Thm 3.1, 3.2, Cor 3.3), mixture-of-experts loss inconsistent. HAM10000, Galaxy-Zoo, HateSpeech, CIFAR-10; baselines classifier, best expert, Hemmer mixture; system accuracy, ECE, set size; 3 seeds.
contribution: Two consistent surrogate losses for learning to defer to multiple experts, with the one-vs-all form giving better calibrated expert-correctness estimates, plus conformal ensembles that choose how many experts to query.
flag: (iii) and (v). One-shot classification. Experts are synthetic or perturbed versions of human annotations, not live humans; handoff itself is not studied so e is not claimed. Most numbers appear only in figures: text gives OvA ECE near 2 percent vs softmax about 4.5 percent on CIFAR-10, and conformal ensembles about 90 percent accuracy vs under 80 for fixed size-5 ensembles. No new theorem for the conformal statistic. No hardware model or latency.

title: In Defense of Softmax Parametrization for Calibrated and Consistent Learning to Defer
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems
evidence: Abstract: "the cause of the miscalibrated and unbounded estimator in prior literature is due to the symmetric nature" of the surrogate losses; Theorem 2 proves the asymmetric-softmax surrogate consistent with bounded estimates.
method: Asymmetric softmax parametrisation and surrogate loss for learning to defer: class cross-entropy plus an expert-correctness term whose output stays in [0,1], giving consistent, calibrated deferral to an expert.
evaluation: Proved: Thm 1 impossibility, Thm 2 consistency, Thm 3 regret transfer. CIFAR-100 synthetic experts, CIFAR-10H, HateSpeech, ImageNet-16H, NIH vs S-SM, S-OvA, A-OvA: CIFAR-10H error 3.65, coverage 94.20, ECE 0.94.
contribution: Shows that unbounded, miscalibrated expert-accuracy estimates in softmax learning to defer come from symmetric losses, and gives an asymmetric softmax surrogate that is consistent and calibrated, improving error and coverage on five benchmarks.
flag: (i) and (v): learning to defer to a human expert with surrogate-loss consistency theory. Single-expert, one-shot classification; no sequential or latency aspect. Experts are simulated or precomputed human labels, no live handoff, so criterion e not claimed; human handoff gap cell is generous and could be dropped. On NIH chest X-ray A-SM coverage (14.24) is not the best (A-OvA 19.47), and on CIFAR-100 its error is not always lowest (e.g. k=60, p=94%: 19.30 vs S-OvA 18.44). Quoted evidence is from the abstract; values read from tables via a summary, standard errors not captured.

title: LEARNING TO REJECT WITH A FIXED PREDICTOR: APPLICATION TO DECONTEXTUALIZATION
venue: 12th International Conference on Learning Representations, ICLR 2024
evidence: Sec 8 (Conclusion): "a theoretically-justified approach to classification with a reject option"; Theorem 5 bounds the excess rejection risk by the square root of the excess surrogate risk.
method: Learns a rejector for a fixed predictor with a convex exponential surrogate of the rejection loss, backed by an H-consistency bound; applied to accept or reject mT5 decontextualization outputs.
evaluation: Proved: calibration gaps and H-consistency bound (Thm 5) for all measurable rejectors. Experiment: 2000 labelled mT5 decontextualizations, 4-fold CV; vs MaxProb and cross-entropy rejectors; coverage at fixed error.
contribution: A surrogate loss for learning to reject with a fixed predictor, with a proved H-consistency bound, that reaches 90.6% coverage at 5.1% error on decontextualization against 64.4% for a cross-entropy rejector.
flag: (v): surrogate-loss consistency for the reject option; the application alone (one-shot rejection of language-model outputs) would be E4. The bound is proved only for the family of all measurable functions under a condition tying alpha, beta and c; extension to other hypothesis sets is asserted, not proved. No deferral to a human or fallback: rejected outputs are simply withheld. Small evaluation (2000 examples, about 89% positives, labelled by the authors); standard deviations are said to be smaller but not given numerically. Abstract claim of about 25% coverage gain when halving error matches body (90.6% vs about 64.4% at about 5.1% error); theoretical limit 93.6%. No hardware or latency.

title: Selective Nonparametric Regression via Testing
evidence: "We show the natural way to construct the abstention rule for nonparametric heteroskedastic regression" (Section 1, contributions)
method: Selective regression: abstain at a point when a hypothesis test on the kernel-estimated conditional variance cannot reject that it exceeds the abstention cost.
evaluation: Proved: optimal rule is variance thresholding (Prop 1), non-asymptotic excess-risk upper bounds (Thm 2). Synthetic 1-D, Airfoil, CPU-small vs plug-in rule; MSE-vs-acceptance curves only, no numeric values in text; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Casts abstention in nonparametric heteroskedastic regression as a test on conditional variance and proves non-asymptotic excess-risk bounds, generalising the plug-in rule.
flag: (v) only: reject-option theory for regression (optimal rule plus non-asymptotic bounds). Borderline: this is one-shot selective prediction with no deferral target, no human and no sequential aspect, so it is E4 unless the maintainer accepts it as foundational theory. Upper bounds only, no minimax lower bound. Empirical results are plots only; I found no numeric metric in the text, so it meets the floor only through the proved results. Low relevance to any RQ.

title: When Does Confidence-Based Cascade Deferral Suffice?
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems
evidence: "In this paper, we initiate a systematic study of the potential limitations of confidence-based deferral for cascades." (Sec. 1 Introduction)
method: Characterises the Bayes-optimal deferral rule for a two-model cascade under a deferral cost; proposes post-hoc deferral: a small MLP on model-1 outputs predicting whether model 2 will do better.
evaluation: Proved: optimal rule (Prop 3.1), excess risk (Cor 3.2), when confidence suffices (Lemma 4.1), finite-sample bound (Lemma 4.2). ImageNet, CIFAR-100 deferral curves vs confidence, entropy, random, oracles; V100 for post-hoc.
contribution: Derives the Bayes-optimal deferral rule for model cascades and shows confidence-based deferral fails with specialist models, label noise or distribution shift, where post-hoc learned deferral does better.
flag: none of (i)-(v) cleanly: deferral is from a small model to a larger model purely for inference cost, which the scope ruling sends to E1; no human, safeguard or safety framing. Maintainer should check whether the proved optimal-rule results earn it (v) instead, since deferral rules are the main contribution and the theory is general. No exact accuracy numbers in the text, only figure curves (axis ranges e.g. ImageNet 0.65-0.75); seeds and variance not stated. Post-hoc MLP size is inconsistent between Sec. 5.3 (64 and 16 units) and App. C.2. No inference latency, only relative cost.

title: Counterfactually Comparing Abstaining Classifiers
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems
evidence: "we introduce the counterfactual score as a new evaluation metric for black-box abstaining classifiers" (Sec. 1 Introduction)
method: Treats abstentions as missing data and defines the counterfactual score, the expected score had the classifier not abstained; doubly robust cross-fitted estimator for comparing two black-box abstaining classifiers.
evaluation: Proved: asymptotic normality and nonparametric efficiency (Thm 3.1, 3.2), anytime-valid sequences (Thm D.1). Simulation n=2000: DR miscoverage 0.05 vs plug-in 0.91, IPW 0.03 (wider CIs); CIFAR-100 three scenarios.
contribution: An offline evaluation method that compares abstaining classifiers by the score they would have achieved without abstaining, with a doubly robust estimator and valid confidence intervals.
flag: none of (i)-(v): an offline evaluation metric and estimator for one-shot abstaining classifiers, not an abstain or defer mechanism; nothing is intercepted at runtime. E1 would also be defensible since abstention is the object evaluated, not the contribution's mechanism. A maintainer could argue (v) on the strength of the proved efficiency results, but they concern evaluation, not the reject rule; relevant to RQ5 only as method for measuring safeguards. Identification needs stochastic abstention (positivity); deterministic abstention is unidentifiable. Efficiency proof is a sketch. Power values not given in text. Read the first 100000 of 108621 characters. No hardware or latency.

title: Adversarial Resilience in Sequential Prediction via Abstention
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems
evidence: "we allow the learner to abstain on adversarial examples for free" (Sec 3.2)
method: Online binary learner outputs 0, 1 or abstain each round; abstains when shattering-probability or disagreement-count evidence is balanced, so clean-label adversarial injections cannot force errors.
evaluation: Pure theory, no experiments. Proved: misclassification <= d^2 log T and abstention <= 6d (known distribution, Thm 5.1); sqrt(T log T)-order bounds for VC-1 and rectangles (Thm 6.1, 6.7).
contribution: Proves that an online learner allowed to abstain each round keeps error bounded by VC dimension rather than Littlestone dimension under clean-label adversarial injections.
flag: (ii) and (v): abstention is a per-round action in an online protocol, with proved bounds. No experiment, no baseline, no latency; runtime_interceptor set no as pure theory. Abstention is free on adversarial rounds, which is a strong modelling assumption. Reader reported an inconsistency in Thm 6.1 (alpha = sqrt(T) in the statement vs sqrt(T/log T) in the proof) and in the constant of Prop 4.2; check against the PDF. Unknown-distribution results cover only VC-1 classes and axis-aligned rectangles. Human takeover is motivation only.

title: Predictor-Rejector Multi-Class Abstention: Theoretical Analysis and Algorithms
evidence: "We introduce several new families of surrogate losses" for which (H,R)-consistency bounds are proved in the predictor-rejector framework (Abstract; Theorems 2, 6)
method: Predictor-rejector multi-class abstention with constant cost c: new single-stage surrogates (MAE, rho-margin, constrained rho-hinge) and a two-stage scheme learning a rejector for a fixed pre-trained predictor.
evaluation: Proved (H,R)-consistency bounds, a negative result (Thm 1), realizable consistency. SVHN/CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 abstention loss, two-stage 0.94/3.31/9.23 percent vs Mozannar-Sontag 1.61/4.48/10.40 and Cao 2.16/3.62/14.99. No hardware or latency.
contribution: Gives the first non-asymptotic (H,R)-consistency bounds and realizable consistency for predictor-rejector multi-class abstention surrogates, with a two-stage rejector that beats score-based baselines on SVHN and CIFAR.
flag: (v) only: foundational surrogate-consistency theory of the reject option. No deferral target, no human, one-shot image classification - without the (v) ruling this would be E4. Single-stage MAE surrogate is no better than baselines (2.22 on SVHN, 14.99 on CIFAR-100); the gain is the two-stage variant. I read the first 100k of 163k characters; the rest is appendix proofs and experimental details (Appendix E) that I did not read. Likely overlaps with other Mao/Mohri/Zhong abstention and deferral papers in the queue.

title: Theoretically Grounded Loss Functions and Algorithms for Score-Based Multi-Class Abstention
evidence: "the cost c implicitly controls the rejection rate when minimizing the abstention loss" (Sec 2)
method: Score-based abstention with an extra abstain score; a cross-entropy surrogate family indexed by mu and a two-stage surrogate that learns the abstention score after a fixed predictor.
evaluation: Proved H-consistency bounds (Thm 1, 3, 4) and realizable consistency; CIFAR-10/100, SVHN abstention loss: two-stage 3.22%, 9.54%, 0.93% vs 4.48%, 10.40%, 1.61% for mu=1 baseline. No hardware.
contribution: Gives non-asymptotic H-consistency bounds for score-based multi-class abstention surrogates and a two-stage algorithm that lowers abstention loss on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and SVHN.
flag: (v): foundational surrogate-loss consistency theory for the reject option. Setting is one-shot image classification with constant cost c; no human, no sequential aspect, no latency, so relevance to the RQs is background only. Fetch covered the first 100000 of 130340 characters, so the appendix proofs and Theorem 8 (realizable H-consistency, said to answer an open problem of Mozannar et al. 2023) were not read in full. mu=1.7 baseline is worse than mu=1 on CIFAR-100 and SVHN (14.99% and 2.16%). Three trials only.

title: Learning to Defer to a Population: A Meta-Learning Approach
evidence: "All existing work on L2D assumes that each expert is well-identified" (Abstract; sentence fragment)
method: L2D-Pop: meta-learned rejector conditioned on a small context set of an unseen expert's predictions, via test-time fine-tuning or an (attentive) neural process, so deferral adapts to new experts.
evaluation: CIFAR-10, Traffic Signs, HAM10000, CIFAR-20 vs single-expert L2D; system and deferred-expert accuracy in figures only; predict time 14.57s (NP) vs 9.83s (single-L2D), 248.38s (finetune) on RTX 3090.
contribution: Formulates learning to defer to a population of experts unseen at training, deriving consistent surrogates and a meta-learned rejector that adapts to each new expert from a small context set.
flag: (i) and (iii). Accuracy results appear only in figures (Figs 3, 4, 9); I could not extract numeric accuracy values from the text, only the Table 2 runtime and parameter counts, so check the quantitative floor against the figures. Experts are simulated (oracle on some classes, else correct with probability p), not real humans. Consistency proofs build on Verma et al. 2023. Evidence quote is a fragment from the abstract.

title: FAIR CLASSIFIERS THAT ABSTAIN WITHOUT HARM
venue: 12th International Conference on Learning Representations, ICLR 2024
evidence: "We propose a post-hoc method that makes existing classifiers selectively abstain from predicting certain samples" (Abstract)
method: FAN: integer program picks abstain and flip decisions per training sample under group-fairness and no-harm accuracy constraints; two MLP surrogates (abstention block, flip block) imitate them at inference.
evaluation: Adult, Compas, Law tabular data; baselines LTD and FSCS; disparity reduction and per-group accuracy only in figures; surrogate accuracy 76-98 percent vs IP solutions; abstention rates 0.1-0.3. Single GPU, no latency.
contribution: Post-hoc fair abstention: an integer program plus two surrogate networks let a classifier abstain or flip labels to meet group-fairness constraints without lowering any group's accuracy.
flag: none of (i)-(v): one-shot selective classification applied to tabular fairness; abstained samples go nowhere (human review is motivation only, and the paper says the LTD decision-maker does not fit its setting). Feasibility theorems (4.1, 4.3-4.5) concern the integer program, not optimal reject rules, so I do not count them under (v) - maintainer may differ. Headline disparity/accuracy comparisons are in figures only; no exact values in the text. Fig. 20 caption numbers match the delta=0.2 row of Table 2, not delta=0.1 as captioned. Hardware given as 'a single T100 GPU' (sic).

title: PLUGIN ESTIMATORS FOR SELECTIVE CLASSIFICATION WITH OUT-OF-DISTRIBUTION DETECTION
venue: 12th International Conference on Learning Representations, ICLR 2024
evidence: Sec 1 (Introduction), contribution (i): "We provide a statistical formulation for SCOD that unifies both the SC and OOD detection problems"; Lemma 3.1 derives the Bayes-optimal classifier and rejector.
method: Derives the Bayes-optimal rejector for joint selective classification and OOD detection (max-probability plus density-ratio term) and plug-in estimators: black-box score combination and a loss-based rejector trained with wild data.
evaluation: Proved: Bayes-optimal rule (Lemma 3.1), MSP failure (3.2, 3.4), excess-risk bounds (4.1, 4.2). Experiments: CIFAR-100 ResNet-56, ImageNet BiT; vs MSP, MaxLogit, Energy, SIRC, OE, CCE, DCE; AUC-RC.
contribution: Formulates selective classification with out-of-distribution detection, derives the Bayes-optimal rejector and excess-risk bounds, and gives plug-in estimators that combine confidence and density-ratio scores.
flag: (v) only: one-shot image classification with a reject option, so without the theory it would be E4. The formal results are lemmas (optimal rule and estimation-error bounds), not a separate consistency theorem; maintainer should judge whether this counts as foundational. No human or fallback deferral is implemented (mentioned only as motivation). Empirical gains are mixed: e.g. CIFAR-100 SVHN AUC-RC 0.223 (plug-in BB L1) vs 0.318 (MSP), but the plug-in BB Res variant is worst on Texture (0.461) and ImageNet-O (0.378); no single variant wins everywhere. No hardware or latency. Text beyond character 100000 of about 119000 (appendix) was not read.

title: Regression with Multi-Expert Deferral
evidence: "Since our work is the first to study regression with multi-expert deferral" (Sec. 6 Experiments; sentence fragment)
method: Learning to defer for regression with multiple experts: single-stage (predictor and deferral learned jointly) and two-stage (fixed predictor) surrogate losses with H-consistency bounds.
evaluation: Proved (H,R)-consistency bounds (Thms 2, 5, 7). UCI Airfoil, Housing, Concrete; system MSE e.g. Airfoil base 23.35 vs 8.53 with 3 experts (single-stage); no external baseline; no hardware.
contribution: Extends learning to defer to regression with multiple experts, giving single-stage and two-stage surrogate losses with proved H-consistency bounds and lower system MSE as experts are added.
flag: (iii) and (v). Experts are neural networks of differing depth, not humans; no human handoff studied. Authors state no prior baseline exists; comparison is against the non-deferring base model and across 1/2/3 experts (Table 1), which I treat as an ablation. Proofs of single-expert Thms 9 and 11 are stated as reductions. Evidence quote is a fragment; verify.

title: Online Cascade Learning for Efficient Inference over Streams
evidence: "We introduce online cascade learning, a new framework for learning model cascades" (Sec. 1, contributions); deferral to the LLM is penalised by a cost term in the MDP (Sec. 3).
method: Cascade of logistic regression, BERT and an LLM over a stream; learned deferral functions pass queries upward; trained online by imitation of the LLM in an episodic MDP with deferral cost.
evaluation: IMDB, HateSpeech, ISEAR, FEVER vs LLM alone, distillation, online ensemble: IMDB 93.01% vs 94.15% GPT-3.5 at about 60% lower cost; HateSpeech 82.66% vs 83.34%, over 90% savings. No latency.
contribution: Online cascade learning trains small models and deferral policies on a stream by imitating an LLM, matching LLM accuracy within about 1-2 points while cutting inference cost by up to 90%.
flag: none of (i)-(v) under the ruling: streaming deferral exists (ii would apply on form), but the cascade defers to a larger model purely for cost, which the ruling names as E1; no safety motivation, no human. Regret results (Thm 3.1, 3.2 o(T)) rest on convexity and a lemma argued at sketch level. ISEAR size given as 7,666 in the body and 3,833 in the appendix; FEVER savings reported as about 17-20% inconsistently between text and caption. Maintainer may want it as background for RQ2 sequential deferral.

title: Cost-Sensitive Learning to Defer to Multiple Experts with Workload Constraints
evidence: "DeCCaF: a novel L2D method that models human behavior under limited data availability" (Section 1, contributions)
method: DeCCaF: a classifier, a human expertise model trained from one expert label per instance, and a constraint-programming assigner allocating cases among classifier and 9 experts under per-batch capacity limits.
evaluation: Bank Account Fraud, 9 synthetic experts, 6 scenarios x 25 variations vs OvA, random, full-rejection, classifier-only; expected cost per 100 instances e.g. 3.4 vs 3.63 OvA; Xeon Gold 5120, 60 s solver timeout; no per-instance latency.
contribution: Assigns fraud alerts among a classifier and a team of experts under cost-sensitive objectives and per-expert workload limits, cutting misclassification cost against one-vs-all learning to defer.
flag: (i) and (iii): deferral to multiple human experts under workload constraints. All experts are synthetic (instance-dependent label noise on a synthetic dataset), no real analysts, so no 'e'; the human handoff gap cell is credited only for the capacity modelling. Abstract claims an average 8.4% cost reduction; I did not locate that averaged figure in the body, only the per-scenario Table 3. The win over OvA is inconclusive in 1 of 6 scenarios and the expertise model has ROC-AUC below 0.50 at the lowest cost ratio. Batch assignment, not online or sequential; no formal proof. New tag constraint-programming added.

title: Towards Calibrated Losses for Adversarial Robust Reject Option Classification
evidence: "we propose an adversarial robust reject option loss l_d^gamma and analyze it for the hypothesis set of linear classifiers" (Abstract); Theorem 10 characterises calibrated surrogates
method: Calibration analysis of margin-based surrogates for a binary reject-option loss under l2-bounded adversarial perturbation with linear classifiers; proposes shifted double-ramp and double-sigmoid losses.
evaluation: Proved: calibration characterization (Thm 10), no convex (Thm 11) or quasi-concave-risk (Thm 12) surrogate is calibrated. Synthetic 2D data, shifted vs unshifted losses, e.g. DRL error 0.229 vs 0.359 at gamma_train 0.2, d 0.2. No hardware.
contribution: Characterises which surrogate losses are calibrated for reject-option classification under adversarial perturbations with linear models, proving that no convex surrogate is, and proposes shifted non-convex losses.
flag: (v) only: surrogate-calibration theory for the reject option. Narrow and partly negative: binary, linear hypothesis class only; the positive claims for shifted DRL/DSL are NOT proved, only supported by conditional-risk plots. Experiments are one synthetic 2D dataset with only the unshifted loss as baseline; some DSL settings collapse to rejecting every sample (RR 1.0), and the high rejection rates (0.8-0.9) behind the low errors deserve scrutiny. DRL mu is 0.55 in the text for figures but 0.95 in Table 2. Maintainer may find this too thin for a foundational-theory include.

title: ASPEST: Bridging the Gap Between Active Learning and Selective Prediction
evidence: Sec 1 (Introduction): "we introduce a new machine learning paradigm: active selective prediction under distribution shift"; inputs whose ensemble confidence falls below a threshold are abstained and deferred to a human.
method: Active selective prediction: over 10 active-learning rounds, query shifted test samples by ensemble margin, fine-tune, self-train on soft pseudo-labels and ensemble checkpoints; abstain by thresholding averaged softmax confidence.
evaluation: MNIST->SVHN, CIFAR-10->CINIC-10, FMoW, Amazon Review, DomainNet, Otto; vs softmax response and deep ensembles with eight acquisition rules; AUACC, coverage at target accuracy; A100 GPUs, training time only.
contribution: An active-learning method with self-training and checkpoint ensembling that raises the accuracy-coverage trade-off of selective prediction under distribution shift, reducing how many inputs go to human labellers.
flag: none of (i)-(v) cleanly: borderline (i). Abstained inputs are said to go to a human, but the human is an assumed-correct oracle, the deferral rule is a plain confidence threshold, and the contribution is the active-learning and self-training procedure that improves a one-shot selective classifier. The rounds are label-acquisition rounds, not abstention as an action over time. No theory. Numbers: MNIST->SVHN M=1K coverage at 90% accuracy 94.91% vs about 0.1% for SR and DE without acquisition; DomainNet R->C AUACC 71.61% vs 68.85% (DE+Margin). The introduction figure of 79.36% -> 88.84% AUACC at M=100 does not match the 78.59% listed for DE+Margin in Table 5; check which baseline is meant. Only the first 100000 of about 188000 characters were read (remainder is appendix).
